# Lua Gameplay/UI API — per-function behaviour notes

This document extends `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13 (the classic `lua_register` idiom, 1,430
individually-named engine C functions across three registrar call sites — `0x00a20840`/1,014
gameplay names, `0x008430f0`+42 wrappers/311 UI names, `0x00845aa0`/113 names). §13 established
*that* the roster exists and *where* each `{namePtr,funcPtr}` pair lives; this document decompiles
individual named entries and records their real argument signature, return value, observable side
effects, and engine subsystem, one top-level section per work item / agent pass, subsections per
function.

**Confidence labels (this project's house style):** `CONFIRMED — disassembly` (read directly from
the decompiled instruction stream — control flow, call targets, field offsets, argument-extraction
shape), `HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred` (a semantic role assigned from consistent cross-call-site
context or an argument-count/shape match against a real public API, not independently proven a
second way), `OPEN — unresolved` (a real gap — exact bitfield/enum meaning, an unresolved callee
argument count, etc.).

**Cleanroom note:** per `WALLS.md`, no raw Ghidra decompiler pseudocode expressions or auto-named
decompiler variables (`piVar8`, `iVar10`, `DAT_...`, etc.) are quoted verbatim anywhere in this
document — behaviour is described in plain English citing only function/data addresses and real,
public, documented Lua 5.1 C API names.

**Method, shared by every subsection below (established once here, not repeated per function):**
every one of this document's entries is a `lua_CFunction`-shaped routine — `int fn(lua_State *L)`
— reached by decompiling the paired function pointer recovered from `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13's
own `{namePtr,funcPtr}` array-walk method. All of them open with the same, evidently
machine-generated binding-wrapper prologue: a call to a 1-argument helper matching the real public
**`lua_gettop(L)`** (`0x00dfde50`) to read the total argument count `N`, followed by a sequence of
positional reads for the mandatory leading arguments and a **trailing-optional countdown** for any
remaining arguments (each optional argument is guarded by a nil/absence test before extraction, and
defaults to a fixed literal when absent or nil — the shape is `if (remaining < 1) use_default; else
if (is_nil_test) use_default; else extract;`, decremented once per optional argument checked, front
to back). The primitives identified and reused across this cluster:

- **`0x00dfde50`** — 1 argument (`L`) → int. Shape matches the real public **`lua_gettop`** exactly
  (only 1-argument Lua 5.1 API returning "how many values are on the stack"). Used first, in every
  function in this cluster, to obtain the real argument count. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred from
  argument-count match + universal first-call position; not independently proven a second way.]**
- **`0x00dfe210(L, idx, 0)`** — 3 arguments, third always a literal `0`. Shape matches the real
  public **`lua_tolstring(L, idx, len)`** exactly (the only 3-argument "read a value off the Lua
  stack" function in the public API; a literal `0`/`NULL` third argument is exactly how the public
  `lua_tostring` convenience macro expands `lua_tolstring(L,i,NULL)`). Every result this document
  observed being used is either kept as an opaque pointer/handle passed straight into a
  name-resolver, or used directly as a string. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred, same basis.]**
- **`0x00dfe1e0(L, idx)`** — 2 arguments → 0/1-shaped int. Shape matches the real public
  **`lua_toboolean(L, idx)`** exactly, and every result this document observed is stored into a
  `bool`-typed local. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred, same basis.]**
- **`0x00dfe040(L, idx)`** — 2 arguments → int, used only as an `==0`/`!=0` gate immediately before
  an optional-argument extraction (never itself supplying the extracted value). Shape matches the
  real public **`lua_type(L, idx)`** (2 arguments), and every call site's `==0` branch is exactly
  where the surrounding code falls through to a hard-coded default — consistent with testing the
  real Lua 5.1 `LUA_TNIL` tag value (`0`). **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred; the exact tag being tested
  is not independently re-derived against `lua_type`'s other tag constants, only against `0`.]**
- **`0x00dfe590(L, v)`** — 2 arguments, called only at the very end of the two functions in this
  cluster that end with a literal `return 1;` (the real `lua_CFunction` convention: the C return
  value is the count of Lua values pushed). Both observed call sites push a 0/1-shaped result.
  Shape matches a real public `lua_push*`-family call (most consistent with **`lua_pushboolean`**
  given the observed value shape, but not independently distinguished from `lua_pushinteger`).
  **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred.]**
- **`0x00dfe160(L, idx)` immediately followed by a zero-argument call `0x00ea2596()`** — a second,
  rarer optional-argument extractor for a numeric/flag-shaped trailing argument (seen where the
  default is a small literal such as `3` or `0`, later consumed as a bitmask, e.g. tested with
  `& 2`). `0x00ea2596` taking no visible `L` argument is inconsistent with the plain public Lua
  C API shape the rest of this list matches cleanly. ~~**[OPEN — the pair's exact real-API identity
  is not resolved; treated here only as "the flags/number extractor," not attributed to a specific
  named public function.]**~~ **RESOLVED, §4.1 ~~(also independently re-confirmed under emulation,
  §5.3 below)~~ (§5.3 emulates `0x00dab330`, not these primitives): `0x00dfe160` is the real public `lua_tonumber(L, idx)`; `0x00ea2596` is not a second
  Lua stack accessor at all, it is the compiler's own inlined float64-to-int64 ~~rounding~~ **[truncating, §4.1, settled 2026-10-01]** cast, called
  immediately after and operating only on the x87 register `lua_tonumber` left behind. [CONFIRMED —
  disassembly, §4.1.]**

Every function below returns via the real `lua_CFunction` convention: a literal `return 0;` (or a
decompiler-inferred `void` fall-through with no `lua_push*` call in the body, which is the same
thing — zero Lua values pushed) means no Lua return value; a literal `return 1;` preceded by a
`0x00dfe590` push means exactly one Lua return value.

## 1. Trigger/mission/objective cluster — 12 functions, all in the 1,014-entry gameplay table (`0x00a20840`)

**Review status summary (2026-09-30):** adversarial desk review of the 14 units of §1 (scope note, 1.1-1.13): 5 DESK-PASS (scope note, 1.1, 1.5, 1.6, 1.8), 4 DESK-PASS with text fixes applied (1.3, 1.4, 1.11, 1.13), 5 NEEDS-EXE (1.2, 1.7, 1.9, 1.10, 1.12; text fixes also applied in 1.9 and 1.12). A desk pass does NOT clear an entry: clearing needs re-derivation against the executable. Every entry, including the desk passes, stays uncleared until that re-derivation (bridge job files `team-a/ghidra/jobs/review-bindings-lua1-2.json`) is read.

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was the 12 highest real-script-call-count names from
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.4's cross-team join (`trigger_enable` 563 calls/59 scripts down to
`object_is_in_trigger` 86/19) that were not already covered by another concurrent pass on this same
new document. All 12 were confirmed present in the 1,014-entry gameplay array exactly as expected;
none needed to fall back to the UI (`0x008430f0`) or third (`0x00845aa0`) registrar. Each entry's
paired function pointer was recovered by taking the full ordered list of every
`MOV dword ptr [stack],imm32` instruction inside `0x00a20840`'s body (`0x00a20840`–`0x00a25f7e`,
2,028 such instructions total, matching 1,014 name/1,014 function pairs with no other instruction
shape competing for the count) and reading the entry immediately following each target name's own
slot — i.e., the same `{namePtr,funcPtr}` adjacency this document's method section and
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.1/§13.2 already established structurally. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly;
full ordered list read directly, not sampled; raw evidence preserved at
`tools/lua_gp_target_pairs.txt`, which also prints ±2/±3 neighbouring array entries around every
target for manual cross-check — every neighbour resolves cleanly to a real name or a real code
address, confirming no misalignment.]** None of the 12 function-pointer targets had previously been
marked as a Ghidra function-start in this project's database (the same "valid code, not yet
boundary-fixed" situation already documented for roughly half of the third registrar's targets,
`spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.5) — each was force-disassembled and given a function boundary as part of
this pass before decompiling.

**Review status (2026-09-30): DESK-PASS — desk review only (checked against the other specs, not re-derived from the executable); NOT yet cleared for implementation.**

### 1.1 `trigger_enable` (`0x00a617d0`) — 563 calls / 59 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory + 2 optional. Arg 1 (string, mandatory) — a trigger name. Arg 2
(boolean, optional, default `true`) — enable/disable. Arg 3 (numeric/flag value, optional, default
`3`) — read via the ~~unresolved flag-extractor pair~~ `lua_tonumber` + integer conversion pair (`0x00dfe160`/`0x00ea2596`, resolved §4.1)
and later tested against bit `0x2`.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`, no push).

**Body:** the trigger name (arg 1) is resolved to a handle via a shared by-name resolver
(`0x005e4e30`) also used by three other functions in this cluster (§1.2/§1.7/§1.12), then gated by
a shared handle-liveness check (`0x00853b10`, returns non-zero for a dead/invalid handle — used
identically by every named-object resolution in this cluster). If the handle is alive: when bit
`0x2` of the arg-3 flag value is set, a setter (`0x0093dbc0`) is called with the handle and the
enable boolean; then, depending on the enable boolean, one of two further subsystem calls
(`0x0093d320` for enable, `0x0093bde0` for disable) is made, each apparently taking only the flag
value in the visible decompilation — **[OPEN — the decompiler shows only 1 explicit argument at
these two tail calls; a hidden calling-convention argument (e.g. the handle passed via a register)
is likely, but not resolved here — does not change the Lua-visible signature above.]**

**Side effects / subsystem:** mutates trigger-subsystem state for the named trigger (an
enable/disable toggle plus a flag-gated secondary behaviour switch). Subsystem: mission/trigger
state. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for control flow and argument shape; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the
exact role of the flag bit and the two tail setters, whose own internal semantics were not traced
further.]**

**Review status (2026-09-30): DESK-PASS — desk review only (checked against the other specs, not re-derived from the executable); NOT yet cleared for implementation.**

### 1.2 `on_trigger` (`0x00a58680`) — 513 calls / 59 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, no optional trailing arguments. Arg 1 — kept as an opaque
string (never resolved through a name lookup itself), used only as a value handed to a
registration call — consistent with a callback/handler name. Arg 2 — a trigger name, resolved via
the same shared resolver as §1.1 (`0x005e4e30`) and gated by the same liveness check
(`0x00853b10`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** once the trigger handle (arg 2) is resolved and alive, a per-trigger field at handle
offset `+0xa8` is checked; if it reads as unset (`0`), a local mode value of `0` together with arg 1
(the callback name) is passed into a registration function (`0x00a56cb0`) — this is the same
registration function §1.7 (`on_trigger_exit`) calls with mode value `1`, strongly suggesting
`+0xa8` is a single callback-list slot on the trigger object tagged by an enter(`0`)/exit(`1`) mode,
not two separate fields. **[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: §20.12 shows by raw disassembly that `0x00a56cb0` is a named-hook-slot-array writer taking a hidden `this` = a sub-record of the resolved handle (there item`+0xc0`, slot 0), so `+0xa8` may be this trigger's hook-array base passed as `this` and `0`/`1` hook slot numbers (registration always happens), not a field checked for zero (registration only when unset) — a Lua-visible difference for re-registration; to be settled against the executable.]** A second field at handle offset `+0xf8` is then checked (`!= -1`); if so,
`0x00d9e140(0)` is called. **Correction, 2026-09-30 (a later pass's direct decompilation of
`0x00d9e140` itself, while documenting an unrelated function that also calls it): this is NOT a
flush/notify call, as this section originally characterized it.** Its real body adds its integer
argument to a fixed global base value and wraps the sum into a fixed range (via a constant-offset
correction of 1,800,000,000), then writes the result through a hidden pointer argument — a
deadline/timestamp computation ("now plus N units, wrapped into a fixed cycle"), not a queue,
broadcast, or opcode-tagged record of any kind. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, `0x00d9e140`'s own
body.]** What this specific call site (argument literal `0`, i.e. "now, no offset") actually does
with the computed timestamp is not established here — the hidden pointer's destination for THIS
call site was not traced — so the reading of `+0xf8`'s check as "pending enter-callback state" is
retained as a plausible motivation for computing a timestamp at all, but "flush/notify" specifically
is withdrawn as a mischaracterization of the callee, not merely refined.

**Side effects / subsystem:** registers a Lua-callable callback name against the named trigger's
enter-mode callback slot. Subsystem: mission/trigger-state (callback registration).
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for control flow, field offsets, and the shared registration-function
identity with §1.7; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the semantic reading of the mode tag / `+0xf8` ~~flush~~ pending-state check (callee computes a timestamp, see correction above).]**

**Review status (2026-09-30): NEEDS-EXE: whether `+0xa8` is a checked field or the hook-array base passed as hidden `this` to `0x00a56cb0` — desk review only (checked against the other specs, not re-derived from the executable); NOT yet cleared for implementation.**

### 1.3 `objective_text` (`0x00a56920`) — 424 calls / 41 scripts

**Arguments:** 6 total. Arg 1 (numeric/slot value, mandatory, read via the same ~~unresolved~~
flag/number-extractor pair as §1.1's arg 3 — `lua_tonumber` + integer conversion, resolved §4.1) — an objective-slot index. Arg 2 (string, mandatory) —
a text key. Arg 3 (string, optional, default a shared empty-string constant). Arg 4 (string,
optional, default the same shared empty-string constant). Arg 5 (numeric/flag, optional, default
`3`, same extractor pair). Arg 6 (numeric/flag, optional, default `0`, same extractor pair).

**Return:** none — no `lua_push*`-shaped call appears anywhere in the body (decompiler infers
`void`), consistent with 0 Lua return values.

**Body:** arg 2 (the text key) is passed to a localization-key resolver (`0x00849df0`); if that
fails, and a global gate (a single flag checked with no further identification attempted here; **[address: the global `0x026e7e68`, per §8.15's identical chain — meaning still OPEN]**) is
set, a second resolver pair (`0x00604740`→`0x00604500`) is tried; if that also fails, the raw key
string itself is formatted into a 512-byte local buffer via what reads as a `sprintf`-shaped
formatter (`0x00db06e0`) as a last-resort literal fallback. Whatever text pointer results, together
with the slot index (arg 1), the two optional strings (args 3/4), and the two optional flag values
(args 5/6), is handed to one final call, `0x007ee110` — six parameters, matching the task brief's
own prediction of "a global objective-text UI slot."

**Side effects / subsystem:** writes a resolved (localized, or raw-fallback) objective string, plus
two auxiliary strings and two flag values, into a global objective-text/HUD slot identified by the
slot index. Subsystem: mission/objective UI (HUD text). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full
argument chain and call graph; HIGH CONFIDENCE that `0x007ee110` is the actual UI-slot writer, since
its address sits immediately adjacent to §1.4's clearing counterpart (`0x007eda00`) and takes
exactly the shape the source arguments assemble; the localization-fallback global gate's exact
meaning is OPEN.]**

**Review status (2026-09-30): DESK-PASS, text fixes applied — desk review only (checked against the other specs, not re-derived from the executable); NOT yet cleared for implementation.**

### 1.5 `mission_end_failure` (`0x00a523e0`) — 160 calls / 36 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings. Arg 1 — passed as-is (never handle-resolved) into a gate
function (`0x006d7240`) that returns a pass/fail boolean; the whole function is a no-op if this gate
fails. Arg 2 — a failure-reason/localization key.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`, on both the gated-out path and the normal path).

**Body:** once the arg-1 gate passes, arg 2 is resolved to an internal id via `0x00604740`, then to
a wide (localized) string via `0x00604500`; a cleanup/bookkeeping call (`0x006d00e0`) runs on arg 2
regardless. If no localized string was found: a literal `"NULL"` wide string is used if arg 2 was
itself empty/zero, otherwise a second, different localization-key resolver (`0x00849df0` — the same
one §1.3 uses) is tried, falling back to a literal `"FAILURE STRING NOT LOCALIZED"` wide string if
that also fails. Whatever wide string results is handed, together with two shared global default
parameters (repeated twice in the call), to a final dispatch (`0x006da400`).

**Side effects / subsystem:** displays a mission-failure message (resolved localized text, or a
diagnostic fallback string) via a UI/dialog subsystem, gated on an arg-1 mission-state check.
Subsystem: mission state + UI dialog/HUD text. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full resolver
chain and gating; HIGH CONFIDENCE for "arg 1 identifies the mission being checked/failed" — the
gate function `0x006d7240` itself was not separately decompiled.]**

**Review status (2026-09-30): DESK-PASS — desk review only (checked against the other specs, not re-derived from the executable); NOT yet cleared for implementation.**

### 1.10 `door_open` (`0x00a488c0`) — 101 calls / 21 scripts

**Arguments:** 6 total — the richest signature in this cluster. Arg 1 (string, mandatory) — a door
name. Arg 2 (boolean, optional, default `false`). Arg 3 (boolean, optional, default `true`). Arg 4
(string, optional, default absent/`0`). Arg 5 (string, optional, default absent/`0`). Arg 6 (string,
optional, default absent/`0`) — each of args 2–6 individually guarded by the same nil-test idiom
used throughout this cluster, decremented one remaining-argument slot at a time.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (boolean-shaped) — a real `0x00dfe590` push followed by a literal
`return 1;`.

**Body:** arg 1 resolves to a door handle via yet another distinct by-name resolver
(`0x006434a0`), gated by the shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`). If arg 4 is absent, a simple
open call (`0x00a31920`) is made with just the two booleans (args 2/3) and its result becomes the
pushed return value. If arg 4 IS present, it is itself resolved via a second by-name resolver
(`0x00a281a0`) to a secondary handle; if that succeeds and a field at door-handle offset `+200` (0xc8)
is non-zero (read as "this door has an attached lock/mechanism"), arg 5 is resolved via

### 1.13 Cross-function observations

Four distinct by-name resolver/registry pairs were found across these 12 functions **[count: four primary-argument resolvers; §1.10 also uses the generic character chain `0x00a281a0`, the name→id table `0x004bf810` and the 5th per-kind resolver `0x005982e0`, and §1.12 the position lookup `0x00a455a0`]**, each paired
with the same shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`) regardless of which resolver produced the
handle — good evidence `0x00853b10` is a generic, object-kind-agnostic handle-validity guard, not
something specific to triggers: trigger/generic-object (`0x005e4e30`, used by §1.1/§1.2/§1.7/§1.12),
spawn-region (`0x006ed4d0`, §1.8), door (`0x006434a0`, §1.10), and a fourth, non-trigger resolver
(`0x005e4dd0`, §1.11) whose target object category is the one open question in this set (**[Resolved: character resolver, §3 preamble/§3.3.]**). Two
independent "set slot"/"clear slot" pairs were also confirmed by address adjacency and argument-shape
symmetry alone, without needing to decompile the setter's own body further:
`objective_text`/`objective_text_clear` (`0x007ee110`/`0x007eda00`, §1.3/§1.4) and the enter/exit
~~callback-mode pair~~ hook slots `0`/`1` sharing one registration function (`0x00a56cb0`, §1.2/§1.7 — a named-hook-slot-array writer, §20.12; the `+0xa8` question stays OPEN, §1.2). No function in this
cluster touches a global objective-text UI slot AND a trigger-state table at the same time — the
task brief's guess that this cluster "plausibly touches a mission/trigger-state table, a global
objective-text UI slot, or similar" resolves cleanly into two disjoint families: trigger/object
state (§1.1/§1.2/§1.7/§1.8/§1.9/§1.10/§1.11/§1.12) and objective/HUD-text state (§1.3/§1.4), plus two

**Primitive identification for this cluster — independently re-derived, upgrading this document's own
§1 from HIGH CONFIDENCE to CONFIRMED for five shared primitives.** Every one of these ten functions
opens with the identical machine-generated `lua_CFunction` prologue §1's method section already
describes (a `lua_gettop` call, then positional/optional argument extraction). This pass went one level
deeper than §1's argument-shape matching: it independently decompiled the *primitives' own bodies* (not
just their call-site argument counts) and matched each one structurally, line-for-line, against real
published Lua 5.1 interpreter source (`lapi.c`/`lauxlib.c`/`lobject.c`/`lstring.c`/`lvm.c` — Lua is
MIT-licensed and its own source is public, the same citation basis `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.1 already
used for `lua_pushcclosure`/`lua_setfield`/`luaI_openlib`):

- **`0x00dfde50(L)`** — body is exactly `(L->top − L->base) >> 4` (a byte-address subtraction shifted
  by 4, i.e. divided by 16 — this project's own already-established `TValue` size). This is the real
  public **`lua_gettop`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE
  reading of the same address.]**
- **`0x00dfdc60(L, idx)`** — the shared internal stack-index-to-pointer helper every other primitive
  below calls first; matches the real Lua 5.1 internal `index2adr`. Not itself public API, cited only
  as supporting evidence. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, structural match.]**
- **`0x00dfe040(L, idx)`** — calls `index2adr`, returns `-1` (`LUA_TNONE`) if the result is the
  interpreter's shared nil-sentinel object, else returns the resolved value's type tag. This is the
  real public **`lua_type`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE
  reading of the same address.]** Lua 5.1's own tag constants (`LUA_TNIL`=0, `LUA_TBOOLEAN`=1,
  `LUA_TNUMBER`=3, `LUA_TSTRING`=4, `LUA_TTABLE`=5) resolve every `==`/`!=` comparison against this
  call's result seen below.
- **`0x00dfe160(L, idx)`** — calls `index2adr`; if the tag isn't `LUA_TNUMBER`, calls an internal
  numeric-coercion helper (structurally `luaV_tonumber`) and bails to `0` on failure; otherwise returns
  the value's number field directly, in the real x87 floating-point return register — the real public
  **`lua_tonumber`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly. This resolves §1's own explicitly OPEN
  item about this same address: it is `lua_tonumber`, not an unidentified "flags/number extractor."]**
- **`0x00ea2596()`** — a zero-`lua_State`-argument float64-to-int64 rounding routine matching the
  classic compiler-generated (MSVC) ~~round-half-correcting~~ float-to-integer conversion helper ~~(exact rounding semantics OPEN, see §4.1)~~ (settled 2026-10-01, job `20261001T020218-team-a-bgcx`: truncation toward zero, see §4.1), always
  seen immediately after a `0x00dfe160` (`lua_tonumber`) call still holding its result in the FPU
  register. This is **not** a distinct Lua API entry point — it is the compiler's own emitted cast code
  for a source-level `(int)lua_tonumber(L, idx)` expression (or the real public `lua_tointeger`, which
  is defined in terms of exactly this same coercion-then-truncate sequence and is observably
  indistinguishable from it at this call shape). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the pairing and role;
  HIGH CONFIDENCE for treating it as equivalent to `lua_tointeger` rather than a hand-written cast, the
  two not being distinguishable from machine code alone.]**
- **`0x00dfe210(L, idx, 0)`** — calls `index2adr`; if not already a string, calls the internal
  `luaV_tostring` coercion, then (matching the real source's own comment that "the previous call may
  reallocate the stack") re-resolves the index via `index2adr` a second time before reading the
  string's length/data fields. This is the real public **`lua_tolstring`**/**`lua_tostring`** (the
  latter being `lua_tolstring(L,idx,NULL)`) line-for-line, including the exact stack-reallocation
  re-fetch its own real source is known for. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE
  reading of the same address.]**
- **`0x00dfe1e0(L, idx)`** — calls `index2adr`, returns `0` only for the nil tag or for the boolean tag
  with a zero value, `1` otherwise — the real public **`lua_toboolean`** line-for-line (`!l_isfalse`).
  **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; upgrades §1's HIGH CONFIDENCE reading of the same address.]**
- **`0x00dfe3a0(L, n)`** — writes `n` into the slot at `L->top`, sets its tag to `LUA_TNUMBER`,
  advances `top`. Real public **`lua_pushnumber`** line-for-line. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe420(L, s)`** — if `s` is `NULL`, writes a `LUA_TNIL`-tagged slot directly (the real
  `lua_pushnil` fast path `lua_pushstring` takes for a `NULL` argument); otherwise, BEFORE interning,
  calls a GC-threshold check (structurally `luaC_checkGC`, also called standalone elsewhere as
  `0x00e014b0`) — this call site's own instruction order places it ahead of the interning step, matching
  where real `lua_pushlstring` calls `luaC_checkGC` (a totalbytes-vs-threshold compare), not the separate

  **`lua_pushstring`** line-for-line

### 2.1 `game_get_platform` (`0x00841c50`) — 659 calls / 244 scripts

**Arguments:** none used. `lua_gettop` is still called first (the shared prologue, §2's method note)

### 2.2 `game_UI_audio_play` (`0x008439e0`) — 616 calls / 158 scripts

**Arguments:** 1, optional. If `lua_gettop` reports at least one argument, argument 1 is read
polymorphically: `lua_type` first; if `LUA_TSTRING`, the string is read via `lua_tolstring` and passed

a heavily stack-protected helper (`0x0045da50`) called with a null position pointer, the `"UI"`
category-id argument, and a literal flag `1` — read as "create a non-positional (2D) voice tagged to
the UI audio category." If both the sound-id and category resolved successfully, a binder call
(`0x0045f5b0`) associates the resolved sound with the new voice; a start/commit call (`0x0045ea70`)
follows unconditionally, its output out-parameter becoming the value eventually pushed back to Lua **[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: §26.17 `game_audio_play` uses the same `0x0045da50`/`0x0045f5b0`/`0x0045ea70`/`0x0045e170` chain with different roles (`0x0045da50` a transient bus object, `0x0045f5b0` linking two secondary sounds, `0x0045ea70` playing the primary sound and returning the handle, `0x0045e170` releasing the bus, 0 values returned when the primary sound does not resolve), which would make `"UI"` the bus, arg 1 the sound played by `0x0045ea70`, and puts the zero-argument return below in doubt; to be settled against the executable.]**; a
final flag-setting call (`0x0045e170`) sets one bit on the voice object (bit `0x4000` at the voice's own
`+0x98` field — a "release after play"/auto-cleanup marker, the same field and companion bit `0x20`
`0x0045f5b0` itself sets during binding).

`"UI"` audio category, optionally binds a caller-supplied sound (by name or by already-resolved
numeric id) to it, starts playback, and marks the voice for automatic release once finished. Returns

### 2.4 `audio_object_post_event` (`0x00a3cb00`) — 427 calls / 47 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory, up to 4 further optional (richest signature in this cluster).

- **Arg 1 (string, mandatory):** an event name, read via `lua_tolstring` and resolved through the same
  Wwise-ID resolver `0x00462960`/`AK::SoundEngine::GetIDFromString` used in §2.2/§2.5. If resolution
  fails, the function pushes `lua_pushnumber(0)` and returns immediately (1 Lua value, value `0`).
- **Arg 2 (optional):** read polymorphically by `lua_type`. If `LUA_TSTRING`, one value is resolved
  through the same name-resolver. If `LUA_TTABLE`, the table is walked via a dedicated length-then-loop
  helper (`0x0083dff0`, detailed below) collecting up to 2 resolved values — a table reporting *more*
  than 2 elements aborts the whole function immediately with the same `push 0; return 1;` failure path
  used for a failed arg-1 resolution.
- **Arg 3 (optional):** identical shape to arg 2 (string-or-table-of-≤2), a second independent
  value/list.
- **Arg 4 (string, optional):** a game-object name. The literal `"#PLAYER1_VEHICLE#"` is special-cased
  (case-insensitively, via the real public CRT `_stricmp`) to redirect to whatever object the separate
  literal `"#PLAYER1#"` resolves to; any other name is resolved through a distinct object-by-name
  lookup (`0x00a29200`). Either way, a resulting object's stored position pair is read (via
  `0x004dcc60`, which itself reads one of two alternate position-field pairs on the object depending on
  a liveness/validity check of the first pair); if arg 4 is absent or fails to resolve, a global
  fallback position pair (`0x0117f808`/`0x0117f80c`) is used instead.
- **Arg 5 (boolean, optional):** read via `lua_toboolean`; **defaults to `true`** if absent or nil —
  the only argument in this whole ten-function cluster observed defaulting a boolean to `true` when
  the corresponding presence-check helper (`lua_type`) reports the slot doesn't exist, rather than when
  it reports the value present-but-nil (both paths reach the same `true` default here).

**Table-walk helper (`0x0083dff0`), used for arg 2/arg 3:** first attempts to read the table's own
`n` field (the classic pre-`#`-operator Lua length convention: pushes the literal string `"n"`, calls
`lua_gettable`) and, if that is a number, uses it directly as the count. Only if `t.n` is absent or not
a number does it fall back to a real generic table walk in the exact compiled shape of
`for k,v in pairs(t) do count = count + 1 end` (§2's method note, `0x00dfe380`/`0x00dfec70`) to count
real entries. Either way, it then re-walks indices `1..count` via `lua_gettable`, resolving each
element through the shared Wwise-ID resolver.

**Return:** normally 1 Lua value (a number: the resulting post-event/play-instance handle, or `0` on
any resolution failure). **Exceptionally 2 values** — a leading `lua_pushnumber(0)` followed by the
normal handle push — specifically when arg 2's and arg 3's resolved-list *counts* differ from each
other; the function does not treat this mismatch as a hard failure, it just prepends an extra `0`
before continuing normally. **[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: the C return value on that path is not recorded — with a literal `return 1` Lua sees only the handle and the extra `0` is discarded, so the Lua-visible arity (1 or 2) is unproven; the fallback position source also conflicts with §2.11 (global pair `0x0117f808`/`0x0117f80c` here vs `+8`/`+0xc` off `L` there), and the resolver behind the `#PLAYER1#` redirect is not named; to be settled against the executable.]**

**Side effects / subsystem:** posts a named Wwise audio event, targeted at a resolved game
object/position (or a global default position if none is given or it fails to resolve), optionally
carrying up to two independent lists of up to 2 resolved switch/value-shaped ids each, and an
optional boolean whose own consumption inside the final post call was not independently traced past
being assembled into a combined argument block. Subsystem: audio (Wwise event posting), plus the same
named-object/position-resolution helpers `audio_play_persona_line` (§2.5) also uses. **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly for the full argument-reading chain, the table-walk helper's `t.n`-then-`pairs` fallback,
the `#PLAYER1_VEHICLE#` special case, and the mismatched-count double-push behaviour; HIGH CONFIDENCE
for the exact role of the assembled position/switch-value block in the final post call, whose own
argument (the block's address) is passed via a register the decompiler did not attribute explicitly —
does not affect the confirmed Lua-visible contract above.]**

**Review status (2026-09-30): NEEDS-EXE: Lua-visible return count on the mismatch path, fallback position source, `#PLAYER1#` resolver — desk review only (checked against the other specs, not re-derived from the executable); NOT yet cleared for implementation.**

### 3.1 `coop_is_active` (`0x00a42bd0`) — 505 calls / 45 scripts

**Arguments:** none. `lua_gettop(L)` is called (the shared fixed prologue every function in this
cluster opens with) but its result is never used to extract anything — every other function here
uses it to locate argument 1; this one's identical prologue call is followed by no extraction at
all, consistent with a genuine zero-argument query rather than an unused/ignored argument.

**Return:** 1 boolean, pushed via the shared push primitive (`0x00dfe590`).

**Body:** queries ~~a co-op session object~~ the session-singleton accessor (`0x0087ba20`, global `0x024d8534`, §8.2); if present, ~~compares its head/tail
member-list pointers and a small state counter~~ **[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: no field offsets are given, so the claim of §6.22/§8.27 that these are other fields than the `+0x58`/`+0x5c` host pair cannot be checked; `0x00681370` and `0x00877a90` are not identified elsewhere; to be settled against the executable.]** **[Settled 2026-10-01 by job `20261001T020213-team-a-dksj`: there is no head/tail pair — see the corrected body below.]**, and additionally checks ~~a network-match-state
accessor~~ (`0x00681370`, **corrected: a one-instruction reader of session `+0x60`, the member count**) before walking the member list once (comparing each entry against a
per-entry validity test, `0x00877a90`).

**Corrected body (re-derived from the executable 2026-10-01, job `20261001T020213-team-a-dksj`).** The Lua function pushes
the result of a core predicate at `0x00867830`. That predicate answers true only when all four of
these hold:

1. the session pointer (accessor `0x0087ba20`, global `0x024d8534`) is non-null — with no session the
   answer is false;
2. either the local machine is the host — session `+0x5c` equals session `+0x58`, the same pair §8.27
   and §10.2 test, and it is the *first* test in the body — or a client-side gate passes: (session
   `+0xf4` ≥ 2, or session `+0x224` ≠ 0, or session `+0xf4` ≠ session `+0xf8`) and the byte at session
   `+0xfd` is 0; **[2026-10-01, job `20261001T114716-team-a-fvfp`: this client-side gate is exactly "the session is not idle
   (the idle test `0x0059fbe0` is false) and is not flagged for destruction (byte `+0xfd` clear)", §26.28.
   CONFIRMED — disassembly: its three terms are the negation of `0x0059fbe0`'s three terms.]**
3. the member count at session `+0x60` (read through `0x00681370`) is **at least 2** — the comparison is
   unsigned, so a count of 0 or 1 fails;
4. every member other than the local one passes the per-member slot check `0x00877a90`. The walk
   starts at the list head, session `+0x54`, follows the next pointer at node `+0xb28c`, and stops at a
   null pointer or on returning to the head; the node equal to session `+0x5c` is skipped. The slot
   check uses the node's byte at `+0x158` as an index into a 5-byte-stride array at (session
   `+0x50`)`+0xc`, whose element count is at (session `+0x50`)`+0x10`; a node passes when the index is
   in range, the element's byte `+2` is non-zero and the element's byte `+0`, taken as a signed char,
   is at least 1. An out-of-range slot counts as −1 and fails.

**[CONFIRMED — disassembly: the four conditions, the ≥ 2 member rule and the walk, from the bodies of
`0x00a42bd0`, `0x00867830`, `0x00681370` and `0x00877a90`.]** Field meanings: `+0x54` is the
member-list head, `+0x58` and `+0x5c` are member records (`+0x5c` the local member, since the walk
skips it; `+0x58` the host member), `+0x60` is the member count **[HIGH CONFIDENCE — from how the
fields are used, not from names]**; `+0xf4`/`+0xf8`/`+0xfd`/`+0x224` form a client-side
connection-state gate **[OPEN — only their gating role is confirmed]**. Consequence: a session with
fewer than 2 members is never "active", whether or not the local machine is the host (§26.28).

**Side effects / subsystem:** none — pure query. Subsystem: co-op/session state. **[CONFIRMED —

### 4.1 Shared primitives — direct decompilation, upgrading ~~three~~ five items in the Method section above and resolving its one OPEN item

The shared Method section above (established by a concurrent pass on this same document) identified
seven stack-access primitives from their **call-site shape** alone (argument count/pattern) and
labelled ~~six~~ five of them HIGH CONFIDENCE, leaving the flag/number-extractor pair OPEN. This subsection
decompiled the primitives' own bodies directly and matched their internal logic, structurally,
against real Lua 5.1 `lapi.c` source — the same evidentiary standard `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.1
already used and had accepted for `lua_pushcclosure`/`lua_setfield`. This upgrades several items to
**CONFIRMED** and resolves the remaining OPEN pair:

- **`0x00dfde50` = real public `lua_gettop(L)`.** Its own body computes the pointer difference
  between two fields of the `lua_State` argument (at fixed offsets `+8` and `+0xc`) and right-shifts
  the byte difference by 4 — exactly the real `(L->top - L->base)` pointer-subtraction macro, divided
  by the real 16-byte Lua 5.1 value-slot stride. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe040` = real public `lua_type(L, idx)`.** Its body resolves the stack index to the
  underlying value slot, reads the slot's own type-tag field (fixed offset `+8` within the slot),
  and — critically, not just a nonzero/zero shape — returns the literal sentinel `-1` specifically
  when the resolved slot is the shared "no such value" singleton object, matching the real API's own
  `LUA_TNONE` (`-1`) special case exactly, not merely a generic tag readout. **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly, including the `-1`/`LUA_TNONE` special case, not only the tag-field readout.]**
- **`0x00dfe1e0` = real public `lua_toboolean(L, idx)`.** Its body returns `1` unless the resolved
  slot's type tag is `0` (nil) or the tag is `1` (boolean) with a stored value of `0` — the exact
  real `l_isfalse` macro Lua 5.1 uses internally, not merely a boolean-shaped wrapper. **[CONFIRMED —
  disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe160` = real public `lua_tonumber(L, idx)`.** Its body checks the resolved slot's type
  tag against the literal `3` (`LUA_TNUMBER`); if it doesn't already hold a number, it calls a
  second internal coercion helper and returns `0` on failure, else reads the numeric field directly
  — the exact real `tonumber()`-macro-plus-`luaV_tonumber()`-fallback structure, returned via the
  x87 register pair the compiler uses for a `double` return. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe210(L, idx, lenOut)` = real public `lua_tolstring(L, idx, len)`.** Its body checks the
  resolved slot's type tag against the literal `4` (`LUA_TSTRING`); on mismatch it calls an internal
  string-coercion helper, then — matching the real API's own defensive re-fetch, since a coercion can
  relocate the underlying object — re-resolves the stack-index-to-slot pointer a second time before
  reading a length field and returning a data pointer offset by a fixed `0x10`-byte string-header
  size. Every one of this section's 11 functions passes the literal `0` for `lenOut`, i.e. the real
  `lua_tostring(L, idx)` convenience macro exactly. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe3a0` = real public `lua_pushnumber(L, n)`** (not previously listed in the shared Method
  section, newly identified here because it appears in this cluster's `get_dist`). Its body writes
  the argument into the slot addressed by the `lua_State`'s own stack-top field, tags that slot `3`
  (`LUA_TNUMBER`), then advances the stack-top field by `0x10` bytes — the exact real
  `setnvalue`+`api_incr_top` expansion. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **`0x00dfe590` = real public `lua_pushboolean(L, b)`**, settling the shared Method section's own
  "not independently distinguished from `lua_pushinteger`" caveat. Its body tags the destination slot
  `1` (`LUA_TBOOLEAN`, not `3`/`LUA_TNUMBER`, which rules out `lua_pushinteger` directly) and writes
  the argument coerced to `0`/`1`, advancing the stack-top field the same way as above — the exact
  real `setbvalue`+`api_incr_top` expansion. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- **The OPEN flag/number-extractor pair is resolved.** `0x00dfe160` (`lua_tonumber`, confirmed above)
  immediately followed by a call to `0x00ea2596` is not a second, distinct stack-accessor pair —
  decompiling `0x00ea2596` itself shows it takes no `lua_State`/index argument at all; it operates
  purely on the x87 floating-point register left behind by the immediately preceding `lua_tonumber`
  call, performing a ~~round-to-nearest~~ double-to-64-bit-integer conversion (~~**[OPEN — rounding semantics: §2's method note, §3's preamble and §3.9 describe this same helper as truncation, round-half-correcting or banker's rounding; the descriptions disagree and the exact semantics is OPEN pending a re-read of `0x00ea2596`'s body. This entry is the single point of reference; other sites point here.]**~~). ~~**[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: still undecided between round-half-even, round-to-nearest and truncation (MSVC `_ftol2`-style), and it affects every integer-coerced argument in this document; to be settled against the executable.]**~~ **[SETTLED 2026-10-01, job `20261001T020218-team-a-bgcx` (full body of `0x00ea2596` in `named/rand_int_0.txt`): the conversion is truncation toward zero, whatever the FPU rounding mode. The helper stores the x87 value to a 64-bit integer under the current rounding mode, reloads it, takes the difference from the original, and moves the result one step back toward zero whenever the stored integer went past the original value in the away-from-zero direction. Net effect: the MSVC run-time's ordinary C integer cast. So 2.9 becomes 2, -2.9 becomes -2, 0.5 becomes 0. Every integer-coerced argument in this document that goes through `lua_tonumber` + `0x00ea2596` truncates; the "round-to-nearest", "round-half-correcting" and "banker's rounding" descriptions elsewhere are struck. Do not confuse it with `0x00dad900` (cited in §16.2 and §22 as "round to integer"), which really rounds, half away from zero (§26.27). CONFIRMED — disassembly.]** This is a shared/compiler-
  provided numeric cast helper, not a Lua C API entry point. **Resolved: this pair is simply
  `lua_tonumber(L, idx)` with its result immediately rounded to an integer — not a second Lua stack
  accessor.** **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**

### 4.2 `get_dist` (`0x00a4bdb0`) — 217 calls / 35 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings (object names) + 2 optional booleans, both default `false`,
each individually guarded by the standard nil-test idiom.

**Return:** 1 Lua value — a real `lua_pushnumber` call followed by a literal `return 1;`.

**Body:** each name string is resolved to a world position via one shared position-lookup function,
`0x00a455a0`. That function itself first tries the generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver
(`0x00a280c0` — see §4.13) and, on failure, falls back through a further chain that can reach ~~what
reads as a coop/network remote-object position cache~~ **[Correction per §20.24/§18.31 #1: for a character seated in a vehicle (`0x009b9160`: `+0x16d4`==3), the vehicle's transform via the cached-vehicle-association resolver]** (`0x004dcf00`, gated by `0x009b9160`/
`0x009b9130`) ~~for objects not resident locally~~, before a final fallback reads a fixed local field
directly off the resolved handle. If both names resolve, the function computes the Euclidean
distance between the two positions, with the middle (vertical) axis of the difference optionally
multiplied by `10.0` (arg 3 `true`) or zeroed out entirely (arg 4 `true` — checked after arg 3 in
the code, so it wins if both are `true`). If either name fails to resolve, the function returns the
IEEE-754 single-precision maximum representable value as a "could not compute" sentinel rather than
signalling an error.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none (a pure read). Touches the world/object-position store and,
conditionally, ~~the coop/network remote-position cache~~ the cached vehicle association (§20.24). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument
shape, control flow, and the distance formula; ~~HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for the remote-lookup
fallback's coop/network role,~~ (coop/network reading withdrawn, see correction above; since `0x00a455a0`'s own call graph was not traced past its first two
branches.]**

### 4.3 `teleport` (`0x00a60e30`) — 181 calls / 33 scripts

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings (arg 1 — the target to move; arg 2 — a destination reference) +
6 further optional arguments, each individually guarded by the standard nil-test idiom: arg 3
(boolean, default `false`), arg 4 (boolean, default `true`), args 5–7 (numbers, default `0.0` each
— read as XYZ position offsets applied on top of the destination's own position), arg 8 (boolean,
default `true`). ~~**[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: the sibling `teleport_to_object` (§22.4) has the same arg 1–7 shape but arg 8 is a number (heading in radians, default `0.0`), and its general applier `0x00996b50` records opcode `0x41`, not the `0x17` §4.13 lists for this function; `+0x4c` is there the orientation record copied by `0x00da4130`; this entry names no apply-callee addresses; to be settled against the executable.]**~~

**Return:** none — no `lua_push*` call anywhere in the body (0 Lua values).

**Body — CORRECTED (2026-10-02, `teleport_coop` investigation, re-derived from the executable):** arg 2 resolves through the registry resolver `0x005982e0` (rejected if `0x00853b10` reports it unusable). Once resolved, its stored position (`+0x40`/`+0x44`/`+0x48`) is read, an orientation is built from its `+0x4c` record via `0x00da4130` (this settles the old OPEN note — `+0x4c` is the orientation record, not an unused position field), and the three optional numeric offsets (args 5-7) are added to the position. Arg 1 (the thing being moved) is resolved separately through `0x00a281a0` (the player-first character chain). **If either resolution fails, the function returns at once without allocating any request** (so a later `teleport_check_done`/§35's status query sees "no request" → true). On success, it **allocates a kind-4 scripted request** for the moved object via `0x006f62b0(target, 4, null callback)` (§35.2's shared request pool — the SAME mechanism `teleport_check_done`, `turn_to_check_done`, `move_to_check_done` and `vehicle_pathfind_check_done` all query), keeping the 16-bit request id. The actual move then dispatches through one of two mutually exclusive paths depending on the resolved target's own class-row bit (`0x02cc9900` indexed by the object's class, byte `+0xa` bit `0x2` — **HIGH CONFIDENCE this is the player class**, not a vehicle sub-category: three independent uses agree, see §35.1): **set →** `0x009e2220(target, position, orientation, 1, 1, arg 3, id, arg 4, 1, 0)`, the asynchronous player-teleport path (queues the move in a two-slot ring and pushes game mode 8 — §35.3); **clear →** streams the destination's zone/cell, resets the target's action state, and calls `0x00996b50(target, position, orientation, 1, 1, 0, id, arg 4, arg 8)`, the immediate-apply path (§35.4) — **arg 3 ("exit vehicles") is NOT forwarded on this non-player path**, only on the player path.

**Side effects / subsystem:** world/position, plus physics/camera/animation-state reset on the
general-apply path; conditionally network-replicated (an opcode-`0x41` record to the target's owner when not locally authoritative — inner type `0x17` for the player path, `0x16` for the other); allocates/completes a kind-4 scripted request tracked by `teleport_check_done` (§35.2). Subsystem: world/position + character-state + the scripted-request pool. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument extraction/defaults, the request allocation, the class-row branch and both apply paths, re-derived 2026-10-02; HIGH CONFIDENCE for "player class" at class-row `+0xa` bit `0x2`, not independently read from a built descriptor row.]**

### 4.4 `release_to_world` (`0x00a5cb10`) — 128 calls / 27 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (object name or `"#PLAYER#"`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the same name string is tried against three different members of the type-gated resolver
family (§4.13) in a fixed order — bit `0x20` at descriptor-row offset `+0xa`; then bit `0x4` at
offset `+0xb`; then bit `0x8` at offset `+0xb` — stopping at whichever succeeds first. On the FIRST
resolver's success, rather than acting on the resolved object at all, the function instead calls a
separate, zero-argument routine that walks its own global linked list (rooted off a fixed
singleton/context object) and invokes a virtual "release" method (vtable slot `+0x5c`) on every
LINKED entry whose own active-flag bit is set — a bulk "release everything currently held" call, not
scoped to the one named argument. **[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: the first resolver (bit `0x20` at `+0xa`) is most likely the script-group resolver `0x005eab60` (§6.6), and the "zero-argument" routine a hidden-`this` drop walking the named group's own member list, so "release every member of the named group" is the likely reading; to be settled against the executable.]** On the SECOND or THIRD resolver's success instead, the SAME virtual
method (vtable slot `+0x5c`) is called directly and only on the one resolved object.

**Side effects / subsystem:** object-possession/ownership release. The registered name matches the
virtual method's own slot (`+0x5c`) in the two direct-call outcomes; the first resolver's global,
not-target-scoped behaviour is a genuine, slightly surprising asymmetry. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly
for the three-resolver sequence and the shared vtable-slot-`+0x5c` identity across all three
outcomes; OPEN — why the first resolver's match ignores the specific resolved object in favour of a

types.]**

### 4.5 `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit` (`0x00a63710`) — 116 calls / 24 scripts

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (vehicle name or `"#PLAYER#"`) + 1 optional boolean, default
`true`.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the target resolves through a dedicated object-to-vehicle-instance resolver (`0x00a281e0`):
it first checks a cached vehicle-handle field pair stored directly on the resolved base object,
falling back to a type-gated name resolution (§4.13) plus a virtual "has vehicle"/"get vehicle"
accessor pair (vtable slots `+0x68`/`+0x70`). If a vehicle instance is found, a fixed sub-offset
(`+0xc68`) inside it is computed, and that exact same sub-record pointer is passed to one of two
near-identical setter functions depending on the boolean argument (this was verified directly from
the raw instruction stream of the caller: both branches `PUSH` the identical `vehicle_instance +
0xc68` value before their respective `CALL` — an earlier decompiler rendering of one branch showing
no visible argument was a display artefact, not a real difference between the branches). Each
setter independently opens the record-and-replicate mechanism (§4.13, opcode `0x46`) and then flips

### 4.13 Cross-function observations

**The generic name resolver, and the `"#PLAYER#"` sentinel.** `0x00a280c0` is the base resolver
every function in this section reaches, either directly (`set_player_can_enter_exit_vehicles`,
`inv_weapon_add_temporary`, `inv_weapon_remove_temporary`, `on_vehicle_enter`'s first attempt) or
transitively (every member of the type-gated resolver family below calls it internally before
applying its own additional bit-gate). **[OPEN — desk review 2026-09-30: this conflicts with §3's preamble, §7 (`0x005982e0` reuses the registry lookup `0x004588f0`) and §9.9 (`0x0062a190` does its own `0x004588f0` lookup), so the conclusion below that every function here accepts `#PLAYER#` is doubtful for the paths that use only a type-gated resolver (§4.3 destination, §4.4, §4.7–§4.9); the five members' addresses are not listed; to be settled against the executable.]** It tries the argument first as a direct name-table lookup,
and — on failure — compares it byte-for-byte against a literal `.rdata` string read directly as
`"#PLAYER#"` (8 bytes, NUL-terminated); on an exact match it resolves to the current player object
via a one-line accessor. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, including the literal sentinel string read
directly, not inferred from call-site shape.]** Every function documented in this section that
accepts an object-name string therefore transparently also accepts the literal `"#PLAYER#"` in its
place.

**The type-gated resolver family.** At least five distinct entry points share one structural body
shape (resolve via the generic resolver above, then additionally require one specific bit of a
per-object-type descriptor row — indexed by the object's own type-id byte, in a fixed global
type-descriptor table — to be set), differing only in which single bit/offset combination is
required: bit `0x2` at row offset `+0xa` (internal to the generic resolver's own numeric-handle fast
path); bit `0x2` at row offset `+0xb` (`teleport`'s destination-reference resolver, §4.3 —
most plausibly the same address as `door_open`'s own third-tier resolver, `0x005982e0`, §1.10:
`teleport`'s own body calls `0x005982e0` for this exact argument, but `0x005982e0`'s internal
bit/offset check was not independently re-derived this pass, so this cross-reference is flagged
HIGH CONFIDENCE, not re-confirmed); bit `0x4`
at row offset `+0xb` (`release_to_world` §4.4 / `on_vehicle_enter` §4.12); bit `0x8` at row offset
`+0xb` (`release_to_world` §4.4 / `vehicle_is_destroyed` §4.9 / `on_vehicle_enter` §4.12); bit `0x20`
at row offset `+0xa` (`release_to_world` §4.4 / `continuous_spawn_stop` §4.7 /
`continuous_spawn_start` §4.8). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, identical body shape read directly at
all five addresses.]** Which single plain-English category each individual bit represents (e.g.
"vehicle," "spawn region," "door") was not independently confirmed beyond the call-site pattern
above in each function's own subsection — flagged OPEN throughout rather than guessed, per this
project's own standing caution against asserting a bitfield's meaning from offset/position alone
(`WALLS.md`).

**The record-and-replicate idiom.** Four of this section's mutating paths — `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit`
(§4.5, opcode `0x46`), `set_player_can_enter_exit_vehicles` (§4.6, opcode `0x46`),
`inv_weapon_add_temporary` (§4.10, opcode `0x41`), and `teleport`'s general-apply path (§4.3, opcode
`0x17` observed) — funnel their actual state change through the identical three-call
"begin/commit/end" sequence (`0x0086f5f0`→`0x0086f110`→`0x0086eb20` in every observed instance), each
tagged with its own numeric opcode, direct confirmation that these are coop/network-synced engine
actions rather than purely local ones. `inv_weapon_remove_temporary` (§4.11) and
`continuous_spawn_stop`/`continuous_spawn_start` (§4.7/§4.8) show no trace of this same idiom in
their own bodies at this call depth — a real, confirmed asymmetry, not an assumption of uniform
replication across the whole cluster. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for all four opcode-tagged call
sequences and both non-replicated counterexamples.]**

**Recommendation for a future pass (not attempted here, out of this task's static-only scope):** a
behavioural oracle — real input/output vectors from actually running these functions — would settle
several of this section's OPEN items fastest: the plain-English category label for each of the five
type-gated resolver bits; `teleport`'s trailing constant arguments and its destination object's
unused `+0x4c` read; `on_vehicle_enter`'s three numeric event codes and two dispatch contexts; and
which of `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit`'s two flag bits (`0x40`/`0x20`) is which. This is a
recommendation only; building or running such an oracle is out of scope for this task.

**Review status (2026-09-30): NEEDS-EXE: whether every type-gated resolver calls `0x00a280c0` (and so accepts `#PLAYER#`) — desk review only (checked against the other specs, not re-derived from the executable); NOT yet cleared for implementation.**

| 600 zero bytes (empty directory) | `0` | `0x00000000` | `0x00000000` | yes |

validated reference exactly, including a non-zero initial seed and the documented
empty-directory special case (`spec-save-format.md` §6.1's own "an empty directory
hashes to 0" note).** **[CONFIRMED — empirical, emulated call, real binary bytes.]** **[Desk recomputation 2026-09-30 (reviewer, independent Python, not a new emulator run): all 7 reproduce with `spec-save-format.md` §6.1's parameterization — reflected `0xEDB88320`, no final XOR, initial value `0` except the one row seeded `0xFFFFFFFF` — and the empty and all-zero rows are non-discriminating (any init-0 CRC gives 0).]**

### 5.2 Two genuinely-open questions checked and found NOT decidable this way — real facts, not tooling notes

- **`continuous_spawn_stop` (§4.7)'s boolean argument** depends on live per-spawned-
  entity state (a virtual-method choice made per instance of whatever is currently
  spawned in the target region at call time) — there is no fixed, callable-in-isolation
  answer, confirmed by tracing the real call chain three levels deep. **OPEN, and
  structurally cannot be resolved by isolated emulation — would need a live/dynamic
  trace with real spawned entities.**
- **`notoriety_force_no_spawn` (§3.6)'s name→code table** is populated by runtime
  initialization code, not present as static data in the executable file at all — a
  cold, isolated call against it would silently return "not found" for every real name,
  a plausible-looking wrong answer rather than a real one. **OPEN, same reason as
  above.**
- **Header-address correction for §4.7/§4.8 (found while tracing the first question above):**
  the original header addresses `0x00a21b62` (§4.7) and `0x00a21b36` (§4.8) were instruction
  addresses inside the registrar-array builder `0x00a20840` (where each slot's `{namePtr,funcPtr}`

## 6. Mission/trigger/notoriety/spawn cluster — 21 functions, all in the 1,014-entry gameplay table (`0x00a20840`)

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was 21 specific names from the task brief's own next-tranche list (ranks 51-150 by real script-call count; per-name counts were not supplied for this tranche the way they were for §1/§3/§4, so subsections below follow the brief's own given order rather than a locally-verified count). All 21 were confirmed present in the 1,014-entry gameplay array (`0x00a20840`) by direct lookup against `tools/lua_all_registered_1430_tagged.txt` (all 21 tagged `gameplay`) followed by a direct read of each name's own `{namePtr,funcPtr}` pair from the same full ordered walk of `0x00a20840` that §3/§4 already published (`tools/scratchpad/lua_gameplay_1014_raw_pairs.txt`) — no new array walk was needed. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; all 21 pairs read directly, not sampled.]** 13 of the 21 targets (`set_mission_author`, `notoriety_set_min_and_max`, `traffic_disable_drawbridge_area`, `notoriety_set_max`, `set_ped_density`, `notoriety_force_no_spawn_group`, `notoriety_set_min`, `spawning_pedestrians`, `set_traffic_density`, `notoriety_reset`, `waypoint_remove`, `notoriety_set_can_decay`, `mission_end_to_activity`) had not previously been marked as a Ghidra function start (the same "valid code, not yet boundary-fixed" situation §1/§3/§4 already documented for roughly half of their own targets) and were force-disassembled and given a function boundary before decompiling; the other 8 (`disable_specific_notoriety_group`, `guardian_angel_register_script_group`, `guardian_angel_unregister_script_group`, `mission_end_success`, `notoriety_set`, `spawning_vehicles`, `tutorial_start`, `mission_set_cancel_warp_location`) were already-defined functions.

Every function below opens with the same shared `lua_CFunction` prologue this document's front matter and §1/§2/§3/§4 already established and confirmed (`lua_gettop`/`lua_type`/`lua_tolstring`/`lua_toboolean`/`lua_tonumber`/`lua_pushboolean` at the same addresses) — not re-derived here, only cited.

**Read `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3.6 first (`notoriety_force_no_spawn`) — several of this cluster's functions extend or run parallel to that section's already-confirmed mechanism, cited throughout rather than re-derived.**

### 6.1 `set_mission_author` (`0x007c9f50`)

**Arguments:** none consumed. The shared prologue's `lua_gettop` call is made but its result is never used to extract anything.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the entire compiled body is the prologue call followed immediately by `return 0;` — no argument read, no push, no other engine state touched. This is a genuine, fully inert binding.

**Side effects/subsystem:** none. **A real, confirmed cross-binary finding, not limited to this one name:** this exact address is reached from at least 32 call sites project-wide, not only from this one registrar slot. One of those call sites was decompiled directly (`0x00a1fa10`, called from `0x00a1fa5a`) and turns out to be a SEPARATE, small Lua-registration table — distinct from the three registrar call sites `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13 already catalogued (`0x00a20840`/`0x008430f0`/`0x00845aa0`) — that registers five names (`script_assert`, `script_profiler_start_section`, `script_profiler_end_section`, `script_profiler_do_printout`, `script_profiler_reset`) into some Lua state, of which the four `script_profiler_*` entries are bound to this EXACT SAME address as `set_mission_author`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; the shared address and the sibling registration table's own name strings were read directly, not inferred.]** The most likely explanation is compiler/linker identical-code-folding merging several independently-written, functionally-empty stub bindings (a debug-only profiler no-op family plus this one) into one shared body — consistent with this project's own established caution (`WALLS.md`) against over-attributing meaning from a shared address alone, so this is reported as an observed fact (the address is shared, `set_mission_author` itself does nothing) rather than a claim about what the OTHER 31 call sites are for. **Flagged for the orchestrator: this `0x00a1fa10` registration site does not obviously match any of `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13's three already-counted registrar call sites and may represent additional, not-yet-inventoried registered names — worth an independent check against that spec's own total before treating the current 1,430-name count as exhaustive; not investigated further here as it is out of this task's scope.** Subsystem: none — a dead/no-op binding. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the function's own body and the shared-address fact; OPEN — why the linker folded these particular bindings together, and whether `0x00a1fa10` is a real additional registrar.]** **[Resolved (second question): `spec-lua-bindings.md` §13.6 — `0x00a1fa10` is the gameplay-state bring-up routine; the 5-name table is a 4th registrar (`0x00e0ef80`), total corrected to 1,435 (later 1,490, §13.7).]**

### 6.2 `disable_specific_notoriety_group` (`0x00a47330`)

**Arguments:** 4, all mandatory, none individually nil-gated (each read directly from its stack position with no presence/type check first — the same "no nil/absence gate" idiom §3.6/§3.14 already established for a boolean argument, seen here applied to every argument in the signature). Arg 1 (string) — a notoriety GROUP name. Arg 2 (number, rounded to an integer via the shared `lua_tonumber`-then-round pair) — a tier/level index. Arg 3 (string) — the name of a specific item within that tier. Arg 4 (boolean) — the value to write.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (boolean-shaped), always pushed (either the real result or `0` on any failure path).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through a dedicated notoriety-GROUP name table (`0x008ed350` — a case-insensitive linear scan over 24 fixed name strings read directly from `.rdata`, the first being the literal `"police"`; returns a group-record pointer or null). This is a DIFFERENT resolver from §3.6's own `0x0094cc60` (which returns a small numeric code with failure sentinel `9`) — a third, independent name→record mechanism in this same notoriety family (see §6.22). If the group resolves, an unidentified zero-explicit-argument call (`0x00d21db0`) runs unconditionally, then arg 2 is range-checked against two fields on the group record (offsets `+0x3e0`/`+0x3e4`, read as a per-group minimum/maximum valid tier). If in range, the actual write is delegated to `0x008ed390`: it computes a per-tier sub-record (48 bytes per tier, from a tier-array base pointer at record offset `+0x3e8`), then linearly scans that tier's own sub-item array (32 bytes per entry, up to a per-tier count at `+0x2c`) for a case-insensitive match against arg 3 among each entry's own name field, and on a match overwrites that entry's own flag byte with arg 4, returning success/failure.

**Side effects/subsystem:** writes a named sub-item's flag byte within a specific tier of a named notoriety group. Subsystem: notoriety/gang state, extending the same family §3.6 traced. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full resolve/range-check/write chain; OPEN — the role of `0x00d21db0`, and which 24 real names populate the group table beyond the confirmed first entry `"police"`.]**

**Arguments:** 3, all mandatory, no nil-gates. Arg 1 (string) — a notoriety track name. Arg 2 and arg 3 (numbers) — a minimum and maximum value.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through `0x00605160` (see §6.22 — a THIRD, independent name resolver in this family: a case-insensitive scan across three parallel 4-entry alias-name arrays, `.rdata` strings beginning `"luchadores"`/`"brotherhood"`/`"los_carnales"`, returning a shared 0-3 index or the literal `5` on no match). **Body:** arg 1 resolves through `0x00605160` (§6.22); unlike §6.5/§6.7/§6.11, this entry point DOES explicitly check the `5` failure sentinel and skips everything on no match (the same guarded shape §6.3 uses). On success, THREE calls run in sequence: `0x00609810` — a simpler, unrelated routine that (only when running as the sole/local co-op authority, via the same `0x0087ba20` ~~head/tail-list-empty~~ host check (`+0x5c`==`+0x58`, §8.27; corrected §6.22) as elsewhere in this cluster) zeroes an 800-byte global buffer (`0x014a4c50`) plus a separate flag (`0x014a4580`) and calls a further no-argument helper (`0x00609030`) — read as a wholesale notoriety UI/meter reset, with **no record-and-replicate fallback at all** if not locally authoritative (a genuine, confirmed asymmetry against its four sibling setters in §6.3/§6.5/§6.7/§6.11, none of which silently do nothing on the non-authoritative path); then `0x00607ea0` and `0x006080d0` (the SAME "set minimum"/"set maximum" setters §6.11/§6.5 use) are both called with the literal value `0xffffffff` — resetting the resolved track's own minimum and maximum bounds back to an "unconstrained" sentinel.

**Side effects/subsystem:** fully resets one named track's min/max bounds to unconstrained AND, only when running as the sole co-op authority, also clears a global notoriety UI/meter buffer. Subsystem: notoriety/gang per-track state, partially network-replicated (the min/max resets go through the same opcode-`0x3f` mechanism as §6.3/§6.5/§6.7/§6.11; the UI/meter clear does not). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for all three calls, the shared sentinel-guard shape, and the confirmed lack of a replicated fallback on the first call.]**

### 6.17 `waypoint_remove` (`0x00a686d0`)

**Arguments:** 1 optional number (standard nil-gated idiom), default `3` — the same "default flag value `3`" convention already seen for `trigger_enable`'s own arg 3 (§1.1).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the argument is passed unmodified to `0x007dd5d0`, which treats it as a bitmask-like mode selector tested by exact value: when the value is `1` or `3`, a local, non-replicated call (`0x007d6dc0`) runs; when the value is `2` or `3`, the change instead (or additionally) goes through the SAME record-and-replicate "begin/commit/end" triplet `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13 already confirmed, tagged with a further new opcode, `0x40` (extends, does not contradict, §4.13's own opcode census). Passing the default `3` (bits for both `1` and `2`) runs BOTH paths.

**Side effects/subsystem:** removes the active waypoint, via a local call, a network-replicated call, or both depending on the mode value. Subsystem: waypoint/HUD-navigation state, network-replicated on the `0x40`-opcode path. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the mode-value branch structure and the record-and-replicate opcode; OPEN — the exact real-world distinction between the two removal paths, and `0x007d6dc0`'s own internal behaviour.]**

### 6.18 `notoriety_set_can_decay` (`0x00a55110`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory boolean, no nil-gate. **Unlike every other `notoriety_set_*` function in this cluster, this one takes NO track-name argument at all — it is a single GLOBAL flag, not a per-track setting.**

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the boolean is passed, through one intermediate wrapper, to `0x006054b0`, whose own body stores the LOGICAL NEGATION of the passed value into a single global byte, `0x014a4c0f`.

**Side effects/subsystem:** sets a single global "notoriety decay suppressed" flag (stored inverted relative to the Lua-visible argument — `notoriety_set_can_decay(true)` clears the global, `notoriety_set_can_decay(false)` sets it — the same "flag stored as the negated sense of an `allow_*`-style argument" convention already confirmed for `character_allow_ragdoll`, §3.16).
