### 6.19 `tutorial_start` (`0x00a603f0`)

**Arguments:** up to 5. Arg 1 (string, mandatory, no gate) — a tutorial/hint identifier. Arg 2 (number, optional, standard nil-gated idiom, default `0`). Args 3-5 (booleans, each optional, standard nil-gated idiom, default `false`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through a dedicated, 210-entry (`0xd2`) fixed name table (`0x00717780`, case-insensitive linear scan, returning the matched index or `-1`) — a name space entirely separate from the notoriety-family resolvers elsewhere in this cluster. On success, the index and the four remaining arguments (with a literal `1` inserted as an internal fourth value not exposed to the Lua-visible signature) are handed to a single large dispatcher, `0x00717780`'s sibling `0x007169e0`. That dispatcher consults a matching 210-entry ~~descriptor table (`0x0151d608`, 36 bytes per entry)~~ **[corrected 2026-10-01, job `20261001T020213-team-a-dksj`: a 210-entry run-time table based at `0x0151d600`, 36 bytes per entry; `0x0151d608` is entry 0's `+0x08` field, a pointer to that entry's separately allocated descriptor record — see the re-derivation below]** and, per an entry-specific flag bit, either issues a simple prompt (`0x00715bf0`) or assembles and dispatches a richer animated/video tutorial widget (`0x00715760`→`0x007fc560`); separately, when running as the sole/local co-op authority (the same `0x0087ba20` check used throughout this cluster) and a further per-entry flag bit (or the hardcoded internal literal `1` above) permits it, the event is additionally funnelled through the SAME record-and-replicate triplet as elsewhere in this document, tagged with yet another new opcode, `0x54`.

**Side effects/subsystem:** dispatches a named tutorial/hint prompt (simple or richly-animated per a per-entry flag), optionally network-replicated. Subsystem: tutorial/HUD-hint scripting. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the resolver, the two display-style branches, and the record-and-replicate opcode; OPEN — the precise real-world meaning of args 2-5 and of several internal per-entry flag bits and threshold constants (e.g. a repeated `0xbc` split between two id ranges) were not independently re-derived past their own gating role.]** **[Partly settled 2026-10-01, job `20261001T020213-team-a-dksj`: the flag bits and the `0xbc` split are described below; the meanings of several globals stay OPEN.]**

**Re-derivation from the executable (2026-10-01, job `20261001T020213-team-a-dksj`).**

*The table.* It is run-time state, zero at load (a `.data` block that is not file-backed), not static
data. Base `0x0151d600`, 36-byte entries (index × 9 dwords), 210 entries. Only the name list is static:
a file-backed table of 210 string pointers at `0x012f5930`, searched by `0x00717780` (§26.28).
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]** Entry layout:

| offset | content | label |
|---|---|---|
| `+0x00` / `+0x04` | next / previous links in a circular doubly-linked list of queued simple prompts (head global `0x0151d588`) | CONFIRMED |
| `+0x08` | pointer to the entry's descriptor record; written only by `0x00715850`, which also sets the state to 0 or 1 **[2026-10-01, job `20261001T114716-team-a-fvfp`: the table is filled by `0x007178c0` through 210 calls to `0x00715850`; `0x007178c0` also writes the 7-id table `0x0152145c`; entries 189–209 start in state 1, entries 0–188 in state 0]** | CONFIRMED |
| `+0x0c` | per-entry **state**, 0–4 (not a kind) | CONFIRMED |
| `+0x10` | not touched by the dumped code | OPEN |
| `+0x14` | argument 2 (the number) | CONFIRMED |
| `+0x18` | 0 if argument 5 is true, else the descriptor's `+0x20` dword | CONFIRMED |
| `+0x1c` | the hidden literal 1 | CONFIRMED |
| `+0x20` | not touched by the dumped code | OPEN |

*Descriptor record* (what `+0x08` points at, only where read): `+0x00` a default widget source;
`+0x14` an optional builder function pointer (called with the descriptor when non-null); `+0x20` a
default parameter copied into entry `+0x18`; `+0x24` flag bits — `0x04` use the rich (animated/video)
widget instead of the simple prompt, `0x08` allowed while a mission is active, `0x10` host-only
(suppressed on a co-op client). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the bit tests; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the
bit names, taken from what each bit gates.]**

*States.* 0 = untouched (zero-fill); 1 = armed/enabled (the dispatcher proceeds from it); 2 = queued as
a simple prompt; 4 = rich widget issued. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, from the writers.]** No code writes
the literal 3; it can only come from the generic setter `0x007163e0` or from undefined code at
`0x00717363`. **[OPEN — what state 3 means. HYPOTHESIS: displayed, waiting for the player to finish the
step.]** `tutorial_advance` (§10.4) succeeds only in state 3.

*Dispatcher order* (`0x007169e0`; A = index, N = argument 2, F = argument 3, B4/B5 = arguments 4/5, P4
= the hidden 1). Each "stop" means do nothing:

1. A < 189 and the global byte `0x0151d5a6` is non-zero → stop (indices 189 and up bypass this byte).
2. The global `0x029443bc` is 1, 2 or 3 → stop. **[OPEN — what that global is.]**
3. A > 209 → stop.
4. A < 189, a session exists, the local machine is not the host (`+0x5c` ≠ `+0x58`) and the
   descriptor has bit `0x10` → stop.
5. `0x00706ab0` returns 6 → stop. **[OPEN — meaning.]**
6. If the byte `0x014f3d34` is non-zero, continue only for A = 188 or 196 ≤ A ≤ 201. If it is zero,
   continue when the descriptor has bit `0x08`, or otherwise only when no mission object is live
   (`0x006d2910` returns −1). **[OPEN — what the `0x014f3d34` mode is.]**
7. A = 76 and the byte `0x0141250d` is zero → A becomes 73. **[OPEN — meaning.]**
8. A ≥ 189 → set state 1 (through `0x00716170`, itself gated on `0x0151d5a6` being zero).
9. F true, `0x0151d5a6` zero and state 0 → set state 1.
10. Continue only if state = 1, or (B4 true and state = 4), or A ≥ 189.
11. Descriptor bit `0x04` set → build the rich widget (`0x00715760` then `0x007fc560`), keep its
    handle in `0x0151d5b4`, set state 4. Otherwise `0x00715bf0`: if the entry is not already queued,
    link it at the tail of the prompt list, set state 2 and fill `+0x14`/`+0x18`/`+0x1c` as in the
    table above.
12. A session exists and the local machine is the host, and (descriptor bit `0x10` or P4 = 1, which
    is always true from Lua) → write an opcode `0x54` record: byte 1, A, a dword from `0x0086be20`,
    P4 (byte), N, B5 (byte); commit and close. A host therefore always replicates `tutorial_start`;
    a client or a machine with no session never does.

**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for steps 1–12 as control flow; the meanings of the globals in steps 1, 2,
5, 6 and 7 are OPEN as marked.]** The "repeated `0xbc` split" above is the boundary between 188
(`0xbc`) and the range from 189 (`0xbd`) up, which skips the suppression byte and the state gate.

**Review status (2026-10-01): re-derived from the executable (job `20261001T020213-team-a-dksj`): CONFIRMED — table base `0x0151d600`, 36-byte stride, 210 entries, zero at load; `+0x08` descriptor pointer; `+0x0c` state 0–4 with states 0/1/2/4 from their writers; the descriptor `+0x24` bit tests; the 12-step order; host-only `0x54` replication. HIGH CONFIDENCE — the names of bits `0x04`/`0x08`/`0x10`. HYPOTHESIS — state 3 = waiting for the player. OPEN — what state 3 means and who sets it; the globals in steps 2, 5, 6, 7; where `0x00715850` gets the descriptors. Updated 2026-10-01 (job `20261001T114716-team-a-fvfp`): CONFIRMED — the fill is `0x007178c0` → `0x00715850` (40-byte descriptors copied to `0x0151f388`); entries 189–209 start in state 1. HIGH CONFIDENCE — the descriptors are compiled-in constants. OPEN — when `0x007178c0` runs; state 3 (see §10.4).**

### 6.20 `mission_end_to_activity` (`0x00a53890`)

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings, no nil-gates. Arg 1 — a mission identifier. Arg 2 — an activity name.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 is gated through the SAME mission-check gate function `mission_end_failure`/`mission_end_success` use (`0x006d7240`, §1.5/§6.12). If it passes, arg 2 resolves through `0x005f4c30` — structurally identical to §6.6/§6.8's own `0x005eab60` (same outer guard, same underlying generic resolver `0x004588f0`, same shared class-descriptor table `0x02cc9900`), here testing a SIXTH catalogued bit/offset combination in this family, bit `0x4` at row offset `+0xc` (an "activity" object kind, inferred from the registered name, not independently confirmed). The resolved (or, on failure/absence/liveness-check failure via `0x00853b10`, null) handle is passed to `0x006da960`, which — itself gated by the same co-op sole-authority check as elsewhere in this cluster — when given a real handle, copies its own position-pair fields (`+8`/`+0xc`, the SAME convention as ~~§1.10/§4.3~~ §3.11/§6.12) into two globals (`0x014c8360`/`0x014c8364`) before unconditionally calling a further dispatcher, `0x006da7b0`.

**Side effects/subsystem:** transitions from a checked mission into a named activity, recording the activity object's world position into two globals along the way. Subsystem: mission-end/state-transition dispatch, sharing its gate function with `mission_end_failure`/`mission_end_success`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full resolve/gate chain and the position-pair copy; OPEN — `0x006da7b0`'s own internal behaviour.]**

### 6.21 `mission_set_cancel_warp_location` (`0x00a53900`)

**Arguments:** 2 optional strings, both standard nil-gated idiom, default absent/`NULL`.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** each argument, if present, resolves through `0x005982e0` — the SAME third-tier by-name resolver `door_open` (§1.10) uses and `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13 already flagged as "most plausibly" identical to `teleport`'s own destination resolver — gated by the shared liveness check `0x00853b10`; a resolution failure is treated the same as an absent argument. If BOTH arguments are absent (or both fail to resolve): `0x006cf050` runs, which — only while a mission is active and not in one specific game-mode state (two global checks, `0x014c8460`/`0x014c7a14`) — clears a single global (`0x014c8540`), read as a "cancel-warp override" pointer/flag. If BOTH resolve successfully: `0x006d1960` runs, gated by the SAME two global checks, and reads a field at offset `+0x4c` from EACH resolved object before combining both into a further call, `0x006d0210`. **If only one argument resolves, neither path runs at all — a genuine, confirmed partial-argument no-op.**

**Cross-section note:** the `+0x4c` field read here is the SAME field `teleport` (§4.3) reads off its own destination object but — per §4.3's own text — never visibly uses again afterward, leaving its purpose OPEN there. This function's own use of the identical field, on an object resolved through the SAME shared resolver family member (`0x005982e0`), is independent corroborating evidence that the field is real, consumed data on this object kind — it does not by itself resolve what `teleport`'s OWN body does with it, and is reported here as additional evidence for a DIFFERENT consuming function, not a resolution of §4.3's specific OPEN item.

**Side effects/subsystem:** sets (or, if both names are omitted, clears) the location the player warps to if the current mission is cancelled, keyed by two named location references. Subsystem: mission-cancel/warp state. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure, the shared resolver/liveness-check reuse, and the `+0x4c` field read; OPEN — `0x006d0210`'s own internal behaviour, and the exact real-world roles of the two arguments (e.g. "from"/"to") relative to each other.]**

### 6.22 Cross-function observations

**Three independent notoriety-track/group name-resolution mechanisms exist side by side, all converging on structurally related record types.** Besides `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3.6's own `0x0094cc60` (numeric-code resolver, failure sentinel `9`, feeding §3.6's own five-track switch `0x008ed1d0` and the batch caller of `0x008ecda0`), this cluster found two more: `0x00605160` (§6.3/§6.5/§6.7/§6.11/§6.16 — a case-insensitive scan across three parallel 4-entry `.rdata` alias-name arrays beginning `"luchadores"`/`"brotherhood"`/`"los_carnales"`, returning a shared 0-3 index or failure sentinel `5`, feeding the five value-setters `0x006079c0`/`0x00607ea0`/`0x006080d0`/`0x006082e0`/`0x00609810`) and `0x008ed350` (§6.2/§6.10 — a case-insensitive scan across 24 `.rdata` group names beginning `"police"`, returning a group-record pointer rather than a numeric code, feeding `0x008ed390`'s tier/sub-item table and, via `0x008ecda0`, the SAME `+0x455` flag byte §3.6 already confirmed on its own five hardcoded track bases). The `+0x455` flag byte and the `+0x3e0`/`+0x3e4`/`+0x3e8` tier-range fields this cluster newly read are consistent, non-overlapping offsets, HIGH CONFIDENCE (not independently proven with a shared-instance check) evidence that §3.6's track records and this cluster's group records are the same underlying object type, reached through name spaces of different granularity (a small fixed enumeration vs. a broader 24-name table) rather than being unrelated structures.

**The record-and-replicate idiom (`spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13) is confirmed to extend to three further opcode values not previously on record there** — `0x3f` (the five notoriety value-setters, §6.3/§6.5/§6.7/§6.11/§6.16, each with its own inner sub-type tag `2`-`5`), `0x40` (`waypoint_remove`, §6.17), and `0x54` (`tutorial_start`, §6.19) — all using the exact same "begin/commit/end" triplet (`0x0086f5f0`→`0x0086f110`→`0x0086eb20`) §4.13 already confirmed. This extends, and does not contradict, §4.13's own opcode census. **Cross-reference, added after review, 2026-09-29: opcode `0x40` is NOT unique to `waypoint_remove` — §9.20 (`inv_weapon_disable_all_slots`) independently uses the identical literal opcode `0x40` for a completely unrelated record. Both individual claims are correct (verified by decompile, `0x007dd5d0`/`0x007f4890` respectively); this document's opcode census is not a claim of uniqueness per name, only that each opcode's use is confirmed wherever cited.**

**A real, confirmed variation on how the record-and-replicate idiom decides "am I the sole/local authority":** §3.7/§3.14/§3.16/§3.17/§4.5/§4.6/§4.10 (already on record) gate that decision on an internal pair, `0x008ae480`/`0x008837a0`. Every record-and-replicate call site newly traced in THIS cluster (the five notoriety setters, `tutorial_start`) instead gates on the SAME accessor, `0x0087ba20`, `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3.1 already established for `coop_is_active`'s own pure query. **Correction, after independent re-verification (2026-09-29): the specific field pair this gate tests, `+0x58`/`+0x5c`, is NOT a previously-unspecified head/tail-member-list-empty pair as an earlier pass in this section claimed — it is the exact same field pair §8.27 (`game_get_is_host`) independently identifies, by the engine's own naming of that accessor, as the "is this machine the network host" check.** ~~§3.1's own head/tail member-list-empty description covers OTHER fields of the same session-context singleton, not this pair~~ **[corrected 2026-10-01, job `20261001T020213-team-a-dksj`: §3.1 has no head/tail pair; `coop_is_active` tests this same `+0x58`/`+0x5c` pair first and then uses the list head `+0x54` and count `+0x60` — see §3.1]** — see §8.27 for the correct reading. This is still a genuine, checked difference between subsystems in how the same underlying "am I authoritative" decision is reached (a host-check here, vs. the internal gate pair in §3/§4's own cluster), not a contradiction of §3.7/§4.13's own findings — flagged here because the task brief asked this pass to actively check for exactly this kind of cross-section inconsistency, and the correction above is exactly such a check catching a real one.

**Two more members of the type-gated-by-name resolver family (`spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §3's front matter / §4.13) were newly catalogued this pass:** bit `0x20` at descriptor-row offset `+0xa` (`0x005eab60`, used by both `guardian_angel_register_script_group` and `guardian_angel_unregister_script_group`, §6.6/§6.8) and bit `0x4` at descriptor-row offset `+0xc` (`0x005f4c30`, used by `mission_end_to_activity`, §6.20) — both structurally identical wrapper bodies over the same shared generic resolver `0x004588f0` and the same shared class-descriptor table `0x02cc9900` already established elsewhere in this document, extending that family from four/five previously-catalogued members to six (correction: `0x005eab60`/bit `0x20`@`+0xa` was already in §4.13/§4.7, so only `0x005f4c30` is newly catalogued here — five/six, one new).

**A second confirmed instance of a trivial, address-shared stub function, alongside `set_mission_author`'s own (§6.1):** `0x008ecda0` (the single-instruction `+0x455` flag-byte setter §3.6 first found and this cluster's `notoriety_force_no_spawn_group`, §6.10, also uses) has 75 callers project-wide — far more than the ones this document actually traces to notoriety state. Per this project's own standing caution against over-attributing meaning from a shared trivial-function address alone (`WALLS.md`), this document does not claim the other ~64 callers touch notoriety state; only the calls independently traced here and in §3.6 are described as such.

**`mission_end_success` (§6.12) and `mission_end_to_activity` (§6.20) both confirmed to share `mission_end_failure`'s (§1.5) own gate function `0x006d7240`**, and `mission_end_success` additionally shares that same section's final dispatch function `0x006da400`, in the same overall parameter shape (a leading flag, a text pointer, then two position pairs) — the three `mission_end_*` entry points documented across this spec so far (§1.5, §6.12, §6.20) form one coherent family built on shared plumbing, not three independent implementations.

## 7. Character/AI/combat flag-setter, hit-points, leash, and hook cluster — 32 functions, all in the 1,014-entry gameplay table (`0x00a20840`)

**Scope note:** this cluster's assignment was the next 32 names by real script-call count after
`spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §1–§4's top 50 (i.e. ranks 51–150's character/AI/combat share). All 32
were located directly in the 1,014-entry gameplay registrar (`0x00a20840`) via the same ordered
`{name,pointer}`-pair walk §3's own method paragraph documents (raw evidence already on disk at
`tools/scratchpad/lua_gameplay_1014_raw_pairs.txt`, re-used rather than re-run); 17 of the 32 had
never been marked as a Ghidra function start and were force-disassembled first, in a fresh disposable
project copy (`tools/gp_charai3`), using the same "force-disassemble, create function, decompile"
script pattern already on record (`AiDecForce.java`). All addresses below were cross-checked against
their own immediately-adjacent `STR:`/`FN:`/`UNK:` sequence entries before use, the same discipline
§3 applied.

**Record-and-replicate audit (explicitly requested for this cluster):** §3.7 documents a "record-
and-replicate" idiom for character/vehicle bit-flag setters — flip a bit directly only when a gate
check indicates the call is already inside a replicated-apply context, otherwise open a network
record first — and this pass was asked to check every structurally-similar simple setter in this
batch against its OWN decompiled body rather than assume uniformity. Result: the idiom is real and
present in most of the flagged names, but in **at least four genuinely different concrete shapes**,
not one:

1. **Double-gate, string-tagged** (the exact §3.7 shape): two successive gate calls (`0x008ae480`
   then `0x008837a0`); both false → open a record carrying two literal debug-tag strings (a category
   + a specific name); otherwise → flip a bit directly. Used by ~~7~~ 9 of this batch's delegates (per §7.33's list). **Note,
   added after independent review, 2026-09-29: `0x008ae480` itself is not an independent predicate —
   it does its own object-resolution/type-check first, then calls the SAME underlying function,
   `0x00884760`, variant 2's own `0x008addb0` wraps directly (with explicit arguments here, vs.
   variant 2's no-visible-argument call). The two call SHAPES are genuinely different, as described,
   but they share one bottom-line predicate — the "4 shapes" are less independent than the count
   alone suggests.**
2. **Single-gate, numeric-mode-tagged**: one gate call (`0x008addb0`, itself a thin wrapper over
   `0x00884760`); false → open a record carrying a small integer mode/sub-opcode instead of a string;
   otherwise → flip a bit or write a value directly. Used by the player-controls/movement pair and
   the hit-points setters.
3. **Single-gate, `0x008ae480`-only** (no second gate, no `0x008837a0` call at all): used only by the
   two leash functions.
4. **No gate at all — always both**: the write happens directly and unconditionally, and the record
   is opened unconditionally too, gated only by an explicit caller-supplied parameter rather than any
   internal replicated-context check. Used by `human_gravity_enable`'s delegate, and (for the record
   side only, with no direct-write alternative at all) by `set_script_animation_state`.

One flagged name, `set_attack_player_flag`, turned out to split its behaviour across **two different
flag locations** — one written unconditionally with no replication at all, the other reached only
conditionally and fully replicated via variant 1 above under a different function. Full detail is in
each function's own subsection below; §7.33 tallies the cross-cutting findings.

### 7.1 `npc_leash_remove` (`0x00a55570`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (NPC/character name).

**Return:** none.

**Body:** resolves via the generic/`#PLAYER#`-then-`#FOLLOWER#` chain (`0x00a28150`); on success,
calls `0x004e3bf0` on the resolved object. `0x004e3bf0` gates on a SINGLE check (`0x008ae480`,
compared for exact equality against `1`, variant 3 above — no second gate call anywhere in this

  each subsection above): double-gate string-tagged (`0x008ae480`+`0x008837a0`, opcode `0x46`) —
  §7.2, §7.6 (via `0x004e0270`), §7.10's secondary flag (via `0x004e0100`), §7.11's fallback (via
  `0x0094b070`), §7.14, §7.19, §7.20, §7.26, §7.29; single-gate numeric-mode (`0x008addb0`, opcode
  `0x32` for player-controls/movement, no opcode-`0x46` reuse) — §7.7, §7.8, §7.11's own outer layer
  (opcode `0x43`), §7.22, §7.25, §7.31 (opcode `0x46`, reusing the string-tag shape despite the
  single-gate check — a genuine cross-variant mix worth flagging on its own); single-gate
  `0x008ae480`-only (no second gate) — §7.1, §7.5; no gate at all, always-both — §7.32; and one
  genuine split-location case — §7.10, where one flag never replicates and a second, separately
  reached one fully does. **The task's own caution not to assume uniformity was well-founded: of the
  9 explicitly-flagged names plus the further ones checked opportunistically in this pass, only
  `set_script_animation_state` (§7.17, unconditional record with no bypass) and `human_gravity_enable`

function only proceeds to its network/queue-side effect when running as host. When both that gate and
a caller-supplied mode-byte bit `0x2` (always set here, the literal `3`) hold: begins a tagged,
opcode-`0x51` buffered record (`0x0086f5f0`), writes a one-byte message-subtype tag (`4`) and the id
byte into it (`0x00881040`), and commits it via `0x0086f1b0`/`0x0086eb20`.

**Side effects / subsystem:** host-only, queues an opcode-`0x51` "conversation" command (subtype tag
`4`) ending the given conversation. Subsystem: dialogue/conversation, host-gated command queue (see
§8.28's cross-function note on this queue mechanism, which this function is the first instance of in
this cluster). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the id-read, the host-gate identity, and the opcode/tag
values; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for "ends a conversation" as the queued command's real effect,
taken from the registered name, since the command's own consumer was not traced.]**

### 8.12 `camera_restrict_set_active` (`0x00a445e0`)

**Arguments:** 2. Arg 1 (boolean, mandatory, read unconditionally via `lua_toboolean` at the first
stack slot) — the active/restrict flag. Arg 2 (string, optional, standard nil-gated) — a target
name.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** a guard starts `true`, and the local setter always runs FIRST regardless of arg 2 — one of
two local setters, `0x0057a780` (clear) or `0x0057a760` (set, with a further call to `0x00d2f540` the
first time it transitions), depending on the active flag. **[2026-10-01, jobs `20261001T021703-team-a-pwgq` / `20261001T021707-team-a-jxxz` (§27.23): `0x00d2f540` is a two-instruction `return 1` stub (load 1, return) with many unrelated callers, one of them inside `0x0057a760`; the call has no effect, so the set path is just the flag write. CONFIRMED — disassembly.]** **Corrected after independent
re-verification (2026-09-29): whether the record-and-replicate path ALSO fires depends specifically on
what arg 2 resolves to, and the "arg 2 absent" and "arg 2 resolves to current player" cases are NOT
the same case — an earlier pass in this section wrongly combined them.** Concretely:
- **arg 2 resolves (via the shared generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver `0x00a280c0`, §4.13) to the
  current player** (`0x009da4e0`, the same accessor §4.13 describes backing the `"#PLAYER#"`
  sentinel): the guard is set `false` — the local setter above runs, and the record-and-replicate
  path is skipped. **This is the only purely-local case.**
- **arg 2 is ABSENT:** the guard is NEVER set `false` — execution lands directly on the local-setter
  label, runs it, then falls through (since the guard is still `true`) straight into the
  record-and-replicate sequence below. **The local setter and the network record BOTH fire — this is
  not a local-only case.**
- **arg 2 resolves to something else (a remote/co-op target):** the local setter is skipped
  (execution never reaches its label), and only the record-and-replicate path runs.

**The record-and-replicate path** (fired for the "absent" and "remote target" cases above): opens an
opcode-`0x43` buffered record (`0x0086f5f0`), carrying a bit-packed payload built from the resolved
target and the active flag (via `0x00881110`, the bit-granularity sibling of the byte-granularity
`0x00881040` writer §8.2's family uses), and commits it the same way (`0x0086f1b0`→`0x0086eb20`).
**Note: this function does *not* use the host-check gate §8.2/§8.5/§8.18/§8.13 share** — its branch is
controlled by what the target resolves to, not by whether this machine is the host.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets a local camera-restriction flag whenever the local setter path is
reached (current-player target OR no target given); additionally queues an opcode-`0x43` command
carrying the target and the flag whenever the target is absent or a remote/co-op target — i.e. the
"absent" case does BOTH, not just the local write. Subsystem: camera state, local-vs-networked split on target
identity. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure, the shared `"#PLAYER#"` resolver
identity (citing `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13 directly, not re-derived), and the opcode/commit
call identities; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for "restriction" as the local flag's role, from the
registered name.]**

### 8.15 `hud_bar_on` (`0x00a4d9e0`)

**Arguments:** up to 6. Arg 1 (numeric, mandatory, read unconditionally) — bar-slot id. Arg 2 (string,
mandatory, read unconditionally — no presence check, the same pattern §2.3/§2.9 already flag) — a
secondary identifier string, passed straight through unresolved. Arg 3 (string, optional, standard
nil-gated, default `""`) — a label/text key. Arg 4 (number, optional, default `0.0`) — a value/percent.
Arg 5 (numeric/flag, optional, default `3`) — same flag-extractor pair as elsewhere. Arg 6
(numeric/flag, optional, default `-1`).

**Return:** none (implicit `void`, no `lua_push*` call — 0 Lua values).

**Body:** if arg 3 is non-empty, it is resolved through **the exact same three-stage localization
chain `objective_text` already established (§1.3)**: `0x00849df0` first, then (gated on the same
global at `0x026e7e68`) the secondary resolver pair `0x00604740`→`0x00604500`, then the same
`sprintf`-shaped last-resort fallback `0x00db06e0` — all three addresses identical to §1.3's own,
confirming this is one shared engine-wide text-resolution helper, not a coincidence of similar shape.
The resolved text, the id, arg 2, the value, and both flag arguments (plus two further globals at
`0x0117f958`/`0x0117f95c`, read as default colour components) are all handed to `0x007edbe0`, a large
per-bar state-writer that only marks the widget "dirty" (a byte flag per changed field, at fixed
offsets of a `0x58`-byte-stride record parallel to the `0x16`-stride array §8.14/§8.16 use) when a
given field actually changed from its previous value, and additionally maintains an interpolate-toward
pair of float fields (immediate value vs. animated target, at record offsets `+0x4c`/`+0x50` relative
to the bar's own base) scaled by a further global (`0x012a2d28`) — the same "current vs. animated
target" shape §8.16's `hud_bar_set_value` also writes into, at a *different* pair of offsets
(`+0x24`/`+0x28`) on the smaller `0x16`-stride array. When flag-argument bit `0x2` is set: queues an
opcode-`0x3e` command (subtype tag `2`, payload the bar id and the flags themselves) via the same
begin/attach/commit shape as §8.2's family (`0x0086f5f0`/`0x00881110`/`0x0086f1b0`/`0x0086eb20`) — **no
host-check gate here**, purely flag-gated. When bit `0x1` is set: marks a further dirty byte and calls
`0x007eaec0` on the bar's own base record — read as an immediate local refresh/show call.

**Side effects / subsystem:** turns a HUD bar widget on with a resolved label, value, and colour
defaults; conditionally (flag-gated, not host-gated) queues an opcode-`0x3e` "HUD bar" command and/or
triggers a local refresh. Subsystem: HUD (bar widgets), sharing its localization chain verbatim with
`objective_text` (§1.3, cited directly) and its command-queue shape with §8.2's audio family (same
begin/commit primitives, different opcode). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the argument chain, the

### 8.16 `hud_bar_set_value` (`0x00a4dc20`)

**Arguments:** 3. Arg 1 (numeric, mandatory, unconditional) — bar-slot id. Arg 2 (number, mandatory,

`0x007eaf30`, but only if the value differs from what is already stored, additionally setting a dirty
byte at `+0x20` when it does.

(`+0x24`, unconditional write, no dirty-tracking), bit `0x2` targets what reads as an *animated target*
field (`+0x28`, change-gated, dirty-flagged) — the same immediate-vs-animated-target split
`hud_bar_on` (§8.15) already shows on its own, larger per-bar record (there at `+0x4c`/`+0x50`).

### 8.17 `hud_prompt_clear` (`0x00a4d080`)

**Arguments:** 1, optional (standard nil-gated) — a target name string; absent/nil/empty resolves to
a null target.

**Body:** a non-empty target resolves through the shared generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver
(`0x00a280c0`, `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13), then is passed to `0x00a36e60`. That function checks
the target against **two** distinct "am I this?" accessors — the current-player one-liner `0x009da4e0`
(§4.13's own `"#PLAYER#"` backing accessor) and a second, separate one-liner `0x009df3d0` ~~, not
independently identified this pass~~ **IDENTIFIED (2026-10-02, ranking tranche 04, §32.1-A.7): the
remote co-op player getter — returns the first live-roster entry that is NOT the local player
(`0x0262edfc`), or null if none, gated on global flag `0x024d4462`; see §14.31's own corrected note** —
and, depending on which (if either) match, or on a null target,
clears either a fixed table slot (`0x02703cac` ← `0x01248ed4`, a "no clear-target" default) and/or
sends a local, non-networked command (`0x005e4520`, literal tag `9` or `10`). When the target
specifically matched the second accessor's own value, and a further gate (`0x00867830`, not opened
this pass) also passes, it *additionally* opens a genuinely network-replicated record — **this is a
further, directly confirmed instance of the record-and-replicate idiom `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md`
§4.13 already established** (the identical three-call sequence, `0x0086f5f0`→`0x0086f110`→`0x0086eb20`,
using `0x0086f110` — not the local-dispatch sibling `0x0086f1b0` this cluster's own audio/HUD command
family otherwise uses, see §8.28) — tagged opcode `0x4a`, carrying a single boolean payload byte and a
resolved handle from `0x009df3d0`→`0x008ae020`.

**Side effects / subsystem:** clears a HUD prompt for the resolved target (or the null/default target
if none given), always locally; additionally, when the target is whatever `0x009df3d0` identifies (not
independently named this pass) and a further condition holds, network-replicates the clear via
§4.13's own idiom. Subsystem: HUD (prompt widget), with a genuine network-replicated path confirmed to
reuse §4.13's exact mechanism rather than this cluster's own local-dispatch variant. **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly for the branch structure and the `0x0086f110`-based replicate call, cross-cited directly

**`0x009df3d0` IDENTIFIED above (2026-10-02); OPEN — `0x00867830`'s own identity.**]**

### 8.18 `hud_set_fake_notoriety` (`0x00a4d0e0`)

**Arguments:** 3. Arg 1 (string, mandatory, unconditional) — a gang/track name. Arg 2 (boolean,
mandatory, unconditional). Arg 3 (number, optional, standard nil-gated, default `0.0`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through `0x00605160`, a case-insensitive scan (real public CRT `__stricmp`)
across **three parallel 4-entry string tables**, read directly (not from Ghidra's own auto-generated
labels, which were independently verified byte-for-byte against the actual string data this pass):
`{"luchadores","deckers","morningstar","police"}` at `0x012ed130`, `{"brotherhood","ronin","samedi",
"police"}` at `0x012ed140`, and `{"los_carnales","vice_kings","rollers","police"}` at `0x012ed150`.
The three tables are indexed by the *same* running counter (0-3), i.e. slot 0 accepts any of
`"luchadores"`/`"brotherhood"`/`"los_carnales"`, slot 1 any of `"deckers"`/`"ronin"`/`"vice_kings"`,
slot 2 any of `"morningstar"`/`"samedi"`/`"rollers"`, and slot 3 accepts `"police"` under all three
names (the same literal string in each table). **These are, respectively, this series' own SR3, SR2,
and SR1 rival-gang name sets** (SR3: Luchadores/Deckers/Morningstar; SR2: Brotherhood/Ronin/Sons of
Samedi; SR1: Los Carnales/Vice Kings/Westside Rollerz) — a genuine cross-title naming-alias table
mapping any of the three games' own gang names onto the same 4 canonical notoriety-track slots,
almost certainly legacy debug/cheat tooling inherited across this engine's shared codebase rather than
anything SR3-specific. Unmatched names fall back to a sentinel slot value `5`. The resolved slot,
arg 2, and arg 3 are passed to `0x007f55c0`, which writes the boolean into a fixed per-slot array
(`0x022b7574`) and the clamped-to-`[0,∞)` float into a parallel array (`0x022b7564`), then — gated on
the **same host-check singleton** §8.2/§8.5/§8.13 already use (`0x0087ba20`/`0x024d8534`,
`+0x5c`==`+0x58`) — opens an opcode-`0x40` record (subtype tag `0x1b`) carrying the slot id and the two
written values, committed via the same local-dispatch shape as §8.2's family.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets a "fake" (debug/override) notoriety level and active flag for a
gang/track slot resolved from any of three cross-title naming conventions; host-gated, queues an
opcode-`0x40` command broadcasting the change. Subsystem: HUD (notoriety meter) / debug tooling.
**[CONFIRMED — disassembly and empirical string dump for the three-table alias structure (verified
directly against the raw bytes, not the decompiler's own auto-labels — this project's own standing
caution against trusting an auto-label without checking, `WALLS.md`); CONFIRMED for the host-gate and
opcode/tag identity.]** **Cross-reference, not a contradiction:** `notoriety_force_no_spawn` (§3.6)
takes a track name too, but its own name→code table was found to be runtime-populated, not static
(§5.2) — this function's own three-table alias structure is a *separate*, fully static resolver for a
different (fake/debug) notoriety mechanism, not the same table under another name.

### 8.19 `hud_timer_set` (`0x00a4f700`)

**Arguments:** up to 4. Arg 1 (numeric, mandatory, unconditional) — a timer-slot id. Arg 2 (numeric,
mandatory, unconditional) — a duration/count value. Arg 3 (string, optional, standard nil-gated,
default `""`) — a text key. Arg 4 (numeric/flag, optional, default `3`).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** the id and value are passed to `0x007eda20`, which indexes a fixed HUD-timer slot array
(base region near `0x022b6658`, stride `0x40`/`0x10` dwords — a distinct array from the bar-widget one

(change-gated, dirty-flagged, the same shape as §8.16's bar-value setter) and — on flags bit `0x2`, no
host-gate, purely flag-controlled, exactly like `hud_bar_on`'s own bit `0x2` (§8.15) — queues an
opcode-`0x3e` command (**the same opcode `hud_bar_on` uses**, subtype tag `1` here vs. `hud_bar_on`'s
`2`) via the identical begin/attach/commit shape. Bit `0x1`, when the slot table isn't already full
(`0x022b6600 < 4`), marks a further dirty byte and calls `0x007eaec0` — **the exact same local-refresh
call `hud_bar_on` makes on its own bit `0x1`** (§8.15), here on the timer array's own base instead of
the bar array's. Back in the top-level function, after the setter returns, a local queue-context

different fields than the host-check pair) is used to clear any stale prior handle, arg 3 (if present)
is resolved through a name-registration helper (`0x00a1fcc0`, a small fixed-capacity name↔id table
keyed by both the slot id and the string) and stored, and finally `0x00a29920` is called with the slot
id, two further globals (`0x026e9568`/`0x026e956c`), and a boolean derived from whether arg 3's name
resolution succeeded.

**Side effects / subsystem:** starts/updates a HUD timer widget's value and (flag-gated, sharing
opcode `0x3e` and the local-refresh call with `hud_bar_on`, §8.15) queues a UI/HUD command and/or
refreshes locally; optionally attaches a resolved text-key name to the timer slot. Subsystem: HUD
(timer widgets), sharing its command-queue mechanics one-for-one with the bar-widget family.

### 8.23 `game_get_key_name_for_action` (`0x008422a0`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string, read unconditionally — an action name.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a string) — `lua_pushstring` (`0x00dfe420`, this document's own newly-opened
primitive, above) of an escaped/re-encoded wide-string result.

**Body:** the action name is passed to `0x005be440`, which checks it, case-insensitively, against
**the exact same two compile-time action tables `spec-tables-ui-controls.md` already fully
catalogues, at byte-identical addresses**: the 34-entry CAA (axis-action) table at `0x01122690`/
`0x01122694` (§4.2 there) and the 166-entry CBA (button-action) table at `0x01122160`/`0x01122164`
(§4.1 there). If the name matches a CBA entry with a bound (non-`-1`) value, the bound key/button code
is resolved directly through `0x005be0d0` — **the exact same low-level key-name helper
`game_get_key_name` already uses** (§2.3) — and that result wins outright. Otherwise, if the name
matched a CAA (axis) entry: axis index `0` (`CAA_CAMERA_ROTATE`) resolves to the localized tag
`"STR_THE_MOUSE"`; axis indices `2`/`3` (`CAA_WALK_FORWARD_BACKWARD`/`CAA_WALK_TURN_LEFT_RIGHT` — the
two-key WASD-style movement axes) each resolve *two* sub-action codes via `0x005be2c0`/`0x005be340`
and format them together as `"<name> / <name>"` via `0x00db0530`; any other axis index (or no match at
all) yields an empty string.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none (pure query). Resolves an action name — either a discrete bound
button/key action (via the CBA table) or a two-key/mouse movement axis (via the CAA table) — to a
localized, display-ready name string, reusing `game_get_key_name`'s own low-level resolver for the
button case. Subsystem: input (action-to-key-name resolution), directly reusing
`spec-tables-ui-controls.md`'s own already-fully-specced CBA/CAA enumerations rather than a separate
table. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure and the byte-identical CBA/CAA table

real-world binding behind axis indices `1` and `4`+ (not covered by any of the three handled branches,

### 8.24 `game_peg_load_with_cb` (`0x00845510`)

**Arguments:** up to 8. Arg 1 (string, mandatory, unconditional) — a request-name/context string,
copied (bounds-checked to 64 bytes) into a per-request tracking-slot's own name field. Arg 2 (numeric,
mandatory, unconditional) — a count `N` of textures to load, used only when in the range `1..6`. Args
3 through `2+N` (each string, gated on presence via `lua_type`, breaking out early on any absent slot)
— PEG/texture filenames.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** claims the first empty slot in a small fixed per-Lua-binding request table (base
`0x02319570`, stride `0x68` bytes, bounded — the loop that finds a free slot bails out past a fixed
address ceiling rather than an explicit count field) and stamps it with the calling script's own
context (`0x00e0ceb0`'s `+0x14` field). For each of the `N` filenames: resolves it through **the exact
same resource-hash-and-lookup chain `game_peg_unload` already established** (§2.7:
`0x00db3530`→`0x00dab330(name,9000)`→`0x006cf2d0`→the PEG pointer array `0x029e1930`), then calls
`0x00dafea0` — a thread-checked (`GetCurrentThreadId` against `0x01329ea4`) load/reference-advance
routine, the direct counterpart of `game_peg_unload`'s own teardown routine `0x00dafad0` (§2.7), tested
against the same per-PEG flag bits at `+0x1e` — and, if the slot's own resolved-PEG capacity allows,
appends the resolved PEG pointer to the slot's own array. After the loop, `0x00845210` is called: it
scans **every** request slot in the same fixed table for one containing the just-resolved PEG pointer,
and only once *all* of that slot's own tracked PEGs report a "fully loaded" state (via the same 6-state
classifier `game_peg_unload` uses, `0x00dafb60`, §2.7 — states `3`/`5`) does it look up and queue a
stored command name (the slot's own `+0x28` name field) carrying the slot's own stored calling-script
context, then reset the slot's count to `0`.

**Side effects / subsystem:** loads up to 6 named PEG/texture resources into a per-request tracking
slot (reusing `game_peg_unload`'s exact hash/lookup/state-classifier chain, §2.7) and, once every PEG
in that slot has finished loading, dispatches the caller's own supplied callback name — the "with_cb"
half of the name. Subsystem: PEG/texture resource management, sharing its full resolution chain with
`game_peg_unload`. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the slot-table structure, the shared hash/lookup
chain (cited directly against §2.7), and the completion-sweep/callback-dispatch structure; HIGH
CONFIDENCE — inferred that the slot's own `+0x28` field is genuinely a stored Lua callback name/token,
from the function's own registered name and the completion-gated dispatch shape, since the actual
Lua-callback invocation was not traced past the queued command lookup.]**

### 8.26 `push_screen` (`0x00842a50`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string, read unconditionally — a screen name.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (boolean) — `lua_pushboolean` then `return 1;`.

**Body:** the name is hashed via the same general-purpose name hash (`0x00d9e8b0`) and looked up
(`0x007b4ad0`, an implicit-`this` method on a screen-stack singleton, checking a registered-screen-type
array at the singleton's own `+0x2c`/`+0x30` fields against each entry's own `+0x74` hash field) to
resolve a screen-definition pointer. That pointer is then pushed onto the *active* stack
(`0x007b4640`, the same screen-stack singleton `pop_screen` already documents by its `+0x24`/`+0x28`
capacity/depth fields, §2.8 — here writing into a separate active-instance array further out in the

### 8.28 Cross-function observations

**A host-gated variant of the local UI/HUD command-queue mechanism recurs across this cluster,
sharing its `begin`/`end` primitives with, but using a different middle "commit" step than, the
already-published network record-and-replicate idiom.** Five functions in this cluster
(`audio_conversation_end` §8.2, `audio_persona_load_2d` §8.5, `audio_persona_remove_2d` §8.6,
`hud_set_fake_notoriety` §8.18, and `fade_in`'s own opcode-`0x53` path §8.13) gate their queuing side
effect on the exact predicate `game_get_is_host` (§8.27) directly exposes to Lua — the shared
session-context singleton `0x024d8534` (reached via `0x0087ba20`), tested for `+0x5c`==`+0x58` — before
opening a tagged record via `0x0086f5f0(opcode)`, writing payload bits via `0x00881040` (byte
granularity) or `0x00881110` (bit granularity), and committing via `0x0086f1b0` then `0x0086eb20`.
**`0x0086f5f0` and `0x0086eb20` are the exact same two addresses `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md` §4.13
already documents as the "begin"/"end" calls of its own network record-and-replicate idiom** — but
that idiom's own middle "attach" call is a *different* address, `0x0086f110` (confirmed distinct: it
appears exactly once across this whole cluster's decompiled output, inside `hud_prompt_clear`'s own
genuinely-networked path, §8.17, at the identical address §4.13 cites — vs. `0x0086f1b0`, which appears
11 times, in every other opcode-tagged call in this cluster). Read together: **the begin/end pair is a
generic "open and finalize a tagged buffered record" primitive, reused by at least two different
downstream consumers** — §4.13's own network-replication attach (`0x0086f110`) and this cluster's own
local command-queue attach (`0x0086f1b0`) — not itself synonymous with "network replication." This
does not contradict §4.13, which only ever cites the network-attach variant; it extends that finding.
Several functions in this cluster use the *identical* opcode-tagged queue mechanism gated purely on a
caller-supplied flag bit instead of the host-check (`hud_bar_on` §8.15 bit `0x2`, `hud_timer_set` §8.19
bit `0x2`, both opcode `0x3e`; `camera_restrict_set_active` §8.12, opcode `0x43`, gated on target
identity instead) — confirming the mechanism itself is generic infrastructure with per-call-site gating
policy, not a single fixed access-control rule.

**A partial opcode catalogue, extending §2.9/§2.10's own partially-named set.** This cluster
independently confirms §2.9's own explicitly-flagged-OPEN opcode `0x53` (`fade_out`'s own bit-`0x2`
path) is the exact same opcode `fade_in`'s own mirrored bit-`0x2` path uses (§8.13) — resolving that
OPEN item to "a fade duration+flags broadcast, plausible co-op fade-timing replication," not
independently confirmed further. New opcodes this cluster adds to the record: `0x51` (audio
conversation/persona commands, subtype-tagged: `0`=persona-2D-load, `1`=persona-2D-remove,
`4`=conversation-end), `0x43` (camera-restrict; already recorded §7.11/§7.17 — a new use, not a new opcode), `0x40` (fake-notoriety, subtype `0x1b`; already recorded §6.17 — a new use, not a new opcode), `0x3e`
(shared by `hud_bar_on` and `hud_timer_set`, subtype `2` vs. `1` respectively), and `0x4a`
(`hud_prompt_clear`'s genuinely network-replicated path, via §4.13's own `0x0086f110` attach rather
than this cluster's local `0x0086f1b0`).

**The engine's general-purpose name hash (`0x00d9e8b0`) recurs across an unusually wide span of this
cluster** — `audio_conversation_load_direct` (§8.1), `audio_remove_mission_cellphone` (§8.8),
`zscene_prep` (§8.21), `vint_set_mouse_cursor` (§8.25), and `push_screen` (§8.26) all hash a name string
through this exact address before a table/array lookup, consistent with the decompiler-database comment
already on record project-wide identifying it as the general name hash rather than anything
conversation-specific (`spec-extensionless-types.md` §4). No new hash algorithm was found in this
cluster.

**`hud_set_fake_notoriety`'s three-table gang-name alias structure is a genuinely new, directly
verified finding** (§8.18) — a cross-title (SR1/SR2/SR3) gang-name resolver mapping any of three
games' own rival-gang names onto 4 shared canonical slots, confirmed by reading the raw string bytes
directly rather than trusting Ghidra's own auto-generated labels for those addresses (per this
project's own standing "verify, don't just eyeball a self-certified reading" discipline, `WALLS.md`).

**Recommendation for a future pass (not attempted here, out of this task's static-only scope):** a
behavioural oracle would settle several of this cluster's remaining OPEN items fastest — whether
`audio_play_persona_line_2d`'s dispatch ever yields non-zero (the same open question §2.5 already
flagged for the same underlying dispatch family), the real axis-index-1/4+ behaviour of
`game_get_key_name_for_action`, and `game_peg_load_with_cb`'s own completion-callback dispatch path.
This is a recommendation only; building or running such an oracle is out of scope for this task (per
`HANDOFF.md` §41.27.3 item 3, first recorded in §38.27.3, emulator use is authorized for isolated computational functions, not for
functions whose behaviour bottoms out in live per-object/per-frame state the way most of this OPEN list
does).

### 9.1 `effect_play` (`0x00a48c30`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string + 3 further optional arguments, each individually guarded by
the standard nil-test idiom (§ Method section): arg 1 (string, mandatory) — an effect name.
Arg 2 (boolean, optional, default `false`). Arg 3 (numeric/flag, optional, default `0`, read via
the shared numeric extractor). No fourth argument is read.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a number) — a real `lua_pushnumber`-shaped push (`0x00dfe3a0`) of a
double-precision value, reached either from the success path (see below) or from a shared
"failed to create" sentinel constant read directly from `.rdata` at address `0x012a3038`
(value `-1.0`, confirmed by a direct memory read of the constant) on any resolution failure.

**Body:** the effect name (arg 1) is resolved through the SAME by-name resolver
`teleport`'s destination argument and `door_open`'s third-tier resolver already use
(`0x005982e0`, §1.10/§4.3/§4.13) — a second, independent confirmed sighting of this exact
address being called on a name, reinforcing (without fully re-proving) its identity as the
type-gated resolver family's bit-`0x2`/offset-`+0xb` member. Once resolved and gated by the
shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`), the resolved object's own effect-definition index is
derived via a dedicated lookup (`0x008eacb0`, called twice in sequence) and a new effect-
instance slot is allocated (`0x005c50b0`, returning `-1` on exhaustion). On success, the new
instance is attached to the resolved object's own position (offset `+0x40`) and a further
`+0x4c` field, together with a 2-byte per-object field at offset `+0x72` (a field also read
by `door_open`'s own third handle, §1.10 — a plausible shared "zone/region tag," not
independently confirmed here), the optional boolean (arg 2), and the optional flag value
(arg 3). A shared finalizer (`0x005cf190`) packs these into the double-precision instance
identifier that becomes the pushed return value.

**Side effects / subsystem:** creates and attaches a named visual/particle effect instance to
a resolved world object, returning a numeric instance handle (or `-1.0` on failure).
Subsystem: effects (`spec-effects-format.md`'s own runtime, addresses `0x00436760`/`0x00437fc0`
already documented there as the emitter step/spawn pair — this Lua entry point is a further,
not-previously-traced caller reaching the same subsystem through its own definition-lookup and
slot-allocation front door). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for argument shape, the resolver/
liveness/definition-lookup/slot-allocation chain, and the shared finalizer; HIGH CONFIDENCE for
the `+0x72` field's "zone/region tag" reading and for the boolean/flag arguments' exact
consumption inside the finalizer, neither independently traced past being packed into the
record.]**

### 9.2 `effect_stop` (`0x00a48bb0`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory numeric value (an effect instance handle/id, the exact return-value
shape §9.1 documents) + 1 optional numeric/flag value, default `3` — the same literal default
seen on several flag-shaped optional arguments elsewhere in this document (`trigger_enable`'s
arg 3, §1.1 of this document's own §1 cluster; `inv_weapon_disable_all_slots`'s own arg 2,
§9.20 below).

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** unlike every named-object function in this cluster, `effect_stop`'s first argument is
read directly as a NUMBER (via the numeric extractor, not a name string) — consistent with it
being fed the numeric instance handle `effect_play` (§9.1) returns, rather than a fresh by-name
lookup. Both the handle and the flag value (arg 2, default `3`) are handed to a single dispatch
(`0x005cfe00`) with a literal middle argument of `1`. That dispatch's own body splits on two
individual bits of the flag byte: bit `0x2` opens the record-and-replicate idiom (§4.13/§9.21
below), opcode `0x45`, recording the handle and the literal `1`; bit `0x1` instead resolves the
handle directly (`0x00458230`, against a fixed handle-table base at `0x031d152c`) and, gated by
a per-object-type descriptor-row bit test (bit `0x1` at offset `+7` of the row indexed by the
resolved object's own type-id byte off a table at `0x02cc9900` — see §9.21) plus the shared
liveness check, applies the stop locally (`0x005c5fd0`).

**Side effects / subsystem:** stops a previously-created effect instance identified by numeric
handle, either applied locally or network-replicated (opcode `0x45`) depending on the flag
value's bit `0x2`. Subsystem: effects. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full dispatch and
both flag-bit branches; OPEN — the exact real-world meaning of the literal `1` middle argument
and of the flag value's remaining bits, read only from the shared default-`3` convention.]**

### 9.3 `explosion_create` (`0x00a49450`)

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory + 4 further optional. Arg 1 (string, mandatory) — read via
`lua_tolstring` but never observably consumed again anywhere in the decompiled body, the same

one of its own arguments — **[OPEN, same caveat as §2.5.]** Arg 2 (string, mandatory) — a
location/object-name reference, resolved through the SAME shared position-lookup function
`get_dist` (§4.2) uses (`0x00a455a0`). Arg 3 (string, optional, default absent) — an
instigator/owner name, resolved through the same object-by-name lookup `audio_play_persona_line`
and `inv_item_equip` (§9.19 below) use (`0x00a281a0`) when non-empty. Arg 4 (boolean, optional,
default `true`). Arg 5 (string, optional, default absent) — if given, routed through a
dedicated lookup (`0x00643a80`) and then the SAME effect-definition-index resolver `effect_play`
(§9.1) uses (`0x008eacb0`), read as an explosion "type" reference; if absent, a 2-byte field is
read directly off the resolved position object instead (offset `+0x72` — the SAME field §9.1
reads off its own resolved object). Arg 6 (number, optional, default `0.0`) — if it exceeds a
global threshold constant confirmed to be exactly `0.0` (address `0x0125e270`), the computed
explosion position is offset along a further vector by this argument's magnitude; the vector's
own source was not independently traced.

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a number) — the shared `-1.0` failure sentinel (`0x012a3038`, same
constant §9.1 uses) on any resolution failure, or the created instance's packed identifier via
the SAME finalize-then-push pair `effect_play` uses (`0x005cf190` then `0x00a48af0`) on success.

**Body:** once arg 2 resolves to a position (via `0x00a455a0`) and, when arg 5 was supplied,
the type-lookup chain above also resolves, the position/type/optional-owner values are handed to
a large, dedicated explosion-application routine (`0x00594460`) together with the position
offset (arg 6, applied beforehand) and several further constants. `0x00594460` was independently

### 9.4 `vehicle_chase` (`0x00a65ac0`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string + 5 further optional. Arg 1 (string, mandatory) — a vehicle
reference, resolved through the SAME dedicated vehicle-instance resolver
`vehicle_suppress_npc_exit` (§4.5) uses (`0x00a281e0`). Arg 2 (string, optional, default the
literal `"#PLAYER1#"` — read directly from `.rdata`, distinct from the `"#PLAYER#"` sentinel
`0x00a280c0` special-cases per §4.13) — a chase-target reference. Args 3-6 (booleans, optional,
defaults `true`/`false`/`true`/`false` respectively), each individually guarded by the standard
nil-test idiom.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** once the vehicle (arg 1) resolves, the chase-target name (arg 2, default
`"#PLAYER1#"`) is resolved against the vehicle's own name/id field pair at offset `+0x40`
(`0x00a3be60` — itself a two-step helper, trying a direct lookup first and falling back to a
plainer by-name resolve, `0x00a28150`, on failure) to obtain a small record. A per-vehicle
drive-mode check (`0x00ad31a0` — reads a nested state field off the vehicle and returns true only
for state values `3`/`4`) selects between two setup paths: if the vehicle is NOT already in
that drive-mode, a fresh chase-record is initialized (`0x00b47110`) and committed via the SAME
per-vehicle sub-record writer at offset `+0xc68` `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit`'s own setters target
(§4.5) — `0x00b4d260`; if it IS already in that drive-mode, the position is instead pushed
through a SEPARATE, record-and-replicate-gated updater (`0x00b3c260`, opcode `0x42` — see §9.21)
that writes the same vehicle sub-record's own position fields directly. Either way, the four
optional booleans (args 3-6) are packed into one flag byte alongside the resolved chase-target
record before being written; **[OPEN — the individual bit-to-argument mapping inside that packed
byte was not independently pinned down, per this project's standing caution against asserting a
bitfield's meaning from offset/position alone, `WALLS.md`.]** Finally, every occupant/attached
part of the vehicle (enumerated via the same count/index accessor pair, `0x00ab4af0`/
`0x00ab5070`, `vehicle_pathfind_check_done` §9.10 below also uses) is checked against a
per-object-type descriptor-row bit test (bit `0x4` at offset `+10` of the row indexed by the
occupant's own type-id byte, off the SAME table §9.2/§9.21 cite, `0x02cc9900`); any occupant
whose row has that bit set triggers a further zero-argument-visible call (`0x004e2350(1)`) —
read as notifying/waking that specific occupant class in response to the chase starting.

**Side effects / subsystem:** starts (or updates an in-progress) AI vehicle-chase behaviour
targeting a named entity, writing into the same per-vehicle behaviour sub-record
(offset `+0xc68`) `vehicle_suppress_npc_exit` (§4.5) also uses, and — when the vehicle is already
chasing — network-replicates the target-position update (opcode `0x42`). Also notifies any
occupant of a specific type category. Subsystem: vehicle/AI-driving behaviour. **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly for the two-path branch, the shared `+0xc68` sub-record identity, the
record-and-replicate opcode on the "already chasing" path, and the occupant-notify loop; OPEN —
the packed flag byte's individual bit meanings and the exact real-world class notified by
`0x004e2350`.]**

### 9.5 `vehicle_speed_override` (`0x00a63630`)

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory: arg 1 (string) — a vehicle reference, resolved through the SAME
dedicated vehicle-instance resolver §4.5 documents (`0x00a281e0`), with NO fallback to the
generic resolver or the coop/remote-position cache (unlike `vehicle_max_speed`, §9.6, and
`teleport_vehicle`, §9.11, below — a real, confirmed asymmetry, not an oversight in this
reading). Arg 2 (number) — a target speed, read unconditionally via the shared numeric extractor
with no presence/nil check at all.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** once the vehicle resolves, the speed value (arg 2) is converted from miles-per-hour
to the engine's internal metres-per-second convention by multiplying by a literal
double-precision constant read directly from `.rdata` at address `0x01119df8`, confirmed by a
direct memory read to be `0.44703999161720276` — the standard mph-to-m/s conversion factor
(`0.44704`), to within IEEE-754 double rounding. The converted value, together with a literal
`0` third argument, is handed to a dedicated setter (`0x00b29ca0`) operating on the SAME
per-vehicle sub-record at offset `+0xc68` §9.4/§4.5 already document: it first clamps the value
to a fixed cap of `1000.0` (both the comparison threshold at `0x012a2d90` and the clamp value at
`0x012a2f68` were read directly and confirmed to be exactly `1000.0`, one stored as a
double-precision constant and one as a single-precision float — i.e., a practical sanity cap far
above any real in-game speed rather than a meaningful gameplay limit), toggles one bit (`0x10`)
of a byte at sub-record offset `+0xa` from the literal third argument (always `0` at this call
site, so this bit is always cleared here), writes the clamped value into a float field at
sub-record offset `+0x9c`, and calls a follow-up recompute/refresh routine (`0x00b26880(1)`,
not traced further).

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets a forced speed override (in m/s, converted from an mph input)
on the same per-vehicle behaviour sub-record `vehicle_chase`/`vehicle_suppress_npc_exit` write.
No record-and-replicate call was found at this call depth — a real, confirmed absence, not an
assumption of uniform replication across this cluster (matching the same kind of asymmetry
§4.13 already noted for `inv_weapon_remove_temporary`/`continuous_spawn_stop`/
`continuous_spawn_start`). Subsystem: vehicle/handling. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the
argument shape, the mph-to-m/s conversion constant's literal value, the clamp thresholds, and
the sub-record field written; OPEN — the exact meaning of sub-record bit `0x10` at offset `+0xa`
and of the follow-up recompute call.]**

### 9.10 `vehicle_pathfind_check_done` (`0x00a66bf0`)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string — a vehicle reference, resolved via `0x00a281e0` (§4.5).

**Return:** 1 Lua value (a number) — `lua_pushnumber` then `return 1;`.

**Body:** once resolved, the vehicle's own occupant/part accessor (the SAME count/index pair
`vehicle_chase`, §9.4, uses — here called with a fixed index `0`, read as "does this vehicle
have an occupant/part in slot 0," most plausibly a driver check) must succeed before a dedicated
pathfind-status check (`0x006f6380`) is consulted. That check's own body was independently
decompiled: it reads a current pathfind-request context (`0x006f6260`) and returns a literal
`2` if none exists; otherwise it tests one bit (`0x1`) of a byte at the context's own offset
`+0x8`, returning `1` (and consuming/clearing the completion via a follow-up call,
`0x006f6040`) if set, or `0` if still pending. The resulting code (`0`=pending, `1`=done and
consumed, `2`=no active request) is pushed directly as the Lua return value. If the vehicle
fails to resolve, or has no occupant/part in slot `0`, a fallback constant read directly from
`.rdata` and confirmed to be exactly `2.0` (address `0x012a2e28`) is pushed instead — the SAME
numeric code the success path itself uses for "no active request," so both routes converge on
one consistent "nothing to check" answer.

**Side effects / subsystem:** none beyond the internal state-consuming call on a genuine
completion (a controlled, intentional side effect of "checking" a completed pathfind request).
Answers whether a vehicle's current pathfinding request has finished. Subsystem:
vehicle/AI-navigation. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full branch structure, the three
numeric codes, and the fallback constant's literal value; HIGH CONFIDENCE that the slot-`0`
occupant/part is specifically the driver, inferred from context rather than independently
confirmed.]**

### 9.15 `door_lock` (`0x00a487e0`)

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory: arg 1 (string) — a door name, resolved via `0x006434a0`
(§1.10/§9.12/§9.14); arg 2 (boolean) — a lock state, read unconditionally with no presence/nil
check, the same unconditional-read shape §9.5/§9.8's mandatory second arguments use.

**Return:** none (`return 0;`).

**Body:** once resolved and gated by the shared liveness check (`0x00853b10`), the boolean is
handed to a dedicated lock-apply routine (`0x008d6f10`). That routine is gated by its own
re-entrancy guard byte (confirmed `0` at rest, address `0x0250a508`): when clear, it opens the
record-and-replicate idiom (opcode `0x3a`, a further opcode not previously documented anywhere
in this cluster or §4.13) tagging the record with a literal `4`; regardless of that gate, it
unconditionally writes the boolean into bit `0x4` of the SAME byte field at door offset `+0x82`
`door_close`'s own setter (§9.14) clears bits `0x10`/`0x20` of — i.e., a door's lock state and
its open/close transient flags share one byte-sized bitfield. If door field `+0xc8` is non-zero
(the SAME "attached lock/mechanism" field §1.10/§9.14 already document), the lock state is
additionally forwarded to that attached object (`0x008d6ba0`), with the re-entrancy guard held
set for the duration of that forwarded call — preventing the attached object's own apply from
re-entering this same routine.

**Side effects / subsystem:** sets or clears bit `0x4` of a door's own `+0x82` flags byte (a
lock state, sharing that byte with `door_close`'s own transient bits), network-replicated
(opcode `0x3a`) when not already inside a re-entrant apply, and forwards the same state to any
attached lock/mechanism object. Subsystem: world/interactive-object (door) state. **[CONFIRMED —
disassembly for the full call chain, the shared `+0x82` byte identity with `door_close`, the
re-entrancy guard, and the `+0xc8` forward.]**

### 9.19 `inv_item_equip` (`0x00a50700`)

**Arguments:** 2 optional arguments, both individually guarded by the standard nil-test idiom
(neither is mandatory, a real departure from most named-object functions in this document):

**Body:** the target (arg 2) resolves through the object-by-name lookup
`audio_play_persona_line`/`explosion_create` also use (`0x00a281a0`, §2.5/§9.3) — a genuine,
confirmed departure from `inv_weapon_add_temporary`/`inv_weapon_remove_temporary`'s own target
argument, which instead resolves through the generic name/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver (`0x00a280c0`,
§4.10/§4.11/§4.13); this document did not independently decompile `0x00a281a0`'s own body to
confirm whether it special-cases `"#PLAYER1#"` internally the way `0x00a280c0` is confirmed to
special-case `"#PLAYER#"` (§4.13) — **[HIGH CONFIDENCE, not independently re-derived.]** If the
target resolves: when no item name was given (arg 1 absent), a large, shared active-item

confirmed here independently by matching the exact `0x7ec`-byte record stride in
`0x00b81220`'s own disassembled scan step) — but keyed here by the string directly rather than
by any pre-filtering flag bit. On a match, the found weapon-definition record is converted to a
small numeric category tag (`0x008dc690`, defaulting to `10` unless the record itself fails an
internal check, in which case it reads a category byte directly off the record's own offset
`+0x54`) and that category tag becomes the SAME routine's selector value instead of the literal

`0x00600720` itself opens a record-and-replicate block (opcode not attributable at this call
site — the begin call's own opcode argument is passed via a hidden register in both observed
call sites, so it could not be pinned to a specific literal this pass, **[OPEN]**) before
switching on the selector value; the two selector values this function's own two call sites
produce (`0` and the record's category byte, e.g. `10`) both land in that switch's `default`
arm, which forwards to a further weapon-select dispatch (`0x005fec20`) — the routine's own
`case`-labelled arms (values including `0xc`-`0x16`) were not reached from either of this
function's own call sites and were not independently traced. **[OPEN — `0x00600720`'s own deep
internals, including the switch's other named arms and the ultimate field(s) it mutates, were
not traced further; this is a large, generic apply routine shared across (at minimum)
`inv_item_equip` and, per §9.20 below, `inv_weapon_disable_all_slots`'s own "clear equipped
weapon" path, not something specific to equipping.]**

**Side effects / subsystem:** equips (selects as the character's active item) either a named
weapon (dispatched via its own definition record's category tag) or, when no name is given,
whatever the routine's own "default" selector value resolves to — for a resolved target
