### 21.11 `vehicle_exit_do` (0x00a67800)

**Arguments:** arg 1 (mandatory string) — occupant/character name; arg 2 (boolean, no nil-gate, default `false`) — "cancel pending entry instead of exiting"; arg 3 (optional boolean, standard nil-gated idiom, default `false`) — a flag folded into a packed status byte; arg 4 (optional boolean, standard nil-gated idiom, default `false`) — a second packed-byte flag; arg 5 (optional string, standard nil-gated idiom, default absent) — an exit-animation-state name, converted to an id via the already-documented shared named-animation-state table 0x004bf810 (§7.33/§14.1/etc.).

Pushes `true`, returns 1. If NOT currently seated but arg 2 (cancel) is set and a second predicate 0x009b91e0 (+0x16d4 ∈ {1,2}, "mid-entry") holds: calls 0x00af3e10(occupant, arg3, arg4) — the "cancel pending entry" path (see item 21.11's callee below) — and returns with **no `lua_push*` call at all** (0 values). Otherwise (unresolved, or neither seated nor mid-entry): pushes `false`, returns 1.

0x00af3cd0 (the struct-fill accessor) and 0x00af3e10 (the cancel-entry apply) are STRUCTURALLY PARALLEL and share real state: both resolve the occupant's cached vehicle-association identity pair (+0x16c0/+0x16c4, the SAME field §12.9/§12.20/item 21.24/item 21.26 all touch) through 0x004dcf00, and both consult the identical per-seat-transition-kind table (a registry keyed off a second shared singleton, 0x02845cb0, via 0x00b08380/0x00b08400 plus an identity-to-index lookup 0x00b08390, stride 0x100 per index, base +0x6a8) — 0x00af3e10 (the cancel path) explicitly handles transition-kind values 1/2/3; 0x00af3cd0's own tail (the main exit path) explicitly excludes kinds 1/2 and instead performs the "real" seat-exit apply (0x00b058f0, mode 0x14) for every OTHER kind — i.e. the two Lua-reachable branches of this one function are dispatching into complementary halves of the identical underlying per-character seat-transition-kind enum.

**Side effects / subsystem:** the primary character/vehicle exit-from-seat mechanism; network-replicated via the identity-key/cached-association path and three fixed timed-event posts. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full three-way branch, the per-path return-arity asymmetry, and the shared-table structural parallel between the two delegate functions; OPEN — the exact real-world identity of the 0x02845cb0 seat-transition registry and its per-kind-value meanings.]**

### 21.22 `move_to_do` (0x00a549e0)

**Arguments:** arg 1 (mandatory string) — the character/object to move; arg 2 (mandatory string) — a destination reference (name OR, depending on arg 6, ignored in favour of a global); arg 3 (mandatory number, rounded) — a move-mode/speed selector (values 1/2/3 branch later into a state code); arg 4 (boolean, no nil-gate, default `false`); arg 5 (boolean, no nil-gate, default `false`); arg 6 (boolean, no nil-gate, default `false`) — selects the destination-resolution mode; arg 7 (mandatory number, rounded, read unconditionally but only consumed in one branch) — a deadline/threshold, only meaningful when arg 6 is true.

**Return:** 1 number — either 0.0 (failure) or a positive per-character sequential "move action id."

**Body — the most complex function in this batch; described at the same level of detail this document's own §17.4/§17.12 use for comparably complex functions, not traced field-by-field.** If arg 6 (destination mode) is false: the destination name (arg 2) resolves through 0x00643a80 — the already-documented thin wrapper around the 5th resolver 0x005982e0 plus the liveness gate (§17.16) — and, on success, its position field at +0x40 (the same small-offset field family §7.15/§7.18/§17.13 document contextually) becomes the move anchor. If arg 6 is true instead: fetches a global "current" object via a zero-argument accessor 0x00643a80's sibling 0x00a53f60 (not independently decompiled, OPEN) and, only if arg 7 (the deadline) is less than that object's own +0x33c field, computes an anchor via 0x00930e90 — **confirmed via raw disassembly that this call passes arg 7's rounded value as an explicit argument, though the decompiled pseudocode renders it with zero arguments** — a hidden-argument correction. Arg 1 then resolves via the generic/`"#PLAYER#"` resolver 0x00a281a0; on success, calls 0x0095acb0(target, 1, 0.2, 0, 0) (the 0.2 recovered from a float constant load, the same MSVC float-literal-as-int-bit-pattern situation §7.4/§17.14 already establish a recovery method for) unconditionally, then — only if an anchor was actually resolved above — checks 0x00a3bae0(target, arg5); on success, packs arg 4/arg 5 into flag bits, and branches on the move-mode number (arg 3): mode 3 additionally probes two fixed lookup codes (0x32/0x34) via 0x004b46c0 on the target's own +0xd24→+0x10 sub-object (falling back to mode 1's own state code if neither resolves) before settling a final state code (1/2/3) written into a local flags byte. Calls 0x006f62b0(target,2,0) then 0x00993630(target, &state); on success, plays a randomized delay effect (0x00d9e180(2000,4000)) and, if a "current" object 0x00971cf0() resolves and arg 6 was false, applies a position-notify (0x0098f250) using that object's own +0x64/+0x68/+0x6c fields. Finally assigns and returns a new sequential id from a global counter at 0x0130cb94 (wrapping, skipping 0), stored into the target's own +0xc34 word field and returned (as a double) to Lua. Any early failure path instead writes the sentinel 0xffffffff into the target's own +0xc30 field and returns 0.0.

**Side effects / subsystem:** the core movement-action dispatcher (shared by this and presumably other `*_move_to*`-named Lua entries, cf. item 21.29 below); per-character move-state fields +0xc30/+0xc34, a positional-notify side effect, and a returned sequential action id usable by a companion "is finished"-style query (not covered this pass). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the overall argument extraction and branch structure, including the hidden-argument correction on 0x00930e90; HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred for the returned id's "action id for later polling" role, by analogy with `action_play_is_finished`'s own id-based pattern (§7.21); OPEN — 0x0095acb0/0x00a3bae0/0x006f62b0/0x00993630/0x0098f250's own bodies and the real-world meaning of move-mode values 1/2/3.]**

## 22. Ranks 351-450 tranche, part B — 30 gameplay-cluster functions (2026-09-30)

Second part of the fresh four-part "ranks 351-450" tranche's own gameplay side (Part B). Addresses resolved from `tools/scratchpad/lua_gameplay_1014_raw_pairs.txt`. Target-level raw disassembly was checked against pseudocode for every one of the 30 functions, plus depth-1 callees; a follow-up Ghidra pass additionally read the raw bytes of every constant address that came up OPEN, landing most as CONFIRMED numeric/string values rather than unresolved citations. None of the 30 resolved addresses land inside the registrar-builder's own body range (0x00a20840-0x00a25f7e), so the known function-pointer-array-entry-vs-real-entry-point trap does not apply to this batch.

### 22.1 `vehicle_pathfind_navmesh_do` (0x00a67e40)

**Arguments:** 6, all mandatory with no nil-gate at all (a real, confirmed asymmetry — every argument is read by straight sequential position, never guarded by a presence/nil check): 1 string (vehicle reference). 1 string (a secondary name — an occupant/group-member reference or a plain named destination). 3 booleans. 1 number (rounded via `lua_tonumber`+round, the shared 0x00dfe160/0x00ea2596 pair §4.1 already establishes).

**Return:** 1 number, via `lua_pushnumber` (0x00dfe3a0).

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through the vehicle-instance resolver 0x00a281e0 (§4.5 et al.). If it resolves, the already-established occupant/part-index accessor 0x00ab5070 (§9.4/§9.10) is queried at index 0, matching `vehicle_pathfind_check_done`'s (§9.10) own "does this vehicle have an occupant/part in slot 0, most plausibly the driver" reading — if that fails, or arg 2 is an empty string, falls straight to a "clear the pending request" tail. Otherwise arg 2 (non-empty) resolves through the group-name resolver 0x0062a1f0, liveness-gated (0x00853b10); on failure, falls back to the 5th per-kind resolver 0x005982e0 (§7.5 et al.) instead. If NEITHER resolves, the vehicle's own destination becomes its own current position/orientation, taken via the default-orientation helper 0x00da38e0 — a fixed 4-field orientation-quaternion copier already cited by role in §12.11's own text, here independently confirmed by full decompilation: it copies 4 consecutive dwords starting at its source's +4 verbatim, no computation. If arg 2 DID resolve to a live group, a general pathfinding/avoidance call, 0x00a3b860, is used instead, built from an up-to-25-entry table of the group's own nearby members/obstacles (its own +0x33c count field), the resolved member index, the rounded number argument, and the vehicle's own +0x40/+0x44/+0x48 position fields — the SAME "general pathfinding/avoidance call" `helicopter_fly_to_do` (§12.11) already documents using on ITS OWN destination-unresolved fallback path, now independently confirmed to also serve THIS caller. Either way, a request id is allocated via 0x006f62b0(vehicle, 2, 0) — a shared per-"kind"-tagged request-id allocator/dedup helper (walks a global linked list at 0x014f4be0 matching the target's own position pair plus a kind tag; on a match, cancels/reuses the existing entry via 0x006f6040; otherwise allocates a fresh 12-bit rolling id, 0x014f6b28, wraps at 0xfff, combined with a generation/layer byte from 0x008677f0, and registers it via 0x006f61b0) — kind 2 here, joining item 22.15's own kind-2 use of the SAME helper for the character-side "move-to" request (confirmed the two share one request-"kind" namespace). The assembled record is passed to 0x00b24fa0 — a rich record-and-replicate dispatcher (single-gate 0x008addb0; false branch → opens a network record, opcode 0x41, serializes the vehicle's identity via 0x0050f790, a packed flag byte from the 3 booleans, and the position; true branch → computes the vehicle's own +0xc68 AI-directive sub-record address (the SAME shared per-vehicle sub-record §4.5/§9.4/§17.1/§17.17/§18.21 already document) and delegates via 0x00b4f150, with a further branch on a code byte at that sub-record's own byte 7 value that either applies a scaled offset via 0x00b2e510/0x0051ddd0 or simply re-arms the single-gate). On success, an occupant-of-that-request-slot cleanup toggle 0x006f6360 runs if needed.

**Side effects/subsystem:** starts (or clears) a vehicle navmesh-pathfind request toward either a resolved group-member/named destination or, if none resolves, the vehicle's own current position — pushing the raw dispatch result as a status code. Shares its request-id "kind" (2) and its general-avoidance fallback call (0x00a3b860) with the already-documented `helicopter_fly_to_do` (§12.11), and its +0xc68 sub-record with the whole existing family (§4.5/§9.4/§17.1/§17.17/§18.21). Subsystem: vehicle AI/pathfinding. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full argument list, resolver chain, and the record/dispatch structure, cross-checked target-level raw disassembly against pseudocode with no discrepancy found; OPEN — 0x00b4f150's own code-byte-7 branch internals and 0x00b2e510's own body.]**

### 22.2 `vehicle_make_corpse` (0x00a62980)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (vehicle reference). 1 mandatory boolean, no nil-gate.

**Return:** none.

**Body:** arg 1 resolves via the vehicle-instance resolver 0x00a281e0. On success, delegates to 0x00a7fef0(vehicle, explodeFlag), fully decompiled: no-ops if the vehicle is already flagged a corpse (bit 0x1 of a status field at +0x16c8) or if a byte at +0xbd0 reads 0; otherwise clears bit 0x2 of that same +0x16c8 field, unlinks the vehicle from whichever doubly-linked list currently owns it (via a list-selector helper, 0x00ac2380, that returns the address of the owning list's own head-pointer slot) and re-links it at the HEAD of a separate GLOBAL circular "corpse" list anchored at a fixed global (0x027c2eb4) — a genuine vehicle-category-list migration, not previously catalogued in this document. A random respawn/despawn-style timer is drawn via 0x00dab660(45000, 75000) and stored at +0x1644; a further wait of 2000-3000 (presumably ms) runs via the SAME wait-helper `player_release_human_shield`'s own delegate 0x009ad6d0 (§18.9) already uses, 0x00d9e180. If the boolean argument is set, ALSO calls an unidentified 0x00aa3b90(vehicle), and — gated on a check 0x008837a0 (one half of the already-documented double-gate pair 0x008ae480/0x008837a0, §3.7 et al. — used here alone, NOT paired with its usual partner, a genuinely different reuse of just one half of that gate) — calls the SAME deadline setter 0x00d9e140(0) THREE MORE times in a row (each call's own hidden destination not independently traced).

**Side effects/subsystem:** converts a live vehicle into a "corpse" object — migrates it into a global corpse-list, clears/sets several status bits, arms a randomized despawn timer, and (only when the "explode"-style boolean is set, and only under the 0x008837a0 gate) fires the shared deadline-setter primitive several additional times, plausibly to schedule staggered wreck/debris sub-effects. **Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (character reference). 1 optional boolean, standard nil-gated idiom, default `false`. 1 optional string, standard nil-gated idiom, default an EMPTY string ("", confirmed by reading the literal bytes at its default address, 0x0129a0e3 — not a sentinel name, a genuine zero-length string) — a vehicle/occupant reference.

Otherwise, if the character's own state-code byte pair (+0x501/+0x504) matches `'&'`/0x12, or the "is entering/in-transition" predicate 0x009b91e0 (+0x16d4 in {1,2}) reports true, the result becomes 0.0 (a genuine "done" code). Finally, if the result differs from a THIRD status constant, 0.0 (byte-confirmed — i.e. "not already the success code"), AND the character's own class-descriptor row has bit 0x2 set at row offset +0xa, a fully-decompiled generic per-character "script-mode" setter, 0x009e3200, runs with mode 0 and no position payload — **a SECOND raw-disassembly-confirmed hidden-`this` finding: the call is rendered 0x009e3200(0,0) with two visible literal arguments, but raw disassembly proves the implicit `this` is the resolved character handle**, matching 0x009e3200's own independently-decompiled `this`/mode/position-struct signature (already established at the SAME address by item 22.15 below, and gated by the SAME single-gate 0x008addb0: false branch → opens a network record, opcode 0x46, two literal debug tags `"player"`+`"script_mode_params"`, serializing a per-object "actor" byte via 0x008add70 — ~~the same serializer `spawn_override_change_hood_alternate_spawning`'s cross-fn note, §16.30, already cites~~ the same per-object id serializer 0x008add70 (§14.29/§15.2) — committed via the genuine multi-target 0x0086f110; true branch → writes the mode into a field at +0x2888 and toggles bit 0x2 of a flags byte at +0x28ac).

**Side effects/subsystem:** polls whether a "vehicle enter" request has finished for a character, returning a 3-value status code (0.0=done, 1.0=still pending/remote, 2.0=nothing to check), and, on a genuine transition, resets a shared per-character "script-mode" record. Subsystem: vehicle-entry/AI state. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, including both hidden-argument findings and all three byte-confirmed status constants; OPEN — the exact real-world meaning of the +0x501/+0x504 state-code byte pair, and 0x009b95c0's own full internal role beyond its own already-decoded branch structure.]**

### 23.1 `pcr_set_voice` (0x00830830) — wrapper 0x008377d0

**Arguments:** arg1 mandatory string (a voice-request tag, compared byte-for-byte against the literal `"play_current"`); arg2 optional boolean, default **true** — a notably different default polarity from most optional booleans elsewhere in this document (which mostly default false).

**Body:** reads a cached "current voice id" off the current player's own +0x2088+0x10 sub-field (current-player accessor 0x009da4e0 called cleanly, zero args, twice — no anomaly here). If arg1 equals `"play_current"`, reuses that cached id; otherwise resolves arg1 through a newly-catalogued by-name voice resolver, 0x009ed7a0 (one clean explicit argument), yielding an index 0-6 or -1 (unmatched). On a match (0-6), a 7-entry switch reads two parallel literal-string tables directly (`Player_WM`/`UI_Voice_WM`, `Player_BM`/`UI_Voice_BM`, `Player_WMA`/`UI_Voice_WMA`, `Player_WF`/`UI_Voice_WF`, `Player_BF`/`UI_Voice_BF`, `Player_HF`/`UI_Voice_HF`, `Player_Z`/`UI_Voice_Z`) and resolves the `UI_Voice_*` name through 0x00462960.

**A genuine finding, confirmed by raw disassembly rather than trusting the decompiler's own symbol label:** immediately after the switch, the decompiled pseudocode renders a call as a thunk-collapsed call to `"Phone_Call"`'s resolver sharing the same label as 0x00462960 — but the actual instruction at that exact call site is `CALL 0x0070a2c0`, a **different real address** than the 0x00462960 the switch cases themselves call directly. The decompiler's thunk-collapsing display is misleading here: the `"Phone_Call"` cue name resolves through 0x0070a2c0, not through 0x00462960 like the per-voice `UI_Voice_*`/`Player_*` names do. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly; the two resolvers are genuinely different addresses despite the shared decompiler label.]**

The resolved `"Phone_Call"` handle is opened on the current player via 0x0070cb60. If arg2 is true: checks whether the player is already mid-conversation (0x0070a440); if so, plays the `UI_Voice_*` cue in "interrupt" mode (0x0070ced0 then 0x0070dd10), else queues it (0x0070dcf0) — and returns immediately, **without** updating the cached voice slot. If arg2 is false: calls a transition/compare helper (0x00bd8360) against the *previous* cached voice, then always writes the new index into the +0x2088+0x10 cache, resolves the `Player_*` name via 0x0070a2c0 — **CORRECTED, 2026-09-30, adversarial review (`ac239d89a67b9ebf8`): raw disassembly at this exact call site shows `CALL 0x0070a2c0`, the SAME address just identified above for the `"Phone_Call"` cue resolve, NOT 0x00462960 — the decompiler collapses both calls under the identical thunk label, and the original write-up caught the artifact once (for `"Phone_Call"`) but missed that it recurs here** — and calls 0x0094e120 (most plausibly "set the player's characterized voice profile").

**Side effects/subsystem:** player voice-line selection — picks and either immediately plays or persists the player's voice profile. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for full control flow and both resolver addresses; OPEN — 0x0094e120/0x0070dd10/0x0070dcf0/0x00bd8360's own internal bodies.]**

Otherwise, walks the SAME 63-slot PCR composite-item list (§16.16: 0x026533ac/b0, 0x0265430c, 0x026534b0) to find the item currently applied for that category, caching its stored tint. Then, for each of the resolved color-table's entries (struct stride 0x30 bytes, RGB floats at +0xc/+0x10/+0x14), opens an event record via the SAME "0x00e0xxxx" event-report family §19.5 already flags (**[Resolved: §26.23]**) (0x00e1a1b0→0x00e0ca80, distinct from the 0x00710cb0 record-and-replicate idiom) — **CORRECTED, 2026-09-30, adversarial review (`ac239d89a67b9ebf8`): the appended-value list below was imprecise and missed a real instance of this tranche's own "decompiler drops a real explicit argument" pattern.** The entry's own index and an optional secondary tag field are appended, then the raw RGB floats; the sRGB-byte-scaled integer versions (same scale constant 0x012a2d88, §16.7/§19.4) are **NOT themselves appended** — raw disassembly shows they exist only as registers feeding a byte-for-byte equality test against the current tint, whose single 0/1 RESULT is the only thing pushed (the append list's original wording made it read as if the scaled ints were a separate reported value). An unmentioned literal `0.0` double append (via the same event-builder family, a bare zero-value push) also sits between the RGB floats and that boolean. Finally, the report-finalize call (0x00e0ce00) is rendered by the decompiler with **zero visible arguments in all three of its branches**, but raw disassembly shows a real, explicit boolean argument pushed at every one — the SAME "decompiler drops a real explicit argument" artifact class this tranche already flags elsewhere (§23.7's literal-4 drop on 0x00821740; §26.13/§26.14/§26.18's drops on 0x00822040/0x00746770/0x00822000/0x007f3520) — present here too, just previously unflagged.

**Side effects/subsystem:** none (pure report/query via the event mechanism, not a Lua return push) — reports the list of available composite colors for a named category, flagging which one is currently active (via a computed boolean, not the raw scaled-int color values) for each entry. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the argument shape, the hidden-arg fix, the cross-family/shared-list reuse, and the corrected append-list/dropped-boolean-argument findings; OPEN — the exact per-entry secondary tag field and the full 0x00e0xxxx event-family semantics (shared OPEN item with §19.5).]**

This is now the THIRD confirmed-by-raw-disassembly sighting of this anomaly found this pass (alongside the two in item 23.5 above), each with a different argument shape (a bare literal, a struct pointer, and now a pointer+integer pair) — reported precisely as observed, not resolved; see the cross-function note below for a candidate explanation (identical-code-folding) offered cautiously.

If arg3 is true, additionally calls 0x006cede0((int)amount) (an extra notify, e.g. a "cash popup" trigger, matching the analogous optional-notify flag `game_award_respect`/§16.2 documents for a similar "show popup" gate).

### 23.23 Cross-function observations

1. **The hidden-register-argument convention (a pointer or "this" captured into a callee-saved register and forwarded with zero visible stack arguments) is confirmed at FIVE distinct call sites/callees this pass**, extending the tally already running in §19's own cross-function notes: 0x008307f0 (hidden-EDI, item 23.5 — independently reconfirming §19.14's own finding at the SAME callee, now TWO tranches deep), 0x00d9e7e0 (hidden-ECX, item 23.8), 0x00960160 (hidden-ECX, item 23.16), 0x005f0f90 (hidden-ECX, item 23.19), and two independent decompiler-dropped-THIRD-argument cases at 0x00821740 (items 23.3 and 23.7, both reconfirming §19.5's exact "literal id 4 on the PCU list" cross-family finding — a third and fourth tranche-internal confirmation of that specific cross-family read).
2. **The open 0x009da4e0-called-with-explicit-arguments anomaly (first flagged at §16.2, `game_award_respect`) is reconfirmed THREE further times this pass, each via raw disassembly (not merely decompiler-pseudocode inconsistency, which this document's own front-matter note already separately cautions about) and each with a genuinely different argument shape:** a bare literal integer and a local struct pointer (both inside `pcr_preview_anim`, item 23.5), and a buffer-pointer-plus-reason-code pair (inside `game_award_cash`, item 23.16). At every one of these sites the call has no stack-cleanup instruction of its own, while every "clean" zero-argument call to the same address elsewhere in this tranche also has no stack-cleanup — consistent with each other but NOT resolving why some sites push arguments at all. **Offered cautiously, not asserted:** one plausible explanation consistent with all observations is identical-code-folding (a linker/compiler optimization merging byte-identical function bodies compiled from originally-different source functions into one shared address) — this would explain a single address exhibiting genuinely different real argument counts at different call sites without any single call site being "wrong." This is a hypothesis for a future pass to test, not a resolved finding.
3. **0x0082e2d0's (the 24-category outfit re-sync routine, first internally resolved at §19.12) category-id argument semantics are now confirmed via a same-tranche cross-reference:** `pcr_restore_clothing` (item 23.2) calls it with the sentinel 0xffffffff ("resync everything"), while `pcr_apply_preset` (item 23.8) calls it twice with literal category ids 10/11 (a scoped resync) — directly confirming the argument is a genuine per-category selector with -1 as an "all categories" sentinel, reconciling §19.12's own more limited characterization.
4. **0x007ac460 (§19.7's "configure interface effect" primitive, 2 numeric parameters) is confirmed reused, not re-implemented, by `game_interface_effect_end` (item 23.14)** — "ending" an effect is just "configure with param1=0."
5. **The shared class-descriptor table (0x02cc9900), bit 0x80 at row offset +6 ("is a vehicle-kind object")**, already established at multiple sites across §17/§19.10 and elsewhere, is independently reconfirmed a further time in `garage_get_repair_cost` (item 23.10) — now spanning the garage subsystem as well as vcust/vehicle-paint and general gameplay call sites.
6. **The shared liveness gate 0x00853b10** is reconfirmed once more (item 23.10) as a fully generic, object-kind-agnostic check, consistent with this document's own standing characterization.
7. **A thunk/symbol-label caution, parallel to (but distinct from) the project's existing setter-vs-global caution:** `game_is_connected_to_service` (item 23.13) decompiles with a call labeled as a thunk, ~~but the real disassembled call target is a different address, 0x0086fde0 (the decompiler's displayed thunk entry point, 0x008703c0, is not the real target).~~ *(Corrected 2026-10-01, jobs `20261001T021703-team-a-pwgq`/`…-jxxz`, as in §23.13: the literal call goes to 0x0086fde0, which is a one-instruction jump stub to 0x008703c0, so 0x008703c0 IS the function that runs; the decompiler's label was right. The general lesson — check the literal CALL operand, and also follow one-instruction jump stubs to their target — still stands.)* Likewise `pcr_set_voice` (item 23.1) shows a call the decompiler labels identically to an earlier 0x00462960 call, but which raw disassembly proves is actually a call to 0x0070a2c0. **Lesson for future passes: a decompiler-displayed thunk/shared symbol name is not proof the call target is the address it appears to name — always check the literal disassembled `CALL` operand.**
8. **New, previously-uncatalogued fields/globals confirmed this pass:** the 63-slot PCR list's per-character "variant" byte array (0x026535b0, parallel to the already-tracked 0x026533ac); the tint-storage dword's (0x026534b0) own alpha byte (+3, i.e. 0x026534b3) used standalone as an intensity value; the garage "currently selected vehicle" 2-part identity pair (0x014a1d28/0x014a1d2c); the per-player garage-vehicle-list pointer field (+0x209c); the dialog self-consistency record array (0x02282d40, 0x184-byte stride, 4 slots, self-id at +0x12c) sitting inside the 0x02282d* region §16.9 already references generically; and the hair-color table's own name field (within the already-tracked 0x48-byte-stride table at 0x02300868).
9. No opcode/network-replicate 0x00710cb0-style record found in 14 of these 22 — only `game_award_cash` (item 23.16, opcode 0xa0) opens one directly; items 23.3/23.4 use the structurally DIFFERENT, still-not-fully-traced 0x00e0xxxx event-report family (§19.5's own open item, now touched by 3 more functions this pass without being further resolved; **[Resolved: §26.23]**).

## 24. Ranks 451-550 tranche, part A — 28 gameplay-cluster functions (2026-09-30)

First part of the fresh four-part "ranks 451-550" tranche's own gameplay side (Part A). Names resolved from `tools/scratchpad/lua_gameplay_1014_raw_pairs.txt` (13 of the 28 needed a force-disassemble+function-boundary fix; the other 15 were already real Ghidra-recognized functions). Every entry was decompiled AND raw-disassembled at its own call site (plus, for several, one level deeper) specifically to hunt hidden-`this`/hidden-argument drops — that check paid off repeatedly, with 8 confirmed hidden-argument findings this pass (see the cross-function observations below).

**Arguments:** none.

### 24.4 `wander_start` (0x00a68b50)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (character/follower name). 1 optional string (a second, position-source object name), standard nil-gated idiom, default absent. 1 optional number (a height/Z-offset value), standard nil-gated idiom, default the already-established constant -1.0 (byte-confirmed at 0x012a2d54, matching this document's own existing citation of that address).

**Two genuine, raw-disassembly-confirmed hidden-argument findings here:**
- If arg2 was NOT given: calls a helper, 0x004e7d10, to fetch a default orientation+position quad. The decompiled pseudocode shows this as a bare zero-argument call; raw disassembly proves the real call is thiscall with a hidden `this` = the resolved character handle + 0x2b0 — completely dropped from the pseudocode.
- If arg2 WAS given: resolves it via 0x005982e0 against the already-established shared multi-kind name-registry singleton (0x02442750 — confirmed again here as this resolver's `this`), with liveness gate 0x00853b10, then reads an 8+4-byte position/orientation chunk from the resolved object's own +0x40/+0x48 fields.

Finally, if the resolved character's own +0x501 byte is zero, calls 0x004e4130(character, 0).

**Side effects/subsystem:** starts a scripted "wander to a position" behavior on a resolved character, sourcing its target position/orientation either from a second named object (via the shared 0x02442750 registry) or from a per-character default (character+0x2b0), with a configurable height/Z value. Subsystem: character AI movement/wander. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the whole chain including both hidden-`this` findings on 0x004e7d10/0x004e3d90; OPEN — 0x004e3d90/0x00da38e0/0x004e4130's own full internals, and the exact real-world meaning of character+0x2f0/+0x501/+0x2b0.]**

### 24.5 `vehicle_spotlight_cancel` (0x00a65d70)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (character OR vehicle name). 1 optional boolean, standard nil-gated idiom — **but the extracted value is never stored or used anywhere: confirmed, via raw disassembly, a genuine dead read** (the `lua_toboolean`-shaped call executes and its result register is left untouched before the very next instruction overwrites it). This entry point silently accepts and ignores a second argument.

**Return:** none.

**Body:** resolves arg1 via the generic/`"#PLAYER#"` chain 0x00a281a0 as a CHARACTER first. If that succeeds: reads a cached 8-byte id-pair off the character — the "active" pair at +0x16d8/+0x16dc if either is non-zero, else a fallback pair at +0x16c0/+0x16c4 — and resolves THAT id-pair back into a handle via 0x00458230 (the already-established generic id-pair-to-handle resolver, previously cited for a different kind in this document) against kind-tag 0x031d152c, called thiscall against a **distinct singleton object, 0x024433a8** — structurally parallel to, but a DIFFERENT object than, the already-established shared multi-kind registry 0x02442750. Gates the result on: bit 0x10 of its own capability byte at +0x33 (a further confirmed bit of the same generic capability-flags byte already tracked at other offsets in this document), a kind-descriptor-table check (bit 0x80 at the row selected by its own +0x34 kind-id byte, into the shared 0x02cc9900 family), and liveness (0x00853b10). If arg1 does NOT resolve as a character, falls back to resolving it directly as a vehicle name via the dedicated vehicle resolver, 0x00a281e0.

Whichever path produced a handle: if its own +0xbd0 byte (the SAME "sub-components valid" gate this document already establishes for a vehicle's +0x1e00 sub-component array) is 1, AND its own +0xa44 sub-object pointer (a previously-uncited vehicle sub-object — presumably the vehicle's own spotlight state) is non-null: overwrites that sub-object's +0x10/+0x14 fields with two fixed globals, 0x011800e0/0x011800e4 — resetting the spotlight's aim/position to a neutral default.

**Side effects/subsystem:** cancels an active vehicle spotlight, reached either directly by vehicle name or indirectly via a character's cached vehicle-id-pair. Subsystem: vehicle spotlight. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the whole chain, including the dead-argument-read finding and the distinct 0x024433a8 singleton; OPEN — the +0xa44 sub-object's own full layout and the 0x011800e0/0x011800e4 globals' real-world meaning beyond "neutral default."]**

### 24.29 Cross-function observations

1. **Eight confirmed raw-disassembly-only hidden-argument findings this pass — the highest density yet for a single tranche of this size** — all cases where the decompiled pseudocode showed FEWER arguments than the real call actually passes: item 24.4 (`wander_start`, TWICE: 0x004e7d10 and 0x004e3d90, both hidden `this` = character+0x2b0), item 24.6 (`vehicle_set_explosion_damage_multiplier`, 0x00a7dd60, hidden `this` = vehicle), item 24.10 (`vehicle_enable_physics`, a vtable+0x78 virtual call, hidden `this` = vehicle), item 24.16 (`set_suppress_synced_melee_attacks_flag`, 0x00948410, hidden `this` = character), item 24.19 (`player_super_powered`, 0x0094a240, hidden `this` = character), item 24.24 (`on_hud_screen_exit`, TWICE: 0x007b4ad0 and 0x00a56df0), item 24.26 (`npc_weapon_spread`, 0x009d7110, hidden `this` = character), item 24.27 (`npc_unholster_best_weapon`, 0x00600720, hidden `this` = character+0x1b78). **Two of these (items 24.16 and 24.19) are especially significant corrections**: read from decompiled pseudocode alone, both looked like a resolved character being used purely as an EXISTENCE GATE before a bare global-boolean write — raw disassembly proves both are actually genuine PER-CHARACTER setters (via the "human_force_flags" double-gate family), a materially different and more specific finding than the pseudocode-only read would support.
2. **A NINTH finding of the opposite kind — the decompiler dropping a real EXPLICIT argument, not a `this` pointer** (item 24.22, `on_random_obj_killed_do`'s 0x00a3b840): a thin validate-then-tail-JUMP wrapper renders as a zero-argument call in pseudocode, when the real (tail-jumped) call genuinely passes the original string argument in its normal stack slot. Confirms this document's standing practice of checking raw disassembly at call sites catches BOTH directions of this artifact class, not just missing-`this` cases.
3. **One confirmed decompiler FALSE POSITIVE, the mirror finding**: item 24.6's own 0x008ae480 call renders in pseudocode with an apparent 4th argument (a stack-cookie local); raw disassembly confirms the real call passes exactly the standard 3 arguments — the "4th argument" is pure noise, matching this document's own already-documented caution about this exact artifact class (and now confirmed present in at least 3 of the double-gate-idiom delegates decompiled this pass: 0x00a7dd60, 0x00948410, 0x0094a240, all sharing the identical artifact).
4. **Two new confirmed sub-record bases for the already-established named-hook-slot-array family** (0x005e4520/0x00a1fcc0/0x00a29920, wrapped by 0x005e4660 and, newly confirmed this pass, by a SIBLING wrapper 0x00a56df0 too): character **+0xf8** (items 24.21 and 24.25, independently confirmed twice — slots 0x11 and 0x19 respectively) and HUD-screen-object **+0x8** (item 24.24, slot 0). This now gives the family at least 5 distinct sub-record bases across this document's running census (+0x1f00, ~~+0xc68,~~ +0xc0, global slots, and now +0xf8 and +0x8; +0xc68 is the vehicle AI-directive sub-record, not a hook base — also known: character +0x68/+0x6c, mover +0x20/+0x24, vehicle +0x30/+0x34 §18.30, door +0x90 §21.19).
5. **A newly-confirmed optional out-parameter on the generic resolver 0x00a280c0**: item 24.21 (`on_taunt`) is the first sighting in this document of this resolver being called with a real (non-null) 2nd argument rather than the literal 0 every other call site in this tranche uses — the resolver writes a genuine out-flag through it, which the caller then branches on to choose between two different hook bases. The out-flag's exact real-world meaning is OPEN.
6. **Two new, distinctly-addressed registry/kind singletons, structurally parallel to but NOT the same object as the already-established shared multi-kind name registry 0x02442750**: 0x024433a8 (item 24.5, paired with the generic id-pair resolver 0x00458230 and kind-tag 0x031d152c) and 0x012fced8 (item 24.24, a dedicated HUD-screen-name registry, paired with resolver 0x007b4ad0). Flagging explicitly per this document's own standing caution against assuming two similar-shaped resolver singletons are the same object without checking.

## 25. Ranks 451-550 tranche, part B — 28 gameplay-cluster functions (2026-09-30)

Second part of the fresh four-part "ranks 451-550" tranche's own gameplay side (Part B). Every function below opens with the document's already-established shared `lua_CFunction` prologue (`lua_gettop` 0x00dfde50, `lua_tolstring` 0x00dfe210, `lua_toboolean` 0x00dfe1e0, `lua_type` 0x00dfe040, `lua_tonumber`+round pair 0x00dfe160/0x00ea2596 per §4.1, `lua_pushnumber` 0x00dfe3a0, `lua_pushstring` 0x00dfe420, `lua_pushnil` 0x00dfe380, general push 0x00dfe590) — cited, not re-described per item.

### 25.1 `notoriety_spawn_group_set_destination` (0x00a561f0)

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings. Arg 1 — a notoriety spawn-GROUP name. Arg 2 — a destination reference name.

**Return:** none.

**Body:** arg 1 resolves through the SAME 24-entry case-insensitive notoriety-group name table already established at §6.2/§6.10/§13.2/§21.3 (0x008ed350), producing the group record. Arg 2 resolves through the 5th/third-tier per-kind resolver already established at §12.10 et al. (0x005982e0) — **raw-disassembly-confirmed here too to be invoked as a method on the fixed literal singleton 0x02442750** (a further, new sighting — see cross-function observations). Both must pass the shared liveness check (0x00853b10, §1.1). On success: a 16-byte block is copied from 4 bytes past the DESTINATION object's own +0x40 field (i.e. +0x44..+0x50) into a local buffer via the already-established fixed default-orientation/position copier 0x00da38e0 (§22.1: "copies 4 consecutive dwords starting at its source's own +4 offset, verbatim"). That buffer is then written onto the GROUP record via a setter not previously catalogued in this document, 0x008edfb0 — **raw-disassembly-confirmed hidden `this` in BOTH this function and its sibling below: the decompiled pseudocode shows a 2-visible-argument call, but the real call is `0x008edfb0(this = the group record, enable = 1, buffer)`.**

**Side effects/subsystem:** sets a named notoriety spawn-group's destination point to a named destination object's position, by copying the destination's own position/orientation block onto the group record. Subsystem: notoriety/gang spawn AI. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full resolve chain and the corrected hidden-`this`; newly-identified primitive 0x008edfb0 (thiscall: this=group record, enable flag, source buffer) — OPEN, its own internal field-offset writes were not further decompiled past the call shape.]**

### 25.6 `mesh_mover_update_control` (0x00a53100)

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (mover reference). 1 mandatory string (a named control parameter). 1 mandatory value whose Lua TYPE selects the write path: a boolean, OR a number with 1 further optional boolean (a "truncate to integer" mode selector).

**Return:** none.

**Body:** arg 1 resolves via the door/4th-kind resolver already established at §1.10 (0x006434a0) — **raw-disassembly-confirmed here to ALSO be invoked as a method on the fixed singleton 0x02442750** (a further new sighting). Liveness-gated (0x00853b10), then the SAME field §1.10 already reads as "this door has an attached lock" (offset +0xc8, there non-zero = locked) must be ZERO here, and a second field at +0xc4 (a "mover-control sub-record" pointer) must be non-null — consistent with movers and doors sharing the same underlying handle/resolver but being mutually-exclusive variants keyed by which of +0xc4/+0xc8 is populated. If arg 3's real Lua type is boolean: reads it and dispatches to 0x0064a1f0. If arg 3's type is a number: reads it as a float and, ONLY if a 4th argument is present AND (per its own type/boolean gates) true, truncates the float to an integer-valued float and dispatches to 0x008cb380; otherwise (4th arg absent or false) dispatches the untruncated float to 0x008cb400. **Raw disassembly confirms a hidden `this` at ALL THREE of these dispatch calls, dropped entirely from the decompiled pseudocode** (which shows e.g. a 2-visible-argument call): the real `this` in every case is the mover-control sub-record at the resolved handle's own +0xc4, with the control-name string and a pointer to the boolean/float value as the two genuine explicit arguments.

**Side effects/subsystem:** writes a named control parameter (boolean- or float-valued, with an integer-truncation mode for the float case) onto a resolved mesh mover's own control sub-record. Subsystem: mesh-mover/physics scripting. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full type-dispatch structure and all three corrected hidden-`this` sites, plus the new singleton-`this` sighting on 0x006434a0; OPEN — 0x0064a1f0/0x008cb380/0x008cb400's own internal field writes.]**

### 25.14 `helicopter_go_to_set_target` (0x00a4fc00)

**Arguments:** 2 mandatory strings: arg 1 — a helicopter/vehicle reference; arg 2 — a target reference, resolved through a 4-tier fallback chain (see body).

**Return:** none.

**Body:** arg 1 resolves via the vehicle-instance resolver (0x00a281e0, §4.5); failure is an immediate no-op return. Arg 2 is tried, in order: (1) the plain generic resolver 0x00a280c0 (no singleton-`this`) — if THIS succeeds, its result is used directly, skipping the rest of the chain entirely; (2) failing that, 0x00a26010/0x00a26110 — the established `"#FOLLOWER#"`-sentinel-adjacent waypoint/index table (§3's front matter) — if it yields a positive index, the corresponding entry is used directly; (3) failing that, the plain character resolver 0x005e4dd0; (4) failing that, the vehicle resolver 0x0062a190. **Both (3) and (4) are raw-disassembly-confirmed to be invoked as methods on the fixed singleton 0x02442750** (further new sightings — see cross-function observations). Whichever of (3)/(4) succeeds and passes the liveness check (0x00853b10) has its own vtable +0x70 queried (this-only, zero explicit arguments — matches the document's established recurring vtable-+0x70 shape, e.g. §12.13/§15.22). The final target value (from whichever tier resolved) is passed with the helicopter handle to 0x00b38280.

**Side effects/subsystem:** sets a helicopter's navigation target, accepting a named object, a `"#FOLLOWER#"`-table waypoint index, a character, or a vehicle as the target reference, tried in that priority order. Subsystem: vehicle AI/pathfinding (helicopter). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the full 4-tier fallback structure and the two new singleton-`this` sightings; OPEN — 0x00a26010/0x00a26110/0x00b38280's own internal bodies.]**

Directly confirms and closes the read-side of §7.17's own write, by field offset (+0x1da8→+0x174) and by sharing the name-lookup table. ### 25.29 Cross-function observations

1. **Major finding: the fixed literal singleton object 0x02442750 is confirmed, by raw disassembly in THIS tranche alone, to serve as the implicit `this` for at least SEVEN further distinct per-kind by-name resolver entry points, on top of the handful already on record** (0x005982e0 per §12.10/§22.4/§22.5/§22.17; 0x00734e90 per §22.4; 0x00739690 per §17.24). The new confirmed members this pass: 0x00729080 (item/pickup kind, §20.12 — §25.7/`item_hide`), 0x005f4c30 ("activity" kind, §6.20 — §25.4/`mission_set_next_mission`), 0x006434a0 (door/4th-kind, §1.10 — §25.6/`mesh_mover_update_control`), 0x005e4dd0 (plain character resolver — §25.14/`helicopter_go_to_set_target` AND §25.28/`character_is_released`, independently at two different call sites), 0x0062a190 (vehicle resolver — §25.14/`helicopter_go_to_set_target`), 0x005eab60 ("guardian angel"/script-group kind, §6.6/§6.8 — §25.16/`group_destroy_do`), and 0x00a3de90 (unidentified kind, §15.22 — §25.22/`debris_flow_add_avoid_object`). Every one of these was previously documented ONLY via its own class-descriptor-table bit/offset test on 0x02cc9900, with no prior confirmation that it is ALSO a method on this one shared object (correction: 0x005e4dd0 §21.2, 0x0062a190/0x006434a0 §21.31, 0x005eab60 §22.18 and 0x00a3de90 §22.21 were already confirmed; only 0x00729080 and 0x005f4c30 are new here). This strongly extends (well past "tentative") the existing "one shared, kind-spanning name→handle registry, not N independent per-kind resolvers" hypothesis already flagged as open at §9.1/§12.10/§17.24/§22.4/§22.5/§22.17 — it is now confirmed across at least 10 distinct resolver function addresses covering effect names, notoriety groups, items, activities, doors/movers, characters, vehicles, script-groups, and at least one more unidentified kind. By contrast, the "generic/#PLAYER#"-family resolvers (0x00a280c0, 0x00a28150, 0x00a281a0, 0x00a281e0, 0x00a26010) checked in this same tranche continue to show NO singleton-`this` call shape (plain explicit-argument calls throughout) — a real, consistent structural split between the two resolver families, not an inconsistency.
2. **The per-character "AI data" sub-object at handle offset +0x2b0** (established at §15.4/§21.21) is now confirmed used by THREE functions in this tranche alone: `human_set_always_sprint` (§25.10), `character_set_can_take_human_shield` (§25.26), and cited in §25.9's own write-up by contrast (`human_set_force_holster` writes the character handle directly, NOT +0x2b0 — a real, checked structural difference between two superficially-similar "set a flag on the resolved character" setters).
3. **A shared, previously-uncatalogued setter, 0x008edfb0** (`this` = a resolved notoriety spawn-group record, explicit args = an enable flag and a source buffer pointer) is confirmed as the exact set/clear pair for `notoriety_spawn_group_set_destination`/`notoriety_spawn_group_clear_destination` (§25.1/§25.2) — the same enable-flag-plus-payload-buffer shape as other set/clear pairs already documented elsewhere in this project, though not claimed to be the SAME primitive as any of those.
4. **Two further, real hidden-`this` corrections beyond the resolver family** were found this pass, each independently confirmed by raw disassembly against a decompiled pseudocode rendering that showed a bare free-function call: `human_set_force_holster`'s call → really `this`=character, flag (§25.9); `group_destroy_do`'s call → really `this`=group record, 0, 0 (§25.16). Both match this document's own standing caution that the decompiler silently drops implicit `this` pointers, and both were only caught by pulling raw disassembly at the call site.
5. **A genuine, confirmed EXCEPTION to this tranche's own hidden-`this` pattern:** `character_set_combat_ready`'s (§25.25) local-apply call 0x00943960(character, flag, number) is a real, plain 3-explicit-argument call — the character IS a genuine visible stack argument here, not a hidden `this` — demonstrating that not every "object, then value(s)" call shape in this codebase is a disguised thiscall; each site still needs its own raw-disassembly check rather than a blanket assumption either way.
6. **`check_script_animation_state` (§25.24) is confirmed to be the direct read-side counterpart of the already-published `set_script_animation_state` (§7.17)**, sharing the same character sub-object (+0x1da8), the exact same consumed/written field on it (+0x174), and the same name→state-id lookup table (0x004bf810, §7.11/§3.15) — a clean, fully closed read/write pair.
7. **A decompiler-rendering artifact, distinct from the hidden-`this` family, was found twice in this tranche:** `hud_inventory_disable` (§25.12) and `character_set_combat_ready` (§25.25) both have their own opening `lua_gettop` call rendered by the decompiler with a spurious extra argument (an adjacent stack-cookie/SEH-frame local coincidentally occupying a nearby slot) — raw disassembly in both cases confirms only the real, single `L` argument is actually pushed. Flagged so a future pass doesn't mistake this for a real second parameter to `lua_gettop`.
8. **A real, confirmed exception to the usual "resolve, then liveness-check" pattern:** `continuous_explosion_follow_target_add` (§25.23) resolves its one argument and proceeds on a bare non-null check alone, with NO call to the shared liveness check 0x00853b10 anywhere in its body — unlike every other resolver-consuming function in this tranche.
9. **An unresolved, explicitly-flagged (not silently patched) tension:** `force_ai_mode_check_done`'s (§25.19) own use of the shared queue-lookup helper 0x006f63c0 and field +0x4aa treats a non-null lookup result as "request done, clear the tag," which reads as the opposite polarity from how §7.28's own text describes the same helper/field pair ("absence means complete"). Both individual readings are accurate to their own respective decompiled bodies; the discrepancy was not reconciled this pass since it requires decompiling 0x006f63c0 itself.
10. **Two genuine "takes no real Lua arguments" functions** were confirmed this pass, both by raw disassembly showing the `lua_gettop` result is read but never consumed downstream: `message_remove_all` (§25.5) and `debris_flow_create` (§25.21).

Third part of the fresh four-part "ranks 451-550" tranche's own UI side (Part C). 17 of the 22 names are in the 311-entry UI-wrapper cluster (0x008430f0); the other 5 (`game_audio_play`, `game_use_radial_menu_item`, `game_set_equipped_grenade`, `game_vkeyboard_input`, `game_is_syslink`) are in the 113-entry loop registrar (0x00845aa0). Every function below opens with the same shared `lua_CFunction` prologue idiom already established in this document's own front matter (`lua_gettop`/`lua_type`/`lua_toboolean`/`lua_tolstring`/`lua_tonumber`+round-cast/`lua_pushboolean`/`lua_pushnumber`/`lua_pushstring`) — cited by reference, not re-derived.

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory number (an eye-color table index), no gate. **Return:** none.

**Body:** fetches the current player (0x009da4e0, zero args — matches its established shape, §3/§11 front matter) and calls the already-documented set/clear-tint primitive (0x009f9f60, §16.7/§19.4/§19.15) with 4 arguments: the player's +0x2088+0x14 per-character composite-item-list base (the exact same 63-slot PCR list §16.16/§19.16 document), the rounded eye-color index, a pointer to a 4-byte local initialized to the sentinel -1, and a literal -1. All 4 arguments were confirmed genuinely explicit via raw disassembly — no hidden-argument surprise here, a clean match to the decompiled pseudocode.

### 26.2 `pcr_strip_clothing` (0x00830750) — same wrapper

**Arguments:** none. **Return:** none.

**Body:** calls the current-player accessor **twice, each time with genuine, disassembly-confirmed explicit literal arguments — 0x009da4e0(1), then 0x009da4e0(5, 0)** — a real, confirmed deviation from its otherwise-universal zero-argument shape (already flagged as an open cross-check item at §16.2/§16.16 for a different function, `game_award_respect`, called there with 1 argument; this is now a second and third confirmed instance of the SAME anomaly, with two different literal argument shapes, inside one tiny function).

**A SECOND, previously-unflagged instance of the stale-stack-slot-reuse mechanism documented below for the 0x00821630 call, CORRECTED 2026-09-30 per adversarial review (`ac239d89a67b9ebf8`):** after the first call, the player's +0x2088 sub-object pointer is passed to a new primitive, 0x009f0cf0 — the original write-up described this as "1 explicit argument, clean," but raw disassembly shows the caller's own `ADD ESP,0x8` (cleaning both the `PUSH 0x1` from the FIRST current-player call and the `PUSH ECX`/+0x2088-pointer push for this one) is deferred until AFTER 0x009f0cf0 returns — so the literal `1` pushed for the earlier call is still sitting on the stack, unpopped, exactly where 0x009f0cf0's own decompiled signature (a pointer parameter followed by a byte parameter) reads its 2nd parameter from. The real call is **0x009f0cf0(player+0x2088, 1)**, not a 1-argument call. This matters: that 2nd parameter gates a hard branch inside 0x009f0cf0 — a value of `0` zeroes a 24-entry table; nonzero (the real case here) instead SETS that table to 1, zeroes several other unrelated fields, and walks a linked list flagging every entry whose category isn't in an 8-value exclusion set — materially different from, arguably the near-opposite of, "clear/reset." Given the function's own name (`pcr_strip_clothing`), "mark everything as needing reapply/dirty" fits at least as well as "clear" — the exact role is left OPEN rather than asserted, per the review's own recommendation.

**A genuine, confirmed hidden/dropped-argument case, found by careful stack accounting on the raw disassembly (a NEW variant of this document's "decompiler drops a real argument" family, distinct from the register-forwarding convention already on record):** after the second 0x009da4e0(5, 0) call, the decompiled pseudocode shows the already-documented reset/notify primitive (0x00821630, §16.7 — confirmed this pass to have the real signature `(context, categoryId, flags)`, walking a per-character list keyed by the context's own +0x14 sub-index and calling a further match-handler, 0x00821590, for each row whose own +0x2c field equals the category id) called with only 1 explicit argument (the player's +0x2088 pointer). Raw disassembly confirms only 1 real `PUSH` immediately precedes this call — but the compiler had **deferred/combined the stack cleanup of the preceding 0x009da4e0(5, 0) call's own 2 pushed arguments until after this call** (a single `ADD ESP,0xc` cleans all 3 pushes at once), so the two literal values 5 and 0 that were pushed for the EARLIER call are still sitting on the stack, unpopped, exactly where 0x00821630's own 2nd/3rd parameters read from. Working through the exact stack offsets confirms the real, full call is **0x00821630(playerSubObject, 5, 0)** — categoryId 5 (in the same 34-entry category table §16.7 documents; the exact name at index 5 was not independently re-read this pass to avoid guessing the table's internal left/right ordering — OPEN), flags 0. This is a genuine instance of the exact hidden-argument check this tranche's brief called out as highest-value, just via stack-slot reuse rather than a register — and, per the adversarial review, is now the SECOND confirmed instance of this exact stale-stack-slot-reuse mechanism within this one function, not a one-off.

**Side effects/subsystem:** character customization — calls 0x009f0cf0(player+0x2088, 1) (role OPEN, plausibly "mark composite items dirty/needing reapply" rather than "clear," see above) and clears one specific category (id 5) from the shared per-character list via the established reset/notify primitive. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, full body, both stale-stack-slot-reuse instances confirmed by instruction-level stack accounting; OPEN — category id 5's exact name, and 0x009f0cf0's own full body beyond the confirmed 2nd-parameter branch structure.]**

### 26.7 `store_weapon_purchase_weapon` (0x008172d0) — 311-entry UI-wrapper table, wrapper 0x00817570 (the same wrapper §16.15 documents for `store_weapon_hide_weapon`), 661-byte body, the largest/most branchy of this batch — summarized per this document's own house style

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory string (weapon category), 1 mandatory number (weapon index within that category, round-cast), 1 mandatory boolean, 1 mandatory number consumed as a genuine **float — the round-cast helper is deliberately NOT called for this 4th argument**, a real, disassembly-confirmed idiom variant (numeric arguments in this cluster don't always get rounded to int; this one is kept as a native double throughout). **Return:** none.

**Body:** the category string is matched case-insensitively (`_stricmp`) against a real, directly-read 9-entry table at 0x01300a78: `unarmed`, `melee`, `pistol`, `smg`, `shotgun`, `rifle`, `explosive`, `special`, `thrown` (unmatched → silent no-op return). The category index combines with the weapon-within-category number to index two parallel global arrays (a flag/state array at 0x022ce048, a weapon-record-pointer array at 0x022ce630, stride 0x14 dwords = 80 bytes per category). If the boolean argument is true, takes a short "preview/toggle only" path via a new primitive (0x00816f00, signature `(target, mode, floatValue)`) on the flag-array entry and returns. Otherwise (the real purchase path): checks an ownership predicate (0x005ee650) on the resolved weapon record; if not yet owned, calls a "grant/give this weapon" primitive (0x005ee630, confirmed via raw disassembly to take exactly 1 explicit argument, the weapon record) — the actual purchase effect; if already owned, instead runs an achievement/completion-tracking pass (counts owned weapons per category via 0x00b76950/0x00b768a0 against a per-category cap at +0x28, and — confirmed via raw disassembly — posts a literal-opcode completion event, 0x00710910(0x2b) (43), when a full 8-category sweep finds every category maxed out — most plausibly an "owns every weapon in every category" achievement).

**Side effects/subsystem:** in-game weapon store — purchases (grants) a specific weapon identified by (category, index), with a preview-only fast path and a floating cost/scale value forwarded to the preview primitive; drives an achievement-completion check when the weapon was already owned. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the category table, the ownership-branch structure, the 1-argument grant call, and the literal achievement opcode; HIGH CONFIDENCE for 0x00816f00's exact role; OPEN — 0x005ee650/0x00816f00's own full internals.]**

### 26.18 `game_use_radial_menu_item` (0x00843e80) — same registrar

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory number (a radial-menu slot index). **Return:** 1 number (never a plain boolean — always returns a double, either a real 0.0/1.0 status or a hardcoded 1.0).

**A genuine, disassembly-confirmed dropped-argument case:** for index values in [0,7], the function calls a general quick-item dispatcher, 0x007f3520, to get the real result; the decompiled pseudocode shows this call with **zero** arguments, but raw disassembly confirms a real, explicit `PUSH` of the index value immediately precedes it — the decompiler simply omitted a real argument from its own rendering (the same class of finding as §26.13/§26.14, now confirmed a third time in this tranche, at a completely different address range).

**Body (now correctly understood via the callee's own decompiled body):** 0x007f3520 is not a simple "is the menu open" predicate — it's a genuine **quick-item-use dispatcher**: for its own argument value 8-11 it delegates to the grenade-equip primitive (0x005fe530, see §26.19) with (value-8); for 0 and 1-7 it resolves the real "currently equipped quick item" through a further chain (0x005fec20/0x00b816d0/0x009c0090/0x005ff7a0) and ultimately performs the actual "use this quick-item slot" action via a large generic dispatcher, 0x00600720, returning success/failure. For the special index 12 (reachable directly, bypassing 0x007f3520 entirely), `game_use_radial_menu_item` fetches the current player and calls 0x00600720 itself directly, via an implicit thiscall `this` = player+0x1b78 (**a genuine hidden-`this`-pointer argument the decompiled pseudocode dropped completely** — confirmed via raw disassembly: `LEA ECX,[player+0x1b78]` immediately precedes the call, and 0x00600720's own independently-decompiled signature is `__thiscall`) with literal arguments (0xc, 1, 0, 0), then always pushes 1.0. **Any OTHER out-of-range index (negative, 8-11 reached through THIS entry point specifically, or 13+) silently falls through to the same "always push 1.0" tail with no real dispatch at all** — a genuine, confirmed no-op-but-reports-success gap, worth flagging since it means indices 8-11 (which 0x007f3520 itself knows how to handle, per its own grenade-delegation branch) can never actually be reached as "8-11" through this specific entry point's own gating logic.

**Side effects/subsystem:** performs the quick/radial-menu item-use action for slots 0-7 (via the shared dispatcher) or the special slot 12 (via a direct call on the SAME player+0x1b78 sub-object §26.19 also uses), always reporting a double rather than a plain 0/1 boolean. Quick-item / radial-menu UI. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly for the dropped argument, the hidden-`this` argument, and the full branch structure; HIGH CONFIDENCE for slot 12's specific real-world identity (OPEN); the always-1.0 fallback for invalid/8-11 indices is CONFIRMED.]**

### 26.19 `game_set_equipped_grenade` (0x00843b90) — same registrar

**Arguments:** 1 mandatory number (a grenade-type id). **Return:** 1 boolean.

**A genuine, confirmed hidden-`this`-pointer-and-register-argument case — exactly the pattern this tranche's brief flagged as highest-value, found precisely because the decompiled pseudocode made BOTH the argument and the current-player call look completely unused.** The decompiled body shows the rounded argument value computed and never assigned to anything, the current-player accessor called with its result apparently discarded, and a bare zero-visible-argument call. Raw disassembly proves all three are real, deliberate, and connected: the rounded argument is held in the callee-saved EDI register across the current-player call; the current-player accessor's return (in EAX) is used to compute ECX = player + 0x1b78 — **the SAME sub-object offset §26.18's own slot-12 special case uses** — loaded as the implicit `this` for a thiscall; and EDI - 8 is pushed as the one real stack argument. The real call is **0x005fe530(player+0x1b78, gradeId - 8)** — a genuine, meaningful equip-grenade-type setter (bounds-checked against a 4-slot table inside 0x005fe530's own body, matching the -8 offset: this binding's own grenade-type ids run 8-11, mapping to internal slots 0-3), not a dead/no-op stub as the raw pseudocode's apparent unused-value pattern would otherwise suggest.

**Side effects/subsystem:** equips a specific grenade type (ids 8-11 → internal slots 0-3) on the player's quick-item sub-object at +0x1b78, returning whether the equip succeeded. Inventory/quick-item UI. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, full instruction-level trace of the hidden `this` and the real stack argument — the single clearest hidden-argument catch in this tranche.]**

### 26.23 Cross-function observations

- **Major new shared-primitive resolution: the 0x00e0xxxx "builder/named-callback" family, previously left OPEN at §19.5 as "a distinct, un-traced mechanism, most plausibly a generic UI/event-reporting builder rather than a network record."** This pass fully decompiled 8 of its members (0x00e1a1b0, 0x00e0ca80, 0x00e0ce40, 0x00e0ce60, 0x00e0cfb0, 0x00e0ce00, 0x00e0cd00, 0x00e0ce20) and can now characterize it precisely: 0x00e1a1b0 is a zero-real-argument accessor always returning ~~one fixed global "value-list builder" singleton object~~ **[corrected 2026-10-01, job `20261001T020200-team-a-nzxf`: the interface (UI) Lua state at 0x02a45450, as `spec-lua-bindings.md` §14.1 says; the builder object is what 0x00e0ca80 returns. This settles the conflict that spec flags between §26.23 and §14.1]**; 0x00e0ca80(targetNameString, builderHandle) "opens"/resolves a **named Lua-side callback target** (its own real signature takes 2 more arguments that, at every observed call site in this tranche, are confirmed via disassembly to be leftover 0/0 values from the immediately-preceding builder-accessor call, not garbage); and the remaining members are thin wrappers around the ALREADY-established `lua_push*` primitives (`lua_pushnumber` for both the double- and float-taking variants, an unnamed `lua_pushnil`-shaped call for the "nil" pushes, `lua_pushstring` for the string-or-nil variant, `lua_pushboolean`), each incrementing a running pushed-value count on the builder object, with a final "finalize/dispatch" call (0x00e0cd00 → 0x00e0cba0, OPEN) that fires the resolved named callback with the accumulated argument list. In other words: **this whole family is a generic "call a named Lua callback with N arguments" mechanism, layered on top of this document's own already-documented `lua_push*` primitives — not a separate network-record system.** This resolves/upgrades §19.5's own OPEN characterization directly. Used by 3 of this tranche's own functions (`pcu_report_item_colors`, `pcu_get_categories_in_area`, `pcu_get_areas`) and also found, independently, inside the newly-decompiled screen-fade primitive below.
- **A second major new-primitive resolution: 0x0059f8c0, previously cited only as "conditionally calls 0x0059f8c0/0x008b7260" at §16.9 with no characterization, is a screen-fade-request primitive** with the real signature ~~(fadeMode, completionCallback, duration)~~ **(durationMs, completionCallback, flag)** **[corrected 2026-10-01 from bridge job `20261001T020200-team-a-nzxf`, read off the raw stack offsets: the integer millisecond duration is the first argument and the flag (stored in 0x013effc8 and passed to Lua first) the third. CONFIRMED — disassembly]**, backed by a small state machine (globals 0x012e6aa0/0x012e6aa4/0x012e6aa8/0x013effc8/0x013effcc/0x013effd0) and internally using the SAME 0x00e0xxxx builder family to fire a named `"screen_fade_do"` callback with 3 numeric parameters. **[2026-10-01, job `20261001T020200-team-a-nzxf`: globals list CONFIRMED and extended with 0x013effc0, 0x012e6aac/0x012e6ab0/0x012e6ab4/0x012e6ab8 and 0x013effc5; the three parameters are `(flag, targetAlpha, durationMs)`. Full state machine in §26.24.]** **This directly explains `sfx_faded_out`'s own query field (0x012e6aa4 == 3) as literally the same fade-state global this primitive itself drives** — a concrete, disassembly-confirmed link between two functions in this very tranche (§26.9/§26.10/§26.6 all touch this one mechanism from different sides).
- **A repeated, newly-identified decompiler-rendering gap, distinct from this document's already-established register-forwarding hidden-argument convention:** at least 4 separate call sites across 3 functions in this tranche (0x00822040 and 0x00746770 inside `pcu_report_item_colors`; 0x00822000 inside `pcu_get_categories_in_area`; 0x007f3520 inside `game_use_radial_menu_item`) show a genuine, single, explicitly-`PUSH`ed stack argument in the raw disassembly that the decompiler's own pseudocode rendering shows as a bare zero-argument call. Unlike the established register-forwarding idiom (where no push exists at all), these ARE real pushes — just dropped from the decompiled text entirely. Worth flagging as its own distinct artifact category for future tranches working in this same address neighborhood (the 0x0082xxxx/0x0084xxxx PCU/radial-menu regions).
- **A second new hidden-argument variant, found in `pcr_strip_clothing`: a real argument reaching a callee not via a register, but via a stale, not-yet-cleaned stack slot left over from an immediately preceding, separately-called function** (the compiler had combined/deferred the two calls' stack cleanups into one `ADD ESP` after the second call). This is mechanically different from both the already-established register-forwarding convention AND the "decompiler silently drops a real push" pattern above — a third distinct flavor of hidden-argument bug this cluster's address range exhibits, all found only by going to raw disassembly.
- **The single clearest and most consequential hidden-argument catch this pass: `game_set_equipped_grenade`.** Its decompiled pseudocode makes the function look almost like a no-op (argument computed and apparently unused; current-player call's result apparently discarded), which would have been easy to mis-report as "another hardcoded stub" by analogy with §26.3/§26.8 of this same tranche — but raw disassembly proves it forwards a real hidden `this` pointer (player + 0x1b78, the SAME quick-item sub-object §26.18's own slot-12 special case touches) and a real adjusted argument into a genuine, meaningful equip-grenade setter. A caution for future passes: an apparently-unused decompiled value in THIS specific cluster is not reliable evidence of dead code — check the raw disassembly before concluding a stub, even when the surface pattern looks identical to a confirmed real stub elsewhere in the same tranche.
- **~~3~~ 2 genuine, disassembly-confirmed hardcoded-stub findings in this one tranche** (`main_menu_check_user_content`, always-true by construction since its literal input trivially satisfies a range check that has nothing to do with real content state; `store_dlc_make_purchase`, literal 0.0 always, argument read but never rounded or used at all) — joining `game_get_party_member_count` (§19.8) as a recurring pattern: **a plausible-sounding Lua binding name does not guarantee the bound function does anything real** in this cluster.
- **+0x2088+0x1c / +0x20f8 field-pair write-direction asymmetry:** `pcu_wear_current_clothing` writes +0x2088+0x1c → +0x20f8 (the reverse of every other function seen touching this pair — §19.1/§19.2/§19.12 and this tranche's own `pcu_discard_slot` all write +0x20f8 → +0x2088+0x1c). Flagged explicitly rather than silently normalized, since it could matter for anyone reconstructing the real field semantics.
- **Newly resolves part of §19.1's own OPEN item** ("the exact meaning of area/category descriptor fields beyond the name string") — this pass's `pcu_get_categories_in_area`/`pcu_get_areas` decompiles directly confirm: area descriptor +0x20/+0x24 = category-pointer-array/count, +0x28 = a "show even if empty" byte flag, +0x2a = a signed visibility-priority byte, +8 = a display-order/sort value; category descriptor +0x2c = item count, +4 = a name/id field (nil-sentinel-checked against the same shared "nil-or-value" idiom, §19.13).
- **A third global identified in the area-state cluster already tracked at §19.1** (0x022ffd40, alongside the already-known 0x022ffd44/0x022ffd48/0x022ffd4c), feeding a shared UI-refresh notifier (0x0082dc40) called identically by this tranche's own `pcu_get_areas` and (indirectly, via the shared revalidate-everything primitive 0x0082e210) `pcu_wear_current_clothing`/`pcu_discard_slot`.
- **A fourth confirmed direct consumer of the exact §16.16/§19.16 shared 63-slot PCR composite-item list**: `pcr_change_eye_color`, joining `pcr_change_composite`/`pcr_set_random_composite`/`pcr_change_skin_color` already on record.
- No opcode/network-replicate record-and-replicate idiom (the 0x00710cb0 pattern) was found in any of these 22 — consistent with §19.16's own observation that the UI/customization cluster doesn't use that idiom; the closest analogue here is the newly-resolved 0x00e0xxxx named-callback builder family, which is a genuinely different mechanism.

### 26.24 Screen fade state machine (exe-derived 2026-10-01)

Source: ~~bridge job `20261001T020200-team-a-nzxf`~~ ~~bridge jobs `20261001T020200-team-a-nzxf` and `20261001T114101-team-a-mnao`~~ bridge jobs `20261001T020200-team-a-nzxf`, `20261001T114101-team-a-mnao` and

**State encoding of 0x012e6aa4** — **CONFIRMED — disassembly**:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | fading in (transition toward transparent running) |
| 1 | fading out (transition toward opaque running) |
| 2 | fully faded in, screen visible — the start-up state |
| 3 | fully faded out, screen covered |

~~Queries: `fade_is_fully_faded_out` and `sfx_faded_out` are true when the state is 3;
`fade_is_fully_faded_in` when it is 2 (§26.9). **CONFIRMED.**~~ **[Superseded, job `20261001T114101-team-a-mnao`:]**
Queries: `fade_is_fully_faded_out` and `sfx_faded_out` are true when the state is 3;
`fade_is_fully_faded_in` and `sfx_faded_in` (0x0059fb60) when it is 2 (§26.9). `sfx_use_load_images`
(0x0059fb90) returns the byte 0x0149365c. All four UI-state natives are registered by 0x005a01d0.
**CONFIRMED — disassembly.**

**Request helpers** — 0x0059f8c0 (fade out) and 0x0059fc40 (fade in), both taking
`(durationMs, completionCallback, flag)`. **CONFIRMED — disassembly, full bodies.** Both Lua wrappers
pass `(trunc(seconds × 1000), 0, 0)`; §26.10 passes `(0, callback, 0)`.

Fade-out request:
1. Posts the 32-bit id 0x5c0b1b1a through 0x0045d990 (via 0x005542f0). HYPOTHESIS: an audio event.
2. If the state and the target are both 3, it calls the callback (if any) with 3 and stops.
3. Otherwise it sets the target to 3 and stores `flag` in 0x013effc8.
4. If a fade-in is running (state 0), it parks the callback in the deferred slot 0x013effd0 and stops.
   The state is left alone and no Lua call is made.
5. Otherwise, if 0x012e6aa0 is not -1 and the UI Lua state defines `screen_fade_do` as a function,
   it calls `screen_fade_do(flag, 1.0, durationMs)` in that state.
6. It sets the state to 1 and stores the callback in 0x013effcc.

Fade-in request, the mirror image:
1. Posts id 0xf0493dc8 when two engine conditions are false (HYPOTHESIS: an audio event).
2. If the state and the target are both 2, it calls the callback with 2 and stops.
3. It sets the target to 2 and stores `flag`.
4. It defers (callback into 0x013effd0, then stops) in two cases:
   - a fade-out is running (state 1);
   - either hold timestamp 0x012e6ab0/0x012e6ab8 is set (value ≥ 0) and the millisecond clock at
     0x01320d9c has not passed it yet (the comparison tolerates a 900,000,000 ms wrap).
5. Otherwise it resets 0x012e6aac/0x012e6ab4 to -1 and makes the same Lua call with
   `(flag, 0.0, durationMs)`.
6. It sets the state to 0, stores the callback, and posts id 0xa577ee9c.

The C side therefore never animates anything. It sets the direction (state 1 or 0), asks the UI script
to run the transition, and parks a callback. A "queued on a UI command queue" reading (2026-09-30) is
superseded: this is a direct call of a Lua global.

**Broadcast helpers** — 0x005a0270 (out) and 0x005a0400 (in). **CONFIRMED — disassembly.** Both do
nothing unless the host gate holds: the session object (0x0087ba20 → 0x024d8534) exists and its
`+0x5c` equals its `+0x58`. Each then opens an opcode-0x53 record (0x0086f5f0) and writes:
- a 1-bit direction flag (1 = out, 0 = in);
- for fade-out only, the current overlay colour as 4 bytes;
- 16 bits of `durationMs`;
- 8 bits of the helper's second argument (0 from Lua).

The record goes to the session's peers (0x0086f1b0) and is closed (0x0086eb20). Each helper also sets
0x013effc5. HIGH CONFIDENCE: the record replicates the fade to co-op clients (the consumer is not traced).

**What completes a fade: `Screen_fade_transition_complete` (0x005a0110).** **CONFIRMED —
disassembly, full listing.** The UI wrapper 0x005a01d0 registers this native in the UI Lua state,
next to `sfx_faded_out`, `sfx_faded_in` and `sfx_use_load_images`. It takes no arguments and
returns nothing. Apart from init/shutdown it holds the only stores of 2 and 3 into the state, so a
fade completes exactly when the UI script calls it (HIGH CONFIDENCE: when `screen_fade_do`'s
tween ends). Its body:
1. If the state is 0 it becomes 2. If the state is 1 it becomes 3, the logo stamp 0x012e6aac is set
   to now + 1000 ms and 0x012e6ab0/0x012e6ab4/0x012e6ab8 are reset to -1. A state of 2 or 3 is
   left alone. The target is not consulted here.
2. If the in-flight callback 0x013effcc is set it is called with the **target** (2 or 3) as its
   only argument; the slot is re-read afterwards.
3. If the state now equals the target and the deferred slot 0x013effd0 is set: when it holds the
   same function as the in-flight slot, both are cleared (the function has just been called) and
   the native returns; otherwise the deferred function is called with the target and the slot is
   cleared.
4. The in-flight slot is cleared (and the deferred slot too when the two were equal).

The native never starts a transition. A request that was parked (target differs from the settled
state) is replayed by the per-frame routine below.

~~**Per-frame routine 0x0059fe70** (callers 0x005d14b0 and 0x007a82c0). **CONFIRMED — disassembly,
full listing.** Each frame, in this order:~~ **[Superseded, job `20261001T122853-team-a-nnlt`:]**
**Per-frame routine 0x0059fe70.** **CONFIRMED — disassembly, full listing.** It is called once per
frame by the main loop's system update 0x005d14b0 (unconditionally, before the mode stack is
pumped) and a second time by the mode callback 0x007a82c0 while ~~mode 5~~ **mode 8** is on the mode stack
(~~HYPOTHESIS: the loading screen~~ **CONFIRMED, 2026-10-02, `teleport_coop` investigation: 0x007a82c0 is the per-frame handler of game mode 8, the asynchronous player-teleport mode registered by `0x007a8530` — see the resolved registrar note below**); the second call changes nothing because the routine only acts on
clock stamps. Each frame, in this order:
- Auto-save indicator: counter 0x013effd4 > 0 and stamp 0x012e6abc unset → stamp := now + 3000 ms
  and call `screen_fade_auto_save_show()`; counter ≤ 0 and stamp reached → call
  `screen_fade_auto_save_hide()` and reset the stamp.
- ~~Mode gate: if the top of the mode stack (0x00706ab0: 0x01503b50 indexed by 0x012f4a80) is 4,
  reset all four fade stamps and stop (OPEN: what mode 4 is).~~ **[Superseded, job `20261001T122853-team-a-nnlt`: next bullet.]**
- Mode gate: if the top of the mode stack (0x00706ab0: 0x01503b50 indexed by 0x012f4a80) is 4,
  reset all four fade stamps and stop. The mode stack is pumped by 0x00706be0 (push/pop requests
  queued at 0x012f4a94; per-mode enter/leave/may-leave callbacks in the 9-dword records at
  0x01503bc0; a mode already on the stack is not pushed twice; a pop waits while the top mode's
  may-leave predicate is false). OPEN: which mode is 4 (no dump names the modes).

  **0x00706a40, the per-mode registrar, CONFIRMED — disassembly, full body, job
  `20261001T172007-team-a-buqd`.** Bounds-checked to `< 0xb` (11 slots, matching the array above), it
  writes one 9-dword (0x24-byte) record per mode index: the first four qwords copied verbatim from
  the caller's second argument (the enter/leave/may-leave callbacks the mode-stack line above already
  names, plus one more field), a dword at `+0x20` also copied from the caller and then overwritten in
  its low byte by the caller's own third (byte) argument, and a `+0x21` byte forced to 1 ("this slot
  is registered"). This confirms the record layout already inferred above, but not which of its ten

  0x007b06f0, 0x007e1d10, 0x0088cf70 — one per mode, for up to eleven slots) is mode 4 or mode 5: the

  candidate at 0x007a82c0 above — is registered by 0x007a8530 (the one call site in the same small
