## 29. Named-object registration — the write side of the `0x02442750` resolver family (2026-10-02)

The dozen-plus by-name resolvers already catalogued throughout this document (§1.1/§1.12 and the many further sightings tallied at §25.29/§28 — `0x005982e0`, `0x005e4dd0`, `0x005e4e30`, `0x005eab60`, `0x005f4c30`, `0x00734e90`, `0x00739690`, `0x004584e0`, `0x00a3de90`, `0x0071f0d0` and others) are all thin, kind-filtering wrappers over **one shared find routine, `0x004588f0`, on an embedded name-map sub-object at `0x02444db0`** (the singleton `0x02442750` plus `0x2660`) — a case-insensitive, multiply-by-33 bucket hash (`0x00dab330`, the same hash the texture registry uses, `spec-texture-format.md` §8.2) over `_stricmp` chain nodes, each storing the object pointer and the name inline. This section documents the **write side** — how a name gets into that map in the first place — investigated 2026-10-02 against the real executable (local Ghidra project, read-only; full trace in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_named_object_resolution.md`, not committed to this spec). **CONFIRMED — disassembly, unless marked otherwise.**

### 29.1 The generic 40-byte record / property-tail construction interface

Every object the registry creates — named or not — is built from one shared in-memory shape: a fixed 40-byte record (`+0x00/+0x04` object handle, `+0x08/+0x0c` owner handle, `+0x10` a 32-bit class-name hash mixed by the engine's integer mixer `0x00dab2b0` into one of 510 buckets and looked up in the registry's own class-name table, `+0x14` a property count, `+0x18` tail length, `+0x1c` a pointer to a variable **property tail**) plus that tail: a sequence of `{u16 kind, u16 size, u32 id}` headers followed by each property's data, grown by `0x00456660` ("add-property") and read back by id/descriptor. The registry's base-vtable slot 11 (`0x00456d80`, or a derived-class override) is the single per-object "initialise from your record" step: if the record names an owner it attaches to it; then, **if the record carries a name and no other live object is already using it, it calls `0x00457650(obj, name)` — the set-object-name method** — before calling the object's own class-specific property reader. `0x00457650` requires the name be 1-32 characters, finds-or-inserts it into the `0x02444db0` map (capped at `0x21` bytes per node), and stores the map node's own copy of the name back into the object's `+0x18` field — which is why no resolver needs a second lookup once an object is found. **This is the only path by which a name reaches the map** (raw call-site census of `0x00457650`/`0x00458850`: no undisassembled caller, no Lua-bound function calls either directly).

### 29.2 Four producers feed the same interface — it is generic, not any one data format's private mechanism

Raw call-site census of the generic create-from-record method, `0x00456e30` (`this` = record; resolves the class, constructs, inserts into the handle table, then calls slot 11 above) finds **173 call sites across roughly 130 functions** — the gameplay, AI/world and vehicle modules, and the Lua binding module. Four distinct producers build 40-byte records and feed them to this one interface:

1. **Zone object placement.** The zone-load module (`0x00863e90`, one step of the ten-step zone-parse chain `0x00865f90` already placed in `spec-zone-data-format.md` §9.5) reads the top-level `{tag, length}` record whose id is the dword at `0x013026d0` — **`0x2234`**, described in the executable's own data section as `"Game objects, as placed in the WE"` — and batch-loads every placed object's 40-byte record from it (`0x00457c60`/`0x00457a50`) through the exact interface above.
2. **A vehicle definition's embedded "cover nodes" batch** uses the same `FBOW`/version-5 batch layout and the same loader.
3. **In-memory records built by engine code**, fed to `0x00456e30` directly — the bulk of the 173 call sites, including spawners, path/navpoint builders, and group objects.
4. **In-memory records built from a serialised stream** by a dedicated deserialiser, `0x00a36a80` — it reads a kind code and a NUL-terminated name taken in place from the stream buffer, then dispatches through a 6-entry jump table to one of five record builders (an "interior" object, a "script mover", and others). This path *replays* a name that already existed on the writing side; it does not originate one. Its property vocabulary (`script_interior_peer`, `script_mover_peer`, …) suggests co-op replication as the transport — **HYPOTHESIS**, the writer side was not traced.

Whether a given producer's record ends up named is simply whether that record carries a `ctg_object_name` property (zone/vehicle stream path) or had the in-memory set-name method called on it (`0x004563f0`, see §29.3) before being handed to `0x00456e30`.

### 29.3 The authored-name property, and the global name map's size

**`ctg_object_name` is the property that carries an object's authored name.** `0x004563f0(record, name)` — the in-memory set-name method — appends a property keyed by the descriptor at `0x01352568` (string `ctg_object_name`), copies the name string into the tail, and stores that data pointer into the record's `+0x1c` field — the exact field slot 11 reads to call `0x00457650`. On the zone/vehicle stream side, the same field is populated from the on-stream record head's `+0x18` "name offset" into the tail, which (HIGH CONFIDENCE, not independently confirmed — no class-specific property reader was dumped this pass) is read as the same `ctg_object_name` property.

**The name map is a single global table, 2,999 slots, enabled once at game start — not per-zone, not per-kind.** The registry's base-vtable slot 2 (`0x00457370`, `init`) is called exactly once, at start-up (`0x008536b0` ← `0x0091f4f0` ← `0x005d25f0`), with a class count of 62 and a **name-map capacity of `0xBB7` = 2999**, which is what fills the map's live count/bucket-count fields and is why every resolver first checks that count before searching. A name registered by any of the four §29.2 producers is therefore resolvable by every per-kind resolver in this document, with no per-producer distinction visible at lookup time.

**For Team B:** the name map itself — the hash, the chain-node layout, the 2,999-slot capacity, the single global instance, and the fact that every resolver in this document is a thin kind-filter over it — is fully specified above and can be implemented directly; nothing about it depends on data this project cannot open.

### 29.4 Where a mission script's fixed name (e.g. `'Killbane'`) actually comes from — and where the trail stops

No Lua-bound function can choose a name for an object it creates: Lua-reachable creation is either unnamed (`spawn_wieldable_prop`, `character_add_prop`, `human_skydive_create_npc_backpack`) or engine-named with a generated, uniquified suffix (`commando_spawn` → `<def-name>_NNN`). Engine code separately registers a handful of literal names (`"homies"`, `"shopkeepers"`, `"-- Cutscene Script Group --"`) and the special-cased `"#PLAYER1#"`/`"#PLAYER2#"` pair — none of which is a mission-specific character name.

**A mission character addressed by a fixed authored name is therefore a placed object whose zone record carries that name as its `ctg_object_name` property (§29.1-§29.3) — i.e. producer (1) of §29.2.** That record lives inside the `.czn_pc` object-placement interior (the `0x2234` top-level record), which **stays PARKED pending the project owner's own direct word** (standing instruction, unrelated to this write-up). **This is where the trail stops: no `.czn_pc` bytes were opened or requested to produce this section** — everything above was established purely from the registry/record code's own call graph and literal data, not from reading any real zone file. A reader that wants to resolve a mission name such as `'Killbane'` would need to parse the `0x2234` record's per-object heads and their `ctg_object_name` property — which requires that parked interior to be opened first.

## 30. Ranking tranche 03 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names, by real runtime call-count priority (2026-10-02)

**Scope.** Team B ranked every Lua-bound native by real runtime call count and found roughly 554 with no dedicated spec coverage; Team A works through them in priority tranches of 25. This is tranche 03 (job `D:\Crreish-sync\for-team-a\team-a\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-03.json`). Investigated 2026-10-02 against the real executable (local Ghidra, read-only; full trace in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_03.md`). All 25 names resolved to exactly one `.rdata` string each, each referenced once inside the 1,014-entry gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`. Shared primitives cited below use this document's own established identities (§3 preamble, §4.1): `0x00dfde50` `lua_gettop`, `0x00dfe210` `lua_tolstring`, `0x00dfe1e0` `lua_toboolean`, `0x00dfe040` `lua_type`, `0x00dfe160` `lua_tonumber`, `0x00ea2596` the truncating float-to-int cast, `0x00dfe3a0` `lua_pushnumber`, `0x00dfe590` `lua_pushboolean`; resolvers `0x00a281a0` (generic character chain), `0x00a280c0` (generic kind-filtered chain), `0x00a281e0` (dedicated vehicle resolver), `0x0062a190` (per-kind vehicle resolver), `0x00853b10` (handle-liveness guard, non-zero = dead); session accessor `0x0087ba20` (global `0x024d8534`, `+0x5c`==`+0x58` = "this machine is the host"); local-player accessor `0x009da4e0`. **CONFIRMED — disassembly, unless marked otherwise.**

### 30.1 Character cluster

**`character_dont_regenerate` (`0x00a41370`).** Arguments: 1 mandatory string (character name, `0x00a281a0`) + 1 boolean (`lua_toboolean`, no nil-gate, absent → false). Return: none. Body: resolves the character, then thiscall `0x0094ce30(flag)`: liveness guard, then single-gate authority check `0x008addb0(character, 0)`. With local authority: writes the boolean into **bit `0x2` of the dword at character `+0x1c98`**; when true stores `-1` into `+0x19c0` (HYPOTHESIS: a regen-restart deadline, disabled while the flag is set), when false restamps `+0x19c0` to "now" via `0x00d9e140(0)`. Without authority: opens an opcode-`0x46` record tagged `"human"` + `"human_force_flagsdont_regen_health"`, the character's network id and the boolean, committed through the multi-target `0x0086f110` — the local flag is NOT written on this path. Side effects: per-character "do not regenerate health" force flag, a new bit in the already-catalogued `+0x1c98` force-flag word.

**`character_clear_combat_move` (`0x00a410e0`).** Arguments: 1 mandatory string (character name). Return: none. Body: resolves via `0x00a281a0`; calls `0x009682d0(character, 1)` (second argument hardcoded true, not from Lua) — does nothing for a null character or one whose word at `+0x1358` is `0xffff` (HYPOTHESIS: "no combat move/state assigned"). Otherwise tests predicate `0x0095d720`: true → `0x0095f250(character, true)`; false → `0x00967f60()` (HYPOTHESIS: receives the character via `ESI`, no stack argument) then three identical calls `0x00957ee0(character, id, 0.2f, 0, -1, 0)` with ids `0x1d53`/`0x1d54`/`0x1d8c`. Side effects: clears a character's current combat movement; the three trailing calls read as action/animation requests with a 0.2 s blend. OPEN: the identities of `0x0095d720`, `0x0095f250`, `0x00967f60`, `0x00957ee0`, and what the three ids name.

### 30.2 `boss_battle_matt_*` cluster

Both resolve the boss through a hardcoded literal — neither takes a character name from Lua.

**`boss_battle_matt_set_player_as_avatar` (`0x00a40930`).** Arguments: 1 boolean (`lua_toboolean`, absent → false). Return: exactly 1 boolean on every path — the result of the worker, NOT the input. Body: calls worker `0x005e5eb0(flag)`, then sets/clears bit 0 of global `0x0268d2d0` per the flag, then pushes the worker's result. The worker reads the local player (`0x009da4e0`) and co-op player (`0x009df3d0`, HYPOTHESIS). No local player → false, no-op. **flag true (become avatar):** several thiscalls, looks up `"npc_bahamut"`; not found → false. Builds a customization item ("Bahamut Suit"/"avatar.cmeshx"/"Bahamut"), applies it to the player's `+0x2088` customization object, resolves a model; failure → false. Success: binds the model, stores the bahamut entry at `+0xf4`, swaps rig to "avatar.rig"/"Avatar", repeats for the co-op player if present, host-side writes 1 to byte global `0x012ec740`, returns true. **flag false (restore):** host clears bit 0 of `0x0268d2d0`; looks up `"StyleTest_PC"`; **not found → returns true without restoring anything**; found: restores the prior model/rig — swaps back to "cf_body.rig"/"PLYF" when character `+0xa41` is 1 (HYPOTHESIS: female body flag) else "cm_body.rig"/"PLYM", host writes 0 to `0x012ec740`. **Returns false after a successful restore** — the Lua return is NOT a plain success flag. OPEN: most callees not dumped at depth 1; the role of bit 0 of `0x0268d2d0` (also touched by several unrelated sites).

**`boss_battle_matt_hide_wings` (`0x00a40850`).** Arguments: 1 optional boolean, nil-gated, **default true**. Return: none. Body: calls the inert always-1 stub `0x00d221a0` (discarded), resolves Matt via `0x005e5ae0` = `0x00a281a0("Matt", NULL)`. If found, `0x005e7590(matt, flag)` walks Matt's circular attached-object list and, for each entry matching a kind-descriptor gate and whose `+0xe0` record hashes to `"Avatar_wings"`, calls `0x008ccb90(entry, flag, 1, 0)` (HYPOTHESIS: 2nd arg = "hidden", per §7's own open note on this same function). If hiding and this machine is host, stores Matt's 16-bit object id (`0x008add70`) into word global `0x012ec742` (only on hide, not cleared on show). The sibling setter `boss_battle_matt_set_matt_flying` is already §18.2.

### 30.3 Global toggles and audio emitters

**`auto_pickup_enable` (`0x00a3c880`).** No arguments read. Return: none. Body: `0x008fb880(1)` — writes the hardcoded byte 1 to global `0x01308698` (file-backed default: enabled). This entry can only enable; a sibling at the adjacent registrar slot `0x00a3c8a0` most plausibly is `auto_pickup_disable` (HYPOTHESIS, not dumped). Consumer: `0x00903330`.

**`audio_ambient_emitter_pause` (`0x00a3c800`) / `audio_ambient_emitter_resume` (`0x00a3c830`).** Identical shape. Arguments: 1 mandatory string (emitter name). Return: none. Body: name → Wwise id (`0x00462960`, the established `AK::SoundEngine::GetIDFromString` path), then scans the world object manager's ambient-emitter list (global `0x03171a64`, count `+0x2b8`, `u16` indices `+0x2b0`, object pointers `+0x58`) for the first `+0x84` match; its `+0x90` handle goes to `0x0045f000` (pause) or `0x0045f0d0` (resume), then a trailing `0x00562ff0(2|3)` (HYPOTHESIS: a state/notification code). No match → nothing. OPEN: the three callee bodies; only the first list match is acted on.

### 30.4 AI cluster — and the 70-entry CAE combat-action table

Both functions below resolve the character via `0x00a28150` (follower sentinels, else the per-kind resolver `0x005e4dd0` on registry `0x02442750`, liveness, virtual slot `+0x70`) and drive the same per-character "combat action" record keyed into a fixed action table.

**The CAE action table (`0x012e1c60`, 70 rows of `0x18` bytes, file-backed — "CAE" is the engine's own name for this system).** Row `+0` name pointer, `+4` category byte, `+8` handler code pointer, `+0x15` flag byte; dwords `+0xc`/`+0x10` are `15000`/`300` in every row. `0x004f2610` maps a name → index (case-insensitive linear scan, 71/`0x47` = not found); `0x004f2840` maps index → name (`"Invalid CAE action"` for 70+). All 70 names, read from the file image: 0 `fire`, 1 `fire sweep`, 2 `fire suppress`, 3 `fire chaos`, 4 `throw grenade`, 5 `throw weapon`, 6 `melee`, 7 `melee vehicle`, 8 `cover take def`, 9 `cover take off`, 10 `cover advance`, 11 `cover stay down`, 12 `cover fire`, 13 `cover popout`, 14 `hold position`, 15 `melee stand back`, 16 `move retreat`, 17 `move regroup`, **18 `move advance`**, 19 `move chase`, 20 `avatar chase`, 21 `move surround`, 22 `move rush`, 23 `move rush to melee`, 24 `move scripted`, 25 `move to navmesh`, 26 `move sidestep`, 27 `move to post combat`, 28 `move to post idle`, 29 `move close in`, 30-40 the `follow ...` family (`make way`, `avoid LOF`, `formation`, `acquire`, `player`, `teleport`, `lemming`, `to car`, `other car`, `carjack`, `browse`), 41-43 `investigate move/look/peek`, 44 `reload`, 45 `pickup weapon`, 46 `human shield grab`, 47 `taunt`, 48 `vehicle passenger`, 49 `vehicle enter scpt`, 50 `vehicle extract`, 51-56 `brute ...` (`throw prop`, `car flip`, `bull rush`, `qte player`, `attack brute`, `gun finisher`), 57-62 `avatar ...` (`shockwave`, `stomp`, `taunt`, `fireballs`, `teleport stomp`, `bullrush`), 63 `quick kill`, 64 `zombie eat`, 65 `zombie explode`, 66 `killbane chase`, 67 `killbane strafe`, 68 `roller blader change`, 69 `idle`. Rows 24 and 49 have a null handler pointer; row 11 is the only row with `+0x15` = 1.

**Per-character action record (character `+0x438..+0x4ff`).** `+0x4a8` a staged ("pending") `0x58`-byte action block — byte `+0x4a8` action index, word `+0x4aa` a value from `0x006f62b0(character, 3, 0)`, dwords `+0x4b0`/`+0x4b4` a target handle pair, `+0x4c0..+0x4c8` a 12-byte target position; `+0x450` the committed copy of the same block; `+0x44c` a flag byte; `+0x445` current action index; `+0x438`/`+0x440` two "now"-stamped deadlines (`0x00d9e140(0)`); `+0x4fe` bits 6-7 flags. HYPOTHESIS: the pending→committed copy semantics, from the `+0x4a8`→`+0x450` copy inside `0x004f4d00`.

**`ai_suggest_action` (`0x00a3eb00`).** Arguments: 3 — arg 1 mandatory character name, arg 2 mandatory action name (one of the 70, or `"NONE"`), arg 3 optional target name (nil-gated, default none). Return: none. Body: unknown name (not `"NONE"`) → prints all 70 valid names via `printf` and returns (no visible console in retail); `"NONE"` → index 71, silent no-op; known name → arg 3, if resolvable through `0x004584e0` + liveness, becomes the target handle, else an all-zero pair; calls `0x004f4b90(character, index, handleLo, handleHi, 1, 0)` (trailing `1` = "force", hardcoded). `0x004f4b90` stages (does not commit) the action into `+0x4a8` unconditionally (force=1 bypasses the busy test); if not under local authority, forwards via `0x004f4830(character, 1, index, 3000)` (HYPOTHESIS: network forward, 3000 ms timeout). OPEN: how/whether the AI later commits or discards a staged suggestion.

**`ai_do_scripted_advance` (`0x00a3e370`).** Arguments: 1 mandatory character name + 1 optional target name (nil-gated, default none). Return: exactly 1 boolean. Body: no target → `0x0053a520` computes an advance destination into the staged block's `+0x4c0`, success → `0x004f4d00(character, 18, 0)` and pushes that result; target given → resolves via `0x00a3df50` then `0x005982e0` (the "5th per-kind resolver", §1.10), copies its position, same commit call, pushes true; neither resolves → false. `0x004f4d00(character, index, 0)` — unlike the suggest path, **commits the action immediately** on the authority machine (copies staged→committed `+0x450`, writes literal `0x12` to `+0x444`, index to `+0x445`, restamps `+0x438`, calls `0x004e4130(character, categoryByte)`); without authority, forwards via `0x004f4830(character, 0, index, 3000)`. Forces action index 18 = `move advance`. Compare §18.3 `ai_do_scripted_take_cover`, which drives the same `0x004f4d00` from the same registrar block.

### 30.5 Vehicle cluster — 13 functions

**Shared vehicle facts.** Two resolution styles: most entries use `0x00a281e0` (tries the generic chain `0x00a280c0` first; if that yields a character currently in a vehicle — `+0x16c0/+0x16c4` non-zero — redirects to that vehicle via `0x004dcf00`; otherwise falls to the per-kind vehicle resolver `0x0062a190`, liveness, a `+0x68` gate, result from virtual slot `+0x70`). **Two entries skip the character redirect entirely** (`vehicle_set_invulnerable_to_player_explosives`, `vehicle_is_vtol` — inline `0x0062a190` + liveness + `+0x70`, no `+0x68` gate). Vehicle class: `0x00ad3200(vehicle)` true when `(+0xbf4)+0x2c` equals 4 = VTOL (the same field §20.3 already tests for zero, car alarm — a class enum). **Four new force-flag bits**, all via the same "variant-1" double-gate record-and-replicate shape (`0x008ae480` then `0x008837a0`; either true → write the bit directly; both false → open an opcode-`0x46` record with hashed tags instead): `+0x1d7c` bit `0x2` `invulnerable_to_player_explosives`; `+0x1d7c` bit `0x4` `radio_controls_locked`; `+0x1d7d` bit `0x20` `disable_exp_and_damage_vfx`; `+0x1d7d` bit `0x40` `special_override_never_ghost` — none collides with the `+0x1d7a` bits §20.1/§21.30 already dispute. Seats: `0x00ab4af0(vehicle)` = 8 unless byte `+0xbd0` is 1 (then dword `+0x824`); `0x00ab5070(vehicle, i)` = occupant of seat `i` (HIGH CONFIDENCE: seat 0 = driver). **Shared script-request-id allocator** `0x006f62b0(object, channel, x)`: cancels any tracked request for the same object+channel, allocates a 12-bit sequence id OR-ed with a machine-index nibble (HYPOTHESIS); channel 0 = `turn_to_do` (§30.6), 2 = `vehicle_pathfind_to_do`, 3 = the AI action writers (§30.4).

**`vehicle_set_invulnerable_to_player_explosives` (`0x00a66270`)**, **`vehicle_disable_explosion_and_damage_vfx` (`0x00a621f0`)**, **`vehicle_set_special_override_never_ghost` (`0x00a63300`)** — all: 1 mandatory vehicle name + 1 boolean (no nil-gate, absent → false); no return; thiscall the matching variant-1 setter for the bits above. `vehicle_set_special_override_never_ghost`'s setter has two further engine callers.

**`vehicle_clear_all_radio_locks` (`0x00a647e0`).** No arguments. No return. Walks every vehicle in the world object manager (`0x03171a64`, `+0xb8`/`+0xc0`/`+0x58`) and clears the `radio_controls_locked` bit on each (literal false, hardcoded) — a per-vehicle authority miss emits one opcode-`0x46` record per such vehicle rather than skipping. The setter has another caller at `0x00a631ba` (HYPOTHESIS: the per-vehicle Lua setter).

**`vehicle_set_2d_tank_controls` (`0x00a62d00`).** 1 boolean, no nil-gate. No return. Body: `0x00a91df0(flag)` — host sends an opcode-`0x42` record (sub-header `0x1f`) before storing the boolean in global byte `0x0278cad8`. HYPOTHESIS: belongs to the RC-vehicle controls (adjacent global `0x0278cad4` is the RC signal range, §30's next entry).

**`vehicle_rc_get_signal_strength` (`0x00a64100`).** Arguments: 2 mandatory strings (vehicle, character). Return: exactly 1 number, 0.0 on resolve failure. Body: `0x00a92430` returns `1 − d/R` where `d` is the **horizontal-only** distance (X/Z, Y dropped) and `R` is float global `0x0278cad4`. **Not clamped — negative beyond range.** OPEN: `R`'s own source (only writer `0x00a906b0`).

**`vehicle_is_vtol` (`0x00a66170`).** 1 string. Return: exactly 1 boolean. Inline resolution (no character redirect); true only when class 4. A second Ghidra candidate `0x00c1e650` is spurious — it has no reference to the name string.

**`vehicle_exit_group_do` (`0x00a67a00`) / `vehicle_exit_group_check_done` (`0x00a66b00`).** Both take a Lua table of character names, walked via `0x0083dff0` (returns `t.n` if numeric, else counts via `lua_next`; −1 for missing/nil). Character vehicle state `+0x16d4`: `0x009b9160` tests `==3` (HYPOTHESIS: seated), `0x009b9230` tests `==2` (HYPOTHESIS: entering/exiting). `0x0096f4f0` is an "is dead/gone" predicate. **`_do`** — arguments: arg 1 boolean (no nil-gate) + arg 2/3 optional booleans (nil-gated, default false) + arg 4 the table (must be 4th — fewer args sees no table and does nothing). Return: 1 boolean, true if ≥1 character got an exit request. For each resolving character in state 3, builds an exit request and hands it to `0x00af3cd0` (OPEN, not dumped); remembers the first vehicle found; calls `0x00a7bdc0(arg3)` on it — **or with a NULL `this` when no vehicle was found** (confirmed from the listing, `XOR ECX,ECX`) — OPEN whether `0x00a7bdc0` tolerates that. **`_check_done`** — 1 table argument. Return: false if any listed character resolves, is alive, and is in state 2 or 3; true otherwise (including empty/missing table) — the polling partner.

**`vehicle_stop_do` (`0x00a67c80`).** 1 mandatory string: a character name (uses its current vehicle) or a vehicle name. No return. Body: character path requires a live vehicle via `+0x16c0/+0x16c4`, else does nothing (vehicle-name path not tried as fallback); authority checked on the character (if via character) or the vehicle (if direct); with authority: `0x00abe510(handle, 1)` or, for the vehicle path when `+0xc68` byte is not 1, `0x00b46ca0` then `0x00a90c70`; without authority: `0x00a66d30` sends an opcode-`0x43` stop request to whoever owns the vehicle. `0x00abe510` (shared with `teleport_vehicle_to_object` below) without authority forwards an opcode-`0x42` record instead; with authority and `+0xbd0`==1/`+0x81c` non-null, clears flags, notifies the local player's own vehicle specially, stops the `+0x808` sub-object (HYPOTHESIS: the AI driving controller). HYPOTHESIS: `+0xc68` is a scripted-path follower record.

**`vehicle_pathfind_to_do` (`0x00a680c0`).** Arguments: 4, positional, no nil-gates — arg 1 vehicle, arg 2 target name, arg 3/4 booleans (absent → false). Return: exactly 1 value whose **type depends on the path** — boolean false on every failure, but on the main path a **number** (0 is truthy in Lua). Body: needs a vehicle with a driver (`0x00ab5070(vehicle,0)` non-null). **Takes `strlen` of arg 2 before the NULL test** — a non-string arg 2 is dereferenced (crash-shaped edge, CONFIRMED from the listing order). Empty string or unresolvable target → false; a path object (`0x0062a1f0`) copies up to 25 points from the vehicle's position plus the path's own nodes; a point-kind target (`0x005982e0`) gives 2 points (vehicle, target); fewer than 2 points → false. With ≥2: takes a request id (channel 2) and calls `0x00b2b140(vehicle, points, count, arg3, 0, arg4, -1.0f, id)`; a 0 result releases the id; either way pushes the integer as a number. OPEN: `0x00b2b140`'s own semantics/return meaning, what arg 3/4 select.

**`vehicle_set_malfunctioning` (`0x00a65540`).** Arguments: 1 mandatory vehicle name + 1 optional boolean, nil-gated, **default true**. No return. **Does nothing unless the vehicle is class 4 (VTOL)** — the only gate. true: adds 100.0 to a float at the **local player's** `+0x1650` (clamped to `[0, runtime max]`), sets byte global `0x02625852` to 1, sets vehicle `+0xf8` bits `0x1`/`0x2`, activates a "cyber_m16_glitch" screen-effect preset slot. false: zeroes the four floats at local-player `+0x1650..+0x165c`, clears `0x02625852`, clears the effect slot, clears vehicle `+0xf8` bit `0x2` only. Both paths send an opcode-`0x43` record with **no authority or host gate — every machine that runs the call sends it**. HYPOTHESIS: `+0x1650` is a screen-distortion intensity; the glitch effect lands on the local player whoever is actually flying the VTOL.

**`vehicle_component_detach` (`0x00a63870`).** Arguments: 2 mandatory strings (vehicle, component name) + 4 optional, all nil-gated — arg 3/4 booleans default true, arg 5 number default 0, arg 6 boolean default false. No return. Body: requires vehicle `+0xbd0`==1; finds the component by case-insensitive name scan (−1 → nothing); `0x00a8eab0(component, vehicle, arg4, arg5, arg3, arg6, 0, 0)` recursively detaches the component and (gated on arg 3 and several internal vetoes) spawns it as a loose piece (arg 4/arg 5 forwarded, HYPOTHESIS physical meaning: spawn position/velocity-shaped), recurses into non-flagged children, and hands `0x40`-flagged children to a separate path only when arg 6 is true. Marks the component detached (bit `0x200000` of `+0xf0`) on every path regardless of outcome.

### 30.6 Character turn, vehicle teleport, team relation

**`turn_to_do` (`0x00a61e10`).** Arguments: 2 mandatory strings (character, target) + 1 optional boolean, nil-gated, default false. Return: exactly 1 boolean on every path. Body: target pose comes from the established resolver `0x00a455a0` (§20.24/§21.24). Character or target missing → **true**. Character already exactly on target position (arg 3 false) → **true**. Otherwise takes a request id (channel 0) and calls `0x00987410(character, point, 0, id, 0)` with the facing point being the target position (arg 3 false) or the character's own position plus the target's own facing (arg 3 true, "face the way the target faces"). `0x00987410`: true for null character; true when a refusal predicate fires (releases the id); **false without local authority** (after sending an opcode-`0x41` turn request); false under a busy flag; otherwise the result of the actual turn-start routine. **The return reads as "already done"** — true when nothing needs doing or it finished instantly, false while pending. HIGH CONFIDENCE on that reading, from both explicit return paths in the listing.

**`teleport_vehicle_to_object` (`0x00a60ae0`).** Arguments: 2 mandatory strings (arg 1 vehicle OR character — its current vehicle; arg 2 target object, via the generic game-object chain `0x00a29200`) + 5 optional, all nil-gated — args 3/4/5 numbers default 0.0 (offsets along the target's own orientation rows 0/1/2), arg 6 number default 0.0 (a heading in degrees, ×0.017453 to radians), arg 7 boolean default true. No return. Body: target unresolved → nothing. Vehicle via character path has no extra gate; vehicle-name path is **refused when `(+0xbf8)+0xa8` is ≥ 0** (OPEN: meaning; applies only to the vehicle-name path). Stops the vehicle (`0x00abe510`, shared with `vehicle_stop_do`), detaches all seats, builds the target's 4×4 pose, offsets/rotates it per args 3-6, calls `0x00a874f0(vehicle, x, y, z, &orientation, arg7, 0)` (OPEN: what arg 7 selects).

**`team_make_unfriendly` (`0x00a60940`).** Arguments: 2 mandatory strings (team names). No return. The exact sibling of §20.6 `team_make_allies`, relation value **1** instead of 4. Both names resolve through `0x0094cc60` (unknown name → id 9 — a crash-shaped edge if that indexes past an 8×8 relation-matrix block, OPEN, not confirmed). `0x009b7130(id1, id2, 1, true)` writes the relation symmetrically, then a local-only opcode-`0x43` record. **Refines §20.6's "team 5" note**: the two "auxiliary arrays" that note names are the SAME relation matrix at rows/column 6 — **whenever team 5 is one side, team 6 gets the identical relation** (team 6 mirrors team 5), confirmed from the address arithmetic directly.

### 30.7 Cross-function observations

The CAE combat-action table is now fully named (§30.4) — any other entry in this document handing a literal index to `0x004f4d00`/`0x004f4b90` can now be named by it. `0x006f62b0` is confirmed as a shared, channel-keyed script-request-id allocator used by three unrelated subsystems (turn/pathfind/AI-action). Four new vehicle force-flag bits and one new character bit (`+0x1c98` bit `0x2`, `dont_regen_health`) are catalogued. Two vehicle entry points inconsistently skip the character→vehicle redirect every other one gets. Several return-value quirks a reimplementation must copy exactly, not "clean up": `vehicle_pathfind_to_do` returns a boolean on failure but a truthy number on success; `turn_to_do` returns true when it has nothing to do; `boss_battle_matt_set_player_as_avatar` returns **false** after a successful restore; `vehicle_rc_get_signal_strength` goes negative past range; `vehicle_exit_group_check_done` returns true for an empty table. Three crash-shaped edges are flagged, not resolved: `vehicle_pathfind_to_do`'s pre-NULL-check `strlen` of arg 2; `vehicle_exit_group_do`'s possible NULL-`this` call; `team_make_unfriendly`'s id-9 relation-matrix index for an unrecognized team name. Inert/discarded calls found: `0x00d221a0`, `0x00d1de80` (both always-1 stubs), and `0x0096f4f0`'s result inside `0x004f4d00`.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 03 resolved and written up (§30.1-§30.6); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items are each tied to a specific undumped callee (depth-1 cap), not guessed past.

## 31. `pause_map_stag_current_district_control` — location and "stag mode" (2026-10-02)

**Why this is here.** Team B's runtime stub ranking showed this name called 303 times with zero host-side spec coverage, unlike its five sibling pause-map names which were already specced.

### 31.1 It is a UI-registrar name, not a gameplay-registrar name

The name does not live in the 1,014-name gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`. The string `"pause_map_stag_current_district_control"` (one `.rdata` occurrence, one code use, at `0x007dfb02`) is used inside wrapper `0x007dfae0`, whose sole caller is the 311-name UI registrar `0x008430f0` (already named in this document's own preamble and in `spec-lua-bindings.md`). The wrapper builds a 9-entry {name, function} array and registers each as a Lua C closure under its name as a global (`0x00dfe4f0` to create the closure, `0x00dfe830` to store it). The full pause-map family it registers:

| # | Name | Function |
|--:|---|---|
| 1 | `pause_map_stag_takeover_do_reward` | `0x007de1c0` |
| 2 | **`pause_map_stag_current_district_control`** | **`0x007de0d0`** |
| 3 | `get_world_income_dollars` | `0x007db9c0` |
| 4 | `pause_map_is_stag_mode` | `0x007d98b0` |
| 5 | `pause_map_is_tutorial_mode` | `0x007d98e0` |
| 6 | `pause_map_set_gps` | `0x007dba10` |
| 7 | `pause_map_add_bookmark` | `0x007df8a0` |
| 8 | `pause_map_drag_map` | `0x007d9910` |
| 9 | `pause_map_zoom` | `0x007dbcc0` |

**[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**

### 31.2 `pause_map_stag_current_district_control` (`0x007de0d0`)

**Arguments:** none. The argument count is fetched (`0x00dfde50`) and discarded; any arguments passed are ignored.

**Return:** normally 1 number — the weighted "owned" fraction, in [0, 1], of the zone currently selected on the pause map; **1.0** if that zone has no members or their total weight is ≤ 0 (including a NaN total). When no zone is selected (the selected-zone global `0x0229a2ac` reads 0), the function does **not** return early — it pushes `0` first, then falls through the same computation a second time (in practice over members with no zone, giving 1.0 — HYPOTHESIS), so it returns **2 numbers**: `0, 1.0`. A reimplementation should reproduce this two-value shape faithfully rather than "fixing" it; a Lua caller doing `local c = ...` only ever sees the first value (0 either way when nothing is selected).

**Body:** reads selected-zone global `0x0229a2ac`; walks a typed member list rooted at the world singleton global `0x03171a64` (count `+0x198`, `u16` indices at `+0x190`, object pointers at `+0x58` — a different typed sub-list of the same world singleton this document's §8.10/§8.11 already use at different offsets); for each member whose pointer field `+0x4c` equals the selected zone, adds its float `+0x3c` (its weight) to a running total, and — if bit `0x02` of its byte `+0x3a` is set — also to a running "owned" sum (both accumulated in double, rounded to single per addition); pushes owned ÷ total as a Lua number, or the constant 1.0 if total ≤ 0.

**Side effects:** none — a read-only query, safe to call with nothing selected (the selected-zone value is only compared, never dereferenced).

**[CONFIRMED — disassembly for all of the above.]**

### 31.3 Where the selected zone comes from

Full reference census of `0x0229a2ac` (7 uses, **CONFIRMED**): written only by `pause_map_set_gps` (`0x007dba10`) and by a pause-map teardown helper `0x007db3e0` (writes 0); read only by §31.2's function and by `pause_map_stag_takeover_do_reward` (§31.6).

- `pause_map_set_gps`, while stag mode (§31.5) is on, does **not** set a GPS route; instead, if the hovered zone (global `0x0229a2e4`) is non-null with a non-null pointer at `+0x44` and an int at `+0x54` greater than 0, it copies the hovered zone into `0x0229a2ac` and fires the Lua hook `pause_map_stag_completion` (already listed in `spec-lua-bindings.md`) through the existing hook lookup/dispatch trio `0x00e0cef0`/`0x00e0ca80`/`0x00e0cd00`, with the dispatch record's `+0x14` set from global `0x0229a364`. Outside stag mode, or with no valid hovered zone, it does nothing. **[CONFIRMED — disassembly.]**
- The hovered zone `0x0229a2e4` is written by the pause map's per-update refresher `0x007dd700` from `0x0084ba60(cursor position, previous)` — the zone-containment lookup `spec-tables-environment.md` §11.8 already documents. So the "district" the Lua name refers to is, at engine level, the **map zone currently selected on the pause map**, and its `+0x44` is that zone's parent district record. **[CONFIRMED for the lookup/comparison; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the "zone"/"district" role names.]**
- `0x007db3e0` clears both `0x0229a2ac` and `0x0229a2e4`; it is reached only from a pause-map screen teardown/close callback table at `0x0115a668`. **[HIGH CONFIDENCE.]**

### 31.4 The "owned" member flag

Bit `0x02` of member byte `+0x3a` is the "owned by the player" flag. `pause_map_stag_takeover_do_reward` calls `0x005e97a0` on each matching member, which — only while bit `0x02` is still clear — calls `0x005e8b30`, the routine that sets bits `0x02`/`0x01` of `+0x3a`, notifies the parent through `0x0084aeb0` when `+0x4c` is non-null, and (with both of its own arguments 0, under a session-state condition) replicates network opcode `0x45` sub-type `0x1d` for the member's id pair at `+0x08`/`+0x0c`. **This settles §28.15 Q14.6's own OPEN note on `0x005e8b30`'s per-object effect** (cross-referenced there). **[CONFIRMED — disassembly, for the bit writes and the opcode; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the "owned" reading.]** The member weight `+0x3c` is a plain float summed per zone (role HYPOTHESIS: the member's contribution to territory control; OPEN: the member's own object kind).

### 31.5 "stag" is a pause-map mode flag, not a staged/committed pair

There is no staged/committed value pair anywhere in this flow. "stag" names a pause-map mode flag, byte `0x0229a317`. Full reference census (12 uses, 10 functions), **CONFIRMED — disassembly:**

- **Set to 1** only by `0x0071b640` (which then makes further calls opening the pause map, starting with `0x007e1d00(1)` — bodies not dumped, HIGH CONFIDENCE). Its sole caller is the target of **case 48** of the reward-apply switch in `0x0071f170` (jump table `0x0071f8d4`, 61 entries, walking records tagged `"Reward"`). Reward type 48 is **`Auto_Complete_City_Takeover_District`** in `spec-tables-progression.md`'s reward-type table — so stag mode means "the player has been granted a free district takeover and must pick a zone on the map."
- **Cleared** by `pause_map_stag_takeover_do_reward` (§31.6) and by a pause-map close handler `0x007dab20` (referenced only as data from `0x0115a684`, which also clears the tutorial-mode flag `0x0229a318` that `pause_map_is_tutorial_mode` returns).
- **Read** by `pause_map_is_stag_mode` (`0x007d98b0`, returns it as a boolean via `0x00dfe590`), by `pause_map_set_gps` (§31.3), by the map refresher `0x007dd700` (in stag mode it shows district values from `0x0084ce80` instead of `0x0084ce30`), by the bookmark function `0x007df8a0`, and by the autosave gate `0x00b95060` (§27.12) — **autosave is suppressed while stag mode is on.**

Value > 0 → `0x009108b0(value)` stores it in global `0x01308af0` only if ≤ 1.0 (above 1.0 silently ignored, prior value kept); value ≤ 0 → `0x009108d0()` stores −1.0 (the file-backed default = "no override"). Converts the total delta to seconds and calls `0x006fe240(seconds, 1, 0, 1)` then `0x005a2440()`. No range check on the input hour/minute (e.g. 30:90 just makes a bigger forward delta). ~~**[CONFIRMED for the delta arithmetic and forward-only wrap; HIGH CONFIDENCE that `0x006ff1f0`/`0x006ff360` are the actual advance/rewind primitives; HYPOTHESIS — a listener-list at `0x014ff330` and a lighting/weather re-key in `0x005a2440`; OPEN — most callees.]**~~ **RESOLVED (2026-10-03, §48): the forward jump and the `0x006ff1f0`/`0x006ff360` primitive identities are CONFIRMED as stated. The listener list at `0x014ff330` is CONFIRMED to always be empty (no writer anywhere in the image) — it has no practical effect. `0x005a2440` does NOT re-key the weather (no call into the weather state machine at all); it re-keys the **clock itself** (not just the lighting): it snaps the just-jumped-to time to the nearest key of the active time-of-day definition, which can move the hour/minute **backward** from what was just requested. So after `set_time_of_day(h, m)`, the hour byte usually does not equal `h` — it holds the nearest key's hour. Full mechanics, the clock's true 20-byte calendar layout, its per-frame driver, and initial-state sourcing are in §48.**

### 32.4 NPC/party (follower) functions

**`party_add_do` (`0x00a5af70`).** Arguments: arg 1 leader name (via `0x00a280c0`); arg 2 table of follower names (length via the established table-walk helper `0x0083dff0`); arg 3 boolean, no nil-gate; arg 4 optional boolean, nil-gated, default false. No return. **Each resolved follower is written into a fixed 5-slot local array with no bound check against the table's reported length — a 6th-or-later follower (a literal 6+-element table, or a `t.n` ≥ 6) overwrites the saved return address and beyond: a real stack-overrun crash/exploit surface reachable directly from a Lua script.** Scripts must pass at most 5 followers. For each resolved follower: if the leader itself failed to resolve, it is re-resolved per-follower, and the special name `"#CLOSEST_PLAYER#"` (or `"#PLAYER#"`) picks whichever co-op player is nearest that specific follower. Admission then goes through an existing-membership check and a join routine with a capacity/force-override gate (skipped entirely when arg 3 is false), network ownership hand-off when leader/follower authority differ, and (for one specific leader-kind bit) a fuller follower AI/registration setup. **[CONFIRMED for the argument positions, the 5-slot overflow, the per-follower closest-player fallback and the overall control flow; HYPOTHESIS for several internal gate meanings; OPEN — several named callees.]**

### 32.5 Named objects, markers and shops

**`object_destroy` (`0x00a57630`).** 1 string; non-string/nil → no-op. No return. Resolves via a dedicated item/placed-object resolver, liveness-checked, then a capability-predicate virtual call gates a destroy virtual call with no arguments. No record opened in this function itself (replication, if any, is inside the virtual). **[CONFIRMED; HIGH CONFIDENCE — the virtual is the object's own destroy/remove method; OPEN — the virtual's per-kind body.]**

**`object_indicator_remove_do` (`0x00a59190`).** Arg 1 string; arg 2 optional number, nil-gated, default 3 (the established local/replicate bitmask: bit `0x1`=apply locally, bit `0x2`=send a record). No return. Resolves, liveness-checks, then calls a shared indicator-remove helper with ≥30 other callers: bit `0x2` opens an opcode-`0x40` sub-tag-4 record; bit `0x1` **removes every indicator attached to the object, not just one** — it loops asking an indicator-lookup for an entry and removing it until none remain. **[CONFIRMED including the loop-until-none removal; OPEN — the indicator-list internals.]**

**`minimap_icon_remove_do` (`0x00a54430`).** Arg 1 string; arg 2 optional number, nil-gated, default 3 (same bitmask). No return. Objects of one specific kind (a descriptor bit marking "carries its own icon fields") go through a dedicated setter that clears the icon fields to "none," conditionally opening an opcode-`0x40` sub-tag-9 record. **Every other kind goes through an indirect call via a 4-entry function-pointer table (`0x0130cb98`) indexed directly by the caller-supplied mask byte, with NO range check** — an explicit mask of 0 calls a null table entry, and a mask of 4+ reads past the table into garbage (confirmed file-backed table data: `[0]`=null, `[3]`=a real local+replicated removal helper) — **both are real crashes reachable from a Lua script argument**, not merely a theoretical bound issue. **[CONFIRMED for the routing and the missing range check; OPEN — the two un-dumped middle table entries' exact behavior, though their general shape (local-only / replicate-only) is HIGH CONFIDENCE from the 1/2/3 mask convention.]**

Picks the target shop from the world object manager's shop sub-list: **the FIRST shop within 15 units is taken immediately — not the nearest** — falling back to the closest shop within 75 units only if none is within 15. If found, and this machine is host, sends an opcode-`0x45` sub-tag-7 record; every machine then sets a "disabled" bit the opposite of the enable flag, and closes the shop if it was left open while now disabled. **[CONFIRMED including the 15/75-unit thresholds and the first-within-15 rule; HIGH CONFIDENCE — host-replicated shop availability.]**

### 32.6 Items

**`item_show` (`0x00a51d50`).** 1 string; nil → no-op. No return. Resolves an item-kind object, then calls the shared item hide/show setter: without authority and not already inside a replicated apply, opens an opcode-`0x45` sub-tag-`0x13` record addressed to the owner instead of changing anything locally; otherwise flips a "hidden" bit (`+0x3b` bit `0x1`) and, unless a second bit is set, calls the object's own visibility virtual. The registrar slot immediately before this one is very likely `item_hide` (name not read this pass — HYPOTHESIS). **[CONFIRMED; OPEN — the meaning of the setter's "extra" argument, hardcoded to 1 here.]**

**`item_anim_play` (`0x00a51ad0`).** Arg 1 item name; arg 2 animation name (nil → id −1); arg 3 optional boolean, nil-gated, default false; arg 4 optional string, nil-gated, default none. No return, no network record at depth 1 (local-only). Both the animation-name arguments map through the established animation-state name table (§7.11). If arg 4 resolves, it drives a two-state blend-transition call (0.3 s blend) and arg 3 is ignored; otherwise if arg 2 resolves, a single-state start call is made with flag `0x40` when arg 3 is true, else `0x10` (HYPOTHESIS: hold/loop vs. play-once); neither resolving is a no-op. **[CONFIRMED for the argument order and branch rule; HYPOTHESIS for the flag meanings; OPEN — the layer-slot internals.]**

### 32.7 Vehicle-targeted

**`radio_set_station` (`0x00a5c1c0`).** Arg 1 vehicle-or-character name (via the vehicle resolver, which redirects through a character's cached vehicle); arg 2 number (station), no nil-gate, truncated to a signed byte. No return. Two independent effects: (1) a local apply that treats stations as **1-based** (station ≤ 0 or above the station count is rejected — this call can never switch the radio off) and does nothing if the vehicle lacks a radio or the chosen station is itself marked refused; (2) **an opcode-`0x45` sub-tag-`0x17` record is always sent whenever the vehicle resolves, even when the local apply above rejected the station outright.** The vehicle is passed to the record-sender in a register (ESI), not on the stack — a genuine non-standard-register argument, confirmed from the raw instruction listing rather than the decompile (which shows it unassigned). **[CONFIRMED including the always-sent record and the register argument; OPEN — the internal station-attach/detach routines.]**

**`helicopter_shoot_vehicle` (`0x00a4d790`).** The vehicle-target sibling of this document's existing `helicopter_shoot_navpoint`/`helicopter_shoot_human` entries, through the same shared fire dispatcher `0x00b37250`. Arg 1 helicopter name; arg 2 target name (vehicle resolver — so a character name targets that character's own vehicle); arg 3 optional boolean, nil-gated, default true (apply spread); arg 4 optional number, nil-gated, default 1.0 (spread radius); arg 5 optional boolean, nil-gated, default true. Returns 1 boolean: false if either name fails to resolve or the helicopter fails its AI-drive-state gate; otherwise the dispatcher's own result. The spread offset is drawn from a helper that **produces a uniformly distributed point on the unit sphere** (z drawn uniformly in [−1,1], angle drawn separately, x/y from cos/sin scaled by √(1−z²)) — this settles this document's own previously-OPEN question about that helper's exact distribution. The shared dispatcher itself has three confirmed oddities: its own return value is invisible in the decompiled view (only visible in the raw listing); it dereferences address `0x54` when a firing occupant's weapon-info pointer is null (a real null-deref crash path, not script-controlled); and its network record may omit the Z coordinate of the aim point if the field-writer it uses is really only 8 bytes wide (OPEN). **[CONFIRMED for the arguments, the drive-state gate and the dispatcher's control flow; HIGH CONFIDENCE for the uniform-sphere reading; OPEN — the dispatcher's weapon-class/ownership internals and the record-width question.]**

### 32.8 Cross-function observations

Three Lua-reachable crash paths were found in this tranche and are flagged, not resolved: `party_add_do`'s unchecked 5-slot stack array (§32.4); `minimap_icon_remove_do`'s unranged 4-entry function-pointer table (§32.5); and the shared helicopter-fire dispatcher's null-pointer dereference on a missing weapon-info record (§32.7, not script-controlled). `0x009df3d0` is confirmed as the remote co-op player getter — the first live-roster entry that is NOT the local player — which corrects this document's own §8.17 and §14.31 (both edited in place above, 2026-10-02) rather than the "matching" reading those entries previously gave it. New flag bits catalogued: character `+0x1c9c` bit `0x1` trailing_aim, bit `0x40` always_uses_seatbelt; character byte `+0x2b9` bit `0x40` never_turn_on_player; player byte `+0x28ad` bit `0x2` warp_to_shore_disabled. New record sites: opcode `0x40` sub-tags 4 and 9; `0x41` sub-tags 4, `0x1c`, `0x38`; `0x42` sub-tag `0x14`; `0x45` sub-tags 7, `0x13`, `0x17`. Decompiler-artifact catches (settled from the raw listing, not engine bugs): a register-passed argument in `radio_set_station` (ESI) and in `object_indicator_remove_do` (EDI); stack literals mis-attributed to the wrong call in `item_show`; a dropped return value in the shared helicopter-fire dispatcher.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 04 resolved and written up (§32.1-§32.7); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above.

## 33. Ranking tranche 05 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Crreish-sync\for-team-a\team-a\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-05.json` (names 51-75 of 554, Team B call-count order; all low-traffic, 2-3 calls each). Every name is a single registration in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; all 25 resolved. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 33.1 Vehicle cluster (11 functions)

**`vehicle_is_helicopter` (`0x00a66070`).** 1 string. 1 boolean. Bypasses the usual vehicle-instance resolver entirely — uses the by-name vehicle lookup directly, so a character/driver name never resolves here. True only when `(vehicle+0xbf4)+0x2c` equals **3**. The same field is tested for "3 or 4" by this document's existing helicopter commands and for "==4" by the two VTOL queries below — **so a VTOL (mode 4) answers false here**, unlike those other commands. HYPOTHESIS: `+0xbf4` is the vehicle's class/definition record, `+0x2c` a flying-type enum (3=helicopter, 4=VTOL).

**`vehicle_is_vtol_hover` (`0x00a64700`) / `vehicle_is_vtol_jet` (`0x00a64770`).** 1 string, via the vehicle-instance resolver. **Both push a stray extra `false` after a successful `true` on the success path and return 2 values instead of 1** (a real stack-discipline defect, not a design choice — the success branch falls through into the failure path's own push instead of returning) — an `if f(v) then` call site still sees the right answer, but a byte-for-byte-faithful reimplementation must reproduce the extra value. Gate: flying-type `+0x2c`==4 (not 3). "Hover" = vehicle `+0x5e8` ∈ {0,3}; "jet" = `+0x5e8` ∈ {1,2} (HYPOTHESIS for the state meanings; a non-VTOL just answers a single false either way).

**`vehicle_is_ready` (`0x00a62820`).** 1 string, via the vehicle resolver. 1 boolean: unresolved → false; else the negation of a "not ready" predicate this document's existing `vehicle_is_destroyed`-adjacent entry already calls without opening — now resolved: not-ready when a byte-`0x3b`-bit-0 flag is set, OR a byte-`0x3a`-bit-0 flag is set, OR the vehicle is null, OR byte-`0x33` bit `0x8` is clear. So **ready = `+0x3b` bit 0 clear AND `+0x3a` bit 0 clear AND `+0x33` bit `0x8` set**; the meanings of the two low bits are OPEN, but `+0x33` bit `0x8` cross-links to the kneecapper setter below (same bit, "vehicle object fully set up," HIGH CONFIDENCE).

**`vehicle_never_flatten_tires` (`0x00a62a60`).** 1 string + 1 optional boolean, default true. No return. Double-gate setter: local write = vehicle byte `+0x1d7b` bit `0x1`; else an opcode-`0x46` record tagged `"vehicle"`/`"m_force_flagsnever_flatten_tires"`. Reader not traced (OPEN).

**`vehicle_set_weapons_disarmed` (`0x00a63520`).** 1 string + 1 boolean (no nil-gate, absent→false). Same double-gate shape: local write = `+0x1d7e` bit `0x4`; tags `"vehicle"`/`"m_force_flagsweapons_disabled"` (the engine's own flag name is "disabled," the Lua name says "disarmed" — same bit).

**`vehicle_set_no_chase` (`0x00a62b80`).** 1 string + 1 boolean (no nil-gate). Setter runs on the vehicle-AI sub-record (handle `+0xc68`), writing sub-byte `+5` bit `0x1`; tags `"vehicle_ai"`/`"vai_force_flagsno_chase"`. **Reaches the exact same setter as this document's existing `vehicle_disable_chase` entry** (through one extra double-negation wrapper there) — the two Lua names write the identical bit; they differ only in default (`vehicle_disable_chase` defaults true, this one defaults false) and the extra wrapper.

**`vehicle_set_kneecappers` (`0x00a62fe0`).** 1 string + 1 optional boolean, default true. Attaches or removes a per-wheel spike/collision controller at vehicle `+0x1550`, drawn from a fixed 48-vehicle pool: enabling when the vehicle isn't yet "set up" (`+0x33` bit `0x8` clear) only sets a **deferred-request bit** (`+0x16cc` bit `0x8`) rather than attaching immediately; once set up, allocates a pool slot and builds one collision box per wheel. Disabling releases each wheel's physics object, destroys any attached id-pair object, and returns the slot to the pool (also clearing the deferred bit if that's all there was). No replication at this level. Whether the deferred bit is later honored automatically is OPEN.

**`vehicle_set_sirenlights` (`0x00a64490`).** 1 string + 1 boolean (no nil-gate). Re-resolves the vehicle by id pair (bypassing the normal resolver) and requires body-active byte `+0xbd0`==1. Switches on a vehicle-class enum at `(vehicle+0xbf4)+0x4c4`: classes 3/5/6/7/8/11 get both flashing headlights (byte `+0x1d7c` bit `0x10`) and siren lights (bit `0x8`); class 12 gets siren lights only; every other class gets both only if a per-class record flag allows it, otherwise both are forced off with no further effect. Except on the forced-off path, also drives the actual siren **sound** (starts/stops a Wwise event on the vehicle's emitter, tracked by a byte flag) to match the boolean.

**`vehicle_set_ambient` (`0x00a62ad0`).** 1 string + 1 optional number, default −1.0. No return. Marks the vehicle (byte `+0x16c0` bit `0x1`), puts its AI sub-record into **mode 6, sub-mode 0x11**, with no target (HYPOTHESIS: ambient/traffic driving) — authority-gated the usual way (opcode-`0x42` sub-code 12 if not authoritative). If the number is ≥ 0.0, also caps the vehicle's speed (clamped to at most 1000.0) via the same setter this document's existing `vehicle_speed_override` entry uses — **but passes the number unconverted**, while that other entry multiplies by the mph→m/s factor 0.44704 first; so the two take different units into the identical setter. Mode 6/sub-mode 0x11's meaning is OPEN.

**`vehicle_spotlight_is_target_spotted` (`0x00a65e70`).** 1 string (vehicle or its driver) + 1 string (target, via the general object resolver). 1 boolean. **Not a pure query**: it first writes the target's id pair into the vehicle's spotlight object (re-aiming it) as a side effect, every call, before testing anything. Requires body-active byte `+0xbd0`==1 and a live spotlight. The test itself: range ≤ 80 units, a ≤10° cone from the light's forward axis, and an unobstructed ray cast to a point 1.85 units above the target's own origin.

### 33.2 AI cluster (4 functions)

All four resolve their character argument through the established `#FOLLOWER#`-family character chain.

**`ai_clear_priority_target` (`0x00a3c320`).** 1 string. No return. Sets the character's AI forced-target field to the null id pair. Uses a **single-gate** (not double-gate) setter — same family previously seen only in the "leash" functions — local write when authoritative, else an opcode-`0x46` record tagged `"human_ai_data"`/`"forced_target_handle"`.

**`ai_set_in_scripted_cover` (`0x00a3c3a0`).** 1 string + 1 boolean (no nil-gate). Returns 1 boolean: false only if the character doesn't resolve. Double-gate setter on the AI force-flag byte (bit `0x1` of the same byte this document's existing ignore-AI-flag entry uses bit `0x2` of); tags `"human_ai_data"`/`"ai_force_flagsin_scripted_cover"`. **When the boolean is false, additionally queues scripted action 13 with no target** (HYPOTHESIS: "leave cover"/idle; sibling of this document's existing scripted-take-cover entry, action 8). Meaning of action 13 is OPEN.

**`ai_pay_attention_to_position` (`0x00a3d720`).** 1 character string + 1 object string (via the general object resolver) + 1 optional boolean, default true. No return. Authority-gated: locally, copies the object's position into the character's "attention" sub-block and sets attention mode **7** (true) or **3** (false) — bit `0x4` of the mode is exactly the Lua boolean; without authority, an opcode-`0x43` sub-code-50 request. Makes an NPC face/attend to a world position once (copied, not tracked). What the mode-7-vs-3 variant changes internally is OPEN (HYPOTHESIS: head-only vs. whole-body facing).

**`ai_do_scripted_rush` (`0x00a3e870`).** 1 character string + 1 optional target string (character or object), default none. Returns 1 boolean. With no target: rushes the character's own current combat target, subject to reachability/distance checks (refused if already close enough, if the target is already engaged in melee, or if a destination can't be found) — accepted immediately if the character's current scripted action is already 22. With a target: copies that target's current position directly. Either way, success starts scripted action **22** ("rush") — the exact structural twin of this document's existing scripted-take-cover entry (action 8), but storing a raw position instead of an id pair.

### 33.3 Action cluster (3 functions)

**`action_play_synced_do` (`0x00a3fe10`).** 2 mandatory actor-name strings + 1 mandatory synced-action-name string + 1 optional anchor-object string, default none. Returns 1 number: **−1** if both actors resolved and actor 1 is dead; **1** if the final play call succeeds; **0** otherwise. **Unlike this document's existing §14.1 `action_play_synced_state` entry (corrected above), an unresolved actor here does NOT short-circuit — the function continues with a null handle.** The synced-action name is turned into an index by `0x0095da50` (name → index lookup — see the §14.1 correction above, which this same investigation settled). In multiplayer, always sends an opcode-`0x43` sub-code-19 record (actor ids, anchor id, action index) in addition to, not instead of, playing locally with the anchor's transform if one was given. What a null actor does inside the final play call is OPEN.

**`action_play_directional_stumble_do` (`0x00a3f7d0`).** 1 character string + 1 reference-object string + 1 optional boolean (selects between two animation-id sets), default false. **Return is a variable number of values — the function never returns early, and pushes `-1.0` for each individual failure (character unresolved, object unresolved/dead, character dead, animation id not found) followed by an unconditional final `1.0`; the actual C return value is the push count.** A clean success returns just `1.0`; a dead character returns `(-1.0, 1.0)` and **still plays the stumble anyway**. **Because nothing returns early, an unresolved object or character leads to a genuine null-pointer dereference later in the function (reads through address `0x64`/`0x68` relative to the null pointer) — a real access-violation crash in the shipped game reachable from bad Lua arguments; an implementation should treat these as script errors, not reproduce the crash.** On the normal path: interrupts the character's current action, blends out animation layers, and picks a "front" vs. "not front" animation depending on whether the reference object's heading is within 45° of the character's own — **the code's apparent intent to also distinguish "back"/"left"/"right" is dead: a second comparison re-tests the same 45° constant with its operands swapped, so that branch can never be taken for any non-NaN input.** CONFIRMED from the listing.

**`action_sequence_end` (`0x00a3c270`).** No arguments. No return. A global "end the current scripted cutscene sequence" teardown: clears a shared sequence object, releases a tracked id pair if one is held, clears a per-player scripted-camera/target field on both the local player and (if present) the remote co-op player, releases one more tracked handle, and — **host only** — broadcasts an opcode-`0x49` record with a single byte, value 2. HYPOTHESIS: "sequence" = an in-engine scripted cutscene; several callees remain OPEN.

### 33.4 Audio cluster (4 functions)

**`audio_set_listener_override` (`0x00a3dc70`) / `audio_clear_listener_override` (`0x00a3c860`).** Set takes 1 object-name string (via the general object resolver, requiring one specific descriptor bit — HYPOTHESIS: "human/character" kind); clear takes none. Both store an id pair (and its compressed 16-bit network id) into a pair of fixed globals and **always** send an opcode-`0x45` record with that id — no authority gate, no local/remote split (clear sends the same record with id 0). The per-frame reader snapshots the override object's position/orientation into a fixed block each frame when the pair resolves to something live, and the listener-update routine substitutes that block for the normal player/camera path whenever the override is active; a peer that only received the network id resolves the pair lazily. Makes the audio listener follow a named object (or, cleared, fall back to its default source).

**`audio_play_for_navpoint` (`0x00a3edf0`).** 1 sound/event-name string + 1 object-name string (via the third-tier by-name resolver) + 1 optional string that is **read and discarded**, never used (the same "read but inert" pattern this document already records elsewhere). Returns 1 number: the playing instance's id, or 0 on failure. Plays a sound event positioned on the named object through this document's own shared audio-play core.

**`audio_any_conversation_playing` (`0x00a3c640`).** No arguments. Returns 1 boolean: true if any session member currently has a valid, non-0xff slot in the global **"mission_conv"** per-session channel — **this settles this document's own previously-OPEN identity question for that channel global** (created by a dedicated helper against the session object, named literally "mission_conv"). The same per-member 5-byte-slot layout this document's existing session-conversation entry already reads on a different channel offset is confirmed as a generic, reusable mechanism — "mission_conv" is just one such channel among possibly several.

### 33.5 Other (3 functions)

**`boss_battle_matt_begin` (`0x00a407c0`).** 1 optional boolean, default true. No return. Fully resets the Matt-boss encounter's dedicated state block (counters, deadlines, cheat slots, four sub-objects, all to their neutral/−1 values), then immediately arms its first deadline (5000 ms if the boolean is true, 0/immediate if false) and marks it active. Also looks up the character literally named **"Matt"** and, if found and alive, sets bit `0x4000` of its dword `+0xec` (meaning OPEN). Pairs with this document's existing Matt-boss cheat-stop entries. No replication.

**`auto_pickup_disable` (`0x00a3c8a0`)** (with its unregistered-this-pass neighbor, almost certainly `auto_pickup_enable`). No arguments, no return. Writes to a **named, session-synchronized variable "allow_weapon_auto_pickup"** (not a bare global — it's registered through a session-variable mechanism with the host as owner), which a pickup-decision routine tests before allowing automatic weapon pickup. Corrected subsystem note: this turns off automatic **weapon** pickup specifically, and the flag is session-wide, not per-player.

**`waiting_for_player_dialog` (`0x00a68ea0`).** 1 boolean (no nil-gate). No return. Reference-counted show/hide of the co-op "waiting for the other player" dialog — nested shows need an equal number of hides; a hide when the counter is already 0 does nothing. Showing increments the counter even when a suppressing game-state check blocks the actual display (in which case only a "pending" flag is set). On the final hide (counter reaches 0), the **host**, while co-op is active, broadcasts an opcode-`0x23` record with 3 bytes (show/hide, and two state bytes); the host also sends the matching show broadcast when the display actually appears. **Open hazard, not resolved:** neither the show nor the hide path ever clears the "currently shown" byte except via an untraced third writer, so after one real display, a second show can silently skip the display branch if that writer never runs — OPEN.

### 33.6 Cross-cutting findings

Two more stack-discipline defects of the same shape already seen elsewhere in this document: `vehicle_is_vtol_hover`/`vehicle_is_vtol_jet` push an extra `false` after a successful `true` (§33.1); `action_play_directional_stumble_do` pushes a variable count ending in a final `1.0` and never returns early, which is also what creates its null-dereference crash path (§33.3). A dead code branch is confirmed in `action_play_directional_stumble_do` (duplicate-constant comparison, §33.3). The §14.1 `0x0095da50` correction (applied in place above) and the `0x014e9ad0`/"mission_conv" identification (§33.4) both resolve previously-OPEN items. New force-flag bits: vehicle `+0x1d7b` bit `0x1` (never_flatten_tires), `+0x1d7e` bit `0x4` (weapons_disabled), vehicle-AI sub-byte `+5` bit `0x1` (no_chase, shared with the existing `vehicle_disable_chase` entry), AI byte `+0xc` bit `0x1` (in_scripted_cover). New record sites: opcode `0x45` always-sent listener override; `0x49` byte-2 (sequence end, host-only); `0x23` waiting-dialog (host-only); `0x43` sub-codes 50 (pay-attention) and 19 (synced play); `0x42` sub-code 12 (vehicle-AI mode).

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 05 resolved and written up (§33.1-§33.5); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: scripted actions 13 and 22's exact meaning, the VTOL `+0x5e8` state values, vehicle-AI mode 6/0x11, bit `0x4000`@`+0xec` on "Matt", and the untraced writer that would reset the waiting-dialog's "shown" byte.

## 34. Character spawn-time defaults — max HP and ignore-AI (2026-10-02)

**Why.** §3.4 and §7.12/§13.20's cross-cutting finding 7 document the Lua *setters* of `+0x1cac` (max-HP cap) and `+0x2bc` mask `0x02` (ignore-AI), but not what value a freshly spawned character holds before any script touches them — needed to resolve a partner-team mission-drive trace's `OPEN_STATE` on these two fields across 98 missions. Investigated against the real executable; the `.czn_pc` object-placement interior stayed PARKED throughout — no zone bytes were opened, only the code that reads that stream.

### 34.1 Spawn sequence

A character is built the same way as any other registry object (§29): class constructor, then registry slot-11 initialise, then the object's own vtable slot 1 ("read my properties from the record"). For a character:

1. **Constructor `0x00954340`** writes placeholder zeros: `+0x1cac` (max HP) = 0, `+0x1cb0` (see §34.2) = 0, `+0x1cb8` (current HP) = 0.0. It also constructs the per-character AI-data sub-object in place at `+0x2b0` (via `0x004e46c0`), whose own constructor clears its `+0xc` word through `0x004dde30` — i.e. character `+0x2bc` = 0 (ignore-AI off) at construction. Two derived constructors (`0x009d4700`, `0x009de970`) both chain to this one; `0x009d4700` also zeroes `+0x1da8` (§34.3).
2. **Base vtable slot 1, `0x0096ec80`**: resolves the character's preset (`human_preset`/`human_preset_name` property → `0x00be3360`, stored at `+0xf0`), picks a level index, and computes the real spawn max HP from a data table (§34.2) via `0x0094d1f0`'s forced/authoritative branch (bonus 0) — `+0x1cac` = that table value, and `+0x1cb8` (current HP) is set to the same value immediately after: **a character spawns at full health**.
3. **Derived vtable slot 1, `0x009d8930`** (overrides slot 1 on the derived classes; chains to step 2 first): checks one more record property (a script-NPC-peer descriptor). Absent → calls `0x009d7480(1, 0)` on the character, which recomputes the identical table-sourced max HP and re-clears ignore-AI (same result as step 2, redundantly). Present → binds a **script NPC** object (§34.3) to the character first, then `0x009d7480` applies that script NPC's own overrides instead.

### 34.2 Max HP (`+0x1cac`) — table-sourced by default, with a script-NPC override

**Default: `+0x1cac` = round(M × `Hit_Points`)**, where `Hit_Points` is the 16-bit field at `+0x0a` of the selected `spawn_info_ranks.xtbl` `<Rank>` record (array `0x029a91a0`, already documented in `spec-tables-progression.md` §10.6). The starting record is the one the character's `character_definitions.xtbl` preset points to at preset `+0x28` (HIGH CONFIDENCE from use — the definition reader `0x00be0630` itself was not opened); `0x00be4830(rank, levelIndex)` re-picks it to the record of the same `type` (`+0x04`) whose `rank_numeric` (`+0x08`) equals the character's level index, except for three rank types (numeric `2`, `6`, `7` — HIGH CONFIDENCE these are Homie/Other/Specialist per the xtbl's own type list, by position not name) which are used as-is without re-picking. The level index is `0x0096e830()` for ordinary classes, or a fixed 0 for one class family (a descriptor-table bit test); OPEN — what `0x0096e830` (and its own gate `0x005f4ad0`/`0x006d2910`) actually reads to choose a level. The multiplier M is 1.0 unless class test `0x00853b30(character, 0x22)` holds, in which case it is a float field (`+0x20` or `+0x1c`, selected by a further test) of the object `0x005f4a50()` returns — HYPOTHESIS: a difficulty/game-settings block; not opened. The row's sibling 16-bit field at `+0x0e` (knockdown points) is written to `+0x1320`/`+0x1324` by the same code path.

**Override:** if the character is bound to a **script NPC** object (character `+0x1da8`, §34.3) whose own record property `script_npc_hp` was present and is ≥ 1, `0x009d7480` uses that value for `+0x1cac` verbatim instead of the table formula. A script NPC's own constructor defaults that field to −1 ("use the table"); `commando_spawn`-produced script NPCs (builder `0x00a33b80`) never set `script_npc_hp`, so they always fall back to the table.

**`+0x1cb0` is the max-HP bonus, not a base** — see the correction already applied in place at §13.20 above (own setter `0x0094d380`, record tag `"max_hit_point_bonus"`). It is 0 on every spawn path; only an explicit later script call changes it.

**Current HP (`+0x1cb8`)** starts equal to the table value (step 2 of §34.1) and is not rewritten by `0x009d7480` itself. Whether it is refilled to match a `script_npc_hp` override that differs from the table value is HYPOTHESIS/OPEN (would need `0x009d7480`'s trailing helpers `0x0096e6e0`/`0x00943cc0`/`0x009659f0` opened).

### 34.3 Ignore-AI (`+0x2bc` mask `0x02`) — engine default off, with a script-NPC override

**Default: off (0)**, cleared by `0x004dde30` at construction and re-cleared by `0x004e5a50(character, 1)` inside `0x009d7480`'s no-script-NPC path (§34.1 step 3).

**Override:** a character bound to a script NPC (character `+0x1da8`, a two-way bind via `0x00a33380` — vtable `0x0117efec`, the same "script NPC"/"script mover" object family `spec-lua-api-behaviour.md`'s own named-object-registration section (§29) already identifies as a Lua-module object) whose record property **`script_npc_flags`** contains the literal flag name **`ignore_ai`** spawns with ignore-AI **on**. The flag-name table (`0x00a33ff0`, built once at startup) hashes `"ignore_ai"` to mask `0x00001000` in the script NPC's own 64-bit flag word (`+0xac`/`+0xb0`); `0x004e5a50` copies bit `0x10` of that word's byte `+0xad` into AI-block `+0xc` mask `0x02` — i.e. character `+0x2bc` mask `0x02`. Releasing the character from its script NPC (unbind, vtable slot 23 = `0x00a33480`) clears both this bit and one other (mask `0x04`) again.

**This resolves §3.4's own OPEN note** (already struck through and resolved in place above): `0x004e2050`'s `this` is confirmed to be character `+0x2b0` (the AI-data sub-object), so its own `+0xc` write and the `+0x2bc` read are the identical byte, mask `0x02`.

### 34.4 The script NPC object and the `.czn_pc` boundary

A script NPC (constructor `0x00a33600`) reads its own record's properties on its slot 1 (`0x00a35b00`): besides `script_npc_hp`/`script_npc_flags` (§34.2/§34.3), it also carries `script_npc_char_preset`(_name), `script_npc_bleed_hp`, `script_npc_knockdown_hp`, `script_npc_hearing_distance`, `script_npc_leash`, `script_npc_team`, `script_npc_personality`(_idx), `script_npc_char_scale`, and `script_npc_items`/`script_npc_loots` — none of those further properties were traced for effect this pass (OPEN). In-memory producers found by this pass (`commando_spawn`'s builder `0x00a33b80`; the script-NPC's own spawn routine `0x00a34f00`) never set `script_npc_hp` or an `ignore_ai` flag. The only **file-borne** producer of any registry record, per §29's own census, is the zone's top-level `0x2234` record ("Game objects, as placed in the WE"). **So for a script NPC placed in the world editor, whether its placement record carries `script_npc_hp` or an `ignore_ai` flag is zone data — the same `.czn_pc` interior §29 already stops at. This investigation stops there too: no `.czn_pc` bytes were opened, requested, or read.**

**Practical reading:** without the zone data, the faithful spawn default for every character is max HP = the rank-table value (bonus 0, current HP = max), ignore-AI = off — **correct for a character whose placement record is not a script NPC, or is one with neither override property set, and wrong exactly for those that do carry one.** Which of a given mission's characters fall into the second group cannot be determined from code alone.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** spawn mechanism CONFIRMED — disassembly for both fields' full default-value chain; the data-table formula and the script-NPC override path are both traced to their respective record properties. Residual OPEN (all code-only, collected from the investigation): `0x0096e830`'s own level-choice logic; the multiplier block `0x005f4a50`; confirming preset `+0x28` from the `character_definitions.xtbl` reader `0x00be0630` itself (currently HIGH CONFIDENCE from use only); whether current HP is refilled under a `script_npc_hp` override; the other `+0x1da8` producers/binders not read this pass (`0x009e35b0`, `0x009e38e0`, the stream deserializer `0x00a354e0`, the mission-module binders `0x00735940`/`0x0072c260`/`0x006d2fc0`). The zone-data question itself (which placed characters are script NPCs, and what their records carry) is explicitly out of scope pending the parked `.czn_pc` interior.

## 35. `teleport_coop` and the scripted-request completion pool (2026-10-02)

**Why.** Three missions (`dlc2_m01`, `m13`, `m19`) sit suspended at `game_lib.lua:2956`, inside `teleport_coop`, because a partner host's `teleport_check_done` stub returns nil. Investigated against the real executable and the shipped `game_lib.lua` (read-only, extracted from `misc.vpp_pc`) to settle what drives completion. Corrections this investigation forced onto §4.3/§15.17/§22.4/§22.15/§26.24 above, and on `spec-world-streaming.md` §11.3, are already applied in place; this section documents the mechanism itself.

### 35.1 `teleport_coop` is a script helper, not an engine binding

The name is absent from the 1,014-entry gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`, the 113-entry loop registrar `0x00845aa0`, and the full 1,490-name tagged roster. It is a plain Lua function defined in the shared library script `game_lib.lua` (definition at line 2940 of the shipped file; `LOCAL_PLAYER`/`REMOTE_PLAYER` are that same file's own string constants `"#PLAYER1#"`/`"#PLAYER2#"`). Its body: call the no-op assertion `assert_screen_is_faded_out` (`0x007c9f50`, already catalogued elsewhere in this document); if `coop_is_active()` is true, teleport `"#PLAYER2#"` to its destination; always teleport `"#PLAYER1#"` to its destination; if co-op is active, show the "waiting for player" dialog and poll `teleport_check_done("#PLAYER2#")` once per scheduler tick until true, then hide the dialog; always poll `teleport_check_done("#PLAYER1#")` once per tick until true (the line the three missions are parked on). In single player `coop_is_active()` is false, so the whole remote half is skipped — the helper reduces to one `teleport` call plus a poll on the local player's own completion.

### 35.2 The shared scripted-request pool behind every `*_check_done` native

`teleport_check_done`, `turn_to_check_done`, `move_to_check_done` and `vehicle_pathfind_check_done` (§9.10) are all thin queries over one small engine module (`0x006f6040`-`0x006f68a2`) that tracks "scripted requests." **Storage:** 200 records of 40 bytes in a static block at `0x014f4be8`, threaded on an active list (head `0x014f4be0`) and a free list (head `0x014f4be4`); `0x006f60b0` (called once, from start-of-game set-up `0x00708330`) resets the block. **Record layout:** `+0x00`/`+0x04` list links; `+0x08` flags (bit `0x1` = done); `+0xc` kind (a small integer — kind 0 = turn-to, kind 2 = move-to/pathfind, **kind 4 = teleport**); `+0x10` a 16-bit request id; `+0x18`/`+0x1c` the target's 8-byte handle; `+0x20` an optional completion callback. **Allocate — `0x006f62b0(object, kind, callback)`:** releases any existing record for the same object+kind first (a new request silently supersedes an old one), forms the id as `(machine index << 12) | counter` (machine index from `0x008677f0` → `0x0087ba20`, **0 with no session**), takes a free-list record, returns the id (or 0 on refusal — null object, a dead/unusable object, or an exhausted free list). **Status — `0x006f6380(object, kind)`** (register-argument: object in ECX, kind in EDI, into the finder `0x006f6260`, which matches on both handle and kind): **2 = no matching record** (never issued, already consumed, superseded, reaped, or an unresolved name); **1 = done** (releases the record back to the free list as a side effect); **0 = pending**. **Complete — `0x006f66d0(id, a, b)`:** local machine nibble → sets the done bit and fires any stored callback with `(a, b)`;
