remote nibble → forwards an opcode-`0x38` sub-type-0 network record to that machine, carrying the id and the `(a, b)` payload. **Cancel — `0x006f6680(id)`:** local → release; remote → opcode-`0x38` sub-type 1. **Reaper — `0x006f6820`** (called every frame from the world-update routine `0x00702a50`, HIGH CONFIDENCE): releases any active record whose handle no longer resolves, is flagged uninitialised, or fails liveness.

So **every boolean `*_check_done` built on this status function returns true for "done" or "no request," and false only while genuinely pending** — this convention is confirmed directly for `teleport_check_done` (§15.17, corrected above), `vehicle_pathfind_check_done` (§9.10, already correct and the reference reading), and `move_to_check_done` (§22.15, corrected above); `turn_to_check_done` (`0x00a61dd0`, kind 0) was confirmed to use the same status function but not independently re-read for its own wrapper logic.

### 35.3 The player path: an asynchronous teleport, game mode 8

`teleport` (§4.3) allocates a kind-4 request, then for a **player** target (class-row `+0xa` bit `0x2`) calls `0x009e2220`, which — with local authority (or when global `0x00bc5610` is set) — stores the request into a 2-slot ring at `0x02242068` (target, destination position/orientation, flag bytes, the 16-bit request id) and pushes **game mode 8**, the asynchronous player-teleport mode (registered by `0x007a8530`: enter `0x007a7cb0`, exit `0x007a7de0`, may-leave predicate `0x007a7db0`, per-frame handler `0x007a82c0` — log strings `"teleport_enter"`/`"teleport_exit"`/`"UI_Async_Teleport"`/`"UI_Async_Teleport_Stop"`). Each frame while mode 8 is active, `0x007a82c0`: waits for any requested screen fade-out to settle; on the first frame for a slot, moves the streaming focus to the slot's destination (`0x0085bce0`, `spec-world-streaming.md` §11.3) and applies its orientation to a view; waits for background loading at the destination to finish idle (`0x007a8140` → `0x00dafa90`); once loading is done, moves the target (`0x009e69d0`) and clears the slot's busy flag; on a later frame with the slot no longer busy, stops the UI and pops mode 8. The exit handler **completes the kind-4 request** (`0x006f66d0`) and, if a fade-out was requested, starts a fade-in. **Net effect: `teleport` returns at once with a pending request; the request becomes done when mode 8 exits — at least one frame after streaming at the destination is idle and any fade-out has finished, plus one more frame to pop the mode.** Without local authority, an opcode-`0x41` record (inner type `0x17`) goes to the target's owner instead, and completion arrives later as an opcode-`0x38` sub-type-0 reply.

### 35.4 The non-player path: immediate completion

For a non-player target, `teleport` calls `0x00996b50` (also used by `teleport_to_object`, §22.4, and many engine callers): with local authority (or during an active cutscene, or for the local player specifically when `0x00bc5610` is set), it applies the move directly (vehicle-exit handling, physics/animation/camera resets, the actual placement) and **completes the kind-4 request before `teleport` itself returns** (`0x006f66d0(id, 0, 0)`, via the common exit point `0x009970b3`). Without local authority, an opcode-`0x41` record (inner type `0x16`) goes to the owner instead, with no local completion.

### 35.5 Co-op/host gating — no host check at all on this path

`teleport` and `teleport_check_done` contain **no** reference to the `0x0087ba20` `+0x5c`==`+0x58` host predicate this document uses elsewhere. The only co-op test anywhere in the chain is the script helper's own `coop_is_active()` (§35.1). The engine side instead branches on an **authority** gate, `0x008addb0(object, 0)` → `0x00884760(object+0x3c, 0)` — which inspects the object's own network-record owner byte (true for a null object, a `0xff` owner byte, or no network record/manager at all; compares the owner byte to the local machine only when a record and manager both exist) — plus the global `0x00bc5610`. The session is consulted only to form the request id's machine-index nibble (§35.2). **With no session installed, every one of these independently resolves to "local": `coop_is_active` false, machine nibble 0, authority true for the local player — so the no-session branch is simply the ordinary local branch: move performed locally (player: via mode 8; non-player: immediately), request completed locally, nothing sent to or awaited from another machine.**

### 35.6 Why Team B's host stalls, and the minimal fix

`teleport_check_done`'s correct answer to "no request exists" is **true** (§35.2) — not nil, and not a value that depends on co-op state. A host that leaves it unmodelled (returns nil) can never satisfy `until teleport_check_done(LOCAL_PLAYER)`, however many ticks pass. **Minimum correct model:** return true unless the host is actually tracking a pending teleport for that character — with no model of asynchronous teleports at all, that is simply "always true," and `teleport_coop` then finishes after exactly one scheduler yield. **Faithful model:** keep a per-(character, kind) pending-request table; `teleport` marks a non-player target's request done immediately, and a player target's request done no earlier than the next tick (after any fade-out/streaming wait the host chooses to model); a "done" read deletes the record, matching the real engine's own release-on-read behavior.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** mechanism CONFIRMED — disassembly throughout (§35.2-§35.5); `teleport_coop` itself CONFIRMED — script text. Real corrections applied in place to §4.3, §15.17 (and its own §15.30 cross-reference), §22.4, §22.15, §26.24, and `spec-world-streaming.md` §11.3. OPEN: class-row `+0xa` bit `0x2` as "player class" is HIGH CONFIDENCE from three consistent uses, not read from a built descriptor row; the role of global `0x00bc5610`/`0x029443bc`; mode 5's exact identity (HIGH CONFIDENCE gameplay mode); the superseded-ring-slot edge case (not reachable in single player); `0x009e69d0`'s own use of the "exit vehicles" flag.

## 36. How a mission's `<stem>_start` is actually invoked (2026-10-02)

**Why.** Team B's host called a mission's `<stem>_start(checkpoint, is_restart)` with `checkpoint = 0` on a fresh start; `dlc2_m02`'s script then indexed its checkpoint table with `0` and got nil. `spec-lua-bindings.md` §14.2 and §14.6-§14.10 had already exhaustively ruled out every EXE-side and Lua-VM-side string-construction mechanism for how a mission's start function is even named, leaving the real invocation mechanism OPEN. This section resolves it (cross-referenced from `spec-lua-bindings.md` §14.11, which carries the narrative of why the prior searches came back negative — not duplicated here).

### 36.1 The start-function name is a data-borne string property, not a built or literal name

A mission is represented by a `scripted_mission_start` object (RTTI name `0x0113c288`). Its own "read my properties" method (vtable slot 1, `0x006e30d0`) reads a cluster of hash-keyed record properties, among them the string **`script_mission_start`**, stored into the object's own `+0x1f0` field. **If that property is absent, the object fails to initialise — a mission object without a start-function name cannot exist.** Sibling properties on the same object name the mission's other entry points: `script_mission_setup` (`+0x1ec`), `script_mission_cleanup` (`+0x1f4`), `script_mission_success` (`+0x1f8`), `script_mission_skipped` (`+0x1fc`) — none of their own call sites were traced this pass. A sibling class, `silent_mission_start` (RTTI `0x0113c530`, its own `silent_cutscene_name`/`silent_success_function` properties), was not investigated. **This pass is code-only — the property reader and the initialisation gate above were disassembled, but no zone or other placement bytes of any kind were opened.** Which carrier actually holds a given mission's record is therefore itself OPEN, not narrowed to one candidate: **HYPOTHESIS** candidates are the zone's `0x2234` placement stream (the same parked `.czn_pc` interior §29 stops at for Killbane), a mission package/table, or another serialised carrier not traced this pass — settling it would need the class's constructor/instantiator traced outward to its creator (not attempted), and, if the trail leads to the zone stream, that parked interior opened. Confirming that shipped missions' `script_mission_start` values actually follow the `<stem>_start` pattern a partner team's census found would need the same step.

### 36.2 The two native call sites

Both reach the identical sequence: `0x00e0ca80(name = currentMission+0x1f0, state = 0x026e7e6c, 0, 0)` — the same named-global-lookup/coroutine-creation primitive this document's own thread-table section already establishes — looks the name up in the gameplay Lua state's globals (a plain global lookup, no special-casing), requires it to be a Lua function, creates a new coroutine, and appends a not-yet-started thread record. The caller then pushes exactly two arguments onto that record — the checkpoint name as a string (`0x00e0cfb0`) and the restart flag as a boolean (`0x00e0ce00`) — and leaves it there; **no immediate call happens.** The per-frame scheduler (`0x00e0cf50`, §29/thread-table) starts the coroutine with those two arguments on a later tick.

| Site | When it fires | Checkpoint-name argument |
|---|---|---|
| `0x006d5460` (stored in the mission start marker's `+0xe8` callback slot; called directly when the player walks into the marker) | Ordinary story-mission entry, after any pre-start phone call | Freshly set, one instruction before the push, to the literal `"mission start"` (`0x0113aa20`) |
| `0x006d9310` (undefined code; the enter handler of one game-mode state, table slot `0x012f473c` — which numbered state is OPEN) | A mission with no pre-start phone call, or any restart | Whatever the current-checkpoint-name global (§36.3) already holds |

### 36.3 The current-checkpoint-name global (`0x014c8354`) and the restart flag (`0x014c8324`)

**`0x014c8354`** holds the mission's current checkpoint name as a heap-allocated Lua string, set via `0x006ce930` ("set current checkpoint name": frees the old string, allocates and copies the new one). Its lifecycle: the mission system's one-time initialiser (`0x006d6010`) sets it to `"mission start"` at start-up, so it is **never null**; every "begin a mission" entry point resets it to `"mission start"` before making the mission current; the one parameterised entry (`0x006d7120`) substitutes `"mission start"` whenever its own name argument is null; and `mission_set_checkpoint`'s native handler (`0x00a52600` → `0x006d5060`, already documented in `spec-lua-bindings.md` §14.7) writes the script's own reported checkpoint name straight into it. **Loading a save unconditionally resets it to `"mission start"`** (`0x006d5f90`) — a checkpoint name is not persisted through a save/quit/resume cycle; the restored state is "fresh start of this mission, but flagged as a restart" (next paragraph). The mission-failed handler (`0x006d8fb0`) itself string-compares this global against `"mission start"` to decide what the failure/retry screen offers — **the engine's own code treats `"mission start"` as the sentinel for "no checkpoint has been reached yet."** No row of either shipped copy of `mission_checkpoints.xtbl` is named `"mission start"` or indexed `0` — checkpoints are only the names a script explicitly reports.

**`0x014c8324`** is the `is_restart` boolean. Set by `0x006d6920` (called by every "begin a mission" entry) to `(the pending in-progress-mission handle `0x014c8328` == this mission)`, which is then cleared. `0x014c8328` is written by a save/network-stream load and by the mission-failed handler just before invoking its retry callback. So on a genuine fresh start — this mission was never already in progress — **`is_restart` is `false`**; it is `true` for a retry after failure or a resume from a save that was itself mid-mission.

### 36.4 Direct answer for a host implementation

**On a genuine fresh start, call `start_fn("mission start", false)` as a new coroutine** — never the number `0`, `-1`, or nil; nothing in this mechanism ever produces anything but the string `"mission start"` and a boolean on a fresh start. **To resume at a checkpoint, call `start_fn(checkpointName, true)`** where `checkpointName` is the exact string the mission's own script last reported via `mission_set_checkpoint` — equivalently, the `CheckpointName` column of `mission_checkpoints.xtbl` for that mission (for `dlc2_m02`: the strings `"1"`, `"2"`, `"3"`, `"4"`, not the numbers 1-4). The function to call is whatever string the mission's `script_mission_start` property holds — for shipped missions this is HYPOTHESIS equal to `<stem>_start`, not independently confirmed from the object's own (parked) data.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** the invocation mechanism itself (data-borne name, two call sites, the two-argument coroutine launch, the checkpoint-name/restart-flag lifecycles) is CONFIRMED — disassembly. HIGH CONFIDENCE that these are the only two native call sites (a module-wide property-read sweep plus a census of every writer of the mission-thread-id global, not a binary-wide census of every `0x00e0ca80` caller — see `spec-lua-bindings.md` §14.11 for the exact census method). OPEN: which game-mode state `0x006d9310` enters; the `silent_mission_start` sibling's own argument shape; `0x006d7120`'s remaining callers (whether any passes a checkpoint name other than the current one or `"mission start"`); where `scripted_mission_start` objects are actually created/serialised from — code-only this pass, no zone or other placement bytes opened; the carrier is unresolved among the parked `.czn_pc` interior, a mission package/table, or another serialised source, not narrowed to one candidate.

## 37. There is no native "delay" — the script wait, its clock, and why a thread can stall (2026-10-02)

**Why.** After the thread-table section's own resume-scheduler fix, one mission's script thread enters a timed wait and never returns. This investigation settles what that wait is, what clock it reads, and whether anything can stop that clock — and, as a side effect, forced the major `0x00702070`/`0x00e0dfc0` correction already applied in place to the thread-table section above (not re-detailed here).

### 37.1 There is no native delay/wait/sleep

An exhaustive string census (every identifier-shaped string containing `delay`, `sleep`, `wait`, `timer`, `elapsed`, `game_time`, `get_time`, `pause`) finds no registered name of that shape — every timer-sounding Lua name is an unrelated domain function (`hud_timer_*`, `trigger_set_delay_between_activations`, etc.). **Only two functions in the entire binary can suspend a Lua thread**: `thread_yield` (`0x00e0f0d0`) and the stock `coroutine.yield` (`0x00fcca20`) — both confirmed by an exhaustive raw-call scan of the VM's own yield primitive (`0x00dffb20`), which has exactly these two callers. So a mission's "delay" is necessarily a **Lua function** — almost certainly in `game_lib.lua` — that loops `thread_yield()` and accumulates time itself; the engine has no part in deciding when it's done beyond resuming the thread. `game_lib.lua`'s own text was not read: it exists in exactly one place, `misc.vpp_pc`, a per-entry-compressed ("mode-a") container whose decompression stays parked — **no file bytes beyond the directory/header were opened.** The only clock a script can read is `get_frame_time` (above); the other time-shaped native, `get_game_time` (`0x00a4ae30`), returns the in-world calendar time-of-day, not an elapsed-time counter. So the delay's shape is constrained to "repeat: yield, add `get_frame_time()` to a running total, until the total reaches the requested seconds" (HIGH CONFIDENCE as a constraint, not a read of the actual loop).

### 37.2 The engine keeps two millisecond clocks, but neither backs `get_frame_time`

`0x00db9970` (the per-tick timer update, §get_frame_time above) also maintains two separate millisecond accumulators, each useful context for a host modelling other engine timers: a **pausable, scaled "game" counter** (`0x029f4db0`, stops while the pause depth `0x029f4dcc` is positive, scaled by a time-scale divisor `0x0132a0bc`) and an **unpausable, unscaled "real" counter** (`0x029f4db4`). A 12-byte engine-side timestamp object family (`0x0086be20`-`0x0086c04a`: set/hold-release/remaining/expired) is built on whichever of the two a caller selects (or, in multiplayer, a session-synchronised equivalent) — this is what backs domain timers like HUD countdowns and AI/respawn delays (§37.1's string census), never a generic script delay. `get_frame_time`'s own global (`0x0132a0b0`) is neither of these two counters — it is the raw, unscaled, unpaused, (near-)uncapped measured frame delta, detailed in this section's own entry above.

### 37.3 Game-pause census: 28 push sites, 32 pop sites, one shared depth counter

Beyond the push/pop quartet already corrected into the thread-table section above (`0x007074a0`/`0x00708a80` push, `0x00707540`/`0x00708330` pop, all keyed on the shared depth `0x01503eb0`), a full site census finds 28 raw push sites and 32 pop sites carrying 11 distinct "reason" codes (cutscene pause-menu, UI dialogs, movie playback, multiplayer lobby, and others — full table in the investigation's own notes, not reproduced here). Two properties matter for a stuck thread: **the depth is one shared counter and the per-reason bytes are bookkeeping only** — a pop decrements the depth whenever it is positive, without checking that its own reason was ever pushed, so the gameplay state stays exempt for exactly as long as the shared depth is positive, regardless of which reason holds it; and **no Lua-registered function ever pushes or pops a pause** (none of the 60 combined sites lies in the Lua-binding address range) — a script can only cause a pause indirectly, through an engine flow such as opening a cutscene's pause/skip menu. **A pause pushed and never popped — an unbalanced cutscene-pause-menu or movie-playback level being the two most likely culprits — freezes every mission thread indefinitely, with no Lua-visible symptom beyond "nothing resumes."** The world-start routine `0x00708330` pops every outstanding level when a new world starts, bounding the damage to at most one play session.

### 37.4 The runner's two resume-veto hooks only affect object-bound threads

Re-reading the runner `0x00e0cba0` finds two optional callbacks, installed once by `0x00a1ff70`, consulted before every resume: a "should this thread be killed" hook and a "skip this resume" hook. **Both act only on thread records whose `+0x18` flags have bit `0x08` set** — for any other record both unconditionally return false. A plain `thread_new` thread (a mission's own main thread, or an ordinary delay loop inside it) is never flagged this way, so these hooks cannot be the cause of a stuck mission delay; they exist for a different, object-bound thread category whose own flag-setter was not traced (OPEN).

### 37.5 Direct answer

**A delay cannot stall on its clock in the shipped engine** — `get_frame_time` always advances, is never scaled or capped below its true value, and is never gated by pause. **It is always the thread, not the clock, that freezes.** The two real-engine mechanisms that stop an ordinary mission thread from being resumed at all are: (a) an outstanding, unbalanced game-pause level (§37.3); (b) the in-game state's own per-frame update skipping its call into the scheduler while a blocking stream load is in progress (`0x00dafa90`, the thread-table section above). **For a host:** if the stuck thread keeps being resumed every tick but its own delay loop never reaches the threshold, the defect is in the host's `get_frame_time` equivalent — most likely it is refreshed on a cadence that does not match the thread-resume cadence (e.g. a headless mission-drive loop that never calls its own frame-time update). If instead the thread is not being resumed at all, check for an unbalanced pause push or a load-gate that never clears — a resume problem, not a clock problem.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** CONFIRMED throughout for the negative (no native delay), the two-clock census, the pause-site census and reason-code independence, and the resume-veto hooks' object-bound scope. OPEN: the exact Lua text and loop order of the real `game_lib.lua` delay (parked mode-a container, not opened); the full meaning of pause reasons `0x02`/`0x05`/`0x0b`/`0x0e`/`0x12`; who sets thread-record flag bit `0x08`; `0x00dafa90`'s own backing field `0x029cffd4`.

## 38. Ranking tranche 06 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Crreish-sync\for-team-a\team-a\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-06.json` (names 76-100 of 554, Team B call-count order; all low-traffic, 2 calls each). 15 of 25 names are in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; the other 10 (`store_vehicle_*`, `store_weapon_*`, `vcust_*`) are **UI names**, in three small sub-registrars reached only through the 311-entry UI registrar `0x008430f0`: `0x008152a0` (`store_vehicle_*`), `0x00817570` (`store_weapon_*`), `0x00820aa0` (`vcust_*`) — any registrar-membership table in this document should list these 10 as UI, not gameplay. All 25 resolved. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 38.1 Vehicle cluster (12 functions) — shared "enter" machinery

Three entries (`vehicle_enter_do`, `vehicle_enter_guardian_angel`, `vehicle_enter_group_do`) build a **0x44-byte request record** and submit it through a common `0x00af22a0(character, vehicle, record)`: it forces "instant" mode under certain character/vehicle flags, runs an eligibility predicate (refuses a seated/entering character, one in a special-movement state, or one failing several further checks), resolves a default vehicle when none was named, claims the first of **8 fixed occupancy slots** per vehicle (no de-duplication — a repeated order for the same character can claim a second slot; the slot-clearing code was not traced), and starts the slot. Separately, three of the four "enter" entries (`vehicle_enter_do`, `_guardian_angel`, `_group_do`) have a hidden side effect: entering a vehicle while following a leader silently flips the character's own **independent-follower flag** (bit 0 of `+0x1e01`) and never clears it again.

**`vehicle_hidden` (`0x00a62610`).** 1 string. 1 boolean: the object's hidden bit (byte `+0x3b` bit 0) — **but an unresolved name answers `true`**, so a bad name, a destroyed vehicle, or a character name all read as "hidden." Same bit `vehicle_show`'s existing entry clears.

**`vehicle_anim_playing` (`0x00a62050`).** 1 string. 1 boolean (false if unresolved). True only if the vehicle's body is active (`+0xbd0`==1) and any entry of its animation-set object has "active" set without "finishing/paused" (HYPOTHESIS on the exact bit meanings).

**`vehicle_engine_check_running` (`0x00a63e50`) — return-value defect.** 1 string. On failure (unresolved, or a specific object flag clear) pushes `false` and returns 1 value; **on success it calls the engine-running-bit getter, discards the result, and returns 0 values** — so this query can never answer `true`; a script sees `nil` for every running vehicle and `false` for every non-running one. A reimplementation that wants byte-for-byte behavior must also return nothing on success; one that wants the evident intent should return the bit instead.

**`vehicle_engine_start` (`0x00a62380`).** 1 string + 1 optional boolean, default true. No return. **An already-running engine is stopped first, then restarted — never left alone.** The stop/start pair writes a per-class engine-state byte (class 2 → one field, classes 3/4 → another, any other class → nothing at all) with the Lua boolean inverted into one of its bits; on a VTOL (class 4) with an active sub-object it also fires an audio event. HYPOTHESIS: the boolean selects "start instantly" vs. a spin-up; classes 2/3/4 = car/helicopter/VTOL (the class enum itself, `0x00ad2f80`, was not opened).

**`vehicle_disable_weapon_physics` (`0x00a62330`).** 1 optional boolean, default true — **calling it with no argument disables the effect** (writes the logical NOT of the argument). No return. Gates whether a weapon hit can knock a vehicle's parts loose. **No host gate, no replication, and exactly one writer anywhere in the binary — once a script disables it, it stays disabled for the rest of the process, across missions and loads.**

**`vehicle_forced_corpse_removal_enabled` (`0x00a624d0`).** 1 bare boolean (absent = false). No return. Writes a global **only when a session exists and this machine is host** — a silent no-op otherwise. The flag is registered as a named session variable (`"vehicle_forced_corpse_removal"`) and reset to **on** at every world init, unlike the previous entry. Its consumer (a per-tick wrecked-vehicle cleanup walking a fixed list) **collects candidates into 48-entry stack arrays with no count check** — more than 48 qualifying wrecked vehicles on the list overruns the stack frame. A real, confirmed missing bound; whether the list can reach 49 entries in practice is OPEN.

**`vehicle_delete_all_corpses` (`0x00a63d30`).** No arguments, no return. Walks the same wrecked-vehicle list; for each locally-authoritative entry, either deletes it and its occupants outright, or — if a per-class "protected" test passes (HIGH CONFIDENCE: script/mission-owned) — hides it and its occupants instead of deleting them, and releases its attached effect handles. **Correction to this document's existing `vehicle_show`-area entry:** the "position pair" arguments it describes for the shared hide helper are actually the vehicle's **handle pair**, resolved through the standard handle lookup, not a position.

**`vehicle_enter_do` (`0x00a67000`).** 7 arguments (character, vehicle, "instant" boolean, then 4 optional: seat index, 2 booleans, seat name). Returns 1 boolean. Resolves the vehicle directly, or — if that fails — as a character's own current vehicle. Three dispatch paths: instant placement; a named-seat placement (seat name resolved through the established animation-state-style name table); or, with neither, an **AI order** that stages a default action template on the character and starts action `0x31`, additionally switching a player-class character's own script-mode field to 2 on success.

**`vehicle_enter_guardian_angel` (`0x00a67670`).** 3 arguments (character, vehicle, optional seat index). Returns 1 boolean. Same resolver/follower-flag shape as the previous entry, but submits a record with "forced" eligibility — it skips several of the shared submitter's own refusal checks that an ordinary enter order is subject to. HYPOTHESIS: this is the relaxed-eligibility entry used by the existing escort/backup ("guardian angel") command family.

**`vehicle_enter_group_do` (`0x00a67330`).** 3 arguments (vehicle, "instant" boolean, a table of character names). Returns 1 boolean — false if the vehicle fails to resolve or any instant placement was refused, else true if at least one member reached its order/placement (an order's own result is never checked, so every member that reaches that branch counts as success regardless of outcome). **Instant mode assigns seats strictly by table position** (the table's first member becomes seat 0 = driver) — a table that doesn't list the intended driver first puts the wrong member in the driver's seat.

**`vehicle_enter_group_check_done` (`0x00a66920`).** 3 arguments (vehicle — no character fallback, unlike the three entries above — a "do not re-order" boolean, a table of character names). Returns 1 boolean: **an unresolved vehicle answers "done" (true)**. Not a pure query: polling it with the "do not re-order" flag false **re-issues the enter order to every straggling member each time it's called.**

**`vehicle_exit_guardian_angel` (`0x00a66c70`).** 1 string (character). Returns 1 boolean: **true means "was seated," not "exit succeeded"** — the exit request itself can be silently refused (e.g. the character's occupancy slot is already mid-transition) while the function still reports true. Also applies a 3-second cooldown to three AI actions (ids 37-39 of the existing 70-entry CAE action table, §30.4 — names not read this pass).

### 38.2 Team and tutorial (3 functions)

**`team_make_hostile` (`0x00a607a0`) — two real memory-safety defects.** 2 strings (team names), no return. Writes relation value **0** (hostile) into the existing byte relation matrix (the sibling of `team_make_allies`/`team_make_unfriendly`, values 4/1 respectively), symmetrically, with the same team-5-mirrors-into-team-6 behavior this document's tranche-03 write-up already established for the unfriendly sibling — then **always** broadcasts an opcode-`0x43` record (sub-code `0x30`), with no authority gate of any kind. **Defect 1:** a non-string team-name argument reaches a null-pointer dereference inside the name-hash helper with no guard. **Defect 2:** an unrecognized team name resolves to id 9, which is larger than the matrix's own row stride — writing past the intended row and corrupting an unrelated team pair's relationship, which then gets replicated to every peer. Both CONFIRMED from the disassembly's own arithmetic.

**`tutorial_visible` (`0x00a602e0`) — not a pure query.** No arguments. Returns 1 boolean (a visibility predicate gated on ~11 further conditions, not individually traced). **Side effect:** when the head of the tutorial-prompt queue carries one specific descriptor bit and no mission is active, polling this function unlinks that prompt and re-inserts it at the tail of the queue, returning false — a new descriptor bit ("may be deferred to the back of the queue") added to this document's existing tutorial-prompt table.

**`tutorial_get_case` (`0x00a60390`).** 1 string. Returns a number (found) or `false` (not found) — resolves the name through the existing 210-entry case-insensitive tutorial table and returns that entry's own `+0x10` field (a previously-unidentified field, now settled). **Crash-shaped:** the name lookup calls the CRT's `strcmp`-family comparator with no null check on the argument; this build's own comparator routes a null pointer into the CRT's invalid-parameter handler, which terminates the process by default unless the game installs its own (not confirmed either way).

### 38.3 Weapon store (3 functions, UI sub-registrar `0x00817570`)

**`store_weapon_purchase_ammo` (`0x008165c0`) — multiple null/wrong-item paths.** Up to 4 numeric arguments (slot/category, item id, amount, price). No return. Two resolution modes (a direct inventory slot, or a scan of the store's listed items by a code derived from the item id) both fall through to charging the price and recording the purchase **even on failure**: an empty or non-matching store-list scan still charges the player and records an unrelated/garbage item; a "give weapon" failure still writes to a fixed offset of a null result with no check. **No affordability check in this function at all** (may be enforced deeper in the generic cash-adjust call, not traced). On success, notifies a registered script callback — host and client take different paths to the same callback, which receives the literal tag `"weapon-ammo"` plus the local player's name; this is the same notification shape `vcust_purchase_wheels` below uses, and HIGH CONFIDENCE the document's other purchase-style entries share it too.

**`store_weapon_change_weapon` (`0x00815f40`) — unchecked index.** A slot-category string + a mandatory item-index number + 2 booleans + an optional number. No return. A category match selects one of two fixed arrays by item index **with no bounds check at all** — an arbitrary script-supplied index reads an arbitrary nearby dword as an item pointer. Also dereferences the local player with no null check on one path. Purely UI preview state (consumed by the store's own per-frame code, not traced).

**`store_weapon_process_post_bg_covered` (`0x00815460`).** No arguments, no return. Writes a single global byte that the per-frame render-scene setup copies into renderer state alongside fog/atmosphere parameters. HYPOTHESIS: a "world rendering/post-effect off while the store background covers the screen" switch; the writer that turns it back on was not traced.

### 38.4 Vehicle store (3 functions, UI sub-registrar `0x008152a0`)

**`store_vehicle_change_mode` (`0x00815120`).** 1 number. No return. A no-op if the number already equals the current mode flag. Mode 0 takes over a pending vehicle into the active selection, tears down the garage UI, and applies the default customization preset; any other value tears down customization instead and attempts to store the player's current vehicle into a garage slot, setting the mode flag to the **literal 1** on success regardless of the argument's actual value (an edge the existing text should note, not "fixed").

**`store_vehicle_retrieve_car_and_exit` (`0x00813020`).** No arguments, no return. Takes over a pending vehicle if the mode flag is 1, then pops the top of the UI screen stack (and a second time if a specific screen id is also on the stack). HYPOTHESIS: that id is the garage list screen.

**`store_vehicle_selection_should_lock_controls` (`0x00813170`).** No arguments. Returns 1 boolean, a pure query over the store's own sub-state and mode flag (details HYPOTHESIS, not independently confirmed beyond the control-flow shape).

### 38.5 Vehicle customization (4 functions, UI sub-registrar `0x00820aa0`) — a shared null-dereference hazard

All four resolve the paint/part sub-object as `vehicle + 0x688` only when the vehicle's body is active (`+0xbd0`==1), and as a **null pointer otherwise**, then dereference an offset of that result unconditionally — **a vehicle that isn't fully set up crashes every one of these four entries**, not just the one detailed below.

**`vcust_preview_color` (`0x0081f860`).** 1 number (color index, unchecked). No return. Applies a palette entry to the current customization zone; the color index is never bounds-checked.

**`vcust_preview_palette` (`0x0081f8d0`) — unguarded pre-check dereference.** 3 numbers (zone, palette, color index — all unchecked). No return. **Reads the zone record and indexes into its palette list BEFORE checking whether the vehicle/zone resolved at all** — a null zone record crashes even when the overall "material" check that follows would have caught it. Also a real inconsistency: the palette is looked up for the given zone argument, but the actual paint call applies it to the *current* zone global instead, which can differ.

**`vcust_preview_wheel_sizing` (`0x0081f5d0`) — null dereference with no target.** 2 numbers (truncated to a byte each). No return. **If there is no live customization target, the vehicle pointer is zero and the very next instruction reads an offset of the null pointer — an unconditional access violation whenever this is called without a live target**, not merely a shared hazard like the other three.

**`vcust_purchase_wheels` (`0x0081fe70`).** 1 number (price). No return. Charges the price (no affordability check, no null check on the local player) and fires the same purchase-notification mechanism `store_weapon_purchase_ammo` above uses (tag `"vehicle-cust"`). **Commits the previewed wheel configuration regardless of whether a price was charged** — and two of the three committed-object pointers are dereferenced with no null check (the third is checked), so a purchase attempted before any wheel preview was actually set up writes through a null pointer.

### 38.6 Cross-function observations

Two distinct return-count defects now exist in this document's catalogue: tranche 05 found functions that push an extra value on success; `vehicle_engine_check_running` here is the opposite shape — it returns **zero** values on success, so it can never answer true at all. "Unresolved" defaults are inconsistent and sometimes surprising across this tranche alone: `vehicle_hidden` → true, `vehicle_enter_group_check_done` → true ("done"), the enter-do family → false, `vehicle_anim_playing` → false — a reimplementation must match each individually, not assume one convention. Several "query" names have real side effects: `tutorial_visible` can rotate the tutorial queue; `vehicle_enter_group_check_done` re-issues enter orders to stragglers on every poll; three of the four vehicle-enter entries silently flip a character's independent-follower flag. A purchase-notification mechanism (registered script handle, host-direct vs. client-forwarded lookup, two string arguments) is now confirmed shared by at least two purchase-style functions across different subsystems (weapon ammo, vehicle wheels) and is HIGH CONFIDENCE shared by the document's other `*_purchase_*` entries too.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED from the disassembly unless noted):** `vcust_preview_wheel_sizing` (null-target dereference, unconditional), `store_weapon_purchase_ammo` (empty-list null read; wrong-item charge on scan miss; null write on a failed weapon grant), `team_make_hostile` (null read on a non-string name; out-of-bounds matrix write on an unknown team name, then replicated), `vcust_preview_palette` (three unchecked indices; a pre-guard null dereference), `vcust_preview_color` (unchecked color index; the shared `+0xbd0` hazard), `vcust_purchase_wheels` (two unchecked committed-preview pointers — reachability OPEN), `store_weapon_change_weapon` (unchecked item index into global arrays; unchecked local player), `tutorial_get_case`/`store_weapon_change_weapon` (CRT invalid-parameter exposure on a non-string name). A separate engine-side defect, gated by `vehicle_forced_corpse_removal_enabled`'s consumer tick, has no bound on its 48-entry stack-array collection loop (§38.1).

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 06 resolved and written up (§38.1-§38.5); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: the vehicle-class enum `0x00ad2f80`'s own value meanings; the relation matrix's true row count; several occupancy/eligibility helper bodies not opened at this pass's depth cap.

## 39. Ranking tranche 07 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Crreish-sync\for-team-a\team-a\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-07.json` (names 101-125 of 554, Team B call-count order; all low-traffic). 16 of 25 names are in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; the other 9 (`store_dlc_*`, `save_system_*`, `store_common_rotate_mouse_drag`, `store_gallery_download_hide_list`, `store_gang_show_question_marks`, `store_clothing_get_store_id`, `store_character_lineup_loaded`) are **UI names** in seven small, screen-local registrars reached by neither the gameplay registrar nor the 311-entry UI registrar `0x008430f0` — each is its own standalone `{name,fn}` table that calls the same `lua_pushcclosure`/`lua_setfield`-to-globals pair directly; who calls each of these seven registrars (and into which Lua state) was not traced (OPEN). All 25 resolved. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 39.1 Character action cluster (5 functions)

**`skydive_move_to_do` (`0x00a5f780`) — a real null-pointer crash reachable from a bad argument.** 6 arguments (character, target name, a bare "use-path" boolean, then 3 optional: point index, 2 booleans). No return. With the use-path flag true, the target resolves through a dedicated path-object resolver and the point index is read from its 12-byte point array (bounds-checked). **With the flag false, the target resolves through the generic third-tier resolver with NO guard on failure: an absent/unresolved name leaves the target pointer at literal zero, and the function then unconditionally copies 12 bytes from address `0x40` into the character** — a genuine access violation, reachable with `skydive_move_to_do(<character>, "no_such_object", false)` or a nil target name. Reproducible only when the character passes three further gates (one of them requiring a specific locomotion state, `+0xcc8`==0xe, HYPOTHESIS: skydiving/free-fall). On success it switches the character into action-state `0x1f` through this document's general action-state-switch helper (`0x004dd380`, ~30 callers — worth its own future entry) and copies the resolved point into the character's own move-to target fields.

**`rappel_enter` (`0x00a5c4a0`) / `rappel_exit` (`0x00a5c690`).** `rappel_enter`: character + optional "queue" boolean (default false) + optional target name + optional integer (default −1). `rappel_exit`: character + optional boolean (default **true** — the opposite default from enter) + optional target name. Both return nothing. A **queued** rappel request is stored in a fixed 2-slot table (slot 0 = local player, **slot 1 = every other character** — two different NPCs' queued rappels silently overwrite each other's slot) and always broadcasts an opcode-`0x41`/op-`0x1f` message to the co-op partner unconditionally, before any ownership check; applying it locally requires authority. An **immediate** rappel instead forwards to the owner only when not locally authoritative. Rappel state: character field `+0xcc8` == `0x12` while rappelling; sub-state `+0xcce` is `0x23` (live) or `0x24` (queued) — a queued exit simply cancels the queue slot rather than running the full landing logic. `rappel_enter`'s own integer argument is bounds-checked (`< 8` unsigned, so the default −1 is always skipped) before use in two further calls whose meaning is OPEN; a global float (`0x0262d160`) must lie in `[0, 90]` for an immediate rappel to proceed (meaning OPEN). Both create/reuse a "ga_cable" attached object.

**`set_cower_variant` (`0x00a5e200`).** Character + a number (no nil-gate, absent reads 0). No return. Clamps to `[0,4]`, maps to animation-set index `13+variant`, validates against the character's own animation set (falls back to 13 if not present), then applies through the double-gate "human"/"cower_stand_variant" setter to `+0x1cd8`. Dereferences a character sub-object pointer (`+0xd24`) with no null check (shared with `skydive_move_to_do`'s own state test — HIGH CONFIDENCE it's always set on a resolved human).

**`set_unrecruitable_flag` (`0x00a5da40`).** Character + optional boolean, default true. No return. Double-gate "npc"/"npc_force_flagsunrecruitable" setter, bit `0x10` of byte `+0x1e02`.

### 39.2 Vehicle/world-object cluster (5 functions)

**`set_unjackable_by_ai_flag` (`0x00a5d920`).** Vehicle + optional boolean, default true. No return. Double-gate "vehicle_ai"/"vai_force_flagsunjackable_by_ai" setter on the vehicle-AI sub-record, bit `0x02` of its own byte `+5` (vehicle `+0xc6d`).

**`rc_set_max_signal_range` (`0x00a5b7d0`).** 1 number (no nil-gate, absent reads 0). **Returns the PREVIOUS range**, not the new one or nothing — swaps the new value into a global float and pushes the old value. The reader computes `1 − horizontal_distance/range` (X/Z only). **`rc_set_max_signal_range(0)` (or no argument) makes the reader divide by zero** — an SSE float divide, so with default masked FP exceptions this yields ±inf/NaN rather than a trap (HYPOTHESIS on the control word, not independently confirmed). The global's own start-up default was not traced (OPEN).

**`spotlight_heli_laser_size` (`0x00a5dec0`).** 1 number (no nil-gate). No return. Writes a global float (default 1.0) that scales the helicopter spotlight/laser beam's half-width. **No clamp, no replication, no host reset found anywhere** — a negative value is accepted with no check on whether it inverts the comparison sensibly (OPEN).

**`roadblock_create` (`0x00a5cbc0`).** 2 strings (template name, placement object). **Returns exactly 1 number: the new roadblock's 64-bit handle converted to a double, or −1 on any failure.** The template lookup **keeps scanning after a match and returns the LAST one** — duplicate template names silently resolve to the last-loaded entry, not the first. Placement fails if the road-network manager reports busy/empty or none of up to 8 candidate spots within 7.0 units of the object passes a per-template acceptance test. HYPOTHESIS (not confirmed either way): a handle above 2^53 would not round-trip exactly through the Lua double, which would make `roadblock_destroy` silently miss it — whether real handles ever get that large is OPEN.

**`roadblock_destroy` (`0x00a5c350`).** 1 number (the handle). No return. **The truncating-cast helper this document already cites elsewhere (`0x00ea2596`) is used here in its full 64-bit form** (`EDX:EAX` both kept, not just the low half most other callers use) — a real, confirmed instance of that helper's wider behavior. Requires the roadblock-kind descriptor bit before releasing via the generic object-release routine.

### 39.3 Spawning/world-state globals (5 functions)

All five write process globals directly with no object resolution; three are also registered through the session-synced-variable mechanism (`0x0086d770`, the same one tranche 05's `auto_pickup_disable` write-up already documents) with the 4th ("authoritative") argument always computed the same way: true exactly when a session exists and this machine is host.

**`spawning_allow_gang_ambient_spawns` (`0x00a5dd00`).** Optional boolean, default true. Writes the SAME value to **four separate global bytes** at once; the reader requires all four non-zero. HYPOTHESIS: four independent category gates that Lua can only ever set in lockstep.

**`spawn_region_enable_los` (`0x00a5fc70`).** Spawn-region name + a **bare** boolean (absent = disables, the opposite framing from most boolean setters in this document). No return. Resolves the region by name (a new descriptor-bit resolver variant) and writes the inverse of the argument into a bit of the region's own byte `+0x94` (HYPOTHESIS: "skip the line-of-sight test when spawning here").

**`set_saints_hated` (`0x00a5d5a0`).** Bare boolean. Writes a byte registered as the synced variable `"saints_hated"`. The Lua setter writes the raw byte directly, with propagation left entirely to the sync mechanism — HYPOTHESIS that a non-authoritative peer's direct write can be overwritten by the next sync (an open co-op-correctness question, same shape noted for the next two entries).

**`set_stag_notoriety_area_active` (`0x00a5d670`).** Bare boolean. Writes a byte registered as `"stag_notoriety"`, AND (if a literally-named `"LOCKDOWN_NOTORIETY"` world object resolves) writes that object's own flag field, AND — only when this machine is host and the value actually changed — runs a host-gated spawn/despawn step that releases every tracked handle in a dedicated table when turning off. The sync mechanism's own change-callback independently re-runs the same object update on a receiving peer — confirmed, not just inferred.

**`set_cops_shooting_from_vehicles` (`0x00a5cf10`).** Optional boolean, default true. Writes a byte registered as `"passenger_cops"`. **Note the asymmetry: the engine's own reset default is false (no shooting), while calling this setter with no argument at all sets it true** — a real, confirmed default mismatch between "what the engine starts with" and "what calling the setter bare does."

### 39.4 Save-system UI cluster (3 functions) — a real off-by-one slot bound

All three operate on one save-system UI singleton; slot records are a fixed table whose count is read from one specific field.

**`save_system_save_game` (`0x007d0dd0`) / `save_system_load_game` (`0x007d0e60`).** Both take 1 number (slot, truncated). No return. Slot `99` is the special "new save" sentinel (space/slot-count checks, then commits); any other slot opens a confirmation dialog whose callback performs the actual save. **Both the save-confirm callback and the load path bound the slot with `slot > count` / `slot ≤ count` (`<=`), accepting `slot == count` — one past the end of the slot table.** This is confirmed a real defect, not a stylistic choice: a sibling handler registered in the very same registrar (not itself in this tranche) bounds the identical count field with a strict `<`, establishing that the field is genuinely a count and the `<=` siblings here are wrong. The actual out-of-bounds write this produces was not independently confirmed (the record-write helper itself wasn't opened), so it's HIGH CONFIDENCE rather than fully proven. Loading additionally has a **HYPOTHESIS crash path**: a deferred load callback re-reads the pending slot index when it finally fires, with no bound check of its own, and two other code paths can reset that same index to −1 in the meantime — if the deferral window can overlap such a reset, the callback indexes the slot table at **−1**, one record before the start of the table. Reachability of that overlap was not settled.

**`save_system_cancel_coop_load` (`0x007d0e90`).** No arguments, no return. Sets the save-system's own state field to 5 unless already there. HYPOTHESIS: 5 = "co-op load cancelled."

### 39.5 Store UI cluster (7 functions, all in their own screen-local registrars)

**`store_gang_show_question_marks` (`0x00811170`) — a real null-pointer crash path.** Bare boolean. No return. Toggles whether the current gang-customization preview slot shows a placeholder "question mark" model or the real one. **If the slot's own asset reference is unset AND the fallback "question mark" asset lookup also fails (the asset isn't loaded), the code takes the "not a question mark" branch anyway and dereferences the resulting null pointer** — a real, confirmed crash path reachable without any obviously-unreasonable precondition. The slot index used to index two small fixed-size tables is not bounds-checked either (HYPOTHESIS risk, not separately confirmed reachable).

**`store_gallery_download_hide_list` (`0x0080f1a0`) — two unchecked pointers.** Bare boolean. No return. The "true" (hide) path clears a large block of a global gallery-list object AND reads a field off the local player — **neither the gallery object's own global pointer nor the local-player pointer is null-checked anywhere in this function** — calling it before the gallery UI is initialized, or with no local player present (e.g. at the front end), reaches an unguarded dereference either way. Reachability of either precondition in a real run was not settled.

**`store_dlc_queue_icon` (`0x007c5b60`) — no-op stub.** Reads a number and a string argument and discards both; no side effects, no return value.

**`store_dlc_is_offer_free` (`0x007c5b00`) — constant stub.** Reads and discards a number argument; **always returns `false`**, regardless of input.

**`store_common_rotate_mouse_drag` (`0x0080dc10`) — reads uninitialized memory.** No arguments, no return. Reads mouse-delta values from three fixed stack slots, **but only copies the real values in when a specific input-mode bit is set** (HYPOTHESIS: mouse is the active input device) — when that bit is clear, the three stack slots are never initialized at all, and the function proceeds to rotate whichever of three possible targets (a gang-customization preview, a store object, or — as the fallback — **the local player with no null check**) by a garbage angle derived from that uninitialized stack memory. A faithful reimplementation must treat "mouse delta unavailable" as zero, not skip the rotation or read whatever happens to be on the stack.

**`store_clothing_get_store_id` (`0x0080db90`).** No arguments. Returns 1 number, the result of an un-opened callee (`0x0080d810`, OPEN).

**`store_character_lineup_loaded` (`0x0080d4b0`).** No arguments, no return. Sets a single latch byte (`0x022ccc52` := 1). HYPOTHESIS: a "character lineup is ready" flag the store screen polls; its readers were not traced.

### 39.6 Cross-function observations

Boolean-default conventions are genuinely inconsistent across this tranche alone and a reimplementation must match each individually rather than assume a project-wide rule: several bare booleans default to **false when absent** (`spawn_region_enable_los` — note this one specifically *disables* on absence, the opposite framing from most of this document's setters — plus `set_saints_hated`, `set_stag_notoriety_area_active`, `store_gang_show_question_marks`, `store_gallery_download_hide_list`); several nil-gated optionals default to **true** (`spawning_allow_gang_ambient_spawns`, `set_cops_shooting_from_vehicles`, `set_unrecruitable_flag`, `set_unjackable_by_ai_flag`, `rappel_exit`); one nil-gated optional defaults to **false** (`rappel_enter`'s queue flag). Three distinct replication shapes recur: the established double-gate string-tagged setter family; a numeric opcode-`0x41`/op-`0x1f` scheme specific to rappel (sub-op 0 = enter, 1 = exit, with the queued-enter variant broadcasting unconditionally before any ownership check — a genuinely different shape from the immediate variant, which forwards only when not authoritative); and the session-synced-global-variable mechanism, where the Lua setter writes the raw byte directly and leaves propagation to the sync layer. `0x00ea2596` (this document's established truncating float-to-int cast) is now confirmed to actually return a full 64-bit value (`EDX:EAX`) — most callers only ever use the low half, but `roadblock_destroy` is a real, confirmed instance that needs both.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED from the disassembly unless noted):** `skydive_move_to_do` (null-pointer-shaped read at address `0x40` on an unresolved non-path target); the save/load slot off-by-one (HIGH CONFIDENCE bug, sibling-confirmed); the deferred load callback's own stale-pending-index read (HYPOTHESIS reachability); `store_common_rotate_mouse_drag` (uninitialized stack delta; unchecked local player on its fallback target); `store_gallery_download_hide_list` (unchecked global gallery pointer; unchecked local player); `store_gang_show_question_marks` (null-plus-offset read when both the slot asset and its fallback are unset); `rc_set_max_signal_range(0)` (divide-by-zero in its reader, likely inf/NaN not a trap).

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 07 resolved and written up (§39.1-§39.5); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: who calls the seven screen-local registrars; several rappel/skydive argument meanings; the save-system's own record-write/mode-2 internals; whether the session-sync mechanism can overwrite a non-authoritative peer's direct write.

## 40. Ranking tranche 08 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Crreish-sync\for-team-a\team-a\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-08.json` (names 126-150 of 554, Team B call-count order; all 2 calls each). 10 names are in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; the other 15, all `pcu_*` ("PCU" = the clothing-store family), are in a dedicated UI sub-registrar `0x00830230`, itself called only from the 311-entry UI registrar `0x008430f0`. All 25 resolved. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 40.1 Sprint overrides (6 functions) and mission-scoped variables

Three independent global integer overrides (sprint, recharge, delay), each a file-backed `-1` ("no override") static: `player_override_set_sprint`/`_set_sprint_recharge`/`_set_sprint_delay` each take 1 number (no presence check — a missing or non-number argument stores literal **0**, not "cleared") and write it straight into the matching global with no player argument and no range check; `player_override_clear_sprint`/`_clear_sprint_recharge`/`_clear_sprint_delay` take no arguments and write `-1`. **All three overrides are global, not per-player** — one value covers every player in a co-op session. All three are also **mission state**: a mission-start/restart routine resets them to `-1` and registers each with the session-synced-variable mechanism (`0x0086d770`) under the names `"mission_sprint_use"`/`"mission_sprint_recharge"`/`"mission_sprint_delay"` — the same mechanism, and the same mission-scoped-variable pattern, already covers `"mission_finishers"`/`"mission_parachute"`/`"mission_streaming"`. **The getters are not symmetric**: the sprint and delay getters return the stored override as-is, but the recharge getter only honors its override when a host-side mode query (`0x007044f0`) returns non-zero — otherwise it silently falls back to a different, unrelated getter and the override is ignored. `0x007044f0`'s own value meanings are OPEN (it also gates §40.2's sing-along flag).

### 40.2 Radio (2 functions)

**`radio_set_sing_along_allowed_during_missions` (`0x00a5b610`).** Bare boolean. No return. Writes one global byte. Its sole reader (the sing-along track selector) refuses to pick a sing-along whenever `0x007044f0()` returns **3** (HYPOTHESIS: "a mission is running") unless this flag is set or a separate forced-target pair is non-zero. The byte is itself reset and registered as mission-scoped variable `"mission_sing_alongs"` — the same mechanism as §40.1.

**`radio_get_station` (`0x00a5b760`).** 1 string (vehicle, or a character whose current vehicle is used, via the established vehicle resolver). Returns exactly 1 number: **-1** if unresolved, **-1** if resolved but tuned to no station, else the **1-based** station index (found by scanning each station's own listener list for the vehicle's handle pair, returning `0xff`/sign-extended-to-`-1` on no match). HYPOTHESIS: station record 0 is itself the "off"/no-station record (handled specially by the reset routine), so the lowest real answer is **1**, not 0 — "no station" and "no vehicle" share the same sentinel value a caller cannot tell apart.

### 40.3 Projectile (1 function)

**`projectile_fire_from_navpoint` (`0x00a5abb0`).** 2 object-name strings (source, target, third-tier resolver + liveness) + 1 weapon-name string + 1 optional number (spread in **degrees**, missing reads 0, converted to radians). No return. No-op if the two positions are exactly equal, if the spread is ≥ 90° (π/2 radians), or if the weapon name doesn't resolve (the weapon lookup is **null-safe and case-insensitive**, so a nil or unknown name is a silent no-op — no crash). The fired direction is target-minus-source, normalized, perturbed inside a cone when spread > 0 (a uniformly-random angle around the axis), scaled by the weapon's own muzzle-speed field for velocity, and spawned via the generic object-creation path with **no owner/shooter** (HYPOTHESIS: a projectile not attributed to any attacker). **No crash shapes found** — every resolution step is properly guarded.

### 40.4 Camera (1 function)

**`players_in_weird_camera_mode` (`0x00a5a1b0`).** No arguments. Returns 1 boolean, true if any of: a global byte that is **never written anywhere in the binary** (effectively always false in the shipped build — a 9-site exhaustive reference scan, including raw immediate/displacement forms, found zero writers); a second global byte (HYPOTHESIS: an RC-gun remote-control flag, set/cleared by two functions referencing the literal string `"RC Gun"`); or — **only for the co-op partner, never the local player** — the partner is in one of two specific states. **The local player's own state is never inspected by this function at all**; in single player the answer comes entirely from the two globals (the first of which is dead code in the shipped binary).

### 40.5 PCU — clothing store (15 functions) — shared data model

All PCU functions operate on one shared model (full detail in the interp note, condensed here): a **local-player-only** inventory (every accessor explicitly checks the passed object is the local player; a co-op partner has none) — owned items (capacity **2048**, both appenders silently refuse when full) and saved outfits (capacity **128**, same silent-refusal shape) are separate fixed-capacity arrays; items/variants/categories are static tables with bounds-checked and unchecked lookup variants side by side; **the numeric "id" argument most of these functions take is actually a different kind of index depending on the function** — a slot id (0-23) for several, a category index for others, an item index, a catalog-outfit index, or a saved-outfit index for the rest (§40.6) — a binding layer must not conflate these. **The local player is never null-checked before its customization pointer is read, in any of the 15 entry points.** Slot `0x17` (23) is the backpack (sets a dedicated player flag); slot `0x13` (19) sets a different player flag and is processed first by two of the apply routines; slots 0-4/21/22 are excluded from bulk "clear" operations, and slots 0/10/11 are further exempted from some of them.

**Real crash-shaped defects, all CONFIRMED from the disassembly:** `pcu_is_bra_category`/`pcu_is_underwear_category` dereference a null category record when the index is out of range; `pcu_get_owned_item_info` dereferences a null item record when the item index is out of range (once any item is owned), and separately its variant search scans with `<=` instead of `<`, reading one variant record past the end of the array; `pcu_purchase_slot` null-checks one global pointer and then dereferences it unconditionally two lines later for a "Backpacks" name compare, and separately dereferences an unchecked variant-lookup result and an unchecked store-entry variant pointer (reachability of both HYPOTHESIS); a colour copy inside `pcu_purchase_slot` writes into a fixed 3-slot stack array with no clamp of its own (latent only — a shared apply routine elsewhere already clamps the source count to 3, but other builders weren't checked).

**Real logic defects, all CONFIRMED:** `pcu_purchase_slot` and `pcu_purchase_outfit` both **ignore the inventory-append function's "full" return value** — a player who is already at capacity (2048 items or 128 outfits) is charged the full price and receives nothing silently; `pcu_purchase_outfit` additionally drops individual outfit pieces past the 2048-item cap one at a time with no notice, while still saving the outfit record itself. `pcu_wear_store_outfit` numbers catalog-outfit nodes by testing "any non-zero flag bit (excluding one specific bit)," while `pcu_get_num_items_owned` and `pcu_purchase_outfit` both number the identical catalog list by testing "bit 0 only" — **the same Lua-supplied index can name two different outfits depending on which of these three functions is called**, a real, confirmed indexing inconsistency. `pcu_get_owned_item_info` reports **variant 0 of the item's own name, not the actually-owned variant's name**, for one of its many returned fields (CONFIRMED from the listing; whether this is an intentional "base item name" or a bug is HYPOTHESIS). `pcu_is_current_item_worn` returns **zero Lua values** (not a boolean) on one of its paths — a real return-arity irregularity a caller must handle. The shared outfit-apply routine (`0x00825cf0`) mutates its source outfit record's own piece ordering in place as a side effect of applying it — calling it twice on the same saved outfit does not reproduce the original piece order.

### 40.6 Cross-function observations

The "id" argument's meaning varies by function within the single PCU family: slot id for the wear-option/variant/purchase-style entries, category index for the bra/underwear/clear-slots queries, item index for one argument of the owned-item-info query, catalog-outfit index for the outfit-count/purchase/wear-outfit-from-catalog entries, and saved-outfit index for the plain wear-outfit entry — five distinct index spaces sharing one "number" argument type across the family. Three of the fifteen PCU entries are pure Lua-callback iterators (wear options, variants, saved outfits) that call back once per qualifying element and return nothing themselves. Purchases across this tranche never verify that the inventory append actually succeeded before treating the transaction as complete — the same shape as tranche 06/07's own purchase-adjacent findings. `radio_get_station` and `players_in_weird_camera_mode` both illustrate a recurring pattern in this document: a sentinel value ("not found"/"no vehicle") that is indistinguishable from a real, valid low value.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 08 resolved and written up (§40.1-§40.5); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: `0x007044f0`'s own mode values and who reads the sprint getters; the mission-scoped-variable mechanism's persistence/replication semantics; several PCU slot/category id meanings beyond the backpack slot; what receives the "clothing"/"vehicle-cust"-style purchase notifications and when it actually runs.

**`inv_item_add_ammo` (`0x00a50e40`).** Character name + item name + amount (truncated, no checks). No return. If the character isn't locally owned, sends a network message instead — **the amount is truncated to 16 bits on the wire**, with no sign or range check anywhere in this path.

**`inv_item_add_do` (`0x00a51dc0`).** Item name + 3 optional arguments (count, default 1; character name, default `"#PLAYER1#"`; boolean, default false). No return. The character's own "player slot index" can be the sentinel `0xff` when no player record is found, and **neither this function nor its callees bound-check that index against the backing pointer array, or check the array entry for null** before dereferencing the resulting record — HYPOTHESIS/OPEN whether a non-player character can actually reach this path, but the missing checks themselves are CONFIRMED.

Returns `(state, -1)` if resolved, else `(-1)` alone — **two different "not available" sentinels depending on WHY**: -1 means "character not found," while **255** (not -1) means "found, but not currently skydiving." ### 41.6 Queries (3 functions)

**`get_vehicle_speed` (`0x00a4c440`) — unchecked virtual result on one resolution path.** 1 name (vehicle, character, or a third object kind — three different resolution tiers). Returns 1 integer speed, 0 if nothing resolves. Reads the vehicle's velocity magnitude through a scale/bias pair (units OPEN) only when the vehicle's body is fully active. **On the third resolution tier, the result of a virtual call is dereferenced with no null check** — the sibling group code (§41.5) null-checks the identical virtual slot, which suggests it genuinely can return null; reachability here is OPEN, the missing check itself is CONFIRMED.

**`get_closest_npc_to_object` (`0x00a4b7c0`).** Reference object name + radius. **Always returns exactly 2 values**: `(distance, name)` for the closest match, or `(float-max, "")` when nothing qualifies. A spatial query collects up to a **safely bounded 32 candidates** (the append helper refuses once full, confirmed no overflow) and only accepts candidates with a genuine non-empty script name — **unnamed ambient NPCs can never be returned by this function.** With more than 32 real candidates in the search box, the true closest NPC could be dropped by the cap (HYPOTHESIS on the practical effect; the cap itself is CONFIRMED).

Bounded, so a garbage-return/information-leak defect rather than a crash.

### 41.7 Garage (1 function)

**`garage_repair_vehicle` (`0x005f88d0`) — a real, confirmed null-pointer crash on a stale/unset garage vehicle.** No arguments, no return. Resolves the garage's current vehicle handle; **if that handle is unset, stale, dead, or not actually a vehicle, the vehicle pointer is left null — and the cost-calculation callee dereferences it unconditionally with no guard of its own.** A sibling garage handler (not in this tranche) calls the identical cost function but only after confirming the resolution succeeded, and substitutes a plain 0 otherwise — establishing that the repair handler specifically is the one missing the guard, not the cost function being inherently unsafe. The cost formula itself: cheaper as the vehicle's health percentage rises, free above a runtime threshold; the player is charged **before** the repair actually runs, with no visible affordability check in this function.

### 41.8 Cross-function observations

Several functions in this tranche return a different NUMBER of Lua values depending on outcome, not just a different value — `mesh_mover_set_damaged_by_player_only`, `mesh_mover_ready`, `get_char_skydiving_state`, and `inv_item_get_weapon_upgrades` all vary their return arity by path; a reimplementation must match each shape exactly, not normalize them. Three names promise a kind check their implementation doesn't perform: `mesh_mover_ready` accepts any object, `helicopter_set_dont_use_constraints` accepts any vehicle (and even a character, redirected to its current vehicle), and `get_vehicle_speed` accepts a character and reports whichever vehicle it's currently in. Several networked setters truncate their numeric payload to 16 bits on the wire with no corresponding range check on the Lua-facing side (`inv_item_add_ammo`, `inv_item_add_do`). Two stub callees (`0x00d34cd0`, `0x00d21330`) are confirmed dead — both always return the constant 1, discarded by every caller.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED missing-check from the disassembly; reachability marked where not separately settled):** `garage_repair_vehicle` (null vehicle into the cost function — reachable whenever the garage handle is unset/stale); `hud_x_of_y_remove` (unbounded index → wild indirect call); `group_show_do`/`group_hide_do` (null member object reaches an unguarded dereference — reachability OPEN); `get_vehicle_speed` tier 3 (unchecked virtual result — reachability OPEN); `inv_item_get_weapon_upgrades` (unchecked player-slot index and array entry — HYPOTHESIS reachability). Non-crash: `get_get_key_names_for_axis_action`'s uninitialized-buffer return.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 11 resolved and written up (§41.1-§41.7); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: the separate registrar `0x00845aa0`'s own role and callers; several Lua names for sibling setter functions not independently resolved this pass; co-op menu types 10/11; speed units; whether a cash debit beyond the player's funds is clamped or refused.

## 42. Ranking tranche 10 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Crreish-sync\for-team-a\team-a\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-10.json` (names 176-200 of 554, Team B call-count order). 21 names are in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; 4 are UI, in two sub-registrars under `0x008430f0` (`pause_menu_change_control_scheme` and 16 siblings in `0x007e18e0`; three `pause_map_*` names and 6 siblings in `0x007dfae0`, which also already holds the Killbane-era `pause_map_stag_*` names, §31). Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 42.1 Pause menu / pause map (4 functions)

**`pause_menu_change_control_scheme` (`0x007e10d0`).** 1 number (control-scheme index). No return. Selects one of two fixed scheme sets (A or B, chosen by a separate selector global this document's init-sibling writes — **selector 0 → set A, anything else, including its own default, → set B**), clamps the index to the set's own count, unbinds the current scheme and applies the new one. **Real edge case: if a scheme set's count is 0, the clamp computes `count-1 = -1` and then clamps the index DOWN to -1** — reading the fixed-size scheme record immediately *before* the array base (reachability of an empty set while the pause menu is open is OPEN, the arithmetic itself is CONFIRMED).

**`pause_map_zoom` (`0x007dbcc0`).** 1 boolean (true=in, false/missing=out). No return. Applies a ±20% multiplicative step to a global zoom factor (clamped to map-specific bounds), then recomputes the map's pan offset from the new zoom — which **divides by the zoom factor**. HYPOTHESIS edge case (not crash-shaped, just numerically degenerate): calling this before the map's own bounds are set leaves both bounds at 0, forcing the zoom itself to 0 and the pan recompute to divide by zero (float semantics: inf/NaN, not a fault).

**`pause_map_set_gps` (`0x007dba10`) — a real null-pointer crash on a stale selection.** No arguments, no return. Three exclusive modes depending on pause-map state bytes: a "stag" completion mode (fires a Lua hook by name, §31's own `pause_map_stag_completion`, no GPS set); a taxi-destination mode (shows an error message, no GPS set); or the ordinary GPS-route mode, which targets the map cursor, a selected blip, or — for a specific selection "kind 3" with a live co-op partner — the partner's own position. **On the success path, the kind-3 branch re-reads the selection-kind global and re-fetches the co-op-partner accessor A SECOND TIME with no null check** — if the partner has since disconnected while a kind-3 (partner) blip is still selected, this dereferences the null result. The outcome of every route attempt (success or failure) is reported to the pause-map's own UI script by calling a Lua function **by name** (`pause_map_interface_event(code)` — 0=GPS set, 1=GPS failed, 2=bookmark added, 3=bookmark removed), not through a return value — this is the general reporting mechanism for the whole pause-map family, confirmed across both this function and the next.

**`pause_map_add_bookmark` (`0x007df8a0`) — two real null-pointer crash paths.** No arguments, no return. Toggles: if a bookmark blip is currently selected, it's removed; otherwise, if fewer than 5 bookmarks exist, a new one is added at the cursor's position (capacity exactly 5, using ids `0x62`-`0x66` of a 10-wide `0x62`-`0x6b` remove range — a real, confirmed mismatch, though not itself a crash). **Add path:** the marker-object creation call can fail (pool exhaustion), and the caller dereferences its null result with no check. **Remove path:** the stored marker object can have already been destroyed by the time removal runs; the handle-to-object resolver correctly returns null for this, but the generic "local ownership" test treats a null object as locally-owned (true), so the removal call proceeds anyway and dereferences the gone object inside a deeper helper. Both are real, confirmed code paths; exact reachability (e.g. streaming/cleanup racing a surviving blip) is HYPOTHESIS.

### 42.2 NPC/party behavior flags (5 functions)

All five double-gate record-and-replicate setters (this document's established §7 variant-1 shape) except the fourth:

**`npc_brute_always_throws` (`0x00a55190`).** Character + optional boolean, default **true**. **Silently a no-op for any character that fails a specific "is a brute" test** (HYPOTHESIS on the test's exact meaning) — the setter is simply never called in that case.

**`npc_detection_enable` (`0x00a55300`).** Character + bare boolean (default false). **Silently a no-op while a specific global byte is set** — its meaning and writer are OPEN.

**`npc_weapon_pickup_override` (`0x00a557d0`) — inverted boolean.** Character + bare boolean (default false). Sets a "can't pick up weapons" AI force-flag to the **logical NOT** of the Lua argument — `true` means weapons MAY be picked up, the opposite of what the stored bit literally represents.

**`override_npc_run_and_cower_run` (`0x00a58ca0`).** Character (resolved directly, no `#PLAYER#`/`#FOLLOWER#` sentinels accepted) + 2 animation-set names. No return, **no replication at all** — writes two animation-index fields directly from a name→index table lookup (nil or an unknown name stores -1, "no override").

**`party_use_melee_weapons_only` (`0x00a59490`).** 1 boolean. No return. Applies to the local player AND, separately, to the co-op partner if one exists — not to any other party member.

### 42.3 Callback registrars — five `on_*` names are hook registrations, not events (5 functions)

All five register a Lua callback NAME into one of this document's existing named hook-slot sub-records (§10.8) — none of them actually fires an event itself. An empty or nil callback name clears the slot. `on_dismount` (character hook slot `0x13`), `on_vehicle_debris_flow_recycled` (vehicle hook slot `0xb`), and `on_hit_ped` (character slot `0x15` OR vehicle slot `5`, depending on which resolver matches — "hit ped" hooks genuinely exist on both kinds) are straightforward. **`on_mount` (`0x00a580f0`) has a real inverted-probe quirk: it first checks whether the target resolves through the GENERIC name chain (which also matches `"#PLAYER#"`) and registers the hook ONLY IF THAT CHECK FAILS** — so `on_mount(callback, "#PLAYER#")` is a confirmed, silent no-op, and more generally any object kind that the generic chain's own first tier matches never gets a mount hook from this function at all; which concrete object kinds that affects is OPEN. `on_m21_player_choice` is a hand-inlined registration against a GLOBAL hook record (not an object), shared with several clothing-store UI call sites — HIGH CONFIDENCE it is a general player-level/UI hook slot, not actually mission-21-specific despite the name.

### 42.4 Script-group HUD markers (4 functions) — the group-wide siblings of this document's existing single-object entries

Group variants of this document's existing `object_indicator_add_do`/`minimap_icon_add_do` family (§10.5/§10.6): instead of one object, they resolve a script-group name and walk its member list(s), applying the same underlying per-object helper to each qualifying member.

**`object_indicator_add_script_group_do` (`0x00a59080`) — a real null-pointer crash on a bad group name.** Group name + 2 numbers + optional flags (default 3). No return (the single-object sibling returns a boolean; this one doesn't). **A nil, unknown, or dead group name leaves the group pointer at literal null, and the very next instruction unconditionally dereferences it** — confirmed in the disassembly, trivially reachable from a script. The sibling remove function and both minimap group functions all guard this correctly, so this is a one-off defect in this specific function, not a pattern across the family.

**`object_indicator_remove_script_group_do` (`0x00a59220`).** Group name + optional flags (default 3). No return. Correctly guarded against a bad group. **Removes EVERY indicator on each qualifying member object, not just the ones this script group itself added** — a real, confirmed over-broad side effect.

**`minimap_icon_add_script_group_do` (`0x00a54220`) / `minimap_icon_remove_script_group_do` (`0x00a544f0`) — null dereference plus an unbounded function-pointer-table index, confirmed to also apply to the already-specced single-object siblings.** Group name + icon name (add only, no null check — a nil/non-string icon name reaches an unguarded dereference) + optional strings/numbers. No return. For each qualifying member, both dispatch through a **4-entry function-pointer table indexed directly by a script-supplied flags argument, with no range check anywhere** — this is the exact same hazard this document's own tranche-04 write-up already found in the single-object `minimap_icon_remove_do`/`minimap_icon_add_do`, and this investigation now gives the actual table contents: index 0 is a file-backed null pointer, indices 1-3 are the only real handlers, and indices 4+ walk straight off the end of the table into unrelated adjacent globals — for the remove table specifically, **index 4 happens to land on the live `open_vint_dialog_check_done` result global (§42.5), so a flags value of 4 calls that integer as if it were code.** Only flags ∈ {1,2,3} are safe for either table.

### 42.5 Mission help / mission state (3 functions)

**`mission_help_table_do` (`0x00a53ba0`).** 10 arguments (text key, 2 booleans, 2 substitution strings, 3 numeric flags/values, 2 more booleans) — full detail in the interp note. No return. Both this function and its sibling `mission_help_clear` return immediately while a specific game-mode global is in a 4-value range (meaning OPEN).
