Resolves its text key through a localization lookup, falling back to a secondary hashed help-text table, falling back to showing the raw key text. **A real logic quirk: an unknown key combined with the default duration argument shows for 10 seconds, not the record's own 7-second default** — the fallback table's bounds-check failure on an unknown key happens to return 10.0 rather than propagating the real default.

**`mission_help_clear` (`0x00a52ab0`).** 1 optional number (flags, default 3). No return. Bit 1 clears locally; bit 2, **only when this machine is host**, broadcasts a clear to clients. **A non-host calling this with the default flags only ever clears locally** — the broadcast half is silently skipped.

**`mission_collectible_collected` (`0x00a523b0`).** No arguments. Returns 1 boolean. Scans a fixed 4-group collectible table (20 entries each) and returns the first qualifying entry's own stored byte, or **true if nothing qualifies at all** — "no blocker found" reads as success, not absence. Semantics beyond the structural read are HYPOTHESIS.

### 42.6 Small globals (4 functions)

**`parking_spot_set_max` (`0x00a59b20`) / `parking_spot_reset_max` (`0x00a59360`).** Set takes 1 number; values **above 18 or negative are silently ignored** (only 0-18 accepted) — not clamped, simply dropped, leaving the previous value in place. Reset writes the hard-coded default **18**. Global, not per-player.

**`open_vint_dialog_check_done` (`0x00a58f10`) — a real stuck-poll hazard.** No arguments. Returns 1 number: a global integer, file-default **-2** ("pending"), written ~~to a real option index~~ by a dialog's own completion callback. **If the dialog itself fails to open (its own open call can fail), the global is left at -2 permanently** — a script polling this in a loop until it's "no longer -2" never finishes. The same -2 default also means a check performed before any dialog was ever opened reads identically to "pending." **CORRECTED (2026-10-03, ranking tranche 18, §50.3): the completion callback's own body (`0x00a58d40`, 5 instructions, directly disassembled) writes this global only to the literal `-1`, and only when its own second argument equals `-1` — it never writes an option index at all. So the only two values this function can ever return are `-2` (pending) and `-1` (the dialog finished with argument `-1`); it can never report *which* option was chosen. Whether every dialog-close path passes `-1`, or only cancel does, is OPEN — if choosing an option passes its index instead, a script waiting for "not -2" after a choice waits forever, which is the same stuck-poll hazard as the open call failing, just triggered by a chosen option instead of a missing one.**

**`path_name_is_path` (`0x00a5a790`).** 1 string. Returns 1 boolean: true only for a live object of the specific "path" kind, via the dedicated path-object resolver. No sentinel names accepted.

### 42.7 Cross-function observations

22 of this tranche's 25 functions return zero Lua values; every one of them fails silently on bad input (no Lua error is ever raised in this tranche). The group-HUD-marker family and the single-object siblings this document already specs diverge in several concrete ways beyond the shared function-pointer-table hazard: the group variants resolve through a different kind-descriptor bit, skip an alternate dispatch path the single-object versions have, and disagree with each other on failure-guard discipline (three guard cleanly, one dereferences null). The hook-name registry shared by all five `on_*` functions here (`0x00a1fcc0`, a fixed 350-entry pool) has two further confirmed quirks worth carrying forward: it matches purely by name HASH with no string compare (so two different names with an equal hash would silently share one hook slot), and a string-allocation failure during registration stores the sentinel id **0** rather than the "failed" sentinel -1 — every caller's own "is this slot registered" check treats 0 as a real, valid registration.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED code paths from the disassembly; reachability marked where not separately settled):** `object_indicator_add_script_group_do` (null group dereference, trivially reachable); `minimap_icon_add_script_group_do` (null icon-name dereference, trivially reachable; plus the shared unbounded table-index hazard, plus a likely CRT crash on a non-string third argument); `minimap_icon_remove_script_group_do` (the same unbounded table-index hazard, including the specific index-4-hits-a-live-global case); `pause_map_set_gps` (null co-op-partner dereference on a stale kind-3 selection — reachability HYPOTHESIS); `pause_map_add_bookmark` (two separate null-pointer paths, add and remove — reachability HYPOTHESIS for the remove case); `pause_menu_change_control_scheme` (negative-index read on an empty scheme set — reachability OPEN).

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 10 resolved and written up (§42.1-§42.6); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: which concrete object kinds trigger `on_mount`'s exclusion; the collectible table's real writer and field meanings; several `mission_help_table_do` record-field meanings and the game-mode range that disables mission-help entirely; the minimap function-pointer tables' own entries 1-2 (not opened).

## 43. Ranking tranche 09 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Crreish-sync\for-team-a\team-a\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-09.json` (names 151-175 of 554, Team B call-count order; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_09.md`). No gameplay-registrar names this time — all 25 are UI customization functions reached only through the 311-entry UI registrar `0x008430f0`: 10 `pcu_` names (clothing store/wardrobe) in sub-registrar `0x00830230` (a 44-row name/function table — the PCU family has 44 Lua names in total, 34 already specced in §26.11-§26.15 and tranche 08), 15 `pcr_` names (character creator/plastic surgeon) in sub-registrar `0x008377d0`. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 43.1 Lua-callback coroutine mechanism settled (closes a tranche-08 OPEN item)

Every UI customization callback (this tranche's "report"/iteration functions and several already-specced ones) runs as a **new Lua coroutine**, not a bare `lua_call`: `0x00e0ca80(name, state)`/`0x00e0c8f0(name, parentRecord)` → `0x00e0c720` looks the name up in the Lua globals table, requires it to be a Lua (not C) function, creates a new Lua thread, and registers it in the same 256-record script-thread table §26.27 documents, keyed by a fresh 16-bit id. `0x00e0cba0` resumes it synchronously; `0x00e0c610` reports whether it finished (no call info, no stack values) or yielded; a finished-or-errored coroutine is released at once by `0x00e0c650` (drops the reference, frees the name, compacts the table and decrements the count), a yielded one keeps its record — so the 256-record cap is only approached by callbacks that yield. All of these return/behave as null when the name is nil, the global isn't a Lua function, or the table is already full — **every caller in this tranche treats that as "skip this element," except `pcu_get_items_in_category` mode 2 (§43.2), which hangs instead.** This closes tranche 08's OPEN question about a nil callback name (handled, null result) and upgrades two of §26.27's HIGH CONFIDENCE items (the 256-count compare, the null-out on release) to CONFIRMED. §19.5/§23.3/§23.4's "opens an event record" wording should be read as "spawns a script coroutine."

### 43.2 PCU (clothing store/wardrobe) — 10 functions, sub-registrar `0x00830230`

`pcu_get_num_items_category` (`0x0082bb50`): 2 numbers (category, catalog-outfit index or -1); 1 number returned. Arg 2 = -1 counts owned items in the category (arg 1 ignored otherwise); arg 2 ≠ -1 walks the matching catalog node's pieces and keeps the *last* piece-category whose own `+0x2c` field exceeds the running result (HYPOTHESIS: meant as "largest owned count over the outfit's categories," but the comparison as written is neither a sum nor a true maximum). **Null-read crash shape:** a piece's slot that maps to no category is dereferenced at `+0x2c` unchecked (data-gated).

`pcu_get_items_in_category` (`0x0082fa30`) — **real infinite-loop hang.** 1 number (category) + 1 string (callback name); 0 return values. Three reporting modes ("Outfits" by name; "owned instances" when item flag `+0x5c` bit 1 is set; "variants" otherwise), each calling the named callback once per element with 10-18 values depending on mode and flags (full layouts in the interp note). **In "owned instances" mode, when the coroutine can't be created (§43.1 — bad/missing callback name, or the thread table is full), the code jumps to a decrement that is immediately undone by the loop's own increment, so the same owned entry is retried forever — a real hang, reachable once the 256-record table fills with yielding coroutines, or with a misspelt/missing callback name.** Separately, mode 1 numbers catalog nodes on *any* non-zero flag while every other reader (§43.4's A.1 shape, tranche 08 E.3/E.11) numbers on bit 0 only — once a player-created outfit (flag value 2, see below) exists, the "Outfits" list index and the purchase/count index disagree for every later node.

`pcu_get_item_defaults` (`0x0082c7f0`): 1 number (item index); returns -1 (out of range) or 35 values — the item's **default** colours/variant/price, the same layout tranche 08's `pcu_get_owned_item_info` uses for an owned instance. Unchecked variant-0 pointer read (data-gated crash shape).

`pcu_delete_outfit` (`0x0082dad0`): 1 number (saved-outfit index); 0 return values. Returns a player-created outfit's block/node to their free pools (see `pcu_create_outfit` below); a store-bought outfit just forgets the saved entry. Whether two saved entries can share one player-created record (leaving one dangling after delete) is OPEN.

`pcu_create_outfit` (`0x0082d850`) — **real null-write crash shape.** 1 string, which is actually a **lookup key into a 12-byte-stride hash table at `0x02317d74`** (HYPOTHESIS: virtual-keyboard results, per the keyboard-input function `0x00845780` sitting next to the resolver), not the outfit's literal name. Returns -1/error-string, or the new node's pool index (1 number). Builds a 0x24c-byte template from the current store working set and allocates a block+node pair from two free lists; **the allocator's result is read and written with no null check, so an empty block-or-node pool is a null write** — and `pcu_can_create_outfit` (below) only tests the block pool, not the node pool, so the "guard" a script is expected to call first does not cover this. A refusal at the 128-saved-outfit cap is ignored, orphaning the already-allocated catalog node. **Player-created outfits are linked into the same catalog list `0x022db9b8` that holds store outfits**, flagged with value 2 (bit 1 only, not bit 0) — this is why they appear in `pcu_get_items_in_category`'s "any flag" numbering but not in the bit-0-only readers.

`pcu_clear_obscured_slots` (`0x0082e7e0`): no arguments; re-syncs the worn table to the store, then queues two jobs (kinds 6/7) on a job queue — a full queue silently drops the job; the jobs' own consumer/meaning is OPEN.

`pcu_clear_item_new` (`0x0082bf40`): 2 numbers (item index, instance number); clears the owned "new" flag (byte `+9`) on the matching entry. **Logic shape:** the match test runs on *any* non-empty entry's position, not only matching items, so arg 2 = -1 (or an unknown item with arg 2 = -1) clears the flag on the first non-empty owned entry regardless of its item.

`pcu_category_nav_clear_slot` (`0x0082f440`) — **real out-of-bounds read + dereference.** 1 number, masked to 16 bits, indexing the 16-entry descriptor array `0x022ffcf0` **with no bound or null check** before comparing the descriptor's name to "Piercings" — unlike every other reader of this array (§19.1/§26.14/§26.15), which does bound-check it. On a match it stashes worn slot 5 (HYPOTHESIS: headwear that would hide piercings) and restores it on any non-match; the backup is single-level, so navigating "Piercings"→"Piercings" loses the original slot-5 item.

`pcu_can_create_outfit` (`0x0082ae00`): no arguments; 1 or 3 values (ok, or false+title+body for "naked" / empty block pool). **Incomplete guard** — doesn't check the free-node pool or the 128-saved-outfit cap that `pcu_create_outfit` also needs, so `true` doesn't guarantee creation succeeds.

`pcu_bra_required` (`0x0082ad10`): no arguments; 1 boolean = local player byte `+0xa41` == 1 (the gender byte, §16.8 — "player is female"). No player null check (crash shape).

### 43.3 PCR (character creator) — 15 functions, sub-registrar `0x008377d0`

`pcr_report_skin_colors` (`0x00832570`): 1 string (callback). Reports every skin entry via a coroutine opened against **the calling script's own thread record** (`0x00e0cb20(L)` → `0x00e0c8f0`), not the global script state — the only report function in this tranche to do so, so it reports nothing when called from an unregistered state. Uses a second "no string id" sentinel, `0x029c9960` (distinct from `0x029c9964`).

`pcr_report_hair_items` (`0x00832cc0`) — **real crash shapes.** 1 number (hair category 0-2) + 1 callback string. Maps the category through a 3-entry table **with no range check** (unlike `pcr_change_hair`/`pcr_get_hair_info`, which do). A linear-search helper returns null for no match and its `+0x2c` is read unchecked (null-read shape); arg 1 outside 0-2 reads the mapping table out of bounds.

`pcr_report_hair_colors` (`0x00833420`): 1 callback string. "Current" colour = derived from entry 0 of the per-store hair-colour table (whatever slot entry 0 happens to belong to); an empty colour table for that store yields a negative "current" with nothing flagged as selected.

`pcr_report_eye_colors` (`0x00830da0`): 1 callback string. Reports **global composite-definition indices** (not per-category eye-colour indices) for every category-1 ("eyes") definition; uses a third distinct sentinel convention, plain **0** rather than `0x029c9964`/`0x029c9960`.

`pcr_report_anims` (`0x00834bf0`): 1 string (style category) + 1 callback string. "melee_combat_style" is a no-op (as §19.14 already found); the other three categories report through **selection-sort pickers that return entries in alphabetical order of the displayed name**, not table order — an O(n²) cost per listing. Facial "BLANK" reports index -1 even though it occupies the real index 15 internally, so a script cannot select BLANK by feeding the reported index back into `pcr_set_anim`. **Data-gated shapes:** byte loop counters compared against dword table counts (never terminate past 255 entries); unbounded flag-array clears; an unterminated 128-byte `strncpy`.

`pcr_randomize_eye_colors` (`0x00835bc0`): no arguments. Collects every eligible composite definition into a **600-entry stack array with no bound check** before picking one at random (data-gated stack-overflow shape).

`pcr_purchase_tattoo` (`0x008333a0`) — **real logic defect.** 1 number (price in dollars, default 0). Only charges cash (reason `0xb`, §16.8a's "cash_adjust" path) — no item, composite, or stat is touched. **No sign check, so a negative price pays the player instead of charging them; no affordability check; no player null check.**

`pcr_lips_randomize` (`0x00834a00`) — **real divide-by-zero and null-read shapes.** No arguments. Picks from a 64-entry stack array (entry 0 = "no lips," no bound check against 64) via the shared PRNG helper `0x00dab660(lo, hi)`, which **divides by `hi-lo+1` with no empty-range guard** — an empty "lips colour" palette (palette index 2) makes this divide by zero. A picked lips item whose name doesn't resolve as a PCU item is dereferenced null immediately after the unchecked lookup.

`pcr_hair_randomize_all` (`0x00837450`) — **real divide-by-zero and a real logic bug.** No arguments. Same unguarded PRNG call against the hair-colour table (divide-by-zero on an empty table). **Logic bug:** when recording the chosen colours, the code uses the hair-style array entry's own slot instead of the category's slot, so colours land under the wrong slot unless the first three hair styles happen to occupy slots 1-3 (intent HYPOTHESIS; read CONFIRMED).

`pcr_get_voice` (`0x00832e60`): no arguments; 0 or 1 values (cached voice index). `pcr_get_triangle_cursor_pos` (`0x008329a0`): no arguments; 2 signed integers. **Spec correction:** the matching setter (§19.3, `0x008329f0`) **truncates** each value to an integer before storing — §19.3's "written directly" wording should say so; fractional cursor positions are lost on write, not just on this getter's read. Neither function null-checks the player.

`pcr_creation_complete` (`0x008335c0`) — **real null-dereference shape.** No arguments. A co-op "both players finished the creator" handshake on two ready-flag globals plus a byte (`0x024e97d2`, HYPOTHESIS: "remote player still in the creator," writer OPEN) that gates a wait. When not ready, opens a waiting dialog from a fixed dialog pool — **if the pool is exhausted, the allocator returns null and the caller dereferences it unchecked.** In single player, "ready" is always true (no remote player exists).

`pcr_cleanup_player_voice` (`0x00830a30`): no arguments. Clears the voice-slot "Phone_Call" cue override that `pcr_set_voice` (§23.1) sets, replicated to clients when this machine is host.

`pcr_apply_regional_preset` (`0x00830600`) — **real null-dereference shape.** 2 strings (region, preset name), resolved through the same two-stage name resolvers `pcr_apply_preset` (§23.8) already uses for its optional arguments. Applies the preset's morph pairs to the player, including a "body gender" special case that swaps the slot-10 base garment when the morph value crosses 0.5. **Neither the preset-apply step nor the morph-apply step null-checks the local player**, so a valid region/preset pair with no local player crashes. The written field (player `+0x2090`) and the morph-apply helpers' own meanings are OPEN.

`pcr_add_default_clothing` (`0x008306a0`) — **real destructive side effect.** No arguments. Refreshes worn slot 10, then calls the shared "refresh body" helper (§16.8a) in its **flag-0 mode**, which — for this tranche, newly traced — **empties the player's entire owned-clothing inventory (sets the owned count to 0) before re-adding only the default garments for the player's gender/ethnicity.** Correct for new-character creation (the intent, HYPOTHESIS); destructive if any shipped script calls it on an established character (Team B reports 2 call sites in 2 scripts; which, OPEN). No player null check on the final store read.

### 43.4 Cross-function observations

Shared conventions already established by tranches 06-08 and the file's own front matter (argument/return primitives, PCU data model, PRNG `0x00dab660`, name hash `0x00d9e8b0`) are reused here, not repeated. New this tranche: **three distinct "no string id" sentinels are in live use across this one UI family** — `0x029c9964` (items/variants/hair styles), `0x029c9960` (skin names), and plain `0` (eye definitions) — a binding layer must not assume a single sentinel convention. **Local-player null checks are the exception, not the rule**, in this tranche: only `pcr_report_anims`, `pcr_get_voice`, `pcr_cleanup_player_voice`, `pcu_get_item_defaults` (partially) and `pcu_can_create_outfit` check; every other root reads the player or its store pointer unguarded. A new wide-string encoder `0x00e22a30` (writes a NUL-free, tagged-byte UTF-16 encoding) is how outfit/hair-colour/anim names reach Lua as C strings; whether the UI side decodes it back to UTF-16 is HYPOTHESIS.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED code paths from the disassembly; reachability marked where not separately settled):** `pcu_get_items_in_category` mode 2 (infinite loop/hang on coroutine-creation failure, §43.1/§43.2); `pcu_create_outfit` (null write on empty pool; orphan node at the 128-outfit cap); `pcu_category_nav_clear_slot` (16-bit index with no bound/null check into a 16-entry array, then dereferenced); `pcr_report_hair_items` (unbounded category index; null-read on a component-lookup miss); `pcr_lips_randomize` (divide-by-zero on an empty palette; null-read on an unresolved item name); `pcr_hair_randomize_all` (divide-by-zero on an empty colour table; plus the wrong-slot logic bug); `pcr_creation_complete` (null dereference on an exhausted dialog pool); `pcr_apply_regional_preset` (null player dereference on a valid region/preset pair); `pcr_purchase_tattoo` (no sign check — a negative price pays the player); `pcr_add_default_clothing` (wholesale owned-clothing wipe, destructive outside new-character creation). Several further shapes are data-gated (unbounded 64-/600-/stack arrays, out-of-range colour-palette indices) — full list and addresses in the interp note's sections E/G.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 09 resolved and written up (§43.1-§43.3); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: queued job kinds 6/7's consumer; player fields `+0x2090`/`+0x5c` bit meanings; the byte `0x024e97d2`'s writer and the co-op "done" flags' reset path; whether any shipped script's customization callback actually yields (which decides how close the 256-record coroutine table can get in practice); whether any shipped script calls `pcr_add_default_clothing` on an established character.

## 44. Ranking tranche 12 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM A\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-12.json` (names 226-250 of 554, Team B call-count order — corrects the dispatch brief's guessed range; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_12.md`). Five registrars: the 113-row `game_` table `0x00845aa0` (spec-lua-bindings §13.5, 14 names), the difficulty/pause-menu sub-registrar `0x007e18e0` (§16.11/tranche 10, 3 names), two **new** UI sub-registrars under `0x008430f0` — a 9-name lobby table `0x007abbb0` (4 names in this tranche) and a 7-name machinima table `0x00bc68a0` (2 names) — and the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840` (2 names). Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 44.1 Eight names are constant stubs

`game_is_pc_dx11`, `game_get_ps3_button_swap`, `game_record_mode_is_supported`, `game_record_mode_is_active` all resolve to `0x00a3c670`, which unconditionally returns false (this executable is the DX9 build; whether a separate DX11 executable binds a different handler is OPEN). `game_show_party_ui` and `game_show_community_sessions_ui` resolve to the existing shared no-op stub `0x007c9f50` (§6.1/§24.2/§27.17). Console-overlay/recording features with no PC implementation.

### 44.2 Co-op, network and Steam (7 functions, `0x00845aa0`)

`game_set_coop_join_type` (`0x00844440`): 1 number, mapped 0→0, 1→1, anything else→2; **ignored entirely on a client**; on the host it's a lobby setting (session `+0x40`/`+0x230` settings block, dword `+8`) published to matchmaking, rate-limited. Getter `game_get_coop_join_type` reads global `0x012f44fc`; meaning of 0/1/2 is OPEN.

`game_coop_kick_player` (`0x00844250`) — **real latent stack-overflow shape.** Optional callback-name string. With a remote player, shows a confirm dialog (formatted via the wide-sprintf wrapper `0x00db0510`, which always tells the CRT its buffer holds 1024 wide characters); **three call sites in this tranche (plus the sibling `game_kick_coop_player`) pass a 256-wide-character stack buffer to that wrapper** — a long enough localized string plus player name overruns the stack frame (data-gated: shipped strings/Steam names are short, HYPOTHESIS not reachable in practice). Confirming removes the player with reason `0xf`. **Callback arity is inconsistent by path:** 0 arguments (no remote player), 1 argument `true` (confirmed kick), or never called at all (cancelled) — and the dialog is shown on clients too, where confirming calls back `true` without actually kicking anyone.

`game_show_coop_partner_gamercard` (`0x008425a0`): opens the Steam friends overlay on the remote player's Steam ID (player `+0x142`) via `SteamFriends()` slot `+0x50` (HIGH CONFIDENCE `ActivateGameOverlayToUser`) — **the interface pointer is not null-checked** here, unlike tranche 11's sibling overlay call.

`game_is_joinable` (`0x00842510`): free-slot count (capacity minus two reserved-slot checks minus player count) tested as **"not zero" rather than "greater than zero,"** so a negative count (more players than capacity) passes — reachability OPEN — plus several session-state field tests whose meanings are OPEN.

`game_is_connected_to_internet` (`0x008428e0`) is the **same handler** as the already-specced `game_is_connected_to_service` — both mean "logged on to Steam" (`SteamUser()` non-null and `ISteamUser::BLoggedOn`), distinct from §27.19's weaker "interface exists" test.

`game_join_syslink_game` (`0x00844610`): 1-based server index, **compared as 8 bits** against the find-server ring (tranche 11) — index 257 silently matches the same record as index 1; an unknown index is a silent no-op. `game_coop_get_starting_syslink` (`0x008426b0`) reads co-op-start byte `0x014ff6c2`, set by the sibling setters `game_coop_start_new_live`/`game_coop_start_new_syslink` (new globals `0x014ff6c1`/`0x014ff6c2`, mutually exclusive).

### 44.3 Lobby (4 functions, new sub-registrar `0x007abbb0`)

`game_lobby_update_map_selection`/`game_lobby_update_char_selection`: store the selection with no bounds check (consumers check); the char setter applies at once on a client but only stages the value on the host, committed later by `game_lobby_set_horde_mode_data`.

`game_lobby_set_horde_mode_data` (`0x007ab8d0`) — **real logic defect.** 1 boolean ("continue from saved wave," HYPOTHESIS). Looks up saved horde progress for the selected map; **an out-of-range map index returns a "no saved progress" code that is mishandled identically to "saved progress = 1," so the player sees a spurious restart-warning dialog, and confirming it starts the mode anyway while the separate map-commit call refuses to write the out-of-range index — the committed map stays whatever it was before, which is -1 on a fresh boot.** Whether a horde start with an uncommitted (-1) map breaks anything downstream is OPEN.

`game_lobby_get_local_player_name` (`0x007ab030`): 0 values with no local player, else 1 string (UTF-16 name, encoded into a 192-byte buffer — at most 63 characters survive).

### 44.4 Machinima (2 functions, new sub-registrar `0x00bc68a0`) — real crash shapes

`game_machinima_playback_enter` (`0x00bc67d0`) has **two real crash shapes and a resource-handling defect:**
- **Null read:** arg 1 is compared inline against the literal `"machinima"` with no null check — a missing/non-string argument reads through null.
- **Uninitialized-buffer crash:** a plain string that wasn't produced by the matching UI string encoder (tranche 09's `0x00e22a30`) makes its decoder counterpart (`0x00e22ac0`, new this tranche — fails silently, writing nothing, on any input not starting with its own tag byte) leave a 520-byte stack buffer uninitialized; that garbage is then used as a `%s` argument to `_swprintf_s`, which can trigger the CRT's invalid-parameter handler and terminate the process.
- **Resource handling:** the clip-file loader (`0x00bc5230`) leaks the file handle on a bad header, never checks `ReadFile` results, can underflow a size computation from a crafted header, and doesn't check its allocation result before reading/parsing — all reachable via a damaged or hostile `.srtt_clip` file in the user-writable clips folder.

`game_machinima_is_recording` (`0x00bc5860`): simple state-dword read (`0x029443bc` == 1).

### 44.5 HUD, state, and gameplay (6 functions)

`game_hud_hide` (`0x00841d80`): **reference-counted** (clamped at 0) across ~11 HUD documents; **calling it with no argument counts as a show**, not a no-op — hide/show calls must be balanced.

`game_is_autosaving` (`0x008427b0`) **omits one of the three "busy" tests** the real autosave routine applies (interp_tabs.md Q5.2) — it can report "not autosaving" while an autosave request would still be refused.

`game_difficulty_select` (`0x007e18a0`, sub-registrar `0x007e18e0`) — **this resolves tranche 11's §41.2 OPEN item** ("`get_current_difficulty`'s real setter, reached via a sibling UI handler, Lua name not resolved that pass"): it is this function, which stores the value only when it is below 3 (unsigned compare), silently ignoring anything else.

`fov_check_xz_plane` (`0x00a20840`) — **real logic defect:** when the target is in view it returns **2 Lua values (true, false)** instead of 1 — harmless for `if fov_check_xz_plane(...) then` but wrong for a caller that counts or forwards results. Otherwise an XZ-flattened cone test; arg 3 is a half-angle in degrees (default 30, i.e. a 60° cone).

`flee_to_navpoint` (`0x00a20840`) queues a per-character AI event (type `0x30`, the same queue §15.4 below uses) with the navpoint position and a threat handle; silently dropped if the event pool is empty, the character is dead, or it is a player-class object; `"#PLAYER#"` is not accepted for the fleeing character itself.

### 44.6 Spec correction: §15.4's `set_always_cower_flag` effect call is an AI event, not a VFX cue

This tranche's `flee_to_navpoint` (§44.5) and `game_lobby_set_horde_mode_data`'s callees both confirm `0x004f5dd0` is a **per-character queued AI event** (event-type byte, source/recipient 64-bit handles resolved through the shared handle table, delay, two flag bytes, an optional 32-byte payload — dropped silently on an empty event-record free list, a dead recipient, or a player-class recipient). §15.4's existing description of `set_always_cower_flag`'s own `0x004f5dd0(0x26, ...)` call as "spawning a visual/VFX cue at the character's position" from a "position pair" read off handle `+8`/`+0xc` is **corrected**: those two dwords are passed exactly where `flee_to_navpoint` passes a 64-bit object handle, so §15.4's call queues AI event `0x26` on the character — not an effect. HIGH CONFIDENCE (the event-type identity `0x26`'s own meaning stays OPEN).

### 44.7 Cross-function observations

Two new UI sub-registrars confirmed under `0x008430f0`: lobby (`0x007abbb0`, 9 names) and machinima (`0x00bc68a0`, 7 names). Host/client asymmetry recurs across this tranche exactly as in prior ones (join-type setter ignored on clients; char-selection staged differently; kick dialog shown but inert on clients). The wide-sprintf wrapper `0x00db0510`'s fixed 1024-wide-character limit (§44.2) is a **project-wide latent-overflow pattern**: besides this tranche's three call sites, tranche 09's dialog-open helper `0x007c3e60` is another caller with a smaller buffer — a full audit of every caller of `0x00db0510` against its actual buffer size is OPEN and worth doing as its own pass. The UI string encoder/decoder pair (`0x00e22a30` encode, `0x00e22ac0` decode, §44.4) is confirmed two-way, and the decoder's silent-failure-on-bad-input behavior is a second place (besides the machinima crash) any caller must pre-initialize its own output buffer to use safely.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED code paths from the disassembly; reachability marked where not separately settled):** `game_machinima_playback_enter` (null read on non-string arg; uninitialized-buffer crash on a plain string; clip-loader handle leak/unchecked I/O, §44.4); `game_coop_kick_player` and sibling `game_kick_coop_player` (latent stack overflow via `0x00db0510`'s fixed 1024-char limit against 256-char buffers — data-gated); `game_show_coop_partner_gamercard` (unchecked `SteamFriends()` result); `game_is_joinable` ("≠0" free-slot test admits a negative count — reachability OPEN); `game_join_syslink_game` (8-bit index wraparound); `game_lobby_set_horde_mode_data` (spurious restart warning plus an uncommitted-map start on an out-of-range index).

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 12 resolved and written up (§44.1-§44.6); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: join-type/session-field meanings (§44.2/§44.5); whether horde can actually start with an uncommitted (-1) map; machinima state 3 and game-play-mode stack values 1-4; a full audit of `0x00db0510` callers' buffer sizes project-wide.

## 45. Ranking tranche 13 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM A\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-13.json` (names 251-275 of 554, Team B call-count order; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_13.md`). 17 names in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; 8 under the UI registrar `0x008430f0` through five sub-registrars, two **new**: dialog `0x007c5630` (12 names, 4 in this tranche), cellphone `0x0083db20` (3 names, 1 here), cell camera `0x0083ae10` (2 names, 1 here), cinema editor `0x00bcd240` (2 names, 1 here), and a one-name registrar `0x0067d660` that pushes its function pointer **before** the name — the first registrar in this series the dump tool's "next slot" heuristic mis-locates (the real handler was read from a `range` dump instead). New shared helper this tranche: `0x00853b30(object, n)`, a generic kind-flag bit test (bit `n&7` of byte `+6+(n>>3)`) that every kind-bit test in tranche 11's table reduces to. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 45.1 Characters and AI (6 functions) — unchecked resolver results are the dominant crash class again

**`character_fake_revival_end` (`0x00a41fc0`) and its untranched sibling `character_fake_revival_start` (`0x00a41f80`) — real null-write/null-read crashes.** 1 character-name string, resolved via the generic chain with **no null check on the result**: `_end` writes through null (clearing bit 16 of `+0xe4`) when the name doesn't resolve; `_start` reads through null first (inside a helper, `+0xcd2`) and would also write through null. Together these establish `+0xe4` bit 16 = "fake revival in progress" (HIGH CONFIDENCE).

**`character_take_human_shield_check_done` (`0x00a46600`) — real null-read crash, variable return arity.** 2 character-name strings (taker, expected hostage). Returns 1, 2, or 3 Lua values depending on what resolves (a script reading only the first value gets the intended "taker holds the expected hostage" boolean). **When the taker doesn't resolve, the root pushes `false` and keeps going into the hostage-lookup helper anyway — which (per tranche 11's finding that the "is locally owned" test returns true for a null object) reads null `+0x1890`.** A character carries two separate hostage-handle fields, one for network-owned characters and one for locally-owned ones.

**`character_set_cannot_exit_rc_vehicle` (`0x00a42140`):** standard double-gate record-and-replicate setter (§7.2's shape), writes bit 9 of `+0x1c9c` locally only when both gates are false and no remote owner exists; otherwise sends an opcode-`0x46` record. Reader of the bit is OPEN.

**`character_hidden` (`0x00a41540`):** reads bit 0 of `+0x3b` — **an unresolved name reads as "hidden" (true)**, not an error. The same bit is the "skip hidden object" test `debris_flow_set_inactive`'s worker uses (§45.2), supporting "object is hidden" as the bit's real meaning.

**`customization_swap_player_rig` (`0x00a43cf0`) — real null-dereference crash shapes.** 2 strings (rig name, a second name) + optional player-mask number (default 3: bit 0 local, bit 1 remote co-op). **Always sends a network message on every call with no host/ownership gate** — in co-op with the default mask, each machine both applies locally and sends to the other, with no de-duplication traced on the receive side (OPEN). Crash shapes: no local player with mask bit 0 reads through null `+0xf4`/`+0xd24`; an unknown rig name (both lookups fail) still indexes through to a null `+0x50` read.

### 45.2 Cutscene, camera, and world state (7 functions)

**`cutscene_was_skipped` (`0x00a42ea0`):** reads bit `0x40` of the cutscene flag byte; **stays true after the skipped cutscene has ended**, clearing only when the next cutscene starts. `cutscene_check_exiting` (`0x00a42e70`): true for cutscene state > 12 (the stop/chain/teardown phases).

**`camera_script_enable`/`camera_script_disable`:** write byte `0x013c9382` ("script camera owns the view," HYPOTHESIS) and, whenever the network module is up, **unconditionally broadcast** (opcode `0x43`/`0x10`) with no host check — either machine can send it. Readers/receiver OPEN.

**`cinema_editor_create_camera_zone` (`0x00bcc1d0`) — real out-of-bounds read.** Returns a new zone handle (1 number) or **0 values on failure (not nil)**. The optional "template handle to copy from" argument's slot index (`handle & 0xff`) is **used to read the pool before being bounded by the pool's actual size** — an out-of-bounds read on a stale/foreign handle (read-only; the subsequent generation compare then almost certainly fails, so no further damage).

**`debris_flow_set_inactive` (`0x00a472d0`) — real null-dereference-through-virtual-call crash, confirmed to also hit the network peer.** 1 debris-flow id. **Always replicates** (opcode `0x45`/`0x25`) with no host/existence check. Its worker resolves each of the flow's stored object handles and, **when a handle is stale/unresolvable, sets the object pointer to null and still calls a virtual method through it** — a null dereference reachable whenever a debris-flow entry outlives its object (a realistic case for destructible debris), and it fires identically on whichever machine processes the replicated deactivate message.

**`flashpoint_mission_status` (`0x00a49b00`):** combines a local status dword and a peer status dword (4=complete confirmed by the result-screen strings it gates; 1=idle/reset, 2=started HIGH CONFIDENCE, 3=HYPOTHESIS failed/aborted) with a documented combine rule favoring "in progress" when the two sides disagree.

### 45.3 Dialog boxes (4 functions, new sub-registrar `0x007c5630`) — a real stall hazard

All four operate on a validated 4-slot dialog-handle pool (slot index + generation check, the same `+0x12c` handle tranche 09 already names).

**`dialog_close_finished` (`0x007c1be0`) — a required handshake with no timeout.** Clears latch byte `0x02282d39`. **The dialog manager's own per-pass routine freezes — showing or closing nothing further — the moment a pass closes a dialog without immediately showing a replacement, until a script calls this function to clear the latch.** If the UI script that owns the close animation never calls it (a script error, an unloaded script group, a skipped callback), **every later dialog stays queued forever with no timeout anywhere in the mechanism.**

`dialog_box_set_current_option`: writes the option index into `+0x11c` with **no range check** (consumer unknown, OPEN). `dialog_option_accept_kbd_input`/`dialog_option_end_kbd_input`: start/end text-entry editing on a dialog option (cursor capped at 191 UTF-16 units, key-state table flushed on start, committed text re-encoded with tranche 09's `0x00e22a30` and delivered to a callback on end).

### 45.4 Cellphone (3 functions, new sub-registrar `0x0083db20`) — real crash shapes

**`cellphone_dial` (`0x0083d930`) — three real crash shapes.** 1 phone-book index (number) + 2 callback-name strings. **The phone-book index has no bound or sign check**, reading an arbitrary 24-byte "entry" for an out-of-range value. That garbage (or legitimately bad data) can then make the activity-record lookup return null, which is **dereferenced unchecked**. Separately, the callback helper (`0x0083cfe0`) is **the first function in this whole tranche series to write through the Lua-callback coroutine mechanism's result (`0x00e0ca80`) with no null check** — null on a bad/missing callback name or a full 256-record thread table — and it also dereferences the "cell_phone" script-group record unchecked.

`cellphone_animate_stop_do`: confirmed no-op (calls the project's already-known no-op stub). `cell_camera_enable`: writes a global that has exactly one other reference anywhere in the binary — its own getter `cell_camera_is_enabled` — confirmed Lua-side-only state with no engine consumer.

### 45.5 Boss battle / Killbane (2 functions) — a real logic defect

**`boss_battle_mars_killbane_active(false)` clears the Killbane QTE-active flag without running the QTE-abort cleanup that `boss_battle_kb_enable(false)` runs.** Both default to enabling when called with no argument. If a script calls `mars_killbane_active(false)` while a Killbane QTE is in progress, the "hud_qte" HUD element and the player's locked control/animation state are never torn down, **and a later `kb_enable(false)` can no longer reach the abort cleanup at all, because the flag it gates on has already been cleared.** Whether any shipped mission script actually triggers this ordering is OPEN.

### 45.6 Smaller findings: ambient gangs, audio suppression, HUD mayhem init

`ambient_gang_spawn_enable`: a single boolean fans out to all four ambient-gang-enable bytes at once — no per-gang Lua control exists at this entry point. `audio_suppress_ambient_player_lines`: host-only, writes a session-synced variable ("persona_supress") with no direct engine reader found anywhere — purely a replicated flag for an unidentified consumer. `autil_hud_mayhem_init` (new one-name registrar `0x0067d660`): one-time native-callback creation plus **per-call** UI-element lookup and data-item subscription — **calling it more than once re-subscribes without de-duplication being confirmed either way**, and an empty native-callback pool on the very first call reads through null.

### 45.7 Cross-function observations

This tranche's crash pattern continues tranche 09/11's theme but adds two new instances of an escalating severity: §45.4's `cellphone_dial` is **the first case in this whole series where a coroutine-call-object result is used completely unchecked** (every prior report/callback function at least implicitly tolerated null by skipping), and §45.2's `debris_flow_set_inactive` is a **null dereference through a live virtual-function call**, not just a flat memory read — and it is confirmed to reproduce identically on a network peer via the replicated message path. Five functions this tranche send a network message unconditionally with no host/ownership/existence gate (`customization_swap_player_rig` opcode `0x41`, `debris_flow_set_inactive` `0x45`/`0x25`, `camera_script_enable`/`_disable` `0x43`/`0x10`), matching opcodes already seen in tranche 11. Two functions are confirmed pure Lua-side state with no engine reader at all (`cell_camera_enable`, and `audio_suppress_ambient_player_lines`'s underlying global), and one is a confirmed no-op (`cellphone_animate_stop_do`) — a reimplementation can treat all three as inert bookkeeping.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED code paths from the disassembly; reachability marked where not separately settled):** `character_fake_revival_end`/`_start` (null write/read on an unresolved character name); `character_take_human_shield_check_done` (null read continuing past an unresolved taker); `customization_swap_player_rig` (null player and null-rig dereferences); `debris_flow_set_inactive` (null virtual-call dereference on a stale debris handle, reproduces on the network peer); `cinema_editor_create_camera_zone` (out-of-bounds template-slot read); `cellphone_dial` (unbounded phone-book index; null activity-record read; unchecked coroutine-call-object write — three separate shapes); `autil_hud_mayhem_init` (null read on an exhausted native-callback pool).

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 13 resolved and written up (§45.1-§45.6); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: the flee-order flag bits and byte constants (§45.1); who reads `+0x1c9c` bit 9, dialog `+0x11c`, and `0x013c9382`; the cellphone activity-record state-machine details and the second callback name's purpose (§45.4); whether any shipped mission actually triggers the Killbane logic defect (§45.5); whether `autil_hud_mayhem_init`'s repeated-call subscriptions are de-duplicated.

## 46. Ranking tranche 14 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-02)

**Source.** Job `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM A\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-14.json` (names 276-300 of 554, Team B call-count order; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_14.md`). 23 names in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; 2 under the UI registrar `0x008430f0` through two further new one-name sub-registrars (`whored_countdown_finished` via `0x006147c0`, `vint_options_remap_reset_bindings` via `0x007cdc00`) — both push the function pointer **before** the name, the same quirk tranche 13 first found, so the dumper's own "next slot" guess misses them and a `range` dump is required. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 46.1 Spec correction: §3.7/§20.1's vehicle-invulnerability bit conflict is settled

This tranche directly disassembled `0x00a7a830`'s merge idiom: it writes the boolean into **bit `0x01`** of vehicle `+0x1d7a` (no shift). **§3.7 was right; §20.1's "bit `0x8`" was the error**, now corrected there (and in §20.1's own cross-referencing OPEN notes and the §12.21/§12.22 entries that cite the same primitive). The sibling `0x00a7a9a0` (the "always apply player damage" flag) writes bit `0x02` of the same byte. Ten vehicle force-flag bits in total are now confirmed across vehicle `+0x1d7a`-`+0x1d7e` and the vehicle AI block at `+0xc68` (full table in the interp note's front matter), each with its own literal engine debug-tag name as the cross-check.

### 46.2 Mission action sequences (3 functions sharing one global state block) — a real null-write crash and a dangling-pointer shape

`action_sequence_setup`, `action_sequence_is_playing`, and `action_sequence_advance` all drive one global state block (`0x012f2ae0`) holding a **raw, unresolved vehicle pointer**, hard-coded per-mission step tables (opening-mission helicopter sequence and a mission-6 set piece, embedded directly in the executable, not data-driven), and a 15-slot player-control-lock pool.

**`action_sequence_is_playing` — real null-write crash.** No arguments, returns a boolean, but has a **side effect hidden inside the query**: it always resets the local player's script mode to 0 via a `this`-call helper. **With no local player, that helper's own null-tolerant "is locally owned" test (established in tranche 11: true for a null object) lets the call through anyway, and it writes through `null+0x2888`** — reachable whenever a script polls this function while the local player object doesn't exist (loading, teardown). When it returns false it can also silently run a deferred sequence-advance step as a further side effect.

**`action_sequence_advance` never waits for its own animations to finish** — a script must poll `action_sequence_is_playing` itself to know when it's safe to advance again. **Real dangling-pointer shape:** the block's raw vehicle pointer is dereferenced by all three functions with only a null test, never re-resolved or liveness-checked — if the vehicle is destroyed or despawned mid-sequence (including by this same tranche's `world_despawn_all_vehicles`, §46.3), the next poll or advance reads freed memory.

**`action_sequence_setup` leaks one control-lock slot (of 15) on every repeated call** that doesn't go through the two specific release functions, and is **asymmetric between host and single player**: calling it with no vehicle name clears the sequence in single player but is silently ignored on a session host.

### 46.3 World despawn and AI switches (6 functions)

`world_despawn_all_vehicles`/`world_despawn_all_pedestrians`: walk dedicated ambient/traffic lists and despawn everything not protected (occupied by a player, flagged, etc.), deferring actual deletion through the engine's normal pending-delete queue rather than freeing synchronously.

`ai_force_team_idle` — **real null-read crash plus a real scope-widening logic defect.** 1 team-name string, **hashed through a null pointer with no check when the argument is nil or non-string.** Separately: **an unknown or misspelled team name silently maps to the sentinel team id 9, which every downstream loop treats as "match every team" — so a typo in a script idles every human and vehicle the machine owns, not just the intended team.**

`ambient_cop_spawn_enable`, `action_nodes_shouldnt_flee`, `action_nodes_restrict_spawning`: simple global-byte toggles gating AI spawn/flee behavior, none replicated — a co-op client calling any of them only changes its own copy.

### 46.4 Scripted vehicle motion (2 functions) — a real null-read crash

**`vehicle_turret_base_to_do` — real null-read crash.** 1 vehicle name + 1 target name + 1 boolean. **The target-string length loop runs before its own null test, so a nil or non-string target name (with a resolvable vehicle that has a seat-0 occupant) dereferences null.** Separately, by design an **object** target can never actually drive the vehicle (it reduces to a single point, below the shared drive routine's 2-point minimum) — only a **path** target works, and a path longer than 24 nodes is silently truncated. Return type is mixed: boolean `false` on failure, a plain number (0/1/2) on an attempt.

`vtol_flyby_animation_for_m18`: a one-off mission-18 helper (teleport + animation + an unconditionally broadcast network record with no host or ownership gate) — hard-coded for that specific set piece.

### 46.5 Vehicle flags and queries (11 functions) — two naming traps, no new crashes

`vehicle_lights_on(v, false)` **does not turn the lights off — it clears both the force-on and force-off flags, returning the lights to automatic control.** `vehicle_tire_indicators_alive` reports **8 ("all alive") whenever the vehicle's tire-indicator object is simply disabled**, not actually alive. `vehicle_set_tire_durability`/`vehicle_set_tire_damage_multiplier` silently ignore any value ≤ 0 (the field can never be reset to 0 from Lua this way) and, for an unresolved vehicle name inside a session, broadcast a network record for vehicle id 0 rather than doing nothing. `vehicle_set_npc_engine_audio`/`vehicle_set_kneecappers_damage`: direct, unreplicated field writes with no ownership gate. `vehicle_is_invulnerable`: reads the now-settled bit `0x01` of `+0x1d7a` (§46.1).

### 46.6 Smaller UI findings

`whored_countdown_finished`: its own guard byte is never written anywhere in the binary (so the guard always passes) and the flag it sets has no direct reader found — in practice this call only ever sends a network broadcast with no host gate. `vint_options_remap_reset_bindings`: re-applies two hard-coded default control-binding tables and rebuilds the key-in-use map; the action index it copies from the defaults data is used **unbounded** against the live binding table (data-gated latent shape), and a negative modifier value is accepted where only -1 should be.

### 46.7 Cross-function observations

Four distinct replication patterns recur across this tranche's vehicle-flag setters: the established double-gate pattern (most force-flag setters); a single-gate broadcast variant with **no local fallback for an unresolved vehicle name** (the two tire setters, §46.5); unconditional broadcast with no host or ownership gate at all (`vtol_flyby_animation_for_m18`, `whored_countdown_finished`); and no replication whatsoever (`vehicle_set_npc_engine_audio`, `vehicle_set_kneecappers_damage`, the three AI-spawn-switch functions of §46.3) — in every no-replication case, a co-op client's call only ever affects its own machine. ~~One open discrepancy worth flagging for a future pass: the gameplay registrar's own registration loop runs 1016 times, while `WALLS.md` describes the same table as having 1,014 entries — not reconciled this pass (OPEN).~~ **RESOLVED (2026-10-02, §47): the registrar genuinely has 1,016 slots (1,015 unique names) — one previously entirely un-rostered name, `on_mission_item_drop`, was found and resolved; see §47.**

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED code paths from the disassembly; reachability marked where not separately settled):** `ai_force_team_idle` (null read on a nil/non-string team name); `vehicle_turret_base_to_do` (null read on a nil/non-string target name); `action_sequence_is_playing` (null write via the script-mode helper when there's no local player); `action_sequence_advance`/`action_sequence_setup`/`action_sequence_is_playing` (dangling raw vehicle pointer across all three — reachability HYPOTHESIS, depends on the vehicle being destroyed mid-sequence).

**Review status (2026-10-02):** all 25 names in tranche 14 resolved and written up (§46.1-§46.6); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: the writer of the action-sequence "busy" byte and what releases its control-lock slot in normal play; several AI-state branch meanings in `ai_force_team_idle`'s per-team reset (§46.3); the vehicle-class enumeration `vehicle_set_sirens` switches on. The 1016-vs-1,014 gameplay-registrar row-count discrepancy (§46.7) is RESOLVED — see §47.

## 47. Gameplay registrar row-count discrepancy resolved — a 1,016th-and-1,015th slot, `on_mission_item_drop` (2026-10-02)

**Source.** A direct, bounded re-count requested by the orchestrator after §46.7 flagged tranche 14's finding that the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`'s own registration loop runs 1016 times against `WALLS.md`'s prior count of 1,014 entries. Verified by reading every one of the registrar's 2,032 individual stack-slot writes end to end (a full range dump of `0x00a20840`-`0x00a25f46`, not a partial grep) — CONFIRMED, zero gaps and zero accidental collisions across the 2,032 stack offsets themselves.

**The registrar genuinely builds 1,016 `{name, function}` pairs.** The function allocates exactly `0x1fc0` bytes of stack = 1,016 × 8-byte slots, and the trailing registration loop confirms it by iterating `0x3f8` = 1016 times over that exact span. `WALLS.md`'s prior "~2,028 MOV / 1,014-entry" figure was an undercount from a dump that was cut one instruction short at the function's tail end, not a real structural fact — corrected in place there.

**Of the 1,016 slots, exactly 1,015 are unique names.** The "2 extra" slots are not 2 different names: one name, `on_mission_item_drop`, is registered **twice** — at two different stack slots, but both times with the byte-for-byte identical name-string address and identical handler address. This is a harmless literal duplicate (the second `lua_setfield` simply overwrites the Lua global with the same value it already held), not two competing functions and not a conflict.

**The one genuinely new, previously entirely un-rostered name is `on_mission_item_drop` (`0x00a57000`).** It is absent from every existing roster this project or Team B maintains, including Team B's own call-count reconciliation table — meaning it has zero observed call sites in Team B's instrumented script corpus, which is exactly why the call-count-ordered ranking-tranche methodology never surfaced it as a candidate.

**`on_mission_item_drop` (`0x00a57000`) — resolved.** 1 string argument (a Lua callback name); no return. **Body (CONFIRMED — disassembly):** if the argument is present and non-empty, it is interned into the same global, 350-slot name-hash pool already documented at `0x00a1fcc0` for the `on_*` hook family (§42.3/§42.7) — the pool matches purely by name hash with no string compare, and a string-allocation failure stores the sentinel id `0` rather than `-1`, exactly as §42.7 already states — and the resulting slot id is written into a persistent global that **is not reset when the argument is nil or empty**, so a no-argument call simply reuses whatever name the previous real call registered. Every call, regardless of whether a new name was supplied, finishes by calling the same shared record dispatcher that 20 other hook/setter functions across this address range call: it opens an opcode-`0x43` record and unconditionally broadcasts it to the session through the project's already-established commit trio (the session getter, the commit call, and the finalizer). **Side effects/subsystem:** HIGH CONFIDENCE this is a **global, non-object callback-name hook registration** — the same shape §42.3 already documents for `on_m21_player_choice` (a hand-inlined registration against a global hook record, not a per-object one) — for a mission "item drop" event, broadcast on every call rather than only on an actual change. OPEN: the receiving side's handling of the opcode-`0x43` record, and which mission script(s), if any, actually call this (zero observed call sites in Team B's corpus).

**Deliverable.** Published a corrected roster, `tools/lua_gameplay_names_only_1015.txt` — the prior 1014-line roster plus this one line, in its correct registration-order position; verified by diff to differ from the prior file by exactly that one inserted line.

**Review status (2026-10-02):** resolved and closed. CONFIRMED unless marked otherwise above.

## 48. The game clock (`0x014ff338`) — initial state, per-frame advance, and `set_time_of_day`'s real effect (2026-10-03)

**Source.** Investigation for a new Team B mission blocker: `dlc3_m01`, `m19` and 2 other missions stop on the clock's hour byte being OPEN. Full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_game_clock.md`. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 48.1 The clock is a full calendar, not just an hour/minute pair

The 20-byte struct at `0x014ff338` (matching the save header's `0x08C`-`0x09F` copy exactly, `spec-save-format.md` §6.2/§6.5) holds: year (u16, `+0x00`), month 0-based (`+0x02`), day of month (`+0x03`), hour/minute/second (`+0x04`/`+0x05`/`+0x06`), weekday 0=Monday (`+0x07`), a 30-day moon counter (`+0x08`), the **authoritative** time of day as a 2^32-per-day fixed-point fraction (`+0x0C`, u32 — the hour/minute/second bytes are *derived* from this, not the other way around), and a **separate** real-seconds play-time float (`+0x10`) — confirming and extending the save spec's own "two different accumulators share one 20-byte block" finding. A day counter exists, but only as a calendar date — there is no plain "days elapsed" integer. Adjacent globals: the time scale `0x014ff34c` (game seconds per real second, not saved), an always-empty two-slot "listener" array at `0x014ff330` (§48.3), and a 32-entry queue of future game-time timestamps at `0x014ff358`.

### 48.2 Initial state at game start — four distinct sources, in order

1. **Engine boot** (`0x006fe150`, once from start-up): sets 13 May 2004, 10:17:33, moon day 0, play time 0.0, time scale **40.0**. This literal date/time is also the co-op-sync epoch (§48.6).
2. **New game** (`0x007ae950`, reached by horde start too): rewrites only the time to **10:00:00**, keeping whatever date the clock already holds (13 May 2004 on a fresh boot, but *not* reset if a new game follows an earlier session), and zeroes the play-time float. Time scale untouched.
3. **World start** (`0x00708330` → `0x00b9d620`): **only when a co-op session object exists and the local machine is its host**, snaps the clock to a **random key** of the active time-of-day definition (key 0 is 3× as likely as any other key — an off-by-one in the index-selection arithmetic, not a deliberate weighting). ~~**Whether single player has such a session object at all is the same standing OPEN item as `game_get_is_host` in single player** — this is the actual fork that decides whether a fresh game keeps 10:00:00 or jumps to a random key.~~ **RESOLVED (2026-10-03, reconciliation requested by the orchestrator): §8.27/§26.28 already CONFIRM, by an exhaustive negative check of the session installer's own call sites, that single player never installs a session at all — not an open question, a settled negative. This gate therefore never fires in single player: a fresh single-player game is CONFIRMED to keep 10:00:00 from the new-game routine (step 2), never a random key. The random-key snap only matters in an actual co-op session.**
4. **Loaded save**: restores the full 20 bytes verbatim (`0x00b9b530` → `0x006fe1c0`, a straight copy with **no field validation**) — runs *after* the world-start random snap, so a save always wins.

Two further one-shot sources: a **respawn with no mission/activity running** also snaps to a random key; a **mission's time-of-day override** (data field at `0x012f2df8`, loaded by `0x006e2150`) can carry a start hour, applied via `0x006fe480` — **HIGH CONFIDENCE this is the actual mechanism by which `dlc3_m01`/`m19` get a defined hour**; which missions carry one is OPEN (it's in their override data, not the executable).

### 48.3 Per-frame advance: 40× real time, frame-rate independent

The steady per-frame gameplay routine (`0x00702a50`) is the **only** per-frame caller of the clock-advance primitives. Each unpaused frame it advances the clock by **frame time × time scale** (default (1/30 s) × 40.0 = 1.333 game seconds/frame = **one game hour per 90 real seconds, one game day per 36 real minutes**) — scales with actual frame time, so it is not a fixed per-frame step. The same call adds the **unscaled** real frame time to the separate play-time float (`+0x10`) — this is a pure real-time play counter, confirming the save spec's own "~0.017 s/frame" guess was exactly the unscaled step at 60 fps, and settling that it is *not* the day/hour/minute clock despite sharing the struct. **The listener array at `0x014ff330` is CONFIRMED to always be empty — no instruction anywhere writes it or its count, so any "on clock change" hook mechanism a host might assume exists here has no effect in the shipped game and can be ignored.**

**Lighting does not track the clock every frame in the shipped game.** The two mode flags that would make it do so (continuous or a 30-second cross-fade between keys) are never written anywhere in the executable — only the per-event re-key calls (world start/respawn snaps, `set_time_of_day`, mission/activity/cutscene jumps, the co-op sync) actually move the separate lighting-time global (`0x01311090`). The clock itself keeps running at 40× regardless, so **hour-based game logic (which reads the running clock) and lighting (which only moves at discrete events) can disagree** — e.g. a "night" hour under day lighting. This is the executable-side half of `spec-tables-environment.md` §16 open item 1 ("how `weather_time_of_day` stage transitions use the clock") — the lighting-blend consumer is the per-frame evaluator `0x00ba8540`, called ~330 times/frame against the lighting-time global, not against the running clock directly.

Cutscenes freeze the clock entirely (time scale forced to 0, with the clock and play time snapshotted and restored around the cutscene).

### 48.4 What `set_time_of_day` actually does — corrects §32.1

§32.1 already correctly describes the forward-jump arithmetic. The correction is what happens next: `0x005a2440` (called unconditionally in the shipped game, since the two mode flags that would skip it are never set) does **not** re-key weather or merely "refresh lighting" — it **snaps the clock itself to the nearest time-of-day key** of the active definition, picking whichever of the two bracketing keys is closer. **This means `set_time_of_day(h, m)` usually does NOT leave the hour byte equal to `h`** — only if `h:m` happens to land on (or very near) an actual key time. The snap can move the clock **backward** from the just-requested time, by up to half a key interval; it also zeroes the moon counter, recomputes the weekday, zeroes the seconds, and truncates the play time to whole seconds. **Confirmed NOT touched by `set_time_of_day`:** the weather/wind state machine (no call into it at all), any day/night object pass, statistics, and network replication (clients instead get corrected by the host's own periodic clock-sync message).

### 48.5 Crash-shaped and correctness hazards

**Empty key list (crash-shaped, reachability HYPOTHESIS):** if a mission's time-of-day override (or, in principle, the base definition) has zero keys, three different routines (the random-snap, the bracketing-key finder, and the stepped-lighting blender) all read `keys[-1]` or `keys[0]` through a pointer that may be null, with no count check anywhere in any of them. **Unvalidated save restore:** a corrupted save's month byte ≥ 12 makes the day-stepper index past its 12-entry days-per-month table. **Backward snap after queue drain:** `set_time_of_day`'s forward jump can fire due game-time timers, and the immediately-following key snap can then move the clock back below the time those timers fired at — the timers stay fired regardless. **Play-time float precision loss (not a crash):** stored as float32 from a double accumulation, the per-frame add falls below the representable step once play time passes roughly 146 h (at 60 fps) or 291 h (at 30 fps); past that point it stalls.

**Review status (2026-10-03):** resolved. CONFIRMED unless marked otherwise above. Residual OPEN items: the actual time-of-day key lists for the base definition and each mission override (loaded data, not in the executable — Team B needs these to predict any specific mission's snapped hour); which missions carry a start-hour override; whether lighting is re-keyed after a save restore. The §48.2 step-3 single-player/host-session question is RESOLVED, not open (see §48.2's own correction) — single player is CONFIRMED to never reach the random-key snap at all.

## 49. Ranking tranche 16 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-03)

**Source.** Job `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM A\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-16.json` (names 326-350 of 554, Team B call-count order; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_16.md`). Ten registrars: the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840` (10 names) and nine UI sub-registrars under `0x008430f0` — six **new** table-driven store screens (store-vehicle `0x008152a0`, stronghold-store `0x00812590`, gang-store `0x008111f0`, gallery `0x0080fab0`, crib `0x0080e540`, screen-fade/sfx `0x005a01d0`) plus two more **one-name, function-pointer-before-name** registrars (the same quirk tranche 13 first found) and one entry in the already-known 113-row `game_` helper table `0x00845aa0`. Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 49.1 Store screens (12 functions) — charge-then-validate and unchecked-lookup crash shapes recur

**`store_stronghold_game_purchase_upgrade`** — **real logic defect, same shape as tranche 12's lobby bug.** No arguments. Charges the stronghold's price **unconditionally** once a stronghold resolves, then calls the level-up setter — which silently no-ops unless the level is in range, a session exists, **and this machine is host**. So: at max level, cash is taken and nothing upgrades; on a co-op client, cash is deducted (routed to the owner) but the level never changes; with no session, nothing happens at all. ~~**This is circumstantial evidence (not proof) that single player does run with a host-shaped session object**, relevant to the standing `game_get_is_host` OPEN item (§48.2 names the same fork) — a single-player-only store flow that depends on "session exists and is host" to do anything would be a strange design otherwise.~~ **CORRECTED (2026-10-03, reconciliation requested by the orchestrator — this inference does NOT survive a check against §8.27/§26.28): the level-up setter's gate is the exact same "session exists and `+0x5c`==`+0x58`" test §8.27/§26.28 already CONFIRMED false in single player by an exhaustive negative check, not an open question. The two findings are fully compatible, not in tension: in single player this gate is CONFIRMED to evaluate false by the "no session" branch alone, so `store_stronghold_game_purchase_upgrade` genuinely charges cash and never upgrades the level there — a real, confirmed single-player no-op/overcharge bug Team B should know about, not evidence of a session object. (Whether real retail single-player play can ever observably raise a stronghold past level 1 some other way — e.g. a session-independent path analogous to `crib_unlock_strongold`'s own no-session fallback for level 1, `interp_tabs.md` Q14.5 — is a separate, still-open question; nothing here suggests this specific native has one.)** No local-player null check (crash shape).

**`store_stronghold_upgrade_end_flyby`** — **real unbounded-stack-write shape.** No arguments. Ends the stronghold camera fly-by and, if a stronghold resolves, collects every "unlocked at this level" entry into a **256-slot stack array with no cap on the match count** — data-bounded (real stronghold tables are expected to have only a handful per level) but unchecked in the code.

**`store_gallery_download_show_list`** — reuses the exact null-dereference shape tranche 09 B.12 already found: the dialog-pool allocator can return null on exhaustion, and this function's own success path reads `null+0x12c` unchecked.

**`shop_purchase_purchase_shop`** (one-name registrar `0x00a03600`, function-pointer-before-name) — **real null-dereference crash, plus a real double-charge defect.** No arguments. Resolves a shop via a trigger-handle lookup that returns null when the trigger is stale or absent, and the very next read goes through that null pointer unchecked. Pays the price (routed to the owner if not locally owned), marks the shop owned **only once** (a guarded bit), but **every other side effect — the payment, the trigger-disable, the owned-object broadcast, and the property fly-by — repeats on every subsequent call with no "already purchased" guard beyond the one-time ownership bit itself.**

**`store_vehicle_do_return_to_crib`, `store_vehicle_allow_garage`, `store_gang_is_unlocked`, `store_gang_bg_covered`, `store_gang_begin_exit`, `store_gallery_upload_character`, `store_gallery_display_character`, `store_crib_init_crib_garage`:** resolved in full (screen-stack pop with a confirmed-dead secondary branch; a 13-named-mission garage-allow denylist; a player cash/unlock-bit gate for the gang store; the store-camera subsystem shared by gang/stronghold/shop screens, new this tranche; a deferred-upload scheduler; a bounds-checked list-index apply; and a three-candidate garage-node picker keyed by crib upgrade level). No further crash shapes beyond the unchecked local-player reads already common to this whole series.

### 49.2 Spawning (7 functions) — an inconsistent-validation pair and a real deferred-null-read

**`spawn_override_set_override_category_for_hood`** — **real null-dereference crash, immediate on a host and deferred otherwise.** 2 strings (neighbourhood, category name). The category-name lookup result is **never checked** before being stored and dispatched: on a host with a session, the very next function call dereferences the null category immediately; everywhere else, the null is merely stored and only dereferenced later, either by the per-hood category reader or by the co-op join-snapshot serializer when a partner joins — a **deferred** null read that can fire well after the original bad call. **Direct contrast within the same tranche:** the sibling **global** category setter (`spawn_global_override_set_category`) *does* check its own lookup and silently ignores an unknown name — the per-hood setter is the one entry missing the guard its own sibling already has.

**`spawning_boats`** writes a host-authoritative, session-replicated byte (registered name `"os_boat"`) with **no host gate on the write itself** — unlike tranche 13's `audio_suppress_ambient_player_lines`, which does gate. **`spawn_global_override_set_category`/`spawn_global_override_clear_category`: the global override is not replicated at all mid-session** — it only reaches a newly-joining client via the one-time join snapshot, so a script that changes it after a partner has already joined has no way to inform that partner.

### 49.3 Characters and AI (3 functions)

**`squad_enable`** — **real asymmetric-effect defect.** 1 character name + 1 boolean (default false). `squad_enable(name, false)` actually dismisses the character from the player's crew (restores stats, removes it from the roster, releases resources); `squad_enable(name, true)` only flips two unrelated flag bits and **does not re-add the character to the crew** — the two calls are not inverses of each other despite the name.

**`skydive_move_to_check_done`** — **real null-pointer-arithmetic-before-null-test crash, a new shape for this series.** In single-object target mode, when the target doesn't resolve, the code computes `null_pointer + 0x40` and tests *that sum* for non-null rather than testing the pointer first — the offset addition survives the "null" case and the function reads through address `0x40` while the character is mid-skydive. The sibling list-mode branch handles the identical failure correctly (returns "done"), confirming this is a one-off miss, not the intended pattern. Worth a project-wide grep for the same `pointer+offset` -then-test ordering in other `*_check_done` natives.

**`set_attack_peds_flag`**: a double-gate AI-flag setter; refines tranche 13 B.3's description of this setter family for the no-owner case (does nothing locally rather than writing, when neither gate passes and no owner exists) — worth re-checking tranche 13's own `0x009493e0` against the same branch (OPEN, not done this pass).

### 49.4 UI helpers (3 functions)

**`set_char_in_string`** — **real crash and unbounded-stack-allocation shapes.** 1 string + 1 **0-based** index (unlike Lua's usual 1-based convention) + 1 single-character string. Builds its result in a stack buffer sized by the index with **no cap** — a large or NaN-derived index can overrun the stack guard outright, reachable from script data alone; separately, either string argument being non-a-string reads through null. **`sfx_use_load_images`** is confirmed a hardcoded `true` in the retail build (already in the spec's screen-fade table, re-confirmed independently here). **`screen_capture_preview_should_upload`**: ~~a denied platform privilege silently becomes the same "cancel" path as an explicit false argument — the calling script cannot distinguish "user said no" from "platform denied it" from the return value alone (there is none — 0 return values either way).~~ **CORRECTED (2026-10-03, ranking tranche 19, §54.2): `0x008703f0` is not a platform privilege check at all — it is a plain "1 ≤ argument ≤ 8" range test with no platform call and no state, and this function's own argument (4) always satisfies it. So the "privilege denied" cancel path described above is dead code on PC: the privilege check can never actually fail, and the only way to reach "cancel" in practice is the explicit-false-argument path.**

### 49.5 Cross-function observations

Two more one-name UI registrars push the function pointer **before** the name (`0x00a03600`, `0x007aff80`), the same quirk tranche 13 first found at `0x0067d660` — any future dump whose only "use" is a bare name-push immediately before the `lua_setfield` primitive should be re-read with a registrar range dump rather than trusted at face value. Unchecked lookups remain the dominant crash class this tranche (shop-trigger lookup, hood-category lookup, dialog-pool allocation, two string arguments) — and this tranche surfaces the clearest *within-tranche* contrast yet between a guarded and an unguarded sibling of the same setter family (§49.2's hood vs. global category setters), which is a strong template for a host-side fix: copy the guard from the sibling that has one.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (all CONFIRMED code paths from the disassembly; reachability marked where not separately settled):** `shop_purchase_purchase_shop` (null shop dereference on a stale/absent trigger); `spawn_override_set_override_category_for_hood` (null category dereference, immediate on a host, deferred via the join snapshot otherwise); `skydive_move_to_check_done` (pointer-arithmetic-survives-null-test shape, reachable mid-skydive); `set_char_in_string` (unbounded stack allocation from a script-controlled index); `store_gallery_download_show_list` (dialog-pool-exhaustion null read, same shape as tranche 09); `store_stronghold_upgrade_end_flyby` (256-slot stack array with no match-count cap, data-bounded).

**Review status (2026-10-03):** all 25 names in tranche 16 resolved and written up (§49.1-§49.4); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: who consumes the `"os_boat"`/`"os_parking"` replicated bytes and several other engine-side readers named throughout; the identity of HUD screen `0x39` and platform privilege 4; whether `0x00911770` tolerates a null hood category; a cross-check of tranche 13's `0x009493e0` against this tranche's refined no-owner-no-op finding (§49.3).

## 50. Ranking tranche 18 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-03)

**Source.** Job `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM A\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-18.json` (names 376-400 of 554, Team B call-count order; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_18.md`). 13 names in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; 12 under the UI bring-up `0x008430f0` across six sub-registrars (pause-menu `0x007af8d0`, pause-map `0x007dfae0` — §31's existing registrar — main-menu `0x007c9fc0`, and three more **function-pointer-before-name** one-name registrars, the sixth and seventh of that shape found so far). Two of the 25 names turned out not to be real bindings at all: `npc_aim_at_point` is the already-documented shared no-op stub, and `minimap_icon_remove_radius_do` is byte-for-byte the same handler as the already-specced `minimap_icon_remove_do` — the registrar slot is the ground truth, the name is misleading. Four names were partial re-reads of already-specced material (§31.5/§31.6/§32.1, and tranche 10's `open_vint_dialog_do`, corrected above at §42.6). Addresses below are CONFIRMED — disassembly unless marked otherwise.

### 50.1 Pause menu and main menu (5 functions) — a real stale-flag-then-null-call crash

**`main_menu_restart_video` — real null-video crash, confirmed structural shape.** No arguments. Recreates the main-menu background video; **the video-creation call can return null (video system busy, 7+ live videos already, or allocator failure), and the caller stores that null and sets the "playing" flag anyway without checking.** The *next* call to this function or to `main_menu_video_has_stopped` then sees the flag set and makes a virtual call through the null video object — a crash on the call *after* the one that actually failed, not the failing call itself. A reimplementation should create the video first and only set the flag on success. Also fires a "stop" Lua hook before tearing down the old video and a "start" hook after the new one exists, so a script always observes stop-then-start in that order even though both happen inside one call.

**`pause_menu_cant_retry_because_host_in_creation`, `pause_menu_cat_mouse_active`, `pause_menu_common_top_finished_loading`, `main_menu_video_has_stopped`:** resolved in full (a co-op-client-specific "host still in character creation" query; a minigame-mode-14 query; a pause-menu sub-screen request handshake; the video teardown half of the pair above). No further crash shapes.

### 50.2 Minimap icons, messages, dialogs, and object indicators (5 functions) — the clearest sibling-asymmetry crash pair yet
