**`cutscene_play_do` — three real logic defects, one of them a crash shape.** A boolean passed as the (optional table-or-boolean) second argument is read and discarded, but leaves an 8-entry stack-local handle array **uninitialized**, which the start routine then unconditionally copies 64 bytes of into the cutscene's parked state or its manager as "script-group handles" — undefined data entering a live cutscene. A destination table must have **exactly two** entries or both end-of-cutscene teleports are silently dropped. Most seriously, **the destinations are written even when the cutscene start itself was refused** (e.g. another cutscene is already running) — overwriting the *running* cutscene's own end-of-cutscene teleport destinations. Separately, inside the cutscene-start routine, a failed scene-manager allocation leaves the manager pointer null while the handle-copy and further writes proceed through it unconditionally (reachability HYPOTHESIS).

**`cutscene_play_check_done` reports "done" prematurely.** For a scene-type cutscene whose underlying scene is still loading, the start routine leaves the state machine in a "scene loading" state with **no manager object allocated yet** — and this query treats "no manager" as equivalent to "finished," returning true while the cutscene has not actually started. A script polling "start, then wait until done" can proceed as if the cutscene already played.

### 57.3 Cribs — 5 functions

**`crib_purchase_purchase_crib` — null-pointer crash plus a charge-before-ownership-check logic defect.** The function resolves the currently-selected-for-purchase crib handle with no fallback; if nothing is validly selected (no selection, a stale handle, or one that fails the crib-kind/liveness check), the crib pointer is left null and the **very next instruction reads price through it** — any call to this binding outside the purchase screen's own normal flow crashes. Separately, the player's cash is **always deducted before** the function checks whether the crib is already owned, so a crib whose "unowned" flag happens to already be clear still costs the player money for no effect. The engine's own sibling `crib_unlock_strongold` checks ownership before charging through the identical shared routine — the fix template already exists in the binary.

**`crib_get_cash_stash`** — naming trap: despite its name, it returns **no value at all**; it instead *collects* a stashed-cash global into the player's cash balance and zeroes the stash, discarding the money if the award could only be forwarded to a network owner rather than applied locally. `crib_is_stronghold` and `crib_is_garage_disabled` resolve in full with no crash shape; `crib_is_stronghold`'s reading of the player's crib record directly confirms §23.19's own corrected field reading (see that section).

### 57.4 World, UI and front-end — 6 functions

**`cell_playlist_save_list` — the tranche's second headline memory-safety finding, two distinct crash shapes in one binding.** Script-supplied track-number arguments are used directly as indices into the radio song table with **no bound check against the table's own song count** — any out-of-range id produces a 16-bit write and a pointer-sized read at an address computed directly from that id, reachable anywhere within roughly ±640KB of the song table. Separately, if the script's track-list table carries a **negative** `n` field, the resulting count is narrowed to 16 bits (so −1 becomes 65,535) and then used as a loop bound that writes that many 16-bit entries into a fixed 512-entry **stack** array — overrunning the stack canary, saved registers, and the return address itself. Both are reachable from ordinary Lua table/number arguments with no special preconditions.

**`continuous_explosion_follow_target_remove`** resolves and removes a handle from the same ≤2-entry follow-target list §25.23 (corrected above) documents; `completion_call_callback` and `community_login_open` resolve in full with no crash shape (the former has the quirk that calling it with **no argument selects callback case 0**, not "no callback"); `city_load_img_load_complete` sets a single gating byte with no crash shape but a latent stall hazard if the calling script never fires it; `cinema_editor_save_clip` (a developer-tool binding, HYPOTHESIS unreachable in shipped play) leaves its destination path buffer uninitialized when any of the three Win32 calls building it fails, then hands that buffer to `CreateFileW` as a path.

### 57.5 Characters — 10 functions (gameplay registrar)

Three names (`character_use_synced_finishers`, `character_prevent_kneecapping`, `character_set_over_the_shoulder`) extend the project's `human_force_flags…` double-gate bit family with three more bits on the same two dwords (`+0x1c9c` bit 15, `+0x1c98` bits 3 and 22). `character_prevent_kneecapping` **clears** immunity when its boolean argument is simply omitted (not left unchanged); `character_set_over_the_shoulder` defaults to **on**.

**`character_parachute_open` — real resource-leak logic defect.** The forced-open path never tests whether the character already has a parachute object attached before spawning another one — every call spawns a new parachute object with no reuse or cleanup of a prior one. `character_take_human_shield_do` has **no range test, no self-target test, and no "already busy" test**, unlike its already-documented player-targeting sibling — a character can be made to take itself hostage with no distance check. `character_fake_revival_start` re-confirms tranche 13's already-documented null-pointer crash for an unresolved character name, and adds a new logic point: its "fake revival in progress" flag bit is set **even when the underlying revival call itself refused** (the character was not actually in the required state), leaving a character incorrectly flagged until the matching `_end` call clears it. `character_is_combat_ready` returns **no value** (nil), not false, for an unresolved character name — a return-shape trap for a binding layer to preserve exactly.

### 57.6 Cross-function observations

**Three new script-controlled memory-corruption instances this tranche, on top of tranche 22's clapboard finding** — `dialog_box_create_internal`'s unbounded callback-name copy and `cell_playlist_save_list`'s two shapes (unchecked song-table index, negative-count stack overflow) are this tranche's highest-priority fix-backlog items: bound the callback name to 63 characters, drop song ids outside the table's range, and clamp a negative table count to 0 before use.

**Resolution failure used as a live pointer, again.** `crib_purchase_purchase_crib` (§57.3) joins the project's now-large family of "failed resolve leaves a null/zero pointer that the very next instruction dereferences" crashes; its own sibling `crib_unlock_strongold`, reached through the identical shared sub-routine, shows the fix (check before calling).

**Side effects that outlive a refused or premature start** — `cutscene_play_do`'s destination overwrite of a running cutscene, `cutscene_play_check_done`'s premature "done," and `crib_purchase_purchase_crib`'s charge-before-check are all the same family as tranche 20's "a call being accepted does not mean its effect was achieved."

**Lua-created dialogs ignore engine priority ordering.** `dialog_box_create_internal` always inserts the new dialog at the head of the open-dialog ring regardless of priority, unlike the engine's own dialog opener, which inserts by descending priority — a low-priority script dialog can pre-empt an engine notice (consequence OPEN).

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (CONFIRMED structure unless marked OPEN):** `dialog_box_create_internal` (unbounded callback-name copy corrupting an adjacent dialog slot or pool block; nil title/body/callback-name crashes); `cell_playlist_save_list` (unchecked song-table index; negative-count stack overflow); `crib_purchase_purchase_crib` (null read with no crib selected); `character_fake_revival_start` (reconfirmed null-pointer crash, tranche 13); `cutscene_play_do`'s failed-allocation null-write path (reachability HYPOTHESIS).

**Review status (2026-10-03):** all 25 names in tranche 23 resolved and written up (§57.1-§57.5); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: whether the shipped Lua wrapper polls `cutscene_play_check_done` immediately after starting a cutscene; where (if anywhere) a non-host crib purchase marks the crib owned; who installs the completion-screen callback pointers `completion_call_callback` selects between; whether a second parachute object left attached by `character_parachute_open` is ever cleaned up elsewhere.

## 58. Ranking tranche 25 — the final 4 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-03)

**Source.** Job `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM A\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-25.json` (names 551-554 of 554, Team B call-count order; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_25.md`). The job file lists only 4 names, not 25 — the tail end of the list. **With this tranche, all 554 previously-unspecced names of the entire 01-25 ranking backlog have an interpretation note.** 3 names in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`; 1 (`Screen_fade_transition_complete`) is a global of the UI Lua state registered by the screen-fade natives table `0x005a01d0` already described at §26.24 (this note gives it its own named entry for the first time). No pointer-before-name registrar. No session inferences drawn.

**`airplane_fly_to_do` — a real logic defect makes one of its two input forms permanently non-functional, plus a crash shape shared with an already-documented sibling.** Flies a crewed airplane (driver present, vehicle-type check) along either a named path or toward a named point, at a given speed. **The navpoint form can never work**: it builds exactly one waypoint (the target's position), but the underlying flight-request routine rejects any request with fewer than two waypoints — so calling this with a navpoint target always returns false and the plane never moves. Its own sibling `vehicle_pathfind_to_do` (already documented) builds two points in the identical branch (the vehicle's own position, then the target) — almost certainly what this binding was also meant to do, lost in a copy-and-modify drift between the two functions. The dead navpoint branch also **leaks a request id**: the id is allocated before the two-waypoint rejection, is never released on this path (unlike the sibling, which does release it on failure), and — because allocating a new request of the same kind on a vehicle supersedes any older one — **silently cancels the record of a previously-started path flight that is still actually flying**, leaving it with no way to report completion. Separately, **the target-name argument is measured for its length before being checked for null** — the identical bug already documented in `vehicle_pathfind_to_do` — so a nil, boolean, table, or (with the argument omitted entirely) any non-string stale stack value crashes the call outright whenever the named vehicle is a living, crewed airplane.

**`add_object_indicator_to_closest_npc` — naming trap: it returns a name, not a boolean.** Finds the horizontally-closest (height ignored) living member of a named script group to a reference character, places a HUD object indicator on them, and returns **that member's own name as a string** — or the empty string `""` (never nil, never false) when nothing qualifies. An unresolved, dead, or misspelled reference character silently changes the query's meaning to "the first living group member" with no distance test at all, and the reference character itself is not excluded from being its own answer. The underlying indicator-adder also discards its own success/id value entirely, unlike the already-documented `object_indicator_add_do`, giving the script no way to know whether the indicator was actually created. A real crash shape (shared with that same already-documented sibling) exists in the one-time UI set-up both reach: if the shared 32-record element pool is already exhausted, the set-up reads a null creation result with no check (reachability OPEN).

**`action_play_custom_do` — a null-character crash from the same template as an already-documented sibling, plus a return-value trap.** Blends out a character's current animation and plays a named `.anim` file, returning −1 (character is dead), 0 (play failed), or 1 (play "succeeded") — except that **an unresolved (null) character skips the dead-check entirely and reaches an unconditional read through a null animation-player pointer**, the identical bug shape already catalogued in a neighboring binding in the same registrar block. Separately, **an unknown animation name is not rejected** by the underlying animation-slot player — it claims a slot anyway and returns a stale leftover value from that slot's prior use, which this binding then reports as success (**1**, and for a player character it even sets script mode 2) even though nothing actually plays. The failure value **0 is itself truthy in Lua**, so only careful `== -1`/`== 1` checks, not a boolean treatment, distinguish all three outcomes correctly.

**`Screen_fade_transition_complete`** is re-verified in full against its existing §26.24 description (agrees step for step) and given its own named entry here for the first time. One new observation: the function **unconditionally clears the in-flight fade callback** after calling it — so if that callback itself immediately requests the opposite fade direction, the new request's own callback is installed and then overwritten with null by this same unconditional clear, silently losing it (reachability OPEN — depends on which native callbacks ever request a fade from inside a completion callback).

**Cross-function observations:** this tranche's two unresolved-pointer crashes (`action_play_custom_do`, `airplane_fly_to_do`) both match an already-documented sibling in the same registrar neighborhood exactly — strong evidence these three handlers were written from one shared template with the same latent bug, worth a dedicated sweep of the remaining registrar for more instances. All three gameplay bindings here read at least one argument unconditionally with no presence check, consistent with the project-wide missing-argument-aliasing finding (tranche 22 §55.6/M.1): omitting an argument reads stale stack content, which directly causes `airplane_fly_to_do`'s null-target crash when its third argument is left out entirely.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (CONFIRMED structure unless marked OPEN):** `action_play_custom_do` (null-character read through the animation player); `airplane_fly_to_do` (null-target `strlen`, reachable with a nil/boolean/table/omitted third argument); the shared object-indicator UI set-up's unchecked null read when its 32-record pool is exhausted (reachability OPEN); `Screen_fade_transition_complete`'s lost-callback shape on a same-call fade re-request (reachability OPEN).

**Review status (2026-10-03):** all 4 names in tranche 25 resolved and written up; none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: the meaning of indicator types 7/8 and the indicator "value" argument; whether every vehicle has the sub-record `airplane_fly_to_do`'s type check reads; whether a living character's animation-player pointer can ever legitimately be null; which native callbacks request a fade from inside another fade's completion callback.

## 59. Ranking tranche 24 — 25 previously-unspecced Lua-bound names (2026-10-03)

**Source.** Job `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM A\ghidra\jobs\ranking\tranche-24.json` (names 526-550 of 554, Team B call-count order; full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_ranking_tranche_24.md`). 11 names across six small UI-side cell/crib/camera registrars; 14 in the gameplay registrar `0x00a20840`. One name, `cell_music_menu_toggle_station`, is registered by a **pointer-before-name one-name registrar** (the sixth tranche to meet this quirk, after 13/16/18/19/21). Every name is 1 call site in 1 script. No session inferences drawn.

### 59.1 Cell-phone UI queries — 6 functions

Six simple boolean queries. `cell_debug_all_enabled` is the constant-false stub; the other five resolve in full with no crash shape, including `cell_camera_is_enabled`, which is **false until a script has explicitly called `cell_camera_enable(true)`** — "never set" and "disabled" read identically, since the backing dword is zero-filled at start. `cell_is_map_disabled` is true only during a hard-coded six-mission list (`m01`, `m02`, `m16`, `m21`, `m24`, `dlc2_m02`) and one additional gating byte. `cell_is_closing` reads false only while two specific phone UI-document types are *both* currently open — meaning it also reads true whenever the phone isn't open at all, a naming trap for anything that treats it as a pure "is the phone closing right now" signal.

### 59.2 `cell_music_menu_toggle_station` (pointer-before-name one-name registrar)

Toggles a hidden "disabled/hidden" bit on a radio-station record selected by a 1-based station number that is truncated to a **signed byte** before use (so 257 behaves as 1, 255 as −1). Out-of-range station numbers are read as "already disabled," so the toggle computed from that silently does nothing — a bad number is a safe no-op, not a crash. Re-enabling the station the local player is currently listening to retunes their radio; disabling a different station has no such follow-up.

### 59.3 Cheat menu — 2 functions

**`cell_cheats_activate_cheat` — a real null-pointer crash reachable from an unbounded script-supplied index, plus a shared-state race between concurrent calls.** The index argument is stored in a single global with **no bounds check anywhere on the activation path** — not before the co-op-warning test, not before the confirmation dialog is opened, and not in the apply routine itself, which treats any index at or past the number of currently-unlocked cheats (including negative values, since the comparison is unsigned) as a **null cheat record** and dereferences it directly. This fires either immediately (if a "no confirmation needed" flag is set) or after the player confirms a dialog that was opened for exactly this bad index — meaning the crash can be deferred behind user interaction. Separately, because the pending index lives in one shared global that the dialog's own result callback re-reads rather than capturing at dialog-open time, **calling this binding a second time before the first dialog is answered silently redirects the first dialog's confirmation to activate the second (wrong) cheat**, with both dialogs left open. `cell_cheats_unlock_cheat` resolves in full with no crash shape, but has its own logic defect: a cheat whose master record carries a non-default content id is **never unlocked through this path at all**, even when that content is installed and enabled — the content gate is only consulted after a different, unconditional rejection test already excludes it.

### 59.4 Scripted camera — 2 functions

**`camera_look_through_do` — a real "effect taken before its precondition is checked" logic defect.** Starts a reference-counted "HUD hidden, cinematic camera" mode and moves the camera to a named object over a given duration, broadcasting the move to the session. The HUD-hide reference is taken **before** the target object is resolved, so an unknown or dead object name still hides the HUD with no camera move to show for it — the HUD then stays hidden until the matching "end look-through" call releases the reference, which it always does unconditionally, independent of whether this call actually took one. `camera_script_is_finished` resolves in full with no crash shape (its three-way answer depends on camera mode, elapsed time vs. duration, and a divide-by-zero-shaped but harmless NaN comparison for a zero duration). This tranche also confirms a **third sub-code** of the already-documented opcode-`0x43` receiver table (indexed by sub-code × 4 from a fixed base) — `0x0e` for camera look-through start/end, alongside the two sub-codes tranche 22 already found.

### 59.5 Matt boss battle — 2 functions

**`boss_battle_matt_qte_begin` — three distinct, independently reachable crash paths, all unguarded.** Starts a named quick-time event against the boss character "Matt" at a given phase, keyed by a fixed 4-entry name table. (1) If "Matt" does not currently exist as a live object (not yet spawned, or already dead — the resolver used here rejects dead objects), the liveness-style pre-check itself takes the wrong branch for a null result and reads straight through it. (2) `boss_battle_matt_set_phase` (the sibling setter) stores **any** value with no bound against the table's own 4-entry size and never resets it even when it rejects the value as out-of-range — so a later `qte_begin` call indexes past the table: phases 5-8 silently start the *wrong* named QTE (reading whatever string happens to sit past the table's end), and phases 9 and above hand a non-pointer number directly to a string-comparison routine, which faults. (3) Independently, when a resolved target object is supplied but the player argument does not resolve to a proper character, the binding still proceeds to register a completion hook through a **literal fixed address** (`0x1f00`) used as the write target — a crash with no data dependency on the phase table at all.

### 59.6 Audio — 7 functions

**Two separate "playing id" spaces exist behind seven very similarly-named bindings, and this tranche settles which is which.** Three event-based bindings (`audio_play_do`, `audio_play_id_do`) return a result that can be **left uninitialized on the stack** if audio itself was never initialized — the underlying event-post routine simply returns without writing its output slot in that case, and the binding reports, records, and broadcasts that stale value as if it were a real id. The other four (character/mover/navpoint object-sound bindings) instead return a monotonically-incrementing **engine serial counter**, not a Wwise playing id at all — correcting an earlier tranche's looser wording on this point. Three of the `_id_`-suffixed bindings additionally truncate their numeric cue-id argument to its **low 16 bits** before use, while the string-name resolution path these siblings share produces full 32-bit ids — a script passing a 32-bit hashed id through one of these three gets the wrong sound or none.

**`audio_play_for_character_weapon_do` — real null-pointer crash, with its own sibling showing the fix.** Reads two fields directly off the resolved character pointer with **no null check**, while its very similar sibling `audio_play_for_character_do` explicitly tests the same resolver's result first — any misspelt, unspawned, or dead character name crashes this binding outright with a perfectly valid cue argument. Return shapes across this family are also inconsistent in ways a binding layer must preserve exactly: an unresolved character makes `audio_play_for_character_do` return **two** values (255 and 0) where every success path returns one; `audio_play_id_for_character_do` pushes its single result **twice**; and failure is reported as 255 by two bindings but as plain 0 by the rest.

### 59.7 Airplanes — 2 functions

`airplane_takeoff_do` reports whether the take-off maneuver actually started (locally, or was successfully forwarded to a remote owner) and resolves in full with no crash shape. `airplane_land_do` has a real **return-value trap**: it always pushes **true** once its two name arguments resolve, regardless of what the underlying landing routine itself reports — the two bindings look like a matched pair but only one of them actually reports its own outcome.

### 59.8 Cross-function observations

**The same "sibling shows the fix" pattern recurs three more times this tranche**, on top of the ones already catalogued project-wide: `audio_play_for_character_do` tests its resolved character where `_weapon_do` does not; the boss-phase setter `boss_battle_matt_set_phase`'s own neighbor bounds the phase correctly where the QTE-start path does not; and the cheat-activation dialog's own pointer is tested before use while the index it applies, in the same function, is not. **A second instance of "a global pending-selection value behind an asynchronous confirmation dialog can be raced by a second call"** (after tranche 22's `game_cancel_mission`) now exists in `cell_cheats_activate_cheat`. `0x00d1e1d0`, a one-more constant-1 stub whose result is discarded by its only caller, joins the project's existing dead-stub family.

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (CONFIRMED structure unless marked OPEN):** `boss_battle_matt_qte_begin` (three independent paths: Matt-absent null read, out-of-range-phase table overrun, fixed-address write with an unresolved player); `cell_cheats_activate_cheat` (null cheat-record read from an unbounded index, deferred behind dialog confirmation); `audio_play_for_character_weapon_do` (null-character read); `audio_play_do`/`audio_play_id_do`'s uninitialized-result shape when audio is not initialized (reachability narrow but structurally unconditional).

**Review status (2026-10-03):** all 25 names in tranche 24 resolved and written up (§59.1-§59.7); none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: what fills the cheat-tag string table and the master-cheat-table's own record count relative to the 200-slot unlocked array; the opcode-`0x45` sub-code `0x16` (cheat activation) and sub-code `0xb` (audio event) receivers; which stop function accepts which of the two audio id spaces; what a boss phase other than 1 actually does differently when it does start a QTE; what makes an airplane take-off maneuver itself fail.

**Backlog status.** With tranches 24 (§59) and 25 (§58) both now folded in, every one of the 554 previously-unspecced names from the entire 01-25 ranking backlog is fully written up in this spec.

## 60. Stub hit-list 2026-10-02 — 27 generic-stub Lua names plus 9 OPEN_STATE items (2026-10-03)

**Source.** `D:\Project Crreish\TEAM B\results\stub_ranking_with_specced_20261002.tsv` — every row Team B's own runtime hit-log marks `n(generic-stub)` (no dedicated host implementation), plus every `OPEN_STATE:` row except `Killbane`'s named-object resolution, which stays parked (§60.4 closes this out). Full write-up in `review/exe-notes-2026-10-01/interp_stub_hitlist_20261002.md`. 21 of the 27 names already had a spec entry here or in `spec-lua-bindings.md`; this note re-verified each against a fresh dump, and 12 of those 21 needed a correction (struck and annotated at their own section below, not just summarized here). 6 names had no entry anywhere and are specified from scratch in §60.1. No pointer-before-name registrar this pass. No new session inferences drawn.

### 60.1 Six names with no earlier spec entry

**`customization_create_character` — real no-session crash, reachable by replaying the engine's own co-op character-creation flow.** Runs the same three-call sequence the engine's own undefined co-op character-creation code runs, ending in a step that **reads the session pointer's `+0x60` field with no null test** — any single-player call that reaches this third step faults (whether the shipped script reaches it in single player is OPEN; the one call site sits past this project's clean-room boundary). `customization_creation_is_open` has a **real logic defect: it always returns true in single player.** One of its four OR'd conditions depends on a global that only a mode-manager state exit callback ever sets non-null — and that mode-manager state (state 9, already established elsewhere in this spec as never requested anywhere in the static binary) never runs, so the condition's null-object default resolves to "open" rather than "closed." A script polling `while customization_creation_is_open() do … end` in single player never exits the loop; a faithful single-player host should simply return `true` to match. `customization_screen_is_ready` and `player_parachute_has_backpack` resolve in full with no crash shape; `mip_streaming_pause` has a real cross-script collision (the Lua path always passes bit index 0, aliasing with every other script's own pause reference on the same bit, so one script's resume call can release every other script's pause); `object_spawn_pause` is the shared no-op stub.

### 60.2 Twelve corrections to existing Lua-bindings/behaviour entries (UI-state family, §18-§21/§31.2)

**`vint_internal_dataresponder_request` (§21.2) — two real crash shapes, correcting "up to 16 trailing arguments" to unenforced.** Seventeen or more trailing arguments overrun a fixed 16-slot array on the function's own stack frame, with the 17th slot's tag landing on the saved return address; separately, the callback name is copied into a 64-byte buffer with no length limit, and a name of 64+ characters corrupts the native handler pointer the function calls next. Both corrected the prior "untyped slot" wording to "an int-0 slot with a stalled argument cursor," not a rejection. `vint_set_property` (§20.1) is corrected on four points: the tween redirect only borrows the target property's *type code* for parsing — the write still lands on the tween's own property, not the target's; an absent or nil value still writes the type's default variant rather than being a no-op; a type-mismatched value writes the default and leaves the argument itself unconsumed for the next read; and the optional trailing "extra" integer plus a type-`0xd` enum-string fallback conversion were missing from the prior description entirely. `vint_dataitem_get` (§19.2) is corrected: a colour field pushes 3 values and a vec2 field 2, so "each field is a scalar, exactly 1 value" is wrong — the return count can exceed the field count. `vint_object_clone` (§18.2) is corrected: the clone call is a virtual dispatch on the *source object's* own vtable slot `+0x14` with arguments `(1, parent)`, not on the document with `(parent, 1)`; the document is only the parent-lookup scope, and the fallback to the source's own stored parent also covers an unresolvable or foreign parent, not just an absent one. `vint_object_first_child` (§18.1) is corrected only at a changelog line that over-generalized "always returns exactly one value" to the whole §18 family — §18.1 itself returns 0 values on a bad handle or no child. `vint_get_time_index` (§19.1), `vint_get_property` (§20.2), `vint_dataresponder_finished` (§21.1), and `pause_map_stag_current_district_control` (§31.2) are all re-verified and AGREE with their existing entries with no changes needed.

### 60.3 Twelve corrections to existing behaviour entries (gameplay family)

**`city_zone_swap` (§1.9) — real logic defect: the mission-prefix branch's swap is silently dropped, never applied.** When the current mission name matches the swap's own prefix, the engine queues the request into a 5-slot queue that an exhaustive reference scan found **nothing ever reads** — so §1.9's prior claim of an "immediate-apply path" for that branch is wrong; the swap is queued and then goes nowhere. `mission_autosave` (§17.23) has its busy-check **polarity inverted** in the prior entry (it saves only when the busy predicate is false, not true) and was missing the function's own silent-return-on-Steam-check-failure path; corrected, it also now explicitly notes the native skips `game_autosave`'s extra mission gates, so it can save mid-mission. `player_controls_disable` (§7.22) is corrected on its arguments entirely: it takes **only one argument** (the player name) — the previously-documented "1 boolean, default false" parameter does not exist; the native always disables, unconditionally, via a literal `1` passed to its setter. `mesh_mover_show` (§9.17) is corrected: its third setter argument is **computed** from the mover's own state dword, not the literal `0` the prior entry (and its own cross-references) stated. `customization_outfit_wear` (§13.4) is corrected: the apply function is a plain four-argument call whose first argument is the character directly, not a `this`-call on an outfit manager, and its two targets are specifically the local and remote co-op players, not a context-resolved character; a collateral correction also fixes `0x009df3d0`'s own documented behavior elsewhere (§14.17/§14.31 item 8) — it returns the first non-local runtime-list player, not "the local-player global." `traffic_disable_lanes` (§12.19) is corrected: it does not enable/disable a trigger volume itself — it leaves the trigger unchanged and instead sets or clears a bit on every traffic record found by a spatial query over the trigger's bounds. `mission_set_next_mission` (§25.4) is corrected: in single player this native takes its no-session path and changes nothing at all; a previously-cited gate constant is confirmed to be a true compile-time constant, not a live "mission system active" flag. `audio_object_post_event` (§2.4), `character_ragdoll_set_last_resort_position` (§7.18), `mesh_mover_hide` (§9.16), `party_dismiss_all` (§14.17), and `sidewalk_disable_nodes` (§15.3) are all re-verified with their prior OPEN items closed (full detail in the interp note) and no corrections needed beyond that.

### 60.4 The nine OPEN_STATE items

Seven of nine are now CLOSED outright; two are closed on the code side with a data- or hold-dependent residue. **The Wwise ids for `SYS_HUD_CNTDWN_POS`** (`0x23ce84e6` / 600736998) **and `SYS_HUD_CONF_SERIOUS`** (`0x36b3e0d8` / 917758168) are both settled by reading the real hashing algorithm directly (32-bit FNV-1 over the lower-cased ASCII name, empirically confirmed against all 751 shipped `.bnk_pc` bank-header ids) — a side effect of this closure is a **real stack-cookie-abort crash shape**: the widening step copies up to 0x200 bytes into a 0x100-byte stack buffer, so a name of 128+ characters overruns it. **The default key bindings for `CBA_SWC_FIRE_GUIDED`** (right mouse button) **and `CBA_VDC_CRUISE_CONTROL_B`** (left Ctrl) are both resolved directly from `control_binding_sets.xtbl`'s shipped defaults, with the full lookup chain and 164-slot runtime table construction documented (a loaded save profile can still override the table). **The co-op join-type global (`0x012f44fc`)** starts at a file-backed constant `1`; its one writer and all three readers are now identified, though the semantic meaning of values 0/1/2 stays OPEN. **The `zscene_prep` blocker** is now correctly identified as reading cutscene state `0x0153b520` (not `0x0153b530`, already closed separately) — both the state and its manager pointer are zero-fill with no static initializer, so with no cutscene ever played the guard is simply false and needs no manager value. **The character ignore-AI flag (`+0x2bc`)** is closed on the code side (default off, confirmed against Team B's own source); which placed characters carry the override is zone data inside the parked `.czn_pc` interior and was **not opened**. **Character max hit points (`+0x1cac`)** has both of its remaining code-side OPEN items closed (the level-index selection logic, including a weighted-random level draw by story progress, and the difficulty multiplier lookup) — the value itself is confirmed to be genuinely random per spawn for an ordinary character, pinned only by class/rank type, with a script-NPC override still parked zone data. **The UI safe-frame source (header `+0x8`/`+0xc` off context `+0x674`+`0x14`)** is partly closed: the context field's own identity and its writers/reset are now traced, but a **new crash shape** surfaces in the process — `vint_get_safe_frame`'s null test on the context pointer does not actually guard the read that follows, substituting a null object and then reading through it unconditionally, four separate times in the same function (reachability OPEN). **`Killbane`'s named-object resolution** was explicitly not touched, per the standing `.czn_pc` hold (§29.4) — nothing beyond what that section already states was opened, read, or inferred.

### 60.5 Cross-function observations

**Twelve of the twenty-one previously-specced names needed a real correction**, not just a re-confirmation — a notably high correction rate for a re-verification pass, suggesting the original single-dump derivations for this particular UI-state/gameplay cluster were more error-prone than the ranking-tranche series' own first-pass accuracy, possibly because several of these functions (`vint_set_property`, `vint_internal_dataresponder_request`) have unusually complex multi-branch argument handling that a shallow dump is more likely to mis-render. **A second project-wide pattern confirmed again:** "a condition whose null-object default resolves to the wrong polarity in single player" (`customization_creation_is_open`) joins the small but recurring family of session/mode-manager-adjacent single-player defaults that silently differ from the apparent intent — distinct from, and not evidence toward, the already-settled single-player-has-no-session question (§8.27/§26.28).

**Crash-shaped findings, summary (CONFIRMED structure unless marked OPEN):** `customization_create_character` (no-session read at a session-pointer-derived `+0x60`, reachability OPEN for single player); `vint_internal_dataresponder_request` (16-slot trailing-argument overflow onto the return address; unbounded 64-byte callback-name copy corrupting a handler pointer); `vint_get_safe_frame` (null-context substitution that still gets dereferenced, four call sites, reachability OPEN); the Wwise name-hashing helper's 128+-character stack-cookie-abort shape (shared by every binding that posts a Wwise id/name).

**Review status (2026-10-03):** all 27 names and all 9 OPEN_STATE items (except the explicitly out-of-scope `Killbane`) resolved; none failed. CONFIRMED unless individually marked HYPOTHESIS/OPEN above. Residual OPEN items: the per-frame consumer of the mip-streaming pause bitfield; whether the shipped single-player script ever actually reaches `customization_create_character`'s crashing third step; the meaning of co-op join-type values 0/1/2; the UI safe-frame context field `+0x14`'s own writer and the proof that its `+0x8`/`+0xc` fields are specifically width/height; which placed characters carry the ignore-AI override (parked zone data).
